docs.title: ScreenGrab — Product Specification
docs.text: Status Draft v0.1 Date 2026-11-01 Requirements owner Dan McCreary Platform macOS only (14 Sonoma or later) Related documents design.md

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
ScreenGrab is a small, free, single-purpose macOS utility that replaces the one part of Snagit that is actually used: grabbing a rectangular region of the screen and putting the image on the clipboard. Snagit moved to an annual license; the owner only uses it for screen grabs, so paying for the editor, library, video capture, and sharing features is not worthwhile.

The working name is ScreenGrab.

docs.title: 2.1 Goals
docs.text:
1. Capture a user-selected rectangular region of any display with a single gesture (hotkey → drag).
  2. Capture the same way after a user-configurable countdown, so transient content (open menus, hover states, tooltips) can be arranged first.
  3. Put the resulting image on the clipboard, ready to paste, by default and without any extra step.
  4. Be tiny, fast, quiet, and invisible until needed (menu bar only).
  5. Be buildable from source on the owner's machine with the tools already installed (Swift Command Line Tools; no full Xcode required).

docs.title: 2.2 Non-goals (v1)
docs.text:
• No image editor, annotation, markup, or effects.
  • No full-screen, window, scrolling, or video capture modes.
  • No capture library / history, tagging, or cloud sharing.
  • No OCR, text grab, or QR scanning.
  • No compatibility with Snagit file formats (.snagx) or its presets.
  • No App Store distribution, notarization, auto-update, or telemetry.

See §12 for the list of ideas deferred beyond v1.

docs.title: 3. Users and context
docs.text:
Single user: the owner. Typical use is capturing parts of web pages, apps, and diagrams to paste into documents, slide decks, chat, and the figures of MkDocs-based intelligent textbooks. Because the user pastes into many different applications, the clipboard image must work broadly (Keynote, Pages, Word, Google Docs, Slack, browsers, Preview "New from Clipboard", etc.).

The user's display is a Retina laptop panel (2560×1664 native); external displays and mixed-DPI setups are possible.

docs.title: 4. Decisions made during requirements clarification
docs.text:
The following answers were given by the owner and are binding for v1.

# Question Decision D1 Technology Native Swift (Swift Package, AppKit, ScreenCaptureKit) D2 How a grab is triggered Menu bar app + global hotkeys (menu items as a fallback) D3 How the delay works Presets + custom value. A visible countdown runs first; when it finishes the region selector appears D4 Output Clipboard only by default. An optional preference also saves a PNG to a folder (off by default) D5 Interface complexity Keep it simple; only Grab Region and Grab Region with Delay exist in v1

One further decision came out of testing during design, and it supports D3 rather than changing it:

# Topic Decision D6 Selection model Freeze-frame. Every display is captured the instant the selector starts, and the overlay shows that still image. Testing on macOS 26 showed that a background app can't display a crosshair, and activating the app changes what is on screen. Capturing first means those changes never reach the image. See design §2.1.

docs.title: 4.1 Assumptions made by the specification author
docs.text:
These were not explicitly discussed; each is a sensible default and is easy to change. Please veto any that are wrong.

# Assumption A1 The mouse cursor is not included in captured images. A2 Images are captured at the display's native pixel resolution (2× on Retina) and are never downscaled. A3 A selection can't span multiple displays; it is confined to the display where the drag began. A4 A short confirmation sound plays on success (can be turned off). A5 Default hotkeys are ⌃⇧4 (Grab Region) and ⌃⇧5 (Grab Region with Delay). Both are user-changeable. A6 Default delay is 5 seconds; presets are 3, 5, 10, 15 s; custom range is 1–60 s. A7 The optional save folder defaults to ~/Pictures/ScreenGrab. A8 Local-only distribution: built from source, ad-hoc or self-signed, not notarized.

docs.title: 5. Platform and constraints
docs.text: Item Requirement OS macOS 14.0 (Sonoma) or later. Developed and tested on macOS 26. CPU Apple Silicon (primary). Intel supported via an optional universal build. Language / UI Swift 5 language mode (toolchain Swift 6.x), AppKit Capture API ScreenCaptureKit (SCScreenshotManager). CGWindowListCreateImage is unavailable on current macOS and is not used. Build tooling Swift Package Manager and the Xcode Command Line Tools only. No Xcode.app dependency. Third-party dependencies None. Sandboxing Not sandboxed (personal tool, not App Store). Network None. The app makes no network connections.

docs.title: 6. Functional requirements
docs.text: Requirement IDs are stable and referenced from the acceptance tests in §10.

docs.title: 6.1 Application presence (menu bar agent)
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-1.1 The app runs as a menu bar agent: no Dock icon, no app-switcher entry, no main window. FR-1.2 A status item (icon) appears in the menu bar while the app runs. Clicking it opens the menu described in §8.1. FR-1.3 Only one instance may run. Launching a second instance exits immediately. FR-1.4 Quit is available from the menu (⌘Q while the menu is open). FR-1.5 Launching the app shows no windows or alerts. A permission request occurs only when the first grab is attempted (see FR-8.x).

docs.title: 6.2 Grab Region
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-2.1 Grab Region can be started from the menu item or its global hotkey (default ⌃⇧4), regardless of which application is frontmost. FR-2.2 On start, every connected display is captured immediately (freeze-frame). An overlay covers each display, including displays showing full-screen apps, and shows that still image dimmed. The system cursor becomes a crosshair. FR-2.3 The user presses the mouse button, drags to define a rectangle in any direction, and releases. Release performs the capture immediately (no confirm step). FR-2.4 While dragging, the selected area is shown un-dimmed with a thin border, and a live label shows the selection size in pixels (e.g. 640 × 480). FR-2.5 Esc or a right-click cancels the grab. Cancelling leaves the clipboard untouched and produces no sound. FR-2.6 A selection smaller than 4 × 4 pixels (an accidental click) is treated as a cancel. FR-2.7 ScreenGrab's own overlay, labels, and countdown HUD never appear in the captured image. FR-2.8 The captured image replaces the clipboard contents (see §6.5). FR-2.9 On success the user gets feedback per §6.9. FR-2.10 Starting a grab while another grab or countdown is already in progress is ignored (except the cancel behavior in FR-3.4). FR-2.11 The grabbed image shows the screen exactly as it was when the selector started. Open menus, hover states, tooltips, and active window title bars are preserved, even if the real windows change underneath the overlay. FR-2.12 When a grab ends by any path, keyboard focus returns to the application that was frontmost before the selector appeared.

docs.title: 6.3 Grab Region with Delay
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-3.1 Grab Region with Delay can be started from the menu item or its global hotkey (default ⌃⇧5). FR-3.2 The delay is a whole number of seconds, 1–60, default 5. Presets of 3, 5, 10, 15 are offered; a custom value may be entered. The current value is shown in the menu item title, e.g. Grab Region with Delay (5 s). FR-3.3 On start, a countdown HUD appears showing the remaining seconds, updating every second. The HUD must not take keyboard focus or activate ScreenGrab, so the application and any open menu or hover state the user is preparing is left undisturbed. FR-3.4 The countdown can be cancelled by (a) clicking the HUD, (b) choosing Cancel Grab in the menu bar menu (the item is visible only while a countdown or selection is active), or (c) pressing the Grab-with-Delay hotkey again. FR-3.5 When the countdown reaches zero the HUD closes, the screen is frozen at that instant, and the same region selector as FR-2.2 – FR-2.8 appears. Anything arranged during the countdown, such as an open menu, is in the frozen image and can be selected. FR-3.6 The delay in effect when the countdown starts is used for that grab; changing it mid-countdown affects only later grabs.

docs.title: 6.4 Region selection behavior
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-4.1 The selection is confined to the display on which the mouse button went down; dragging beyond that display's edge clamps to the edge. FR-4.2 The overlay must appear above normal windows, the menu bar, and the Dock, and on whichever Space is active. FR-4.3 The overlay must work on mixed-DPI setups (e.g. Retina laptop panel plus a non-Retina external monitor); the captured area exactly matches what was highlighted. FR-4.4 The size label is placed near the pointer and stays fully on screen (flipping side near edges). FR-4.5 Pointer coordinates and the label are updated at interactive frame rates (no visible lag when dragging). FR-4.6 The overlay is dismissed on every exit path (success, cancel, error) and the cursor is restored.

docs.title: 6.5 Output
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-5.1 Default behavior: the captured image is written to the general pasteboard as PNG and TIFF representations so it pastes into the widest range of applications. FR-5.2 Retina fidelity: the image keeps native pixels (2× on Retina). Its size/DPI metadata is set so that the pasted image appears at the same on-screen size as the captured region (72 × scale DPI). FR-5.3 The app writes nothing to disk unless the optional save preference is enabled (no temp files, no logs containing image data). FR-5.4 Optional save (off by default): when enabled, the same image is also saved as a PNG in the chosen folder, in addition to the clipboard. FR-5.5 Saved filename: ScreenGrab yyyy-MM-dd 'at' HH.mm.ss.png (local time, mirrors macOS's own screenshot naming). If the name already exists, a numeric suffix is added: … (2).png. FR-5.6 The save folder is created if it doesn't exist. If saving fails (permissions, disk full), the clipboard copy still succeeds and the user is shown an error describing the save failure.

docs.title: 6.6 Preferences
docs.text:
A single small Preferences window, opened from the menu (⌘, ) — see the layout in §8.4. Changes apply immediately (no OK/Apply).

ID Requirement FR-6.1 Delay: presets 3 / 5 / 10 / 15 s and Custom… with a numeric field (1–60). FR-6.2 Hotkeys: one recorder control for each of the two actions, each with a reset to default affordance. FR-6.3 Play sound on successful grab (default on). FR-6.4 Also save to folder checkbox (default off) with a Choose… button and the current path displayed. FR-6.5 Preferences persist across launches (user defaults). FR-6.6 A quick Delay submenu in the menu bar menu offers the presets and checks the current one, so the delay can be changed without opening Preferences. FR-6.7 Opening the app while it's already running shows Preferences, which gives a way in if the menu bar icon is hidden behind the notch.

docs.title: 6.7 Global hotkeys
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-7.1 Hotkeys work while any application is frontmost and while ScreenGrab is not the active app. FR-7.2 Registering hotkeys must not require Accessibility or Input Monitoring permission. FR-7.3 A hotkey must include at least one of ⌃ ⌥ ⌘ (a bare key or ⇧-only combination is rejected by the recorder). FR-7.4 The two actions can't be assigned the same shortcut. FR-7.5 If the OS refuses a registration because another app already owns the shortcut, the Preferences window shows a warning next to that control and the menu item remains usable. FR-7.6 The assigned shortcuts are displayed next to the menu items.

docs.title: 6.8 Permissions
docs.text:
macOS requires Screen & System Audio Recording permission to capture the screen.

ID Requirement FR-8.1 Each grab checks permission before doing anything else (for a delayed grab, before the countdown). If permission is missing, the app asks macOS to show its system prompt; macOS itself limits how often that prompt appears. FR-8.2 If permission is missing, the grab is aborted and the user sees an alert explaining what is needed, with a button that opens System Settings → Privacy & Security → Screen & System Audio Recording. FR-8.3 The alert states that the app may need to be quit and reopened after the permission is granted. FR-8.4 A grab never produces a silently blank or wallpaper-only image because of missing permission.

docs.title: 6.9 Feedback and errors
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-9.1 Success is signalled by (a) the menu bar icon switching to a checkmark for about one second, and (b) a short system sound, unless sound is turned off. FR-9.2 Cancel is silent and leaves no visible trace. FR-9.3 Errors are shown in a standard alert with a plain-language message. Covered cases: missing permission, no display found, capture failure, clipboard write failure, save failure. FR-9.4 The overlay and HUD are always torn down, even when an error occurs. FR-9.5 If a display is connected or disconnected mid-grab, the grab is cancelled cleanly without a crash.

docs.title: 6.10 Installation
docs.text: ID Requirement FR-10.1 src/install.sh tests, builds, signs, and installs the app with one command, then opens it. FR-10.2 The default destination is /Applications, falling back to ~/Applications if that isn't writable. A destination can also be chosen. FR-10.3 A failed test or build leaves any installed copy untouched. If replacing the installed copy fails, the previous version is restored. FR-10.4 The installer refuses to replace or remove an app with a different bundle identifier that happens to be named ScreenGrab.app. FR-10.5 The installer checks its prerequisites first and gives a specific instruction for anything missing. It refuses to run as root. FR-10.6 The installer can uninstall the app, optionally deleting its preferences, and can clear the app's Screen Recording entry. FR-10.7 src/README.md documents installation, permissions, usage, troubleshooting, and development.

docs.title: 7. Non-functional requirements
docs.text: ID Category Requirement NFR-1 Responsiveness Overlay visible within 300 ms of the hotkey (excluding countdown). This includes capturing the frozen frames. NFR-2 Capture speed Release-to-clipboard within 300 ms for regions up to ~1 megapixel and within 1 s for a full Retina screen. NFR-3 Idle cost ~0 % CPU while idle; resident memory under 50 MB idle. Frozen frames are released as soon as a grab ends. NFR-4 Privacy No network access, no analytics, no persistence of image data unless FR-5.4 is enabled. Preferences contain no image data. NFR-5 Reliability No crash on cancel, rapid repeated hotkeys, display changes, or empty clipboard states. NFR-6 Quality of image Pixel-exact capture: output pixel size equals selection size × display scale; no resampling blur. NFR-7 Footprint Source of about 2,000 lines of Swift, excluding tests; no third-party packages. NFR-8 Maintainability Pure logic (geometry conversion, file naming, delay clamping, hotkey validation) is separated from UI and unit-tested. NFR-9 Accessibility Menu items and Preferences controls have accessibility labels; every grab can be cancelled from the keyboard (Esc). NFR-10 Buildability src/scripts/build-app.sh produces a runnable ScreenGrab.app on a Mac that has only the Command Line Tools.

docs.title: 8.2 Region selector overlay
docs.text:
• The frozen image of the display, under a translucent black layer of roughly 35 % opacity.
  • Selected rectangle is cut out (shown at full brightness) with a 1 px white border plus a faint dark outline so it is visible on both light and dark content.
  • Crosshair cursor everywhere on the overlay.
  • Size label — white text on a dark rounded pill, e.g. 640 × 480 — follows the pointer, offset down-right, flipping to stay on screen.
  • Before the drag begins, the label shows the pointer's position in pixels (e.g. 1280, 832) to help with precise starts.

docs.title: 8.3 Countdown HUD
docs.text:
• Rounded, translucent dark panel ~140 × 140 pt, horizontally centered near the top of the display containing the pointer.
  • Large white number (remaining seconds) and a small caption Click to cancel.
  • Floats above all windows (including full-screen apps), does not take focus.

docs.text: Setting Default Delay 5 s Grab Region hotkey ⌃⇧4 Grab Region with Delay hotkey ⌃⇧5 Play sound On Save to folder Off Save folder ~/Pictures/ScreenGrab Include mouse cursor No (not configurable in v1)

docs.title: 10. Acceptance tests
docs.text:
Manual acceptance tests (the geometry/naming logic is additionally covered by automated unit tests; see design.md).

ID Scenario Expected result Covers AC-1 Launch the app Icon in menu bar; no Dock icon, no window FR-1.1, 1.2, 1.5 AC-2 Launch a second copy Second copy exits; one icon remains FR-1.3 AC-3 Press ⌃⇧4 in another app, drag a region Overlay appears, size label updates, release copies image; sound plays; icon shows ✓ FR-2.1 – 2.4, 2.8, 2.9 AC-4 Paste into Preview (File → New from Clipboard) and into a Keynote/Pages doc Image is exactly the selected region at expected size FR-5.1, 5.2, NFR-6 AC-5 Start a grab, press Esc Overlay disappears; clipboard still has its previous content FR-2.5, 9.2 AC-6 Start a grab, click once without dragging Treated as cancel; clipboard unchanged FR-2.6 AC-7 Start a grab, right-click Cancels FR-2.5 AC-8 Capture a region containing a Retina photo on a 2× display Pasted image has 2× pixel dimensions and no blur FR-5.2, NFR-6 AC-9 With two displays of different DPI, grab on each The captured pixels match the highlighted area on both FR-4.1, 4.3 AC-10 Drag past the edge of the display Selection clamps at the edge FR-4.1 AC-11 Press ⌃⇧5; wait HUD counts 5…1, then the selector appears; grab completes normally FR-3.1 – 3.5 AC-12 During the countdown, open an app menu and leave it open Menu stays open during the countdown (the HUD did not steal focus). At zero the selector appears with the menu visible, and the grabbed image includes it FR-2.11, 3.3, 3.5 AC-13 During the countdown, click the HUD Countdown cancelled; no overlay appears FR-3.4 AC-14 During the countdown, press ⌃⇧5 again Countdown cancelled FR-3.4 AC-15 During the countdown, use Cancel Grab Countdown cancelled FR-3.4 AC-16 Change delay to Custom 8 s and run a delayed grab HUD counts from 8 FR-3.2, 6.1 AC-17 Check that the HUD and overlay are absent from captures Neither appears in any pasted image FR-2.7 AC-18 Enable Also save a PNG, grab twice in the same second Two PNGs in the folder, the second with (2) FR-5.4, 5.5 AC-19 Point save folder at an unwritable path Clipboard copy works; error alert about save FR-5.6 AC-20 Save preference off No files written anywhere FR-5.3 AC-21 Revoke Screen Recording permission, then grab Alert with Open System Settings; no image copied FR-8.1 – 8.4 AC-22 Record ⌃⇧6 for Grab Region in Preferences, press it New shortcut works, old one doesn't; persists after relaunch FR-6.2, 6.5, 7.1 AC-23 Try to record a bare "A" or ⇧A Rejected FR-7.3 AC-24 Assign a shortcut already used by another app Warning shown in Preferences FR-7.5 AC-25 Press ⌃⇧4 repeatedly while the overlay is up Ignored; no duplicate overlays FR-2.10 AC-26 Unplug a display during a grab Grab cancels; no crash FR-9.5 AC-27 Observe app idle for 1 minute ~0 % CPU in Activity Monitor NFR-3 AC-28 Grab a region that includes the title bar of the frontmost window Title bar and traffic lights appear active (in color), not greyed out FR-2.11 AC-29 Type in a text editor, press ⌃⇧4, complete a grab, then keep typing without clicking. Repeat, cancelling with Esc The text goes into the editor both times FR-2.12 AC-30 Open the app from the Applications folder while it's running Preferences appears FR-6.7 AC-31 Run src/install.sh on a clean machine, then again as an upgrade App is installed and running both times; preferences are kept FR-10.1, 10.2 AC-32 Make the build fail, then run the installer Error shown; the installed app is unchanged and still running FR-10.3 AC-33 Put a different app named ScreenGrab.app in the destination, then install and uninstall Both refuse to touch it FR-10.4 AC-34 Run src/install.sh --uninstall --purge App and preferences are gone; saved PNGs remain FR-10.6

docs.title: 11. Risks and known operating-system behavior
docs.text: ID Risk / behavior Mitigation R1 macOS ties the Screen Recording grant to the app's code signature. An ad-hoc signed app gets a new identity whenever its code changes, so the permission must be re-granted after such a rebuild. The scripts accept a SIGN_IDENTITY so a stable self-signed certificate can be used, as documented in src/README.md. The installer warns when the signature has changed. Rebuilds are rare for personal use. R2 Since macOS 15, the system periodically asks the user to re-confirm Screen Recording access for apps that capture the screen. Out of the app's control; documented. R3 The selector has to activate ScreenGrab to show a crosshair, which closes other apps' open menus and greys their title bars. Freeze-frame: the image is captured before activation, so none of this appears in grabs. The remaining effect is that a menu open when the selector starts is closed once the grab ends, including a cancelled one. R4 The chosen shortcuts may collide with other apps. Configurable hotkeys; collision warning (FR-7.5). R5 Content protected by DRM (some video players, Apple TV) captures as black. OS behavior; documented, no workaround. R6 Mixed-DPI coordinate conversion bugs (top-left vs bottom-left origins, points vs pixels). Single tested conversion function; see design §6. R7 Screen capture uses a macOS API that Apple continues to evolve. Isolated behind one ScreenCapturer type. R8 Because the screen is frozen, video and animations appear paused during selection. Intended: the pixels selected are exactly the pixels copied.

docs.title: 12. Out of scope and future ideas
docs.text:
Intentionally not part of v1, in rough priority order if the app grows:

  1. Launch at login.
  2. Hold Space while dragging to reposition the selection; arrow-key nudging.
  3. Pixel magnifier loupe near the cursor for precise edges.
  4. Optional include cursor setting.
  5. Window-snap capture (hover a window to highlight and click to capture it).
  6. Small floating thumbnail after capture with Save As….
  7. Full-screen capture, scrolling capture, delayed full-screen capture.
  8. Basic annotation (arrows, boxes, callouts) — the only Snagit feature likely worth a future investment for documentation work.
  9. Notarized, universal binary distribution.

docs.title: 13. Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Region An axis-aligned rectangle on a single display chosen by dragging. Point (pt) macOS logical unit. A Retina display has 2 pixels per point. Overlay The borderless, translucent windows that cover each display during region selection. HUD The countdown panel shown during a delayed grab. TCC Transparency, Consent and Control — macOS's privacy-permission system that governs screen recording.

docs.title: Snagit Price History, 2010–2026

This table covers 17 calendar years, from the first commercial Mac release in 2010 through 2026. Prices are in US dollars for one new individual license usable on Mac, excluding tax, promotions, education discounts, and upgrade-only pricing. Some releases arrived in the preceding calendar year, so transition years show both prices.

Snagit for Mac entered public beta in December 2009, offered free, before its first paid release on November 9, 2010. There was no commercial Mac purchase price before that release. Earlier Windows-only prices, including the 1997 price, are excluded. See Macworld's beta announcement and commercial release announcement.

The earlier prices bought a perpetual license to that version; the recent $39 price is a recurring annual charge. Maintenance and major-version upgrades could cost extra under the older model.

This is a sourced reconstruction of advertised prices, not a complete archive of every price change. The 2024 subscription price has weaker historical evidence than the launch prices above; its linked contemporary report is from a user discussion. Research date: November 1, 2026.

Because the table excludes promotions, it doesn't show the author's recollection of buying a one-time macOS license for around $40 on a special sale. No receipt or published sale price has been found to confirm that purchase.

For more detail on current licensing, see Snagit Pricing, November 2026.

docs.title: Snagit Pricing, November 2026
docs.text: Snagit Individual costs $39 per user per year, billed annually, according to TechSmith's pricing page. It covers two computers, but only one can be in use at a time. These figures were checked on November 1, 2026 and will go out of date, so check TechSmith's page before relying on them.

docs.title: Annual Prices
docs.text:
Plan Price per user per year Source Snagit Individual $39 TechSmith Business About $48 Third-party sites only Student About $20 Third-party sites only

TechSmith's page has tabs for its business and education plans, but it didn't show their prices in what could be retrieved, so treat those two figures as approximate. Snagit is also included in all Camtasia plans, which start at $39 per user per year.

docs.title: Computer Limit
docs.text:
TechSmith says each user may install and use one copy on up to two computers for their sole use, provided only one is in use at any given time. Its activation notes give the same two-machine limit for a single user.

The two-computer wording comes from TechSmith's licensing and activation pages, some of which refer to key-based licenses. The current pricing page doesn't state a device limit, and it says subscriptions use account sign-in rather than product keys. Nothing found suggests the limit changed for subscriptions, but no current page confirms it either.

The author recalls using one Mac license key from around 2010 on two work computers without problems, and doesn't recall the limit being enforced at the time. This is a personal recollection and may not apply to current subscriptions.

docs.title: Transfers
docs.text: Individual subscriptions are non-transferable. TechSmith points anyone who needs to move a license between users to a business or multi-seat plan.

docs.title: Earlier Pricing
docs.text:
The earliest documented price found is from TechSmith's pricing and registration page, captured on October 10, 1997. A single-user copy for Windows cost $39.95, and a 10-copy multi-user pack cost $200. The price at Snagit's 1990 launch has not been found.

Mac versions were first sold in 2010. They were one-time purchases at $49.95 to $62.99 until annual subscriptions replaced them in 2024, as the Snagit Price History shows year by year.

The author recalls buying the macOS version of Snagit as a one-time license for around $40 on a special sale. This is a personal recollection, and no receipt or published sale price has been found to confirm it.

docs.title: Chapters
docs.text: This textbook is organized into 15 chapters covering 206 concepts.

docs.title: Chapter Overview
docs.text:
1. Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat - Defines software, features, versions, and release cycles, then shows how bloat, feature creep, and growing resource footprints arise, contrasted with the single-purpose utility.
  2. Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule - Examines how people actually use software, covering power and casual users, the long tail of features, interface complexity, and the roadmap pressures that keep adding features.
  3. Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives - Compares one-time licenses with subscriptions, starting from copyright, and explains how recurring revenue, switching costs, and lock-in change what vendors choose to build and charge.
  4. Total Cost of Ownership - Teaches readers to calculate per-computer and multi-year costs, break-even points, and the hidden maintenance, learning, and opportunity costs behind a software choice.
  5. Generative AI and Coding Agents - Introduces generative AI, source code, and coding agents such as Claude Code, covering prompts, sessions, permissions, human review, hallucination, and overconfident reporting.
  6. Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software - Frames buy, subscribe, and generate as three options, and weighs disposable and long-lived personal software against the risks and support duties of owning a tool.
  7. Requirements and Minimal Specifications - Moves from user needs to functional requirements, non-goals, and acceptance criteria, showing how a specification that leaves features out defines ScreenGrab's region, delay, and clipboard scope.
  8. Software Design and Platform Constraints - Covers design decisions, trade-offs, prototypes, and zero-dependency design, then applies them to ScreenGrab's menu bar app, global hotkey, screen recording permission, and freeze-frame selection.
  9. Generating, Building, and Installing the Code - Follows generation through compiling, build and installer scripts, code signing, and Git, and closes by assembling the complete ScreenGrab case study.
  10. Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing - Explains input, output, cache write, and cache read tokens, along with context windows, cache expiration, pricing, and how model tiers affect selection.
  11. Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost - Applies token pricing to real sessions, separating wall-clock from active time and breaking the $6 build and $14 session into their cost drivers and assumptions.
  12. Software Testing: Automated and Manual - Introduces verification, unit and integration tests, isolation, stubs, and simulated input, then the manual, acceptance, and smoke tests that automation cannot replace.
  13. Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans - Works through reproduction, root cause analysis, and unexplained failures, then teaches evidence-based reporting and verification plans that separate automated tests from checks a person must run.
  14. Maintenance and Open Source Sharing - Covers technical debt, operating system and toolchain changes, and patch releases, then open source licensing, public repositories, forks, pull requests, and long-term stewardship.
  15. The Final Decision and the Capstone Project - Brings the course together with decision criteria, a decision matrix, and cost per feature used, leading to the capstone: build a replacement tool and publish a cost comparison.

docs.title: How to Use This Textbook
docs.text:
Read the chapters in order the first time through. The sequence follows the book's argument, from how software bloats, to what it costs, to generating, measuring, verifying, and maintaining a replacement, and every concept appears only after the concepts it depends on. Chapter 15 draws on nearly everything before it, so if you plan to complete the capstone, start thinking early about which paid tool you want to replace.

Note: Each chapter includes a list of concepts covered. Make sure to complete prerequisites before moving to advanced chapters.

docs.title: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
Summary
docs.text: This chapter builds the vocabulary for the whole book: what a software product is, how features accumulate into a feature set, and how versions and release cycles keep adding to it. It then defines software bloat and feature creep, measures their footprint in install size and idle resource use, and contrasts them with the single-purpose utility that does one job to be done. After this chapter, you will be able to define software bloat and recognize its symptoms in a tool you use.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter assumes only the prerequisites listed in the course description.

Hi, I'm Pinch

I'm Pinch, a hermit crab who is frugal, curious, and a little suspicious of anything heavy that I'm asked to carry. Here is the whole job description, in the order you'll meet me in each chapter:

  1. Welcome: I tell you why the chapter is worth your time.
  2. Think: I mark an idea that should change how you reason about software.
  3. Tip: I hand you a shortcut you can use today.
  4. Warn: I flag a trap and show you the way out.
  5. Encourage: I admit that a passage is hard and suggest a way through.
  6. Celebrate: I name exactly what you just learned.

If I'm not doing one of those six things, I'm not in the chapter. By the end of this one you'll be able to spot software bloat in a tool you pay for. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Software, Products, and Features
docs.text:
Every program on your computer began as text that a person, or lately an AI agent, wrote and a machine can follow. That is the plainest definition of software: a set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. A screen grab utility is software. So is the operating system it runs on, the web browser beside it, and the firmware in your keyboard.

Software on its own is not something you buy. You buy a software product: software packaged with everything needed to obtain and keep using it, namely an installer, documentation, a license, a price, updates, and usually someone to call when it breaks. The same instructions can be sold as several products, and one product can bundle many separate programs. This distinction matters for the rest of the book, because most of what you pay for is the packaging and the promise, not the instructions themselves.

The book's running example makes the difference concrete. The author owns a screen grab utility that cost $9 and ran on every one of the author's computers. The software is the compiled program that copies pixels from the display into an image. The product is that program plus the installer, the license that lets three computers run it, the update service, and the vendor's support page.

Software comes in layers, and it helps to know which layer you are looking at. Firmware lives in a device and starts it up. The operating system manages the hardware and runs other programs. Applications, such as a screen grab utility, sit on top and do work for a person. A developer writes software as human-readable source code and a tool translates it into the compiled form that the computer runs. When you install an application, you receive the compiled form. When the application is open source, you can also read the source.

Software has one economic property that shapes everything in this book: copying it costs almost nothing. A carpenter's second chair costs nearly as much as the first. A programmer's millionth copy costs nearly the same as the second. All of the cost sits in writing, testing, and maintaining the instructions once. That is why vendors sell products and licenses rather than the instructions themselves, and why a price can be set by what customers will accept instead of by what the copy cost to make.

The generated utility described later in this book gives a sense of scale. At first install it was about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, with no third-party dependencies. A line count is a crude measure, but it shows that a tool that does its job completely can be small enough for one person to read in an afternoon.

The packaging around the software is where products differ. The table below separates what a buyer pays for into parts. Each row is something the buyer receives or is promised, and only the first row is the software.

Part of a software product What the buyer receives Present in a free script? The software Instructions the computer can run Yes The installer A way to put the software in place and remove it Sometimes Documentation Guides, help pages, and tutorials Sometimes The license Permission to use the software under stated terms Yes, implicitly or explicitly Updates New versions that fix problems or add capability Rarely Support A person or service to ask when it breaks Rarely

The same software can appear as several products. A vendor might sell a "standard" and a "professional" edition built from one code base, with a different set of unlocked features and a different price. Equally, one product can bundle several programs, as an office suite does. The questions "what software is this?" and "what product am I buying?" have different answers, and a confusing price usually comes from the second.

Inside a product, the things a user can do are its software features. A feature is one distinct capability that serves a purpose a user can name. "Grab a rectangular region of the screen" is a feature. "Grab the same region after a five-second delay" is another. "Add an arrow to a captured image" is a third. Notice that each is described by what the user gets, not by how the code works. The complete collection of capabilities a product offers is its feature set. When a vendor says a product has "over 100 features," they are describing the size of the feature set.

Deciding what counts as one feature takes judgment. A feature should be something a user can name, notice, and in principle do without. "Grab a region" passes that test. "Uses a faster image buffer" does not, because the user cannot tell and would not miss it if it were gone. A feature is also different from a setting: choosing the image format is a setting of the grab feature, not a feature of its own. Vendors who count generously, with every setting and menu item as a feature, produce impressive numbers on a box. Counting strictly, as a user would, produces smaller ones.

The following table lists a feature set for the kind of screen grab utility used as the running example. The features are generic to the category and illustrative of the way a product accumulates them; they describe no particular vendor's product.

Feature Group Minimal utility After several releases Grab a rectangular region Capture Yes Yes Grab after a delay Capture Yes Yes Grab a whole window Capture No Yes Scrolling capture of a long page Capture No Yes Draw arrows and boxes on an image Edit No Yes Blur a region Edit No Yes Record the screen as video Record No Yes Extract text from an image Analyze No Yes Upload to a cloud gallery Share No Yes Team libraries and comments Share No Yes

A feature set has breadth, the number of distinct things it can do, and depth, how fully it handles each one. Bloat is nearly always a growth in breadth. A tool with a deep grab feature and nothing else is a different kind of product from one with a shallow version of forty features. It is also useful to separate the core of a feature set, the features that serve the product's original job, from its periphery, the features added later. In the table, the first two rows are the core, and the remaining eight are the periphery.

The distinction predicts who benefits from growth. Core features are used by nearly everyone who bought the product for that job. Peripheral features are each used by a minority, and different minorities use different ones. Each peripheral feature is valuable to somebody, and that is exactly why it was added. The cost lands on the people who use none of them.

Before looking at the diagram below, here are the relationships it shows. A product contains software and wraps it in a license, installer, and support. A feature set is made of features. A product ships as numbered versions, and a release cycle decides when the next version appears. Those last two terms come in the next section; you can click any node to see its definition and check yourself with the six matching questions.

docs.title: Diagram: Software Vocabulary Concept Map
docs.text:
Software Vocabulary Concept Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: bloat-software-concept-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/computer-science/tree/main/docs/sims/oop-benefits-concept-map Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify six described examples under the correct term among software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, and software release cycle, scoring at least 5 of 6 on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, software release cycle (each defined in the chapter sections "Software, Products, and Features" and "Versions and Release Cycles").

Evidence of Mastery: In the matching quiz, the learner picks one of the six terms for each of 6 described examples. An answer is correct when it equals the Correct term column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Clicking nodes to read definitions is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Software and software product are the same thing. (2) A feature set is the same as a feature. (3) A version is the same as a release cycle.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying a concrete example under an abstract term makes the learner apply the definition instead of recalling its wording, which is the Understand-level behavior. The concept map gives the learner the relationships to reason from.

Content:

The map has eight nodes. Clicking a node opens its definition.

Node Definition shown on click Software A set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. Software Product Software packaged with an installer, documentation, a license, a price, updates, and support. Software Feature One distinct capability of a product that serves a purpose a user can name. Feature Set The complete collection of features a product offers. Software Version A numbered snapshot of a product at one point in time. Software Release Cycle The schedule on which a vendor publishes new versions. Software Bloat Growth of a feature set beyond what most users need or use. Single-Purpose Utility A small tool built to do one job and little else.

The edges, shown with their labels, are:

From Label To Software Product packages Software Software Feature is one part of Feature Set Feature Set belongs to Software Product Software Version is a snapshot of Software Product Software Release Cycle schedules Software Version Software Bloat is what an oversized Feature Set Single-Purpose Utility keeps a small Feature Set

The matching quiz has 6 items in this fixed order. The answer bank is the six terms software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, and software release cycle.

# Description shown Correct term Why (shown as feedback) 1 The Swift source files that make up a screen grab app software They are instructions for the computer, with no license, price, or support around them. 2 The app, its installer, its license for three computers, and its update service sold under one name software product Software becomes a product when it is packaged with the means to obtain and keep using it. 3 Grabbing a region of the screen and copying it to the clipboard software feature It is one capability a user can name. 4 All 40 commands in a hypothetical editor's menus, taken together feature set It is the complete collection of capabilities, not a single one. 5 Release 4.2 as published in March software version It is a numbered snapshot of the product at one moment. 6 A new paid release published every fall software release cycle It describes the schedule on which versions appear, not any one version.

Provenance: Node definitions come from the chapter sections above. Quiz items 1, 2, 3 and 5 follow the chapter's screen grab example; items 4 and 6 are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

Rules: Each quiz item is answered once. An answer is correct when it equals the Correct term for that item. The score is the count of correct answers out of 6. Mastery is a score of at least 5 on the first attempt through the quiz.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner clicks any node to read its definition and sees which nodes it connects to.
  2. The learner starts the matching quiz and reads item 1.
  3. The learner chooses one of the six terms and sees the feedback at once.
  4. The learner continues through items 2 to 6 and sees the final score.

Feedback: Six items in fixed order, one attempt each. A correct answer shows "Correct" and the Why text. An incorrect answer shows the Why text for that item and highlights the correct node on the map. The score "n of 6" is shown after the last item, with the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 5.

Starting State: The map is shown with no node selected and the quiz not started. The prompt reads "Click a node to see what it means, then test yourself."

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the author's screen grab utility cost $9, that three computers share one license, that a feature set is the complete collection of a product's capabilities, and that the map has six quiz items.

Software is cheap to copy

Think of it like a recipe: once it is written, every extra copy costs almost nothing. So what a vendor charges for is not the instructions, it is the product around them. Keep that in mind whenever a price changes.

A worked example shows how the terms separate. Suppose a utility starts with two features: grab a region, and grab a region after a delay. Its feature set has two items. The vendor adds "annotate with arrows," "record a video," "scan text from an image," and "share to a cloud gallery." The feature set now has six items, the software has grown, and the product has acquired a cloud account, a larger installer, and a longer support page. None of the original two features changed, yet the thing a customer buys is now quite different.

docs.title: Versions and Release Cycles
docs.text:
A product does not stay still. Each time a vendor publishes a changed copy, it assigns a software version, a number or name that identifies that exact snapshot of the product. Version numbers usually have two or three parts, such as 4.2 or 4.2.1. By convention, a change in the first part signals a major release with significant new capability, a change in the second signals a smaller set of additions, and a change in the third signals fixes only. Vendors follow that convention loosely, so treat the number as a hint rather than a guarantee.

A worked example of reading a version number: suppose a product moves from 4.2.0 to 4.2.1, then to 4.3.0, then to 5.0.0. The first step changes only the third part, so it should contain fixes and no new capability. The second step changes the second part, so it should add something modest. The third changes the first part, so it signals a major release, and often one that costs money. A reader who sees 5.0.0 should therefore expect larger changes than 4.2.1 and should read the release notes before upgrading.

Change Example What it usually signals What a careful user does Third part (patch) 4.2.0 to 4.2.1 Bug and security fixes Install promptly Second part (minor) 4.2.1 to 4.3.0 New features, same design Read the notes, then install First part (major) 4.3.0 to 5.0.0 Large changes, possibly a new price Check what changed and what it costs

Do not confuse a version with a build. A build is one particular compiled copy, which may be produced many times a day by the vendor's automated tools. A version is a build the vendor chose to name and publish. Users only ever see versions.

Versions exist so that people can talk precisely. A bug report that says "the delayed grab fails in 4.2" is useful. One that says "it fails in the new one" is not. Versions also let a vendor sell the same product more than once, a point that Chapter 3 returns to when it covers upgrade revenue.

The software release cycle is the schedule on which a vendor publishes new versions. Some vendors publish a new major version every year, some every few months, and some update continuously with no visible numbers at all. The cycle shapes what the customer experiences. A slow cycle gives users time to learn and a stable tool. A fast cycle gives the vendor a steady reason to announce something new, whether or not users asked for it.

Release cycles differ in rhythm and in what they reward. The table lists four common patterns and the pressure each puts on a vendor and a user.

Release cycle Typical rhythm Pressure on the vendor Experience for the user Annual major release One big version a year Must announce enough new capability to justify a new purchase Large, occasional changes, sometimes with a new price Quarterly updates Four versions a year Needs regular, visible additions Frequent small changes to learn Rolling release Changes appear when ready Must keep the product feeling alive Changes without clear version names Continuous delivery Many tiny changes a day Releases are cheap, so change is constant The product shifts under the user without warning

The pattern a vendor follows is connected to how it is paid. A vendor paid once per major version needs each release to look worth buying. A vendor paid every year needs the product to look worth renewing every year. Chapter 3 follows that thread.

Consider an illustrative product that follows an annual cycle. Version 1 ships with 6 features. Each later annual version adds 4 more. After ten versions, the product has 42 features. The numbers here are illustrative, not measurements of any real product, but the arithmetic shows the pattern: a modest, steady addition per release becomes a feature set seven times larger than the original.

Version Illustrative features in feature set 1 6 2 10 5 22 10 42

Now consider what a single user needs across those ten versions. If the author needs only two of the features, a grab and a delayed grab, then every version after the first delivers the same value to that user while the product grows around them. The explorer below lets you pick a version and a kind of user, and then calculate how much of the product that user actually touches.

docs.title: Diagram: Feature Growth and Usage Explorer
docs.text:
Feature Growth and Usage Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: bloat-feature-growth-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the percentage of an illustrative product's features that a given user never uses, for a given version, to within 1 percentage point.

Prerequisites: software feature, feature set, software version, software release cycle (defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For 3 challenge cases, the learner enters the unused percentage as a whole number before the sim reveals it. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 1 of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Moving the version control and choosing a user type is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) A product that adds features gives every user more value. (2) The share of unused features stays the same as the product grows.

Instructional Rationale: Calculating before seeing the answer makes the learner apply the formula to new inputs. Free exploration afterward shows the share of unused features climbing with every version.

Content:

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

The number of features in version v is F(v) = 6 + 4 x (v - 1).

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Version v 1 10 1 1 version number

There are three user types. Each has a count of features they want to use.

User type Features wanted Author (grab and delayed grab only) 2 Casual user 4 Power user 18

A user uses the smaller of the features wanted and F(v).

# User type Version F(v) Features used Model value: unused % Feedback when wrong 1 Author 10 42 2 95 Unused = (42 - 2) / 42 = 0.952, which is 95%. 2 Casual user 10 42 4 90 Unused = (42 - 4) / 42 = 0.905, which is 90%. 3 Power user 5 22 18 18 Unused = (22 - 18) / 22 = 0.182, which is 18%.

Provenance: Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter; no real product is measured. The Author row echoes the book's case in which the author needs two features.

Rules: Used(v) = min(wanted, F(v)). Unused percentage = 100 x (F(v) - Used(v)) / F(v), rounded to the nearest whole number. Rounding uses half up. When F(v) equals Used(v), unused is 0.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the version control and chooses a user type, and sees the number of features, the number used, and the used and unused shares update.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. For each, the sim shows the user type and version, and the learner enters the unused percentage.
  3. The learner presses Check and sees the Model value next to their entry.
  4. After the third challenge, the learner returns to free exploration and should notice that the Author's unused share rises with every version while the Power user's rises more slowly.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: % of features unused." Incorrect on the first attempt: the Feedback when wrong text without the final number. After the second wrong attempt the Model value is revealed and the challenge counts as missed. A count "Correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Version 1, Author selected, showing 6 features, 2 used, 67% unused. The question on screen is "How much of this product do you use?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that F(v) is 6 at version 1, adds 4 per version, and reaches 42 at version 10; that the author needs 2 features; and that the numbers are illustrative.

docs.title: What Software Bloat Is
docs.text:
Software bloat is the growth of a product's feature set, code size, and resource demands beyond what most of its users need or use. The word "bloat" carries a judgment, so it helps to be precise about what makes growth bloat rather than healthy improvement. Growth is healthy when it solves a problem that many users actually have. It is bloat when the added capability serves few users yet is carried, installed, updated, loaded, and paid for by everyone.

Bloat is therefore a statement about the gap between what a product contains and what a given user needs. A video editor with 400 features is not bloated for a professional editor who uses most of them. The same editor is bloated for someone who wants to trim one clip. Bloat is relative to a job, which is why the next section introduces the job to be done as the measuring stick.

The book's central case shows the pattern. The author's screen grab utility cost $9 and did its job well. Over the years it gained many more features, and it now costs $30 per year for each computer. The author uses a grab and a delayed grab. A common rule of thumb says that 95% of users use only 5% of a product's features, which Chapter 2 examines closely. If that holds even loosely, the other 95% of the feature set is bloat from that user's point of view, and the user pays for all of it.

Bloat is about the gap

The same product can be bloated for me and just right for you. Before you call a tool bloated, ask: bloated compared to which job?

Bloat takes several forms, and a product can suffer from some and not others. The table separates them so that a vague complaint like "it feels bloated" can be turned into a specific one.

Form of bloat What grows How a user notices it Feature bloat The feature set Menus and toolbars full of commands never used Code bloat The size of the program and its libraries Large downloads and long installs Resource bloat Memory, processor, and battery use A slow computer and a fan that spins up Price bloat The cost of the product A bill that rises faster than the value received Process bloat Accounts, sign-ins, and prompts Having to log in to use a tool that never needed it

Of the five, price bloat is the one this book follows most closely, because it is the one a user can calculate. Chapters 3 and 4 turn it into arithmetic.

Two related terms describe how bloat arrives and what it produces. Feature creep is the gradual, unplanned addition of features beyond a product's original purpose. The word "creep" is apt: no single addition looks unreasonable. Each is a small request from a few customers, a feature a competitor just announced, or an idea from a meeting. Taken one at a time, each is easy to justify. Taken together over ten releases, they produce a product its first customers would barely recognize.

A worked example shows the mechanism. A screen grab tool begins as "grab a region." A user asks for a delay, which is reasonable. Another asks for arrows on the image, also reasonable. A third wants to record video, and since the tool already captures pixels, that seems close enough. A fourth asks for cloud sharing, and now the tool needs accounts, servers, and a privacy policy. At every step the team said yes to something small. After the fourth step, the product is half an image editor, half a video recorder, and half a cloud service, and no one ever decided that it should be.

Watch for the 'just one more' step

Feature creep hides because each step looks small. Write the product's one-sentence purpose down first, and test every proposed addition against it: if the sentence has to change, say so out loud.

Bloatware is software that has become noticeably bloated, or software bundled onto a device that most users never asked for and cannot easily remove. In everyday use, it names the symptom, a product so large and slow that the size is the main thing people notice. Chapters later in this book use "bloat" for the growth itself and "bloatware" for the resulting product.

docs.title: The Job To Be Done
docs.text:
A job to be done is the specific task a person hires a product to accomplish. The phrase comes from product design, where it replaces the question "what features does this product have?" with "what is the customer actually trying to get done?" A person who buys a drill does not want a drill; they want a hole. Someone who installs a screen grab utility wants an image of part of the screen, in the clipboard, so that it can be pasted into a message.

The idea is useful here because it gives bloat a measuring stick. Features that serve the job are signal. Features that serve other jobs, or no job, are the candidates for bloat. Writing the job down in a single sentence also makes a requirements document short, a point that returns in Chapter 7 when you specify a tool to be generated.

Consider three people and one product. A support engineer's job is "capture an error dialog and paste it into a ticket within seconds." A trainer's job is "produce a polished tutorial with arrows, numbered steps, and a video." A casual user's job is "send my friend a picture of this recipe." All three open the same utility, but they hire it for different jobs, and a feature set built for the trainer is mostly dead weight for the other two.

Person Job to be done Features that serve the job Features that do not Support engineer Capture an error dialog and paste it into a ticket Grab a region, copy to clipboard Video recording, cloud gallery Trainer Produce a polished tutorial Annotations, step numbers, video Little of the feature set is unused Casual user Send a picture of a recipe Grab a region Nearly everything else Author (this book) Grab a region, optionally after a delay, to the clipboard Grab, delayed grab Everything else

A job statement works best in a fixed form: "When [situation], I want to [action], so I can [outcome]." Take the author's job: "When I need to show someone what is on my screen, I want to grab a region and have it on the clipboard, so I can paste it into a message." Each part carries information. The situation tells you when the tool is used, the action tells you the minimum behavior, and the outcome tells you how to judge success. Notice that nothing in the statement mentions annotation, video, or a cloud account. Those are answers to other people's jobs.

A job statement also gives you a quick test for any proposed feature. Ask whether removing the feature would stop the job from getting done. For the author's job, removing delayed grab would matter, because a menu or a tooltip that disappears when you click away can only be captured on a timer. Removing the video recorder would change nothing at all.

A single-purpose utility is a small tool built to do one job well and little else. It is the opposite end of the spectrum from bloat: its feature set is small by design, and each feature serves the one job. Plenty of such tools are famous for it, and the Unix command-line tools are the classic case. The Unix philosophy is the design guideline, associated with the early Unix developers, that each program should do one thing well and that programs should be easy to combine. A single-purpose utility is that philosophy applied to a graphical tool.

The table compares the two approaches on the qualities a user feels. Neither column is always the better choice; the point is to see what each one trades.

Quality Single-purpose utility Large multi-purpose product Time to learn Minutes Hours to weeks Fit for a user's one job Exact, if the job matches Covered among many other jobs Coverage of different jobs Narrow Broad Install size and idle use Small Large Effort to inspect or verify Low, because there is less to read High Ongoing change Slow; few reasons to update Constant; many reasons to update

The trade-off is real. A single-purpose utility will never cover every need, and a user with five jobs may need five tools. The benefit is that each tool is small, fast to learn, easy to inspect, and cheap to maintain. Generative AI changes the calculation, as later chapters explain, because it makes it cheap to produce the one small tool that fits your exact job.

Write your job in one sentence

Before you evaluate any tool, finish this sentence: "I need to ___ so that I can ___." If you need more than one sentence, you probably have more than one job.

docs.title: Resource Footprint
docs.text:
Bloat shows up on your computer as well as on the price tag. A program's resource footprint is the total amount of computer resources it consumes: disk space to store it, memory to run it, processor time, battery, network traffic, and the startup time it adds to your day. Footprint is measurable, which makes it the most objective evidence of bloat. A feature set is an opinion about what a product does, but a footprint is a number you can read from your system's monitor.

Two parts of the footprint deserve their own names. Install size is the amount of disk space a program occupies once installed, including its supporting files. It is the easiest figure to find, and it grows with every added feature, bundled library, and embedded asset. Idle resource use is the memory, processor time, and battery a program consumes while it is running but not doing anything for you. A utility you open for ten seconds a day, yet which keeps a helper process running all day to watch for a hotkey, has idle use that dwarfs its active use.

Idle use is where bloat becomes a tax on everything else you do. A small helper that loads at login, checks for updates, syncs a gallery, and reports usage statistics may use little at any moment, but it never stops. Multiply by every such program on the machine, and the computer slows for reasons no single program explains.

The upgrade treadmill is the cycle in which each new version demands a larger footprint and more learning, which pushes users to upgrade their hardware, their skills, or their payments just to stay where they were. The treadmill is the combination of two pressures already named: a fast release cycle supplies the new versions, and feature creep makes each one heavier. Users run harder, with new hardware, new training, and new fees, to remain in the same place.

You can see footprint without special tools. On a Mac, Activity Monitor lists every running process with its memory and processor use, and the Finder's Get Info window shows an application's size on disk. A useful habit is to open Activity Monitor, sort by memory, and ask of each entry near the top: did I open this today, and does it do something I need right now? Anything you cannot answer yes to is idle use you are paying for in battery life and speed.

A worked example compares two illustrative programs that both do the author's job. The numbers below are invented to show the shape of the comparison and are labeled illustrative. They are not measurements of any real product.

Measure Full-featured product (illustrative) Single-purpose utility (illustrative) Ratio Install size 1,200 MB 15 MB 80 times Idle memory 450 MB 30 MB 15 times Background helper processes 3 1 3 times

Looking at that table, a reader might guess that every measure differs by the same factor. It doesn't. Install size differs most, because storage holds every unused feature. Idle memory differs less, because both programs must keep something running to catch the hotkey. The helper count differs least. Each measure answers a different question, and a fair comparison reports all of them.

A footprint is a bill you pay every day

Install size is a one-time cost, but idle use is charged every minute the machine is on. Which of the programs on your computer are running right now, and which of them did you open today?

Use the comparison chart below to see the three measures side by side and to test your intuition about which ratio is largest before the numbers are revealed.

docs.title: Diagram: Resource Footprint Comparison
docs.text:
Resource Footprint Comparison

Type: chart sim-id: bloat-footprint-comparison Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the resource footprint of an illustrative full-featured product and an illustrative single-purpose utility on three measures, correctly ranking which measure differs most between them.

Prerequisites: resource footprint, install size, idle resource use, single-purpose utility (defined in the chapter section "Resource Footprint" above).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the values are revealed, the learner ranks the three measures from the largest to the smallest ratio between the two programs. The ranking is correct when it equals install size, idle memory, background helper processes. Mastery is a correct ranking in one attempt. Hovering bars after the reveal is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A smaller program is smaller by the same factor on every measure. (2) Install size is the only footprint that matters.

Instructional Rationale: Predicting a ranking before the reveal forces the learner to reason about why storage differs more than running cost, which is comparison rather than reading numbers off a chart.

Content:

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

Measure Unit Full-featured product Single-purpose utility Ratio Why the ratio is what it is (shown on hover) Install size MB 1200 15 80 Storage holds every feature, used or not. Idle memory MB 450 30 15 Both programs must keep something running to catch a hotkey, so the gap is smaller than for storage. Background helper processes count 3 1 3 Both need one helper for the hotkey. The full product adds an update checker and a sync agent.

Ratio = full-featured value divided by single-purpose value.

Provenance: Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter. They are not measurements of any real product.

Rules: The ratio for each measure is the full-featured value divided by the utility value. Measures are ranked from the largest ratio to the smallest. Ties, if the values were changed, keep the table order.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the three measure names with the values hidden and orders them from largest to smallest ratio.
  2. The learner presses Reveal and sees the grouped bars and the ratios.
  3. The learner hovers over a bar and reads the Why text for that measure.
  4. The learner should notice that the largest ratio belongs to the measure that costs the user the least each day.

Feedback: One attempt at the ranking. Correct: "Correct: storage differs most, helpers least." Incorrect: the correct order is shown with the Why text for the measure the learner placed wrongly. The reveal always happens after the ranking.

Starting State: Three measure names are shown with no values. The question on screen is "Which measure differs most between the two programs?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the six illustrative values 1,200 and 15 MB, 450 and 30 MB, 3 and 1 helpers, and the ratios 80, 15 and 3 times.

docs.title: Putting the Vocabulary to Work
docs.text:
You now have the vocabulary for the rest of the book. A product is built from software, offers a feature set, and ships as versions on a release cycle. When the feature set grows past what most users need through feature creep, the product is bloated, and the evidence appears in its resource footprint and its price. A single-purpose utility is the contrast case, and the job to be done is the yardstick.

You can name the parts of bloat

You can now tell a software product from the software inside it, trace how a feature set grows through versions, and separate bloat from feature creep and from footprint. That is the vocabulary every later chapter builds on.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Software is instructions; a software product is software packaged with a license, installer, updates, and support.
  • A feature set grows through versions published on a release cycle.
  • Software bloat is a gap between a feature set and the job a user needs done. Feature creep is how the gap opens.
  • Resource footprint, including install size and idle resource use, is the measurable side of bloat.
  • A single-purpose utility, guided by the Unix philosophy, is the contrast case.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
docs.text: Test your understanding of software products, feature sets, release cycles, bloat, the job to be done, and resource footprint with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a software product, as the chapter defines it?
docs.text:
1. The compiled program that copies pixels from the display into an image
  2. Software packaged with an installer, documentation, a license, a price, updates, and support
  3. The complete collection of capabilities a program offers
  4. A numbered snapshot of a program at one point in time
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A software product is software plus everything a buyer needs to obtain and keep using it: installer, documentation, license, price, updates, and usually support. Option A describes the software alone. Option C describes a feature set, and option D describes a software version. Keeping these four terms separate explains why a confusing price usually comes from the product wrapped around the code.

Concept Tested: Software Product

See: Software, Products, and Features

docs.title: 2. What is a software version?
docs.text:
1. A number or name that identifies one exact snapshot of a product that the vendor chose to publish
  2. Any compiled copy that the vendor's automated tools produce during a day
  3. The schedule on which a vendor releases new capability
  4. The set of features that most users actually use
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A version is a build the vendor chose to name and publish, such as 4.2 or 4.2.1. Option B describes a build, which users never see. Option C describes the software release cycle, which is the schedule that produces versions. Option D has no connection to versioning. Versions let people talk precisely, so a bug report that names the version is far more useful than "the new one."

Concept Tested: Software Version

See: Versions and Release Cycles

docs.title: 3. Which statement best describes feature creep?
docs.text:
1. A deliberate redesign that removes rarely used features
  2. A sudden doubling of a product's price in a single release
  3. The gradual, unplanned addition of features beyond a product's original purpose
  4. The slow growth of a program's idle memory use over time
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Feature creep is how a feature set grows: each addition looks small and reasonable, such as a delay, then arrows, then video, then cloud sharing, yet together they change what the product is. Option A is the opposite of creep. Option B describes price bloat, and option D describes resource bloat. Creep hides because no single step looks unreasonable.

Concept Tested: Feature Creep

See: What Software Bloat Is

docs.title: 4. What does install size measure?
docs.text:
1. The memory a program uses while it is running but not doing anything for you
  2. The number of features a program offers
  3. The total time a program adds to your computer's startup
  4. The disk space a program occupies once installed, including its supporting files
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Install size is the disk space an installed program occupies, including supporting files. It is the easiest footprint figure to find and grows with every added feature, bundled library, and embedded asset. Option A describes idle resource use. Option B describes the size of the feature set, and option C describes startup time, which is a separate part of the resource footprint.

Concept Tested: Install Size

See: Resource Footprint

docs.title: 5. A video editor with 400 features is not bloated for a professional editor but is bloated for someone who wants to trim one clip. What does this show about bloat?
docs.text:
1. Bloat depends only on how many features a product has
  2. Professional editors tolerate bloat better than casual users
  3. Bloat is a gap between what a product contains and what a particular user needs
  4. Bloat appears only in video software
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter defines bloat as growth beyond what most of a product's users need or use, which makes it a statement about a gap, measured against a job. The professional uses most of the 400 features, so the gap is small. The clip trimmer uses a handful, so the gap is large. Feature count alone (A) cannot decide the question, and the idea applies to any product category (D).

Concept Tested: Software Bloat

See: What Software Bloat Is

docs.title: 6. Why does the chapter say idle resource use can matter more day to day than install size?
docs.text:
1. Install size is charged every minute the machine is on, while idle use is paid once
  2. Idle use is charged continuously while the program runs in the background, whereas install size is a one-time storage cost
  3. Idle use only affects disk space, which is always scarce
  4. Install size cannot be measured, but idle use can
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A helper that loads at login, checks for updates, and syncs a gallery keeps consuming memory, processor time, and battery whenever the computer is on. Install size is paid once, as storage. Option A reverses the two. Option C is wrong because idle use concerns memory, processor, and battery rather than disk. Option D is wrong because both can be read from system tools such as Activity Monitor and Finder's Get Info.

Concept Tested: Idle Resource Use

See: Resource Footprint

docs.title: 7. A product moves from version 4.3.0 to 5.0.0. What should a careful user do before upgrading?
docs.text:
1. Install it immediately, because only the third number signals bug fixes
  2. Ignore the release, since first-number changes only affect the vendor
  3. Wait for 5.0.1, because 5.0.0 never contains fixes
  4. Check what changed and what it costs, because a first-part change signals a major release and possibly a new price
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. By convention, a change in the first part of a version number signals large changes, and vendors often attach a new price to a major release. Reading the release notes tells you whether the new capability is worth the cost to your job. Option A confuses major and patch releases. Options B and C make claims the chapter does not support. Because vendors follow the convention loosely, treat the number as a hint, not a guarantee.

Concept Tested: Software Version

See: Versions and Release Cycles

docs.title: 8. Why do vendors sell products and licenses rather than just the instructions themselves?
docs.text:
1. Instructions cannot legally be sold
  2. Copying software costs almost nothing, so price is set by what customers will accept and the cost sits in writing and maintaining it once
  3. Every copy of software requires a separate custom build
  4. Customers always prefer to buy support rather than software
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Software's millionth copy costs nearly the same as its second, so the real cost is writing, testing, and maintaining the instructions once. A vendor therefore sells the packaging and the promise, and sets a price based on what customers will accept rather than on copy cost. Option A is false, and option C contradicts the near-zero copying cost. Option D invents a customer preference the chapter never claims.

Concept Tested: Software Product

See: Software, Products, and Features

docs.title: 9. In the chapter's illustrative comparison, install size differs by 80 times, idle memory by 15 times, and helper processes by 3 times. What best explains why install size differs most?
docs.text:
1. Both programs must keep a helper running to catch the hotkey, so running costs cannot differ at all
  2. Idle memory is always about one fifth of install size
  3. Storage holds every feature whether it is used or not, while running costs include a minimum both programs must pay
  4. Single-purpose utilities never install any supporting files
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Install size grows with every feature, library, and asset stored, used or not. Idle memory and helper count have a floor, because both programs need something running to catch the hotkey, so the gap is smaller. Option A overstates the point, since the numbers do differ. Options B and D are not supported by the chapter. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of real products.

Concept Tested: Resource Footprint

See: Resource Footprint

docs.title: 10. Using the author's job of grabbing a region, optionally after a delay, to the clipboard, which feature fails the test "would removing it stop the job from getting done?"
docs.text:
1. The video recorder, because removing it would change nothing about the job
  2. The delayed grab, because menus that vanish on click can only be captured on a timer
  3. The region grab, because it is the core capability
  4. The clipboard copy, because it delivers the outcome
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The test asks whether removing a feature stops the job. Removing delayed grab matters because transient menus and tooltips need a timer, and removing the region grab or clipboard copy would end the job outright. Removing the video recorder changes nothing, so it serves other people's jobs and is a bloat candidate. The test turns a vague feeling of bloat into a specific, checkable judgment.

Concept Tested: Job To Be Done

See: The Job To Be Done

docs.title: References: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
docs.text:
1. Software bloat - Wikipedia - Defines bloat as code and features that consume resources without matching user value, with examples of growing install sizes. Gives this chapter its central vocabulary and its measurable footprint ideas.

  2. Feature creep - Wikipedia - Explains how continuous addition of features beyond the original scope inflates complexity and schedules. Supports the chapter's account of how the gap between features and the user's job opens over time.

  3. Unix philosophy - Wikipedia - Summarizes the design maxims of small, single-purpose programs that cooperate, from McIlroy to Raymond. Provides the contrast case of the single-purpose utility used throughout the chapter.
