  4. The Mythical Man-Month (Anniversary Edition) - Frederick P. Brooks Jr. - Addison-Wesley - Brooks named the second-system effect, where a designer's cautious first system is followed by an overloaded second one. His essays explain why feature accumulation feels reasonable at every step yet ends in bloat.

  5. The UNIX Philosophy - Mike Gancarz - Digital Press - Gancarz distilled Unix design into nine tenets, including small is beautiful and make each program do one thing well. His short, quotable rules are the clearest statement of the lean alternative to bloat.

  6. Strategy Letter IV: Bloatware and the 80/20 Myth - Joel on Software - Spolsky argues that every user needs a different 20 percent of features, so bloat is less irrational than it looks. A useful counterweight that this chapter's bloat claims must answer.

  7. A Plea for Lean Software - Niklaus Wirth, IEEE Computer, 1995 - Wirth's classic essay shows how software grows slower and larger faster than hardware improves, and demonstrates a compact, lean system. Source of Wirth's law, quoted when the chapter discusses resource footprint.

  8. Worse Is Better - Richard P. Gabriel - Gabriel contrasts simple, minimal designs with complete, feature-rich ones and explains why the simple ones often spread faster. Gives students a design-culture lens on why lean tools win and lose.

  9. The Art of Unix Programming: Basics of the Unix Philosophy - Eric S. Raymond - Lists seventeen design rules such as parsimony, modularity, and the rule of silence. Gives concrete, checkable criteria for judging whether a tool like ScreenGrab stays small.

  10. The suckless.org Philosophy - suckless.org - Argues for software that is simple, minimal, and small enough to read fully, and names code bloat as the enemy. A modern, opinionated example of a community that practices the lean contrast case.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: Having seen how products grow, this chapter asks who uses what they gain. It covers usage telemetry, power and casual users, the long tail of features, and the 95/5 rule of thumb alongside the Pareto Principle, along with the cognitive load that unused features impose. It closes with the roadmaps, competitive matching, and checklist marketing that keep features coming. After this chapter, you will be able to compare a product's feature list with how it is actually used.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 14 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Feature Usage 26 Usage Telemetry 1 Power Users 8 Casual Users 8 Long Tail Of Features 8 Pareto Principle 8 95/5 Rule Of Thumb 7 Unused Features 2 Cognitive Load 31 Interface Complexity 2 Feature Discoverability 1 Product Roadmap 5 Competitive Feature Matching 2 Feature Checklist Marketing 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat

Who actually clicks all those buttons?

Last chapter showed how a product piles up features. This one asks the question vendors rarely publish: who uses them? By the end you'll be able to hold a feature list up against real usage and see how much shell you are carrying for nothing. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Measuring Feature Usage
docs.text:
Feature usage is the record of which features of a product people actually use, and how often. It is the missing half of any feature list. A list says what a product can do. Usage says what it does do for the people who own it. The two numbers are often far apart, and the distance between them is the practical meaning of bloat from Chapter 1.

Usage is measured as a share of users, a count of events, or both. "42% of users opened the blur tool at least once last month" is a share. "The blur tool was opened 8,000 times last month" is a count. They answer different questions, because a few enthusiasts can generate thousands of events while most users never touch the tool.

Vendors collect these numbers through usage telemetry: automated reports that a product sends back to its maker, recording which features were used and when. Telemetry is how a vendor learns that a feature nobody opens is still taking up a quarter of the menu. It also raises a privacy question, which is why a product should say plainly what it reports and let you turn it off.

A worked example uses the illustrative data below. A hypothetical screen grab utility has 20 features. The table gives the share of its users who used each feature at least once in a month. The numbers are invented for the chapter and labeled illustrative; they are not measurements of a real product.

Rank Feature Share of users (illustrative) 1 Grab a region 92% 2 Grab a window 55% 3 Save to a file 48% 4 Grab after a delay 30% 5 Draw an arrow 22% 6 Add text 16% 7 Custom hotkeys 12% 8 Blur a region 11% 9 Scrolling capture 9% 10 Record the screen 8% 11 Extract text from an image 6% 12 Upload to a cloud gallery 5% 13 GIF export 4% 14 Team library 3% 15 Capture timeline 3% 16 Comments 2% 17 Image compare 2% 18 Stamp library 2% 19 Batch rename 1% 20 Plugin interface 1%

Reading the table, only two features are used by more than half of the users. Eight features are used by at least 10%. The bottom twelve are each used by fewer than one user in ten.

Telemetry has limits worth knowing. It shows what people did, not why they did it. A feature with low use may be unneeded, or it may be hard to find, or it may matter intensely to a small group who would leave without it. A careful vendor treats low usage as a question to investigate, and a careful reader treats a vendor's claim of "unused" the same way.

Audit your own usage

Pick a tool you pay for and list every feature you used in the last month. Then count the features it advertises, and divide. That one ratio is your own bloat score.

docs.title: Power Users, Casual Users, and the Long Tail
docs.text:
Usage is not spread evenly across people. A power user is someone who uses a large share of a product's features, often and in combination, and who is usually willing to learn a complicated tool to get more from it. A casual user is someone who uses a small number of features, occasionally, and wants the tool to work without study. Both are real customers, and the same product serves both, though not equally well.

Power users matter to vendors out of proportion to their number. They write reviews, request features, and set the standard that reviewers use. A vendor listening mainly to its power users will keep adding depth, and each addition seems reasonable to the person who asked for it. Casual users rarely ask for anything; they simply stop opening the tool, or they keep paying and say nothing.

Here is the worked example, using the 20-feature data above. Three illustrative users open the same utility. The author uses 2 features, a grab and a delayed grab. A casual user uses 4, adding "save to a file" and "grab a window." A power user uses 18 of the 20. The author touches 10% of the feature set, the casual user 20%, and the power user 90%. The product is one thing; its usefulness depends on who is holding it.

The two groups differ in more ways than feature count, and the differences explain many design arguments. The table summarizes them.

Trait Power user Casual user Features used Many, often in combination A few Frequency Daily or hourly Occasional Tolerance for complexity High, if the payoff is control Low Typical request "Add an option for..." "Make it simpler" Effect on the roadmap Pushes depth and options Rarely heard

The long tail of features is the pattern in which a few features are used by almost everyone while many others are each used by very few. Plot the 20 features from most used to least used, and the chart falls steeply and then flattens into a long, low tail. The name comes from the shape. The head of the chart is short and tall, and the tail stretches away to the right.

The tail is not worthless. A feature used by 2% of 100,000 users still serves 2,000 people, and for those people it may be the reason they bought the product. The difficulty is that every user, whether in the head or the tail, pays for and carries the entire tail. Use the explorer below to move a usage threshold along the chart and watch how few features survive as the threshold rises.

docs.title: Diagram: Long Tail of Feature Usage Explorer
docs.text:
Long Tail of Feature Usage Explorer

Type: chart sim-id: usage-long-tail-explorer Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: examine Learning Objective: The learner will examine an illustrative 20-feature usage distribution and state how many features are used by at least a chosen share of users, correctly for 3 of 3 thresholds.

Prerequisites: feature usage, power users, casual users, long tail of features (defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For 3 challenge thresholds, the learner enters how many of the 20 features are used by at least that share of users, before the sim highlights them. An entry is correct when it equals the Count column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt. Dragging the threshold freely and hovering bars is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Most features are used by most users. (2) A feature used by few users is unimportant to the vendor's revenue.

Instructional Rationale: Counting features above a threshold makes the learner read the distribution rather than glance at it, and the threshold control lets them see how steeply the count drops.

Content:

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative. The chart shows the 20 features in this order, from most to least used, with the share of users in percent.

Rank Feature Share of users (%) 1 Grab a region 92 2 Grab a window 55 3 Save to a file 48 4 Grab after a delay 30 5 Draw an arrow 22 6 Add text 16 7 Custom hotkeys 12 8 Blur a region 11 9 Scrolling capture 9 10 Record the screen 8 11 Extract text from an image 6 12 Upload to a cloud gallery 5 13 GIF export 4 14 Team library 3 15 Capture timeline 3 16 Comments 2 17 Image compare 2 18 Stamp library 2 19 Batch rename 1 20 Plugin interface 1

The adjustable quantity is the threshold.

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Usage threshold 1 100 1 50 percent of users

Challenges, in this order:

# Threshold (%) Count Why (shown as feedback) 1 50 2 Only grab a region (92) and grab a window (55) reach 50. 2 20 5 Adding save to a file (48), grab after a delay (30) and draw an arrow (22) gives 5. 3 10 8 Add text (16), custom hotkeys (12) and blur a region (11) bring the count to 8.

Provenance: Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter, shared with the chapter's table; no real product is measured.

Rules: A feature is counted when its share is >= the threshold. The count is shown as "n of 20" and as the percentage n / 20, rounded to the nearest whole percent. At threshold 100 the count is 0. At threshold 1 the count is 20.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the sorted bars and moves the threshold; bars at or above the threshold are marked as counted and the count updates.
  2. The learner starts the challenges. For each, the sim shows the threshold and the learner enters a count.
  3. The learner presses Check; the counted bars are marked and the Why text appears.
  4. After challenge 3, the learner returns to free exploration and should notice that the count falls from 20 to 8 between thresholds 1 and 10, then from 8 to 2 between thresholds 10 and 50.

Feedback: Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: n features." Incorrect on the first attempt: "Not quite. Count the bars that reach the threshold." After the second wrong attempt the correct count and the Why text are shown and the challenge counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

Starting State: The 20 bars are shown with the threshold at 50 and a count of 2 of 20. The question on screen is "How many features do most users really use?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the data has 20 features, that only 2 are used by more than half of the users, that 8 are used by at least 10%, and that the bottom 12 are each used by fewer than 1 user in 10.

The tail is paid for by the head

Notice who carries what: the head users need almost nothing from the tail, yet they download, update, and pay for all of it. Whenever a feature list is long, ask who it is long for.

docs.title: The Pareto Principle and the 95/5 Rule
docs.text:
The Pareto principle is the observation that a small share of causes produces a large share of effects. It is named for the economist Vilfredo Pareto and is usually summarized as the 80/20 rule: roughly 80% of results come from 20% of causes. Software offers many examples. A small share of the code causes most of the bugs, a small share of customers produces most of the revenue, and a small share of features gets most of the use.

The cumulative view makes the Pareto shape easy to read. Each row adds the next-most-used feature to the running total of 332 points in the illustrative data.

Features included Share of the 20 features Cumulative use points Share of all use Top 2 10% 147 44% Top 4 20% 225 68% Top 5 25% 247 74% Top 8 40% 286 86% All 20 100% 332 100%

The 80/20 figures are a pattern, not a law, and the real split varies. Our illustrative data can be tested. The total of all 20 feature shares is 332 percentage points. The top four features account for 92 + 55 + 48 + 30 = 225 of them, which is 68%. The top 20% of the features (4 of 20) therefore carry about 68% of the use. That is the Pareto shape, but a softer version than 80/20.

The 95/5 rule of thumb is the claim, used throughout this book, that about 95% of users use only about 5% of a product's features. It is a sharper version of the Pareto idea, applied to people rather than to causes, and it is a rough guide rather than a measurement. For a product with 40 features, 5% is 2 features, exactly what the author uses. For a product with 100 features, it is 5.

Rule of thumb, not a law

The 95/5 figure is easy to repeat and hard to prove for any single product. Treat it as a hypothesis to test, and check your own tool's usage before you quote it: a product's true split might be 90/10 or 99/1.

Unused features are features that a given user never uses, or that almost no one uses. The phrase has two meanings, and it is worth keeping them apart. For one person, every feature outside their own use is unused, which is nearly the whole feature set. For the product as a whole, a feature is unused when telemetry shows that essentially no one opens it. The second kind is the strongest evidence of bloat, since no user receives value from it, yet it remains in the code, the menu, and the documentation.

docs.title: Why Unused Features Cost Something
docs.text:
An unused feature seems free: it sits there, and you don't have to touch it. That is not quite true, and the reason is cognitive load, the amount of mental effort a task demands of working memory. People can hold only a handful of items in mind at once. Interface designers reduce load by showing only what the task needs. Every extra button, menu, and dialog adds something to scan, read, and rule out.

A worked example makes it concrete. The author's job is to grab a region after a delay. In a minimal tool, a menu offers two commands, and the right one is found at a glance. In a product with 20 features, the same command is one of twenty menu items grouped under several headings, and the user must read, reject, or remember where it lives. Nothing in that menu is broken. The author simply spends effort on the 18 commands that are irrelevant, every time.

Researchers describe cognitive load in parts. Intrinsic load comes from the difficulty of the task itself, such as deciding what to capture. Extraneous load comes from how the task is presented, such as a cluttered menu. Designers can reduce only the second kind, and unused features are one of the largest sources of it.

Interface complexity is the number and arrangement of controls, menus, and options that a user must understand or navigate to use a product. It grows with the feature set, and it grows faster than the feature count, because each new feature must be placed relative to all the old ones. Complexity is the visible part of cognitive load, the part you can count by opening the menus.

Feature discoverability is how easily a user can find a feature they need. It pulls in the opposite direction from a large feature set. A small tool makes its few features obvious. A large tool buries the useful ones among the rest, so even a feature that exists and would help may never be found. A bloated product can therefore fail twice: its unwanted features crowd the screen, and its wanted ones become hard to find.

Features you never use still cost you attention

Think of a drawer with 5 tools versus a drawer with 50. You pay for the extra 45 each time you rummage, even if you never pick one up. What could you take out of your busiest tool?

docs.title: Why Features Keep Arriving
docs.text:
If most features go unused and add load, why do vendors keep adding them? Three forces explain most of it. The first is the product roadmap, the vendor's plan for what to build and in what order. A roadmap is a reasonable thing to have, but it is written by a team that needs to show progress, and "we shipped five new features" is easier to show than "we made the existing three simpler."

A worked example of a roadmap shows the tension. Suppose a team plans four releases. Release one adds cloud sharing, release two adds team comments, release three adds a plug-in interface, and release four adds an AI summary. Each looks sensible in a planning meeting. None of them was requested by the users who bought the original tool for a quick, local grab. The roadmap serves the vendor's growth, and the old users inherit its results.

The second force is competitive feature matching: adding a feature because a rival has one, whether or not customers ask for it. If a competitor announces screen recording, the pressure to add recording is immediate. No team wants to explain why it lacks something on the other product's page. When all the rivals follow each other, the whole category drifts toward the same long feature list.

The third is feature checklist marketing: promoting a product by the length of its feature list rather than by how well it does a job. A comparison table with a check mark in every row is the typical form. It works on buyers who cannot judge quality in advance, because a count is easier to compare than a fit. It rewards adding a shallow version of every feature, which is bloat by construction.

The sorter below presents eight situations and asks you to name the force behind each one, with a fourth option for the one healthy cause, a feature added because usage data and customers showed a real need.

docs.title: Diagram: Why Features Get Added Sorter
docs.text:
Why Features Get Added Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: usage-feature-driver-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish four reasons a vendor adds a feature by assigning each of 8 described situations to the correct reason, scoring at least 7 of 8.

Prerequisites: usage telemetry, product roadmap, competitive feature matching, feature checklist marketing (defined in the chapter sections "Measuring Feature Usage" and "Why Features Keep Arriving").

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each situation to one of four reasons. An assignment is correct when it equals the Correct reason column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt through. Reading the reason definitions is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Every feature exists because customers asked for it. (2) A longer feature list always means a better product.

Instructional Rationale: Sorting similar-looking situations forces the learner to attend to the trigger behind each addition, which is the distinction at the Analyze level.

Content:

The four reasons, with the definition shown to the learner:

Reason Definition shown Customer need shown by usage The vendor adds the feature because telemetry or customer requests show many users need it. Product roadmap The vendor adds the feature because it is on a plan made to show progress and growth. Competitive feature matching The vendor adds the feature because a rival has it. Feature checklist marketing The vendor adds or counts the feature so the product wins a feature-by-feature comparison.

The 8 situations, in this fixed order:

# Situation shown Correct reason Why (shown as feedback) 1 A rival announces AI summaries, and the vendor ships its own within a quarter. Competitive feature matching The trigger is the rival's move, not any request from users. 2 Telemetry shows 40% of users resize every grab by hand, so the vendor adds a resize handle. Customer need shown by usage Usage data shows a widespread need. 3 A three-year plan names cloud collaboration as the headline of next year's release. Product roadmap The feature comes from a plan, not from a stated need. 4 A package says "120+ features" and counts every menu item and setting. Feature checklist marketing The count is chosen to look large in a comparison. 5 Many support tickets ask for a delay timer, so the vendor adds one. Customer need shown by usage Repeated requests from users are a direct signal of need. 6 A comparison page ticks every row against the rivals, including a rarely used plug-in interface. Feature checklist marketing The row exists to earn a check mark, not to serve a job. 7 A planned platform release schedules a plug-in interface for the second half of the year. Product roadmap The date and scope come from the vendor's plan. 8 After a competitor adds screen recording, the vendor adds recording although no customer asked. Competitive feature matching The competitor's feature, not demand, is the cause.

Provenance: All 8 situations are illustrative scenarios invented for this chapter; the sim labels them illustrative.

Rules: Each situation is assigned once to exactly one reason. The score is the number of correct assignments out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7 on the first pass.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the four reasons and their definitions.
  2. The learner sees situation 1 and chooses one reason.
  3. The sim shows whether the choice was correct, with the Why text, and the learner moves to the next situation.
  4. After situation 8, the learner sees the score and which reasons they confused most often.

Feedback: Eight items in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" with the Why text. Incorrect: the correct reason and the Why text. The final screen shows "n of 8" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 7.

Starting State: The four reasons are listed with situation 1 shown. The question on screen is "Why was this feature added?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the sorter has 8 situations and 4 reasons, and that one reason, customer need shown by usage, is the healthy one.

You can read a feature list critically

You can now compare a feature list with real usage, explain the long tail and the 95/5 rule, and say why unused features cost attention. Next stop: the money behind it all.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Feature usage measures what a feature list cannot: who uses what, and how often.
  • Usage is uneven. A few features serve almost everyone, and a long tail serves few.
  • The Pareto principle and the 95/5 rule of thumb describe that unevenness; treat the numbers as hypotheses.
  • Unused features cost cognitive load, add interface complexity, and hurt discoverability.
  • Roadmaps, competitive matching, and checklist marketing keep adding features that usage does not justify.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule
docs.text: Test your understanding of usage telemetry, power and casual users, the long tail, the Pareto principle, cognitive load, and the forces that keep features arriving with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is usage telemetry?
docs.text:
1. A survey in which customers rank the features they would like to see added
  2. A list of every feature a product advertises on its box
  3. Automated reports a product sends back to its maker, recording which features were used and when
  4. A monthly count of how many licenses a vendor has sold
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Usage telemetry is how a vendor learns which features are used, such as discovering that a feature nobody opens still occupies a quarter of the menu. Option A describes a survey, which records opinions rather than behavior. Option B is a feature list, the half of the picture that usage fills in. Option D concerns sales. Telemetry also raises a privacy question, so a product should say what it reports and allow you to turn it off.

Concept Tested: Usage Telemetry

See: Measuring Feature Usage

docs.title: 2. What does the long tail of features describe?
docs.text:
1. A pattern in which a few features are used by almost everyone while many others are each used by very few
  2. A pattern in which every feature is used by about the same number of people
  3. A list of features scheduled for future releases
  4. A group of users who use every feature in the product
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Plot features from most used to least used and the chart falls steeply, then flattens into a long, low tail. In the chapter's illustrative data, only two of twenty features are used by more than half of users, and the bottom twelve are each used by fewer than one user in ten. Option B contradicts that shape. Option C describes a roadmap, and option D describes power users.

Concept Tested: Long Tail Of Features

See: Power Users, Casual Users, and the Long Tail

docs.title: 3. Which statement best defines the Pareto principle?
docs.text:
1. Exactly 95% of users use exactly 5% of features in every product
  2. Every cause contributes equally to a result
  3. Software defects are always spread evenly across the code
  4. A small share of causes produces a large share of effects, commonly summarized as 80/20
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The Pareto principle, named for the economist Vilfredo Pareto, observes that roughly 80% of results come from 20% of causes. In software, a small share of the code causes most bugs, a small share of customers produces most revenue, and a small share of features gets most of the use. The chapter calls it a pattern, not a law. Option A overstates the 95/5 rule of thumb, and options B and C describe the opposite of Pareto.

Concept Tested: Pareto Principle

See: The Pareto Principle and the 95/5 Rule

docs.title: 4. What is feature checklist marketing?
docs.text:
1. Testing each feature against a checklist before release
  2. Promoting a product by the length of its feature list rather than by how well it does a job
  3. Asking users to check off the features they use in a survey
  4. Listing a product's known bugs in the release notes
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Checklist marketing, typically a comparison table with a check mark in every row, works on buyers who cannot judge quality in advance, because a count is easier to compare than a fit. It rewards adding a shallow version of every feature, which is bloat by construction. Options A and D describe quality assurance and release notes, and option C describes a survey, none of which promote a product.

Concept Tested: Feature Checklist Marketing

See: Why Features Keep Arriving

docs.title: 5. A feature shows very low usage in telemetry. What is the most careful conclusion?
docs.text:
1. Low usage is a question to investigate, because the feature may be unneeded, hard to find, or vital to a small group
  2. The feature is useless and should be removed immediately
  3. Users prefer simpler tools in every case
  4. The telemetry system is broken
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Telemetry shows what people did, not why. A rarely used feature may be unneeded, but it may also be poorly discoverable, or it may matter intensely to a small group who would leave without it. A careful vendor treats low usage as a prompt for investigation, and a careful reader treats a vendor's claim of "unused" the same way. Options B, C, and D jump to conclusions the data cannot support.

Concept Tested: Usage Telemetry

See: Measuring Feature Usage

docs.title: 6. Why does the chapter say unused features still cost the user something?
docs.text:
1. They always increase the monthly subscription fee
  2. They cause the program to crash more often
  3. They add extraneous cognitive load, because every extra button and menu must be scanned and ruled out
  4. They reduce the intrinsic difficulty of the task
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Cognitive load is the mental effort a task demands of working memory. Intrinsic load comes from the task itself, but extraneous load comes from how the task is presented, and a cluttered menu is a major source. In the chapter's example, the author finds one command among twenty menu items and spends effort on 18 irrelevant ones every time. Options A and B are not claims the chapter makes, and D reverses the effect.

Concept Tested: Cognitive Load

See: Why Unused Features Cost Something

docs.title: 7. Under the 95/5 rule of thumb, roughly how many features would a typical user of a 100-feature product use?
docs.text:
1. 1
  2. 5
  3. 50
  4. 95
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The 95/5 rule of thumb says about 95% of users use only about 5% of a product's features, and 5% of 100 features is 5. For a 40-feature product the same rule gives 2, which is exactly what the author uses. The chapter stresses that this is a rough guide, not a measurement, so a product's true split might be 90/10 or 99/1 and you should check your own tool's usage.

Concept Tested: 95/5 Rule Of Thumb

See: The Pareto Principle and the 95/5 Rule

docs.title: 8. In the chapter's illustrative data, the top four features have use shares of 92%, 55%, 48%, and 30%, and all twenty features total 332 percentage points. What share of all use do the top four carry?
docs.text:
1. About 20%
  2. About 44%
  3. About 86%
  4. About 68%
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The top four sum to 92 + 55 + 48 + 30 = 225 points, and 225 divided by 332 is about 68%. Four of twenty features is 20% of the feature set, so the top 20% of features carry about 68% of the use. That is a Pareto shape, but softer than the 80/20 figure, which is why the chapter calls 80/20 a pattern rather than a law.

Concept Tested: Pareto Principle

See: The Pareto Principle and the 95/5 Rule

docs.title: 9. Why does a vendor that listens mainly to its power users tend to keep adding depth to a product?
docs.text:
1. Power users make up most of a product's customers
  2. Casual users prefer complicated tools
  3. Power users request features, and each addition seems reasonable to the person who asked, while casual users rarely ask and simply stop opening the tool or keep paying silently
  4. Telemetry only records the actions of power users
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Power users matter to vendors out of proportion to their number: they write reviews, request features, and set the standard reviewers use. Casual users rarely ask for anything. They either stop opening the tool or pay without comment. The result is a roadmap that pushes depth and options. Option A is wrong because casual users are typically the larger group, and options B and D are not supported by the chapter.

Concept Tested: Power Users

See: Power Users, Casual Users, and the Long Tail

docs.title: 10. A rival announces screen recording, and a team immediately adds recording to its own tool although no customer asked for it. Which force is at work, and why is it risky?
docs.text:
1. A healthy usage-driven decision, because the data showed a real need
  2. Competitive feature matching, which adds features because a rival has them and pushes the whole category toward the same long feature list
  3. Feature discoverability, which makes the new feature easy to find
  4. Interface simplification, because recording replaces several older features
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Competitive feature matching means adding a feature because a rival has one, whether or not customers ask. The pressure is immediate because no team wants to explain why it lacks something on the other product's page. When rivals follow each other, the whole category drifts toward the same long list of features. Option A describes the one healthy cause, which requires usage data. Options C and D name unrelated ideas.

Concept Tested: Competitive Feature Matching

See: Why Features Keep Arriving

docs.title: References: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule
docs.text:
1. Pareto principle - Wikipedia - Covers the 80/20 observation that a small share of causes drives most effects, with its history and limits. Frames the chapter's advice to treat 95/5 figures as hypotheses, not laws.

  2. Cognitive load - Wikipedia - Describes intrinsic, extraneous, and germane load in learning and working memory. Explains why unused features still tax users by adding menus and choices they must scan past.

  3. Progressive disclosure - Wikipedia - Explains the interface technique of revealing advanced options only when needed. Offers the main design remedy for the interface complexity that unused features create.

  4. About Face: The Essentials of Interaction Design - Alan Cooper et al. - Wiley - Cooper introduced goal-directed design and the idea that most users are perpetual intermediates, neither beginners nor experts. That framing explains why a few features carry nearly all real use.

  5. The Design of Everyday Things (Revised Edition) - Don Norman - Basic Books - Norman's vocabulary of affordances, signifiers, and the gulf of execution explains why buried features go undiscovered. His examples make discoverability a measurable design property, not a vague complaint.

  6. Progressive Disclosure - Nielsen Norman Group - Shows research-backed patterns for deferring advanced features to secondary screens, and how to avoid hiding too much. Gives practical guidance for taming a large feature set.

  7. Choices (User Interface Design for Programmers) - Joel on Software - Spolsky argues that every added option is a decision the user must make, and that too many questions signal a lazy designer. Ties unused features directly to cognitive cost.

  8. Hick's Law - Laws of UX - States that decision time grows with the number and complexity of choices. Gives a quantified reason why each extra feature or menu item slows every user, used or not.

  9. Feature Adoption Report - Pendo - Presents product-analytics data on how many shipped features are rarely or never used. Shows how vendors measure feature usage and why such vendor-supplied figures need careful reading.

  10. 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design - Nielsen Norman Group - Includes the heuristic of aesthetic and minimalist design, warning that extra information competes with what matters. Offers a widely taught checklist for judging whether an interface carries unused weight.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter follows the money behind the features. Starting from copyright and the software license, it compares one-time and perpetual licenses with subscriptions and per-computer licensing, then shows how recurring revenue, upgrade revenue, switching costs, and lock-in shape vendor incentives. After this chapter, you will be able to describe how a pricing model changes what a vendor chooses to build and charge.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 20 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Copyright 120 Software License 118 End User License Agreement 1 One-Time License 9 Perpetual License 1 Subscription License 51 Annual Fee 37 Per-Computer Licensing 7 Per-User Licensing 1 Recurring Revenue 4 Upgrade Revenue 3 Vendor Incentives 2 Customer Lifetime Value 1 Switching Costs 7 Proprietary File Format 6 Vendor Lock-In 5 Software As A Service 1 Price Increase 1 Freemium Model 1 Free Alternatives 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
  • Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule

Follow the money, not the menu

Features come and go, but the way a tool is paid for decides which ones get built. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to read a license and a price tag and predict what a vendor will do next. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Copyright and the Software License
docs.text:
Start with copyright, the legal right that gives the author of a creative work control over who may copy, distribute, and adapt it. In most countries, software is protected by copyright automatically the moment it is written, with no registration required. The author of the code, which might be a person or the company that employs them, owns that right from the start.

That ownership has a direct consequence for anyone who wants to use the software. By default, you have no permission to copy it, run it, or change it, because those acts belong to the copyright holder. The holder grants permission through a software license: a legal agreement that states what the user may do with the software and under what conditions. The license is the document that turns a program into something you can lawfully use.

Three ideas are easy to confuse and worth separating. Copyright is the owner's underlying right. A license is the permission the owner grants to a user. Ownership of a copy is something different again: when you buy a license, you usually do not buy the software itself. You buy permission to use a copy on the owner's terms. That is why a vendor can change future terms, and why a license can say "per computer" or "per year" and still be perfectly lawful.

You rent permission, not the software

Notice what you actually hold after you pay: not the program, but a permission slip from the copyright holder. Who can change what the slip says?

A worked example makes the split concrete. The author wrote the screen grab app described in this book with an AI agent and now publishes it under the MIT License, a very permissive license. As the copyright holder, the author decided what permission to grant, and chose to grant a great deal: anyone may use, copy, modify, and share the code at no charge, so long as they keep the license notice. The vendor of the paid utility made the opposite choice and granted only the right to run the program on stated terms.

Question The copyright holder A licensed user Who may copy the code? The holder Only as the license allows Who may modify it? The holder Only as the license allows Who may choose the price? The holder No one; the user accepts or declines Who may change the terms for a future version? The holder No one Who may use it? The holder Whoever the license names, under its conditions

Copyright has a boundary that matters a great deal for this book. It protects the expression of an idea, meaning the particular code, text, or artwork, and not the idea or the function itself. Nobody owns the idea of "grab a region of the screen." A vendor owns its specific code and its specific designs, and anyone is free to write different code that does the same job. That boundary is why a new tool can lawfully do what an older one does, as long as it does not copy the older one's code or protected designs. Questions at the edges of that line are for a lawyer.

This book does not give legal advice. The aim is to read a license well enough to understand what a price buys and what it doesn't. For anything involving a dispute or a business, ask a lawyer.

Licenses vary in the elements they contain. Most spell out who may use the software, how many copies or machines are covered, how long the permission lasts, whether the user may modify or share it, and what happens if the terms are broken. Reading those five items tells you more about a product than its feature list does.

License element Question it answers Example from the book's case Who Who is allowed to use it? The person who bought it How many How many copies or machines? One license per computer How long For how long is the permission valid? One year, then renew What may change Can the user modify or share it? No, in a proprietary license What if broken What happens on violation? The license can be ended

Licenses sit on a spectrum from tightly closed to wide open. The table lists the common kinds and what each lets a user do.

Kind of license Use it Read the code Change and share it Typical price Proprietary Yes, on stated terms No No One-time or subscription fee Permissive open source (the MIT License) Yes Yes Yes, keeping the notice Free Copyleft open source Yes Yes Yes, if shared changes stay open too Free Public domain Yes Yes Yes, with no conditions Free

An end user license agreement, or EULA, is the license that a user accepts when installing or first opening a program, typically by clicking "I agree." It is long, written for lawyers, and rarely read in full. It is still a binding statement of what the vendor has granted and what it may do in the future, including raising prices and ending support.

Clicking Agree is signing

Most people accept a license without reading it, and that is how surprises arrive. Next time, search the text for "term," "renew," "transfer," and "devices" and read just those paragraphs.

docs.title: One-Time and Perpetual Licenses
docs.text:
A one-time license is a license purchased with a single payment that grants the right to use a specific version of the software. This is the classic model of boxed software: pay once, install, use. The $9 utility at the start of this book was sold this way. The buyer paid $9 once and ran it on all of their computers.

A perpetual license is a license that has no expiry date, so the right to use that version continues indefinitely. The term is usually paired with the one-time payment, and it is worth being exact about what it covers. A perpetual license usually means you may keep using the version you bought forever. It does not usually mean you will receive every future version, updates, or support. The vendor may stop issuing fixes, or may charge for the next major version.

Walk through the worked example. A buyer purchases version 3 for $9. Version 3 keeps working as long as the buyer's operating system runs it. When the vendor releases version 4 as a paid upgrade for, say, $5 more, the buyer can pay or stay on version 3. Staying carries a risk: the operating system may someday change in a way version 3 cannot handle. The choice is the buyer's, and the cost is visible, which is the key advantage of this model.

Feature of a one-time perpetual license Benefit to the user Risk to the user Single payment Cost is known up front Upgrades may be sold separately No expiry The tool keeps working Support and fixes may stop Tied to a version No surprise changes Newer features need a new purchase

docs.title: Subscriptions and Annual Fees
docs.text:
A subscription license is a license that grants the right to use the software only while the user keeps paying a recurring fee. When the payments stop, so does the permission. The product may stop launching, refuse to open files, or fall back to a restricted mode. This reverses the logic of the one-time license. You no longer buy a version; you rent access to a service that changes.

What happens when the payments stop varies by product, and it should be a question you ask before you subscribe. Some products keep working in a limited mode. Some stop opening your own files. Some delete your cloud copies after a grace period. In the book's case, a user who pays for three years and then stops has paid $270 and holds no right to run the tool, while the user who paid $9 once still has a working program.

An annual fee is a subscription payment charged once per year. It is the simplest recurring charge to reason about, because multiplying by years gives a total. The book's case has a fee of $30 per computer per year. The arithmetic is short enough to do by hand, and doing it is the point of this section.

The total for any per-computer subscription follows one formula.

\[ C = n \times f \times y \]

where:

  • \( C \) is the total cost in dollars
  • \( n \) is the number of computers
  • \( f \) is the annual fee per computer in dollars
  • \( y \) is the number of years

Take the author's situation. There are three computers, each needing a license. The annual cost is \( 3 \times \$30 = \$90 \). Over five years, it is \( 5 \times \$90 = \$450 \). The one-time purchase it replaced cost $9 in total. The table below shows the running total at the end of each year.

End of year Annual cost (3 computers) Running total One-time $9 license for comparison 1 $90 $90 $9 2 $90 $180 $9 3 $90 $270 $9 4 $90 $360 $9 5 $90 $450 $9

Put the same figures from the vendor's side. A customer on the one-time license yielded $9 in total. A customer on the subscription, staying five years on three computers, yields $450. The same customer is worth fifty times as much. No feature changed the economics of that customer; the licensing model did. A reader who wonders why vendors moved to subscriptions need look no further than that multiplication.

The comparison hides a subtle change. Under the one-time license, the vendor's incentive stops at the sale. Under a subscription, the incentive continues for as long as the customer pays, which affects every decision about the product. The sections that follow develop that point.

The same pricing model appears under a common label. Software as a service, or SaaS, is software delivered over the internet and paid for by subscription, usually running on the vendor's servers rather than on the user's computer. A desktop utility with a yearly license is not strictly SaaS, but it shares the same revenue pattern.

A price increase is a rise in what the vendor charges for the same product. Subscriptions make increases easy: the vendor can raise the fee at renewal, and the customer must decide immediately whether to pay. Suppose, as an illustration, that the fee rose 10% each year from $30. The charges would be $30.00, $33.00, $36.30, $39.93, and $43.92, for a five-year total of about $183.15 per computer, or about $549 for three. The numbers are illustrative, and the book's actual figure is $30 flat.

Calendar the renewal

Subscriptions often renew automatically, at whatever the fee is on that day. Put the renewal date in your calendar a week early, so you can compare the new price with the alternatives while cancelling is still an option.

docs.title: Counting Licenses: Per Computer and Per User
docs.text:
A per-computer license is a license that is counted by the number of machines on which the software is installed. Each computer needs its own license. This is the model behind the book's $30 fee. A person with a desktop, a laptop, and a second laptop needs three.

Per-computer pricing has a worked consequence. The same $30 fee that looks modest for one machine multiplies with each device, and the multiplication falls hardest on the people who own the most. The author's three computers triple the cost compared with a one-computer user, for the same single job.

A per-user license is a license that is counted by the number of people who use the software, regardless of how many machines each person uses. It is common for business tools, where one employee works on several devices. For an individual with several computers, per-user pricing is usually cheaper than per-computer pricing. For a family or a team, the arithmetic can reverse.

Model What is counted Cost for 1 person with 3 computers at $30 Cost for 3 people with 1 computer each at $30 Per computer Machines $90 $90 Per user People $30 $90

The two sorting dimensions, how often the money is paid and what is counted, combine to form every offer in this chapter. The sorter below presents six offers and asks you to place each on both dimensions.

docs.title: Diagram: License Offer Sorter
docs.text:
License Offer Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: licenses-offer-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-linux/tree/main/docs/sims/open-vs-closed Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify six described software offers by when payment is made (one time or recurring) and by what is counted (per computer or per user), getting both answers right for at least 5 of 6 offers.

Prerequisites: one-time license, subscription license, per-computer licensing, per-user licensing (defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each offer, the learner picks a payment pattern and a counting unit. An offer is correct only when both choices equal the Correct values in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 offers correct on the first pass. Reading the definitions is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) A one-time price means the license is per computer. (2) A subscription always counts users rather than machines.

Instructional Rationale: Placing each offer on two independent dimensions shows the learner that payment timing and counting unit are separate choices, which is the distinction the chapter teaches.

Content:

The two choices are payment pattern (One time or Recurring) and counting unit (Per computer or Per user).

# Offer shown (all prices illustrative) Correct payment Correct counting unit Why (shown as feedback) 1 Pay $9 once and install it on each of your own computers. One time Per user One payment; the license names the person, not the machines. 2 Pay $30 per year for each computer it is installed on. Recurring Per computer The fee repeats yearly and is multiplied by machines. 3 Pay $12 per month for each person on a team, on any number of devices. Recurring Per user Monthly payments repeat, and the count is people. 4 Pay $40 once for each computer; the next major version costs extra. One time Per computer One payment, but each machine needs its own license. 5 Pay $60 per year per person, with unlimited computers. Recurring Per user The fee repeats yearly and the count is people. 6 Buy a $25 key that works on one specific computer with no expiry. One time Per computer A single payment with a license tied to one machine.

Provenance: All offers and prices are illustrative and invented for this chapter; the sim labels them illustrative.

Rules: Each offer is answered once with two choices. An offer is correct when both choices match. The score is the number of correct offers out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads offer 1 and picks One time or Recurring.
  2. The learner picks Per computer or Per user.
  3. The learner presses Check and sees whether each choice was right, with the Why text.
  4. The learner moves through offers 2 to 6 and then sees the score.

Feedback: Six offers in fixed order, one attempt each. Each choice is marked right or wrong, and the Why text is always shown. The final screen shows "n of 6" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 5.

Starting State: Offer 1 is shown with no choices selected. The question on screen is "How is this offer paid, and what is counted?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the book's case has a fee of $30 per computer per year, that three computers cost $90 per year, and that the sorter has 6 offers.

docs.title: How Pricing Shapes Vendor Behavior
docs.text:
Pricing models differ in who gets the money and when, and that determines what a vendor works on. Recurring revenue is income that a business receives repeatedly from the same customers, usually monthly or yearly. It is valued because it is predictable. A vendor with 10,000 customers each paying $30 per year can plan for about $300,000 every year, as long as the customers renew. Compare that to a vendor who must find 10,000 new buyers to earn the same amount a second time.

Upgrade revenue is income earned from existing customers who pay to move to a newer version. Under one-time licensing, upgrades are the main way to earn from a customer after the first sale. That creates an incentive to make each new version look significantly different, even when the old one did the job well.

Customer lifetime value is the total revenue a vendor expects from one customer over the whole time they remain a customer. As an illustration, a customer paying $30 per year who stays five years is worth $150. The figure justifies a vendor's spending on advertising, support, and features aimed at keeping customers. A one-time $9 sale has a customer lifetime value of $9 plus any upgrades.

Vendor incentives are the pressures, financial and otherwise, that push a vendor toward some decisions and away from others. The same person at the same company will choose differently when the revenue model changes. Under a one-time license, the strongest incentives are to win new buyers and persuade old ones to upgrade. Under a subscription, the strongest incentives are to keep customers from canceling and to raise the fee they pay.

Pricing is a steering wheel

Think of the revenue model as the thing steering the product roadmap. The vendor's engineers and managers may be perfectly honest, and the incentives will still lean on every decision. Ask: what does this vendor earn when I do nothing?

The explorer below lists eight vendor decisions and asks you to predict which pricing model makes each one more likely. There is no trick here. The goal is to see that the incentive follows from the way the money flows.

docs.title: Diagram: Vendor Incentive Explorer
docs.text:
Vendor Incentive Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: licenses-vendor-incentive-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: attribute Learning Objective: The learner will attribute each of 8 vendor decisions to the pricing model, one-time or subscription, whose incentives make it more likely, scoring at least 7 of 8.

Prerequisites: one-time license, subscription license, recurring revenue, upgrade revenue, customer lifetime value, vendor incentives (defined in the chapter section "How Pricing Shapes Vendor Behavior").

Evidence of Mastery: The learner chooses One-time license or Subscription license for each of 8 decisions. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct model column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first pass. Reading the revenue summaries is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Vendors behave the same way under every pricing model. (2) Subscription pricing only changes how customers pay and not what vendors build.

Instructional Rationale: Attributing a decision to an incentive makes the learner trace a cause, which is the Analyze-level act, instead of memorizing which model is better.

Content:

The revenue summaries shown before the decisions:

Model Where the next dollar comes from The vendor's strongest incentive One-time license A new buyer or an upgrade purchase Win new buyers and make upgrades look worth buying Subscription license A renewal or a higher fee Prevent cancellation and raise what each customer pays

The 8 decisions, in this fixed order:

# Vendor decision shown Correct model Why (shown as feedback) 1 Add a showy feature so owners feel they must buy the next version. One-time license Upgrade revenue depends on making the next version look new. 2 Keep customers satisfied so they renew every year. Subscription license Each renewal is the next dollar, so keeping the customer matters. 3 Charge for each major version. One-time license The sale of a version is the revenue event. 4 Make cancellation steps long and hard to find. Subscription license Each canceled customer ends the recurring revenue. 5 Stop fixing bugs in old versions to push owners to the new one. One-time license Owners of old versions pay nothing more until they upgrade. 6 Raise the annual fee, expecting most customers to renew. Subscription license Customers who are locked in may pay more rather than switch. 7 Compete mainly on the number of new customers won each quarter. One-time license Without renewals, revenue depends on new sales. 8 Add reminders and features that bring users back every week. Subscription license Frequent use makes renewal feel worthwhile.

Provenance: All eight decisions are illustrative scenarios invented for this chapter and derived from the incentives defined in the chapter text; the sim labels them illustrative.

Rules: Each decision is answered once. The score is the number of correct answers out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the revenue summaries for the two models.
  2. The learner reads decision 1 and chooses a model.
  3. The sim shows right or wrong with the Why text.
  4. The learner moves through decisions 2 to 8 and then sees the score.

Feedback: Eight decisions in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" with the Why text. Incorrect: the correct model and the Why text. The final screen shows "n of 8" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 7.

Starting State: Both revenue summaries are visible and decision 1 is shown. The question on screen is "Which pricing model makes this decision more likely?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that 10,000 customers at $30 per year produce about $300,000, that a five-year customer paying $30 per year is worth $150, and that the explorer has 8 decisions.

docs.title: Switching Costs, File Formats, and Lock-In
docs.text:
A subscription's strongest advantage for the vendor is not the price. It is the moment of renewal, when the customer must decide yes or no once more. Every decision to stay is easier when leaving is expensive.

Switching costs are the costs a customer bears to move from one product to another, including money, time, effort, and risk. They can be small, like downloading another app, or large, like retraining a team and converting ten years of files. They matter to vendors because a customer who would face a high switching cost will tolerate a price increase that a free-to-leave customer would not.

A proprietary file format is a file layout that is defined and controlled by one vendor, and that other tools cannot reliably read or write. If your work is stored in such a format, leaving the vendor means converting every file, losing some information in the conversion, or abandoning the work. By contrast, an open format such as PNG for images or plain text for notes can be opened by many programs. The format is a hidden part of the price.

Vendor lock-in is the condition in which a customer's switching costs are high enough that they stay with a vendor even when a better or cheaper option exists. Lock-in is the combined result of the two terms above: the more of your work lives in a format only the vendor can read, the higher the cost of leaving. Lock-in need not be malicious. It is often a side effect of a vendor building features that only work within its own system.

The distinction between open and proprietary formats can be seen in a short comparison. Each row asks: if the vendor disappeared tomorrow, could you still use the file?

Kind of file Format Readable by other tools? Lock-in risk A screen image saved as PNG Open Yes, by nearly everything Very low A note saved as plain text Open Yes Very low A project saved in a vendor's own editor format Proprietary Only by that vendor's tools High An image library kept in a vendor's cloud gallery Proprietary storage Only through the vendor's service High

For the book's case, the author's job produces a plain image on the clipboard. The output is already in an open format, so the switching cost of leaving is close to zero. That is a large part of why a two-feature replacement is realistic.

A worked example shows the calculation. Suppose a user has 200 files in a vendor's format, and each takes 1 minute to convert. Their time is worth $40 per hour, and learning a replacement tool takes 4 hours. The conversion takes \( 200 \times 1 / 60 = 3.33 \) hours, which at $40 costs $133.33. Learning costs \( 4 \times \$40 = \$160 \). The total switching cost is $293.33. If the move saves $90 per year in fees, the cost is recovered in \( 293.33 / 90 = 3.26 \) years. A vendor that knows this can raise the fee a little each year without losing the customer.

Test the exit before you enter

Before you commit to a tool, export one file into an open format and open it somewhere else. If that is hard now, it will be harder after a thousand files.

The calculator below lets you change the inputs and compute the years needed to recover a switching cost. It also includes the open-format case, where the conversion cost is zero.

docs.title: Diagram: Switching Cost Calculator
docs.text:
Switching Cost Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: licenses-switching-cost-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the years needed to recover a switching cost from the annual fee saved, to within 0.1 years, for 3 challenge cases.

Prerequisites: switching costs, proprietary file format, vendor lock-in, annual fee (defined in the chapter sections above).

Evidence of Mastery: For 3 challenge cases, the learner types the years to recover the switching cost before the sim shows it. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 0.1 of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the inputs freely is exploration and is not scored.

Misconceptions: (1) Switching is free if the new tool is free. (2) Files in an open format cost nothing to move, so lock-in is unrelated to file format.

Instructional Rationale: Computing the payback period from the learner's own inputs makes the learner apply the chapter's formula and see how conversion work stretches the recovery time.

Content:

All figures are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Files in the vendor's format 0 1000 50 200 files Minutes to convert one file 1 10 1 1 minutes Value of the learner's time 10 100 5 40 dollars per hour Hours to learn the replacement 0 20 1 4 hours Annual fee saved 10 300 10 90 dollars per year

Challenge cases, in this order:

# Files Minutes per file Time value ($/h) Learning hours Fee saved ($/yr) Switching cost ($) Model value: years 1 200 1 40 4 90 293.33 3.3 2 600 2 30 2 90 660.00 7.3 3 0 1 40 4 90 160.00 1.8

Feedback text per case: case 1 "Conversion is 200 x 1 / 60 = 3.33 h = $133.33; learning is $160; total $293.33; 293.33 / 90 = 3.26, which rounds to 3.3." Case 2 "Conversion is 600 x 2 / 60 = 20 h = $600; learning is $60; total $660; 660 / 90 = 7.33, which rounds to 7.3." Case 3 "No files means no conversion cost; learning is $160; 160 / 90 = 1.78, which rounds to 1.8."

Provenance: The case 1 numbers are the chapter's worked example. Cases 2 and 3 are illustrative and invented for this chapter.

Rules: Conversion cost = files x minutes / 60 x time value. Learning cost = learning hours x time value. Switching cost = conversion cost + learning cost. Years to recover = switching cost / annual fee saved, rounded to 1 decimal place. The annual fee saved is always at least 10, so division by zero cannot occur.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner changes the five inputs and sees the conversion cost, learning cost, switching cost, and years to recover update.
  2. The learner starts the challenges; for each, the sim sets the five inputs and hides the result.
  3. The learner types the years to recover and presses Check.
  4. The learner returns to free exploration and should notice that doubling the file count roughly doubles the conversion cost but not the learning cost.

Feedback: Three cases in fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: n years." Incorrect on the first attempt: the matching feedback text without the final number. After the second wrong attempt, the full feedback text and the Model value are shown and the case counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

Starting State: The defaults are shown (200 files, 1 minute, $40 per hour, 4 hours, $90 per year) with the result 3.3 years displayed. The question on screen is "How long until switching pays for itself?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example states 200 files, 1 minute each, $40 per hour, 4 hours of learning, a switching cost of $293.33, $90 saved per year, and recovery in 3.26 years.

docs.title: Free Options and the Freemium Model
docs.text:
Not every route is a paid one. The freemium model gives a basic version of a product away for free and charges for advanced features or higher limits. The free version attracts users cheaply, and some fraction of them convert to paying customers. Freemium works well for the vendor when the free tier is useful enough to spread, but limited enough that heavy users upgrade.

A worked example: a utility offers free grabs but charges $30 per year to remove a watermark or unlock the editor. For the author's two-feature job, the free tier may already be enough. For someone who needs the editor, the free tier is a trial. Freemium pricing therefore depends on the vendor believing that most users will not pay, and structuring the product so that the bloat is behind the paywall.

Free alternatives are products offered without charge that do jobs similar to a paid product's. They come from open-source projects, from operating systems that bundle a basic version, and from small developers. Free alternatives change the calculation of a price rise: the real switching cost is no longer the fee of another product but only the effort of moving. Whether a free alternative is good enough depends on the job to be done, which Chapter 1 told you to write down first.

You can follow the money

You can now trace a product's price from copyright through the license to the subscription, and say how recurring revenue, switching costs, and lock-in steer what a vendor does. That is the machinery behind the $9 to $450 story.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• Copyright gives the author control; a software license is the permission the author grants.
  • A one-time perpetual license buys a version for good; a subscription rents access and repeats the charge.
  • Per-computer pricing multiplies the fee by machines; per-user pricing multiplies it by people.
  • Recurring revenue, upgrade revenue, and customer lifetime value shape what a vendor builds.
  • Proprietary file formats raise switching costs, and high switching costs produce vendor lock-in.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
docs.text: Test your understanding of copyright, licenses, subscription pricing, vendor incentives, switching costs, and lock-in with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does copyright give the author of a piece of software?
docs.text:
1. Ownership of every idea the program implements
  2. The legal right to control who may copy, distribute, and adapt the work
  3. A guaranteed price for every copy sold
  4. Permission to use the program on any computer without a license
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Copyright is the legal right that gives the author of a creative work control over copying, distribution, and adaptation, and in most countries it arises automatically when the software is written. It protects the particular expression, meaning the code and designs, not the underlying idea. Nobody owns the idea of grabbing a region of the screen. Options A, C, and D claim rights that copyright does not grant.

Concept Tested: Copyright

See: Copyright and the Software License

docs.title: 2. What is a software license?
docs.text:
1. The program's compiled code
  2. A receipt that proves the buyer owns the source code
  3. The owner's underlying right to the work
  4. A legal agreement stating what the user may do with the software and under what conditions
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A license is the permission the copyright holder grants to a user, and it turns a program into something you can lawfully use. Copyright (option C) is the owner's underlying right, and the license is derived from it. Buying a license usually does not mean buying the software itself, so option B is wrong. The compiled code (option A) is the software, not the legal agreement around it.

Concept Tested: Software License

See: Copyright and the Software License

docs.title: 3. What does a perpetual license usually give the buyer?
docs.text:
1. The right to keep using the version they bought indefinitely, but not necessarily future versions, updates, or support
  2. The right to receive every future version at no charge
  3. The right to modify and resell the source code
  4. The right to use the software only while paying a recurring fee
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A perpetual license has no expiry date, so the version bought keeps working as long as the operating system runs it. It does not usually include later versions, updates, or support, and the vendor may charge for the next major version. Option B overstates the grant. Option C describes open-source licenses, and option D describes a subscription license.

Concept Tested: Perpetual License

See: One-Time and Perpetual Licenses

docs.title: 4. What are switching costs?
docs.text:
1. The fees a vendor pays to change its licensing model
  2. The price difference between a monthly and an annual plan
  3. The costs a customer bears to move from one product to another, including money, time, effort, and risk
  4. The cost of upgrading from one version to the next
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Switching costs can be small, such as downloading another app, or large, such as retraining a team and converting ten years of files. They matter to vendors because a customer facing a high switching cost will tolerate a price increase that a free-to-leave customer would not. Options A, B, and D describe other costs that do not capture the customer's cost of leaving.

Concept Tested: Switching Costs

See: Switching Costs, File Formats, and Lock-In

docs.title: 5. Why can a vendor lawfully change future terms or charge "per computer" or "per year"?
docs.text:
1. Because the buyer owns the software but has agreed to rent it back
  2. Because license terms never change after purchase
  3. Because copyright expires once the software is sold
  4. Because the buyer usually purchases permission to use a copy on the owner's terms, not the software itself
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter separates copyright, the owner's right, from the license, the permission granted, and from ownership of a copy. A buyer typically holds a permission slip from the copyright holder, and the holder decides what the slip says. That is why per-computer or per-year terms are perfectly lawful. Option A reverses the relationship, option B is false, and option C is wrong because copyright does not expire at sale.

Concept Tested: Software License

See: Copyright and the Software License

docs.title: 6. What happens to a subscription license when the user stops paying?
docs.text:
1. The permission to use the software ends, and the product may stop launching, refuse to open files, or fall back to a restricted mode
  2. The user keeps full rights to the latest version forever
  3. The user receives a refund for all earlier payments
  4. The vendor must release the source code
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A subscription grants the right to use the software only while the fee is paid, which reverses the logic of the one-time license: you rent access instead of buying a version. What happens next varies by product, and it is worth asking before subscribing. In the book's case, someone who pays for three years and stops has spent $270 and holds no right to run the tool, while the $9 buyer still has a working program.

Concept Tested: Subscription License

See: Subscriptions and Annual Fees

docs.title: 7. Using the formula C = n × f × y, what is the total cost of a per-computer subscription for 4 computers at $30 per computer per year over 3 years?
docs.text:
1. $120
  2. $360
  3. $270
  4. $480
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Multiply the number of computers (4), the annual fee per computer ($30), and the number of years (3): 4 × $30 × 3 = $360. Option A is one year for four computers, option C matches the author's three computers over three years, and option D would be four computers for four years. The same formula gives the book's $450 for three computers over five years.

Concept Tested: Annual Fee

See: Subscriptions and Annual Fees

docs.title: 8. A single person owns three computers, and a tool costs $30 whether counted per computer or per user. Which licensing model is cheaper for this person, and by how much?
docs.text:
1. Per computer, by $60
  2. They cost the same
  3. Per user, by $60
  4. Per user, by $30
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Per-computer licensing costs 3 × $30 = $90, while per-user licensing costs one person × $30 = $30, a saving of $60. For an individual with several machines, per-user pricing is usually cheaper. For three people with one computer each, the two models both cost $90, and for larger groups the arithmetic can reverse, so always count what the license counts.

Concept Tested: Per-User Licensing

See: Counting Licenses: Per Computer and Per User

docs.title: 9. How does moving from a one-time license to a subscription change a vendor's strongest incentives?
docs.text:
1. The vendor no longer cares about customers after the sale
  2. The vendor focuses on winning new buyers and persuading old ones to upgrade
  3. The vendor stops charging for new features
  4. The vendor focuses on keeping customers from canceling and on raising the fee they pay
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Under a one-time license, incentives center on winning new buyers and selling upgrades to old ones, and they largely stop at the sale. Under a subscription, the vendor earns only as long as the customer keeps paying, so retention and the renewal price dominate decisions. Option B describes the one-time model. The chapter notes that honest engineers and managers are still steered by the revenue model.

Concept Tested: Vendor Incentives

See: How Pricing Shapes Vendor Behavior

docs.title: 10. A user has 200 files in a vendor's proprietary format. Each takes 1 minute to convert, their time is worth $40 per hour, and learning a replacement takes 4 hours. If switching saves $90 per year in fees, about how long does it take to recover the switching cost?
docs.text:
1. About 1 year
  2. About 3.3 years
  3. About 6 years
  4. It can never be recovered
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Conversion takes 200 ÷ 60 = 3.33 hours, which at $40 costs $133.33. Learning costs 4 × $40 = $160. The total switching cost is $293.33, and dividing by the $90 annual saving gives about 3.26 years. A vendor that knows this can raise the fee a little each year without losing the customer. An open format such as PNG would have made the conversion cost zero.

Concept Tested: Proprietary File Format

See: Switching Costs, File Formats, and Lock-In

docs.title: References: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
docs.text:
1. Software license - Wikipedia - Covers proprietary, free, and open-source licensing models and how a license governs use, copying, and redistribution. Supplies the legal baseline for per-computer and per-user pricing discussed in this chapter.

  2. Software as a service - Wikipedia - Describes subscription-delivered software, its pricing models, and its trade-offs for customers and vendors. Background for the recurring-revenue incentives the chapter analyzes.

  3. Vendor lock-in - Wikipedia - Explains how switching costs, proprietary formats, and dependency tie customers to one vendor. Directly supports the chapter's treatment of file formats and exit costs.

  4. Information Rules: A Strategic Guide to the Network Economy - Carl Shapiro and Hal R. Varian - Harvard Business School Press - Shapiro and Varian built the lock-in analysis that sums a customer's switching costs and shows vendors how to raise them. Their framework explains why subscriptions and proprietary formats are so profitable.

  5. Free Software, Free Society - Richard M. Stallman - GNU Press - Stallman framed software freedom as four user rights: run, study, share, and modify. That ethical framing gives students a clear yardstick for judging what any license actually lets them do.

  6. What Is Free Software? - GNU Project - Defines the four essential freedoms and explains why they matter to users. A primary-source counterpoint to the proprietary licensing models in this chapter.

  7. The Open Source Definition - Open Source Initiative - Lists the ten criteria a license must meet to count as open source. Lets students separate truly open licenses from merely source-available ones.

  8. SPDX License List - Linux Foundation SPDX - Catalogs standard identifiers and full texts for hundreds of software licenses. A practical lookup when reading the license of a tool or choosing one for generated code.

  9. Choose a License - GitHub - Compares common open-source licenses in plain language with a permissions, conditions, and limitations summary. Helps students see how license choice changes what others may do with software.

  10. Various Licenses and Comments about Them - GNU Project - Reviews dozens of software licenses and says which grant the freedoms of free software. Lets students read how real license terms differ in what they allow.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter turns licensing terms into numbers, using the book's example of a $9 tool that became $30 per year on each of three computers. It covers purchase price, cost per computer, multi-year cost, and break-even points, then adds the maintenance, learning, and opportunity costs that a price tag leaves out. After this chapter, you will be able to calculate the multi-year total cost of ownership of a per-computer subscription.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 9 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Purchase Price 35 Cost Per Computer 6 Multi-Year Cost 5 Break-Even Point 1 Opportunity Cost 23 Software Maintenance 41 Maintenance Cost 28 Learning Cost 28 Total Cost Of Ownership 27

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
  • Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule
  • Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives

From price tag to real cost

A price tag is the cheapest part of owning most tools. In this chapter you'll learn to add up everything else, so you can compare a subscription, an old one-time license, and a tool you generate yourself on equal terms. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Purchase Price and Cost Per Computer
docs.text:
The purchase price is the amount a buyer pays to acquire a product, usually at the moment of acquisition. For a one-time license, it is the whole payment. For a subscription, it is the first fee, or even nothing at all if the first period is free. The purchase price is the number a vendor puts on the box, and it is the number people compare. It is also only one of several numbers that decide what a tool really costs.
