The book's case offers three ways to acquire a screen grab tool, and their purchase prices look very different. The original utility was a one-time purchase of $9. The current version of the paid product asks for $30 per year, per computer. The generated replacement described in this book cost about $6 in API fees to build and install, and about $14 for the whole session, including testing. These are estimates drawn from the course description, and they cover the code only.

Path Purchase price What the price covers Original one-time license $9 The license for that version, on the author's computers Current paid subscription $30 per computer, charged yearly One year of use on one computer Generated replacement About $6 to build, about $14 for the whole session The AI session that wrote the code, not the author's time or later upkeep

The cost per computer is the total cost of owning a tool, divided by the number of computers that use it. It matters because many licenses are sold per computer, and because the same tool installed on three machines costs three times as much to license even though it does one job. In the worked example, the subscription costs $30 per computer per year, so the cost per computer per year is simply $30, and the cost for three is $90.

Cost per computer can also be a way to spread a fixed cost. A generated tool that costs $14 once and runs on all three computers has a purchase price per computer of about $4.67. The comparison with $30 is not quite fair, because the $30 recurs every year and the $14 does not, which is the subject of the next section.

docs.title: Multi-Year Cost
docs.text:
A multi-year cost is the total expense of a product over a stated number of years, found by adding the costs of every year. It is the figure that exposes recurring charges. A fee that looks small in one year becomes large across five, and any decision about a tool you plan to keep for years should be made on the multi-year number.

For a per-computer subscription, the calculation uses the formula from Chapter 3, now with the year count chosen by the buyer.

\[ C = n \times f \times y \]

where:

  • \( C \) is the total fee in dollars
  • \( n \) is the number of computers
  • \( f \) is the annual fee per computer in dollars
  • \( y \) is the number of years

For the author, \( n = 3 \) and \( f = 30 \). Over one year, \( C = 90 \). Over five years, \( C = 450 \). Over ten years, \( C = 900 \), a hundred times the original $9. The table shows how the gap grows.

Years Subscription fees (3 computers at $30) Original one-time license Difference 1 $90 $9 $81 3 $270 $9 $261 5 $450 $9 $441 10 $900 $9 $891

The horizon you choose changes the answer, which is why you should state it. A tool you will use for two months should be judged on two months. A tool you will use for a decade should be judged on ten years. Pick the horizon honestly, before you compare.

Judge a tool by its horizon, not its sticker

A $30 fee is small if you look at it once and large if you look at it every year for as long as you use the tool. How long do you actually keep your tools?

A break-even point is the moment at which the total costs of two options become equal, after which one of them is cheaper. For a generated tool compared with a subscription, it is the time when what you have saved in fees equals what you spent on the tool. Using only purchase prices, the $14 generated tool breaks even against the $90-per-year fees after \( 14 / 90 \approx 0.16 \) years, which is under two months. The later sections add the costs that move this number.

docs.title: Opportunity Cost
docs.text:
Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative that you give up when you make a choice. Money spent on a subscription cannot be spent elsewhere, and time spent building a tool cannot be spent on other work. Opportunity cost is not a bill you receive. It is a cost you notice only by asking what else the same resource could have done.

The idea lets you put a number on time. Suppose an hour of your time is worth $40, either because that is what you earn or because it is what you would pay to have the hour back. Spending 70 minutes with an AI agent has an opportunity cost of about \( 70 / 60 \times 40 = \$46.67 \), as an illustration. That is more than the $14 of fees. The honest total for building the tool includes both.

Now the worked example runs the other way. A subscription costs $90 per year, and that money could have gone to something else. At 5% annual return, the $90 saved in the first year would be worth $94.50 a year later. The effect is small at these amounts, and the larger opportunity cost for a small tool is almost always time. Both views point to the same practice: price everything, including your own hours, in the same currency.

Put a price on your hour

Decide once what an hour of your time is worth, then use it for every build-or-buy comparison. A rough number you apply consistently beats a precise number you invent each time.

docs.title: Software Maintenance and Its Cost
docs.text:
Software maintenance is the ongoing work required to keep software useful after it is first delivered. It includes fixing bugs, adapting to new operating system releases, patching security problems, and making small changes as needs shift. Software does not wear out like a machine, but its surroundings change, and a program that does not change with them slowly stops working. Maintenance is why a tool that worked perfectly last year may fail after an update to the operating system.

Maintenance has to be done by someone. In a paid product, the vendor does most of it, and the fee pays in part for the work. In a personal tool, you or your AI agent do it. The book's own case shows a small example: after the first version was installed, a later fix was needed for Macs that had only the Command Line Tools. A tool built for one person still needs upkeep, though usually far less than a product built for millions.

Kind of maintenance What it fixes Who does it for a paid product Who does it for a personal tool Corrective Bugs and failures The vendor You or your AI agent Adaptive Changes in the operating system or hardware The vendor You or your AI agent Security Newly found weaknesses The vendor You or your AI agent Enhancement New wishes The vendor, if it matches the roadmap You, whenever you choose

The maintenance cost is the money and time spent on maintenance over a stated period. It is easy to underestimate because it arrives in small, irregular pieces. A useful way to estimate it is to count the hours per year you expect to spend, multiply by the value of an hour, and then multiply by the number of years.

Take a worked example. If you expect to spend one hour a year keeping a small tool working, and an hour is worth $40, the yearly maintenance cost is $40, and over five years it is $200. That is more than twelve times the $14 it cost to generate, which shows why a build price alone would mislead. For the paid product, the same upkeep is in the fee, but you still spend a little time on renewals and updates.

Don't compare $14 with $450

The build bill is only the entry fee. Before you claim a saving, add maintenance and your own time to the generated side, and add the same to the paid side, or you're comparing a part to a whole.

docs.title: Learning Cost
docs.text:
The learning cost is the time and effort needed to become able to use a tool well, valued in money or hours. It is paid up front when you adopt a tool, and again each time a major version changes the interface. A large feature set raises the learning cost because there is more to learn and more to skip. A tool you wrote yourself, for your own job, lowers it, since you already know what it does.

A worked example: suppose learning a new editing tool takes 4 hours, and an hour is worth $40. The learning cost is \( 4 \times 40 = \$160 \), which is larger than a year of the book's $90 fee. If the vendor redesigns the interface in a later release and relearning takes 1 hour, that adds another $40. Learning cost is one of the quiet reasons that people stay with a product they no longer like. The effort already invested seems to be lost on leaving, and the cost of learning a new tool seems higher than a year of fees.

Learning cost also applies when you generate a tool, though in a different form. You must learn to describe what you need, to review what the agent built, and to run the tests. Later chapters teach that skill, and it should be counted as a one-time cost that falls with practice.

docs.title: Total Cost of Ownership
docs.text:
The total cost of ownership, or TCO, is the sum of every cost of acquiring, using, learning, and maintaining a product over a stated period. It collects the numbers this chapter has introduced into a single comparable figure. The formula is straightforward.

\[ \text{TCO} = P + n \times f \times y + m \times r \times y + L \times r \]

where:

  • \( P \) is the purchase or build cost in dollars
  • \( n \) is the number of computers
  • \( f \) is the annual fee per computer in dollars
  • \( y \) is the number of years
  • \( m \) is the maintenance time in hours per year
  • \( r \) is the value of an hour of your time in dollars
  • \( L \) is the one-time learning or setup time in hours

The time terms use \( r \), the value of an hour, which is how opportunity cost enters the formula. A worked example compares three paths over five years on three computers, with an hour valued at $40. All of the time estimates are illustrative.

Cost item Paid subscription Original $9 license Generated tool Purchase or build cost \( P \) $0 $9 $14 Annual fees \( n \times f \times y \) $450 $0 $0 Maintenance (hours per year) 0.5 0 1 Maintenance cost \( m \times r \times y \) $100 $0 $200 Learning or setup (hours) 1 0 1 Learning cost \( L \times r \) $40 $0 $40 TCO over five years $590 $9 $254

Three lessons come out of the table. First, the original $9 license was far cheaper than either alternative, but it is no longer on offer, so the real choice is between the other two. Second, the generated tool's total of $254 is about eighteen times its $14 build price, because time dominates. Third, even after counting the time, the generated tool costs well under half of the subscription over five years. The result depends on the time estimates, which is why you should change them and see what happens.

Under these assumptions, the two paths break even quickly. The subscription starts at $40 of learning time and grows by $110 a year, while the generated tool starts at $54 and grows by $40 a year, so they cross after \( 14 / 70 = 0.2 \) years, about ten weeks. If the generated tool needed three hours of upkeep a year instead of one, its yearly cost would reach $120 and it would never catch up.

The calculator below lets you set the inputs for each path and read off the TCO.

At m = 2.75 the yearly costs are equal; the control's step grid does not reach 2.75, so the "never cheaper" case is reached at m >= 3.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner moves the maintenance control and sees the generated tool's line change slope and the crossing point move.

"Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

You can price a tool honestly

You can now compute the multi-year cost of a per-computer subscription, add maintenance, learning, and opportunity cost, and compare the total with a generated alternative. That is the arithmetic behind every build-or-buy decision in the next chapters.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• The purchase price is one number among several; the multi-year cost exposes recurring fees.
  • Opportunity cost lets you price your own time, and the value of an hour is an input you must choose.
  • Software maintenance never ends, and its cost can exceed the cost of building the tool.
  • Learning cost is paid up front and again after redesigns.
  • Total cost of ownership adds purchase price, fees, maintenance, and learning over a stated horizon; the break-even point shows when one option overtakes another.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Total Cost of Ownership
docs.text: Test your understanding of purchase price, multi-year cost, opportunity cost, maintenance, learning cost, and total cost of ownership with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a break-even point?
docs.text:
1. The price at which a vendor stops making a profit
  2. The moment at which the total costs of two options become equal, after which one of them is cheaper
  3. The date on which a subscription renews
  4. The purchase price divided by the number of computers
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A break-even point is where two options cost the same in total. After it, one option is cheaper. For a generated tool compared with a subscription, it is the time when fees saved equal what you spent on the tool. Using only purchase prices, the $14 tool breaks even against $90 per year in fees after about 0.16 years. Options A, C, and D describe other ideas.

Concept Tested: Break-Even Point

See: Multi-Year Cost

docs.title: 2. What is opportunity cost?
docs.text:
1. The bill a vendor sends when a subscription renews
  2. The fee charged for early cancellation
  3. The cost of buying a tool at a discount
  4. The value of the best alternative you give up when you make a choice
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Opportunity cost is not a bill you receive. You notice it only by asking what else the same money or time could have done. Money spent on a subscription cannot be spent elsewhere, and time spent building a tool cannot go to other work. For a small tool the larger opportunity cost is almost always time, which is why the chapter prices your own hours in the same currency as everything else.

Concept Tested: Opportunity Cost

See: Opportunity Cost

docs.title: 3. How does the chapter define total cost of ownership (TCO)?
docs.text:
1. The sum of every cost of acquiring, using, learning, and maintaining a product over a stated period
  2. The purchase price plus the first year's fee
  3. The vendor's cost of developing the product
  4. The price of the product divided by the number of years of use
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. TCO collects purchase or build cost, recurring fees, maintenance, and learning into one comparable figure over a stated horizon. The time terms use the value of an hour, which is how opportunity cost enters the formula. Option B counts only part of the costs. Option C is the vendor's view, not the owner's, and option D is a per-year average of the price that ignores fees, upkeep, and learning.

Concept Tested: Total Cost Of Ownership

See: Total Cost of Ownership

docs.title: 4. Why might a program that worked perfectly last year fail after an operating system update, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Software wears out through use like a machine
  2. Vendors deliberately disable old programs
  3. Software does not wear out, but its surroundings change, and a program that does not change with them slowly stops working
  4. Updates always delete user programs
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Software maintenance is the ongoing work of keeping software useful after delivery, including corrective, adaptive, security, and enhancement work. Adaptive maintenance responds to changes in the operating system or hardware. Option A is wrong because software does not physically wear out. Options B and D attribute intent or effects the chapter does not claim. Even a personal tool needs upkeep, as the book's Command Line Tools fix showed.

Concept Tested: Software Maintenance

See: Software Maintenance and Its Cost

docs.title: 5. Why does learning cost help explain why people stay with a product they no longer like?
docs.text:
1. Learning a product always takes longer than a year
  2. The effort already invested seems lost on leaving, and learning a new tool can look more expensive than a year of fees
  3. Vendors forbid users from learning competing tools
  4. Learning cost is waived for users who stay
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Learning cost is the time and effort needed to use a tool well, valued in money or hours. In the chapter's example, 4 hours at $40 is $160, more than a year of the $90 fee. It is paid up front and again after interface redesigns. Option A overgeneralizes, and options C and D invent policies. A tool you generated for your own job lowers this cost because you already know what it does.

Concept Tested: Learning Cost

See: Learning Cost

docs.title: 6. In the chapter's break-even analysis, which input matters most in deciding whether the generated tool is ever cheaper than the subscription?
docs.text:
1. The maintenance time of the generated tool
  2. The color of the application icon
  3. The number of features in the subscription product
  4. The vendor's marketing budget
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The generated tool costs more up front in this example ($54 including setup) and then accumulates maintenance time at the value of an hour. If upkeep stays near one hour a year, it overtakes the subscription in about ten weeks. If upkeep rises to three hours a year, its yearly cost of $120 exceeds the subscription's $110, and it never catches up. The other options do not enter the TCO formula.

Concept Tested: Break-Even Point

See: Total Cost of Ownership

docs.title: 7. An agent session takes 70 minutes, and an hour of your time is worth $40. What is the opportunity cost of that time?
docs.text:
1. $14.00
  2. $28.00
  3. $70.00
  4. About $46.67
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Divide 70 minutes by 60 to get 1.167 hours and multiply by $40, which gives about $46.67. That is more than the $14 of API fees for the session, so the honest cost of building the tool includes both. Option A is the fee figure alone, and option C wrongly treats minutes as dollars. Pricing your own hours in the same currency as fees keeps comparisons honest.

Concept Tested: Opportunity Cost

See: Opportunity Cost

docs.title: 8. You expect to spend one hour a year keeping a small tool working, and an hour is worth $40. What is the maintenance cost over five years?
docs.text:
1. $40
  2. $14
  3. $200
  4. $450
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Maintenance cost is hours per year times the value of an hour times the number of years: 1 × $40 × 5 = $200. That is more than twelve times the $14 it cost to generate, which is why a build price alone would mislead. Option A is a single year, and option D is the five-year subscription fee for three computers, not a maintenance figure.

Concept Tested: Maintenance Cost

See: Software Maintenance and Its Cost

docs.title: 9. Using C = n × f × y, what is the subscription cost for 3 computers at $30 per computer per year over 10 years?
docs.text:
1. $900
  2. $90
  3. $300
  4. $450
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Multiply 3 computers by $30 and by 10 years: 3 × $30 × 10 = $900, a hundred times the original $9 license. Option B is one year, option D is five years, and option C ignores the number of computers. The chapter stresses stating your horizon honestly, because a tool you keep for a decade should be judged on ten years, not one.

Concept Tested: Multi-Year Cost

See: Multi-Year Cost

docs.title: 10. If the generated tool needed three hours of upkeep a year instead of one, why would it never catch up with the subscription?
docs.text:
1. Its build price would double
  2. The subscription would become free
  3. Learning cost would disappear for the subscription
  4. Its yearly cost of $120 would exceed the subscription's yearly growth of $110, so the gap would widen each year
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In the chapter's model, the subscription starts at $40 of learning time and grows by $110 a year from fees and half an hour of upkeep. The generated tool starts at $54 and, at three hours of upkeep at $40, grows by $120 a year. Because it starts higher and grows faster, the curves never cross. This is why maintenance time is the input to test hardest.

Concept Tested: Maintenance Cost

See: Total Cost of Ownership

docs.title: References: Total Cost of Ownership
docs.text:
1. Total cost of ownership - Wikipedia - Describes how purchase price, operation, maintenance, and disposal are summed over a stated horizon. The core method this chapter applies to software options.

  2. Software maintenance - Wikipedia - Classifies corrective, adaptive, perfective, and preventive maintenance and discusses their cost. Supports the chapter's claim that maintenance never ends and can exceed build cost.

  3. Break-even point - Wikipedia - Explains how to find the volume or time at which two cost curves cross. Gives the formula behind the chapter's break-even comparisons between buying and building.

  4. Software Engineering Economics - Barry W. Boehm - Prentice Hall - Boehm introduced the COCOMO cost model and the first systematic economics of software, including maintenance effort. His work made lifecycle cost a calculable quantity instead of a guess.

  5. Facts and Fallacies of Software Engineering - Robert L. Glass - Addison-Wesley - Glass collected evidence that maintenance typically consumes 40 to 80 percent of lifecycle cost, and presented it as blunt, citable facts. A readable source for the chapter's maintenance claims.

  6. Technical Debt - Martin Fowler - Explains Ward Cunningham's metaphor of shortcuts accruing interest that future work must pay. Gives students a concrete way to think about the ongoing cost of owning code.

  7. Is High Quality Software Worth the Cost? - Martin Fowler - Argues that internal quality pays back within weeks because it speeds later changes. Challenges the assumption that cheaper-now choices are cheaper overall.

  8. Things You Should Never Do, Part I - Joel on Software - Spolsky uses the Netscape rewrite to argue that discarding working code hides large costs. A cautionary case for the build side of the total-cost comparison.

  9. Technical Debt Quadrant - Martin Fowler - Sorts debt into deliberate or inadvertent and reckless or prudent. Helps students label the maintenance costs they include in a total cost of ownership table.

  10. Design Stamina Hypothesis - Martin Fowler - Argues that good design slows early progress slightly but wins after a short time as changes get cheaper. Explains why the cheapest option at purchase is rarely cheapest over a long horizon.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter introduces the technology that creates a new option. It explains generative AI and source code at the level this course needs, then shows how an AI coding agent such as Claude Code works through prompts, clarifying questions, tools, planning, and permissions within an AI session. It also sets out why human review matters, given hallucination and overconfident reporting. After this chapter, you will be able to explain what a coding agent does and where a person must stay in the loop.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat

A New Way to Get Software

The first four chapters showed what a bloated tool costs you. This chapter shows the tool that makes a different answer possible: an AI that can write a small program to order. By the end you will know how it works, what it needs from you, and where you must keep watching. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Generative AI
docs.text:
Generative AI is a kind of software that produces new content, such as text, images, audio, or program code, instead of only sorting, searching, or measuring content that already exists. You give it a request. It writes something that did not exist a moment ago.

Older software follows rules that a programmer wrote down in advance. A spreadsheet adds the cells you tell it to add, and a search box looks up pages that match your words. Generative AI works differently. Its behavior comes from patterns it absorbed from a very large collection of examples, so it can respond sensibly to requests nobody wrote a rule for. That flexibility is the whole attraction, and it is also the source of the problems later in this chapter, because the same flexibility lets it produce an answer that sounds right and is not.

Here is a worked example. Suppose you type this request into a generative AI tool: "List three features that every screen grab tool needs." A rule-based program would have no idea what to do with that sentence. A generative AI tool might answer: grab a region of the screen, put the image on the clipboard, and save the image to a file. Ask the same question again and you may get a slightly different list, perhaps with a keyboard shortcut in place of the file. The answer is generated fresh each time, not looked up.

Generative AI is not limited to text. Image generators turn a sentence into a picture, music generators produce audio, and code generators produce programs. This course cares about the last kind, because a program is the product we are trying to replace. In the ScreenGrab case study, the entire app was generated from a short request and a handful of answers to questions. No one typed the Swift code by hand.

The word "generative" also marks a boundary. A classifier looks at a photo and says "cat." A generator is asked for a photo of a cat and produces one. The first judges what exists, while the second makes something new, and making something new is exactly what lets a person describe a tool in words and receive a working version.

Before the table below, note the two phrases it uses. A deterministic program gives the same output for the same input every time. A probabilistic program may give different outputs for the same input, because chance plays a part in choosing the answer.

Question Traditional software Generative AI Where does its behavior come from? Rules a programmer wrote Patterns learned from many examples What happens with an unusual request? Error message or no result A best-effort answer Same input twice? Same output (deterministic) Often a different output (probabilistic) Can it be wrong and sound sure? Rarely; it fails visibly Yes; wrong answers read fluently Typical output A calculation or a search result New text, images, or code

Generated, Not Looked Up

Notice the shift: a calculator retrieves, while a generative tool composes. Composing is what lets it write a whole program from a paragraph, and it is why you must check the result instead of trusting it the way you trust arithmetic.

docs.title: Large Language Models
docs.text:
A large language model, or LLM, is the kind of generative AI that works with text, and it is the engine inside coding agents. It is a program trained on an enormous amount of written material, including books, web pages, and a great deal of program code. During training it learns which pieces of text tend to follow which other pieces.

To keep this precise, define one more term. A token is a small chunk of text, often a short word or part of a word, that the model reads and writes one at a time. Chapter 10 returns to tokens because they set the price of using an AI. For now, the key fact is that an LLM generates its answer one token at a time. At each step it estimates which token is most likely to come next, picks one, adds it to the text so far, and repeats.

A worked example makes this concrete. Give an LLM the unfinished sentence "To copy an image to the clipboard, you first need to". The model scores many possible next tokens. A word like "clear" or "get" might score high, because the training text often continued that way, while "banana" scores very low. It picks a likely word, appends it, and asks the same question again with the longer sentence. A few hundred repetitions later, you have a paragraph or a function.

That one-token-at-a-time process explains both the strength and the weakness of an LLM:

  • It is strong at fluent, well-formed text, because it has seen millions of examples of well-formed text.
  • It is strong at code, because program code is highly regular text with strict patterns.
  • It is weak at knowing whether its output is true, because it was trained to continue text plausibly, not to check facts.
  • It can use only what is in front of it: the instructions and files you give it in the current conversation, plus what it absorbed in training.

This book does not teach how an LLM is built inside, and you do not need that to use one well. You need the working model above: it continues text plausibly, and plausible is not the same as correct.

Plausible Is Not Correct

Think of an LLM as a very well-read improviser: it always has a fluent next line ready, whether or not it knows the facts. Every safeguard later in this chapter exists because fluent and true are different things.

Ability Why an LLM is good or poor at it Writing a short function in a common pattern Good: this pattern appears constantly in its training text Explaining an error message in plain language Good: it has seen the message and many explanations Knowing today's version of a small library Poor: it may remember an older version Confirming that its own code works Poor: it can only continue text; running the code is a separate step Remembering a conversation from last week Poor: it only has what is in the current session

docs.title: Source Code and Lines of Code
docs.text:
Source code is the human-readable text of instructions that tells a computer what to do. A programmer, or an AI, writes it in a programming language. A separate program called a compiler (Chapter 9) later translates it into the form the computer actually runs. When people say a tool is "open source," they mean its source code is published for anyone to read and reuse.

Source code differs from the app you double-click. The app is a finished, compiled product. The source code is the recipe that produced it. If you hold the recipe, you can change the dish: fix a bug, remove a feature, or move the tool to a new machine. If you hold only the app, you can use it as the vendor made it, and nothing more. This is one reason the generated alternative appeals. You own the recipe, in files you can read, instead of renting the dish.

You do not need to read code fluently to follow this book, but you should be able to look at a few lines and see that they are plain, structured text. Before the example, here is what it does. The three lines below belong to a program that puts a picture on the macOS clipboard, the shared holding area that the Copy and Paste commands use. The first line asks the system for the shared clipboard. The second empties it. The third places the picture there. The words pasteboard and image are names the programmer chose; NSPasteboard is the macOS name for the clipboard.

let pasteboard = NSPasteboard.general
pasteboard.clearContents()
pasteboard.writeObjects([image])

Three lines handle the clipboard step, which is the last step of a screen grab. A complete tool has many such pieces that must fit together: finding the screen, letting the user draw a region, capturing the pixels, and more. Counting how much code a tool contains gives a rough measure of its size. Lines of code (LOC) is that count of lines in the source files. It is an imperfect measure, since one clever line can replace ten plain ones, but it is easy to compute and good enough to compare scales. A worked comparison: a tool with 2,000 lines is roughly the size of a short story, while a large commercial product can contain millions of lines. When you ask an agent for a minimal tool, a small line count is a sign that the specification left features out.

The ScreenGrab case study supplies real numbers. The first install of the generated app contained about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, with no third-party dependencies. The whole project, including tests, scripts, and documents, came to about 5,200 lines.

Part of the first install Approximate lines App code (Swift, 19 files) 2,000 Tests (94 automated tests) 1,370 Install and build scripts 500 Specification, design, and README 1,340 Total 5,200

Count the Lines Before You Judge

When someone says a tool is "huge" or "tiny," ask for the line count and the number of files. About 2,000 lines of app code is small enough that a person can skim every file in an afternoon.

docs.title: Prompts and Natural Language Requests
docs.text:
A prompt is the input you give an AI model to tell it what you want. It can be a single question, a paragraph of instructions, a pasted error message, or a whole file. The model's output is shaped heavily by the prompt, so the quality of your prompt largely sets the quality of the result.

A natural language request is a prompt written in ordinary human language rather than a programming language or a special command syntax. "Make me a screen grab tool that copies a region to the clipboard" is a natural language request. It needs no code, no menu choices, and no special vocabulary, which is why people with no programming background can now ask for software.

Natural language requests are forgiving in one way and unforgiving in another. They accept almost any phrasing, so there is nothing to memorize. They also accept almost any level of vagueness, so the burden of being specific falls on you. Whatever you leave unsaid, the agent will fill in with its best guess, and its best guess is usually the most common feature set it has seen.

A worked example shows how much a prompt matters. Compare two requests for the same tool.

Prompt What the agent has to guess "Make a screenshot app." Which screens, which formats, where the file goes, whether to include editing, sharing, or cloud storage "Make a macOS menu bar app that grabs a screen region after an optional delay and puts the image on the clipboard. No saving, no editing." Very little: the platform, the two features, the output, and the exclusions are all stated

The first prompt invites a large, general tool, because the agent fills each gap with a popular guess. The second prompt does the job of leaving features out, and that is the habit this book builds. Chapter 7 develops it into the minimal specification.

docs.title: Prompt Iteration
docs.text:
Prompt iteration is the practice of refining a prompt in a series of tries, using what each result shows you. You read the output, notice what is missing or wrong, and adjust the request. First attempts are rarely perfect, and that is normal; treat the first answer as a draft and the second prompt as an edit.

A worked example: the first prompt asks for a screen grab tool and the agent proposes saving files to a folder. You reply, "No file saving; the image goes to the clipboard only." The second result is smaller and closer to what you wanted, and the correction cost one sentence. Each round also teaches you something about your own request, which is why a short prompt iterated three times often beats a long prompt written once.

docs.title: AI Coding Agents
docs.text:
An AI coding agent is a program that uses an LLM to carry out multi-step software tasks on your behalf. A plain LLM chat answers a question and stops. An agent keeps going: it reads your files, decides what to do, writes or edits files, runs commands, looks at the results, and tries again. The LLM is the reasoning engine, while the agent supplies the hands. Most of what an agent does well comes from this combination, and most of what goes wrong comes from the same place: the engine can be plausible without being right, and the hands will act on whatever it decides.

An ordinary chat with an LLM is like asking a knowledgeable friend by text message: you get advice, and then you do the work yourself. An agent is like hiring that friend to sit at your desk. It can open the project, make the change, run the build, and show you what happened. The table below summarizes the difference once both terms are clear.

LLM chat AI coding agent Output Text you read and copy Changes made directly in your project files Can it run the code? No Yes, through tools such as a build command Does it see the result? Only if you paste it back Yes, and it can react to errors on its own Typical number of steps One reply per question Many steps toward one goal Where you stay involved Copying and pasting Approving actions and checking the result

A worked example of one trip around the loop shows why the agent is more than a chat. The agent writes a new source file and then runs the build command. The build fails with a message that a variable name is misspelled. The agent reads that message, which is new information it did not have when it wrote the code, fixes the spelling, and builds again. The second build succeeds. You asked for none of those steps individually; the agent chose them to reach the goal you stated. This is also why agents can fail in more interesting ways than a chat: a wrong step early in the loop can carry through everything that follows.

The loop is the key idea. An agent receives a request, works out a plan, takes an action with a tool, observes the result, and repeats until the task is done or it needs you. The MicroSim below lets you step through that loop. Before you use it, here are the stage names it shows, each explained in the sections that follow: the request, clarifying questions, the plan, tool use, the report, and human review. A permission check is a moment when the agent stops and asks you to approve an action before it runs.

docs.title: Diagram: AI Coding Agent Loop Stepper
docs.text:
AI Coding Agent Loop Stepper

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-coding-agent-loop-stepper Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-agent-anatomy Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain the order of the seven stages an AI coding agent moves through, by predicting the next stage correctly in at least 5 of 6 steps.

Prerequisites: AI coding agent, prompt, natural language request, clarifying questions, agent planning, agent tool use, agent permissions, human review (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: At each of six steps the learner commits a prediction of the next stage before it is revealed. A prediction is correct when it matches the "Next stage" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try. Reading the stage descriptions and pressing Next without predicting is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The agent writes all the code in one step and then stops. (2) The agent never needs the person after the request. (3) The agent's report that work is done proves the work is done.

Instructional Rationale: Predicting the next stage forces the learner to rebuild the loop from the meaning of each stage instead of reading a list. The concrete ScreenGrab example visible at every stage keeps the abstract loop tied to a real case.

Content:

The seven stages, in order, each shown with its ScreenGrab example:

# Stage What happens ScreenGrab example (from the chapter) 1 Request The person states the goal in a natural language request A short request for a tool that grabs a region and copies it to the clipboard 2 Clarifying questions The agent asks the person to settle open choices Four multiple-choice questions answered by the author 3 Plan The agent lists the steps it intends to take Specification first, then design, code, tests, installer 4 Tool use: write The agent creates or edits files, after a permission check Writing the Swift source files 5 Tool use: run The agent runs commands such as a build or the tests, after a permission check Building the app and running the automated tests 6 Report The agent states what it did and what it believes the result is A summary that the app was built and installed 7 Human review The person checks the report against evidence and decides what happens next Trying the hotkey and a first real screen grab

Prediction steps (six): the learner is shown stage N and picks the next stage from three choices: the correct next stage and two other stages from the table.

Step Shown stage Choices Correct next stage Why (shown as feedback) 1 Request Plan; Clarifying questions; Human review Clarifying questions The agent settles open choices before it commits to a plan 2 Clarifying questions Plan; Report; Request Plan With the choices settled, the agent lays out its steps 3 Plan Tool use: write; Report; Human review Tool use: write Files must exist before anything can be built or tested 4 Tool use: write Tool use: run; Request; Plan Tool use: run New files are built and tested to see whether they work 5 Tool use: run Report; Clarifying questions; Request Report After running commands, the agent summarizes the outcome 6 Report Human review; Plan; Tool use: write Human review A report is a claim, and the person must check it

Provenance: Stage names and definitions come from this chapter, sections "AI Coding Agents", "Prompts and Natural Language Requests", "Human in the Loop" and "Human Review". The ScreenGrab examples come from the course description section "How the first version was built".

Rules: The stage order is fixed. Stages 4 and 5 each show a permission check before they run. After stage 7 the sim states that the loop can return to stage 1 with a new or refined prompt. Choices are shown in a fixed order for each step.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees stage 1 with its description and example, and the question "What comes next?"
  2. The learner picks one of three choices and locks it in. The sim reveals the correct next stage.
  3. The learner moves to the next step and repeats until all six predictions are made.
  4. After step 6, a summary lists the seven stages in order and marks the two permission checks and the final human review.

Feedback: Six predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. On a correct prediction the sim shows "Correct" with the Why text. On an incorrect prediction it shows the correct stage and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 6" is shown. At the end, 5 or 6 correct displays "You can explain the loop"; fewer than 5 invites a restart.

Starting State: Stage 1, Request, is shown with its example and the question "What does the agent do after it receives the request?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that there are seven stages: request, clarifying questions, plan, tool use (write), tool use (run), report, and human review, and that the author answered four multiple-choice questions.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
Claude Code is Anthropic's AI coding agent, and it is the one used to build ScreenGrab. It runs in a terminal window on your own computer, which means it can read the files in a project folder, edit them, and run the same commands you would type yourself. You describe what you want, and it works through the stages above, asking for your approval at the points you have configured.

A worked example from the case study: the author gave Claude Code a short request, answered four multiple-choice questions, and later asked for the app to be installed with a README. The work moved through a set order of specification, design, code, tests, and installer. Claude Code did the typing, but the author decided what the tool should do and what should be left out. The same pattern applies to any coding agent; Claude Code is simply the concrete example in this book.

Two features of Claude Code matter for this course. First, because it runs on your computer and not as a web page, it works on real files in a folder you can open and read afterward. Everything it makes is inspectable, which is what makes human review possible. Second, it keeps a record of each session, which the later chapters use to measure time, tokens, and cost. Other coding agents exist and share these traits, so the skills in this book transfer even if the tool changes.

docs.title: Clarifying Questions
docs.text:
Clarifying questions are questions an agent asks before it starts work, to settle choices that the request left open. Good ones turn a vague request into a precise one at almost no cost. In the ScreenGrab session the four multiple-choice questions let the author pick among options instead of writing long answers.

A worked example, with illustrative wording: the agent asks, "Where should the captured image go? (a) Clipboard only, (b) Save to a folder, (c) Both." The author picks (a). That single answer rules out a file-saving feature, a folder setting, and a file-format option, three things that would otherwise have been generated, tested, and maintained. Clarifying questions are therefore also a tool for leaving features out, so answer them deliberately and pick the smaller option when you are unsure.

docs.title: Agent Tool Use
docs.text:
Agent tool use is the agent's ability to take actions beyond writing text, such as reading a file, writing a file, running a command, or searching a project. Each action is a call to a tool, a small capability the agent is allowed to use. Tool use is what turns a chatty assistant into something that can build and test a program.

A worked example: asked to fix a failing build, an agent might read the build output, search the project for the file named in the error, open that file, edit one line, and run the build again. That is four tool calls in a row, each one visible in the session log. Because tools act on real files and real commands, they are also where permissions apply, as described later in this chapter.

docs.title: Agent Planning
docs.text:
Agent planning is the step where the agent breaks a task into ordered actions before it starts acting. A visible plan lets you catch a wrong direction early, when changing course costs one sentence instead of a rewrite.

A worked example: for ScreenGrab the plan follows a set order of specification, design, code, tests, and installer. If the plan for a tool you wanted to keep small included "add an editing toolbar" or "sync captures to the cloud", you could cross those items out before any code existed. Reading the plan is the cheapest review you will ever do, because nothing has been built yet.

docs.title: Keeping a Person in the Loop
docs.text:
Human in the loop means a person takes part in the process at points where judgment is needed, instead of leaving the whole thing to the machine. For an AI coding agent, those points are the request, the answers to clarifying questions, the approval of risky actions, and the final check of the result. The agent is fast, but it cannot know what you meant to leave out, and it cannot be held responsible for what it ships.

A worked example from the case study shows the loop doing its job. The author stated the goal and made the choices when asked. The agent proposed, wrote, built, and tested. The author then tried the Control-Shift-4 hotkey and made a real screen grab. That final step is the one an agent cannot do for you, because the question is whether the tool matches what you needed.

Staying in the loop does not mean watching every keystroke. It means choosing the checkpoints where your judgment adds the most value. The table below lists four checkpoints, the question you answer at each, and what goes wrong if you skip it.

Checkpoint Question you answer Risk if skipped Request What do I actually need, and what can go? A bloated tool that does what is popular, not what you use Plan Does this list of steps match my intent? Wasted work in the wrong direction Permission prompts Is this action safe and expected? Deleted files or changed settings you did not mention Final check Does the real tool do the real job? Relying on a claim nobody verified

docs.title: Human Review
docs.text:
Human review is the act of a person reading the agent's output and checking it against evidence before relying on it. Review is not the same as skimming the agent's summary. It means opening the files, running the tool, and looking at test results.

A worked example: after the agent reports that the screen grab works, a reviewer does three things. They launch the app, press the hotkey, and grab a region. They paste the result into an image viewer to confirm the clipboard really holds the picture. They check that the session log shows the tests actually ran. Each step takes a minute or two, and together they replace trust with evidence. Review also scales with risk: a throwaway script deserves a glance, while a tool you will use daily deserves the full routine.

docs.title: Agent Permissions
docs.text:
Agent permissions are the settings that control which actions an agent may take without asking. Reading files might be allowed freely, while deleting files or running unfamiliar commands requires your approval. Tighter permissions mean more interruptions and more safety, and you choose the balance.

A worked example of how a sensible setup might look for ScreenGrab:

Action Suggested setting Reason Read project files Allow without asking Reading changes nothing Edit files in the project folder Ask at first, allow once you trust the plan The project is under version control, so edits can be undone Run the build and the tests Allow These are the commands the project documents Delete files or run commands outside the project Always ask Hard to reverse, and outside the task

docs.title: Agent Instructions File
docs.text:
An agent instructions file is a text file in a project that tells the agent how to behave there: the build commands, the style rules, and the things never to do. The agent reads it at the start of each session, so you state a rule once instead of repeating it in every prompt. This book's own project works this way: the file CLAUDE.md contains one line that points to AGENTS.md, and AGENTS.md holds the rules every coding agent must follow when working on the book.

Approve With Your Eyes Open

A common trap is clicking "allow" on every permission prompt to make the interruptions stop. That hands the agent the keys. Read what it wants to run, approve the ordinary steps, and stop on anything that deletes files or changes settings you did not mention.

docs.title: AI Sessions and Session Logs
docs.text:
An AI session is one continuous working conversation with an agent, from the first prompt until you end it. Everything in the session, including your messages, the agent's replies, the files it read, and the results of its commands, forms the working memory the agent draws on. A new session starts almost fresh, apart from what the instructions file tells it.

Sessions matter in this book for a practical reason: they are what you measure. The cost, the time, and the number of tokens all attach to a session. The case study reports the whole session as about 70 active minutes, which Chapter 11 breaks down.

A worked example illustrates why sessions behave the way they do. Suppose you spend an hour with an agent building a tool, close the window, and open a new session the next day. The new session does not remember that you rejected a cloud-storage feature yesterday. If that decision lives only in the old conversation, the agent may suggest the feature again. If it lives in the instructions file or the specification, the new session reads it and complies.

The practical lesson is to write decisions into files, not into the conversation. A conversation is temporary, and a file in the project is permanent and visible to every future session and every future reader. A long session also has a cost: everything the agent has read and written stays in its working memory, so a very long conversation can become slower, more expensive, and more prone to confusion. Chapter 10 explains the cost side. Starting a fresh session for a new task, with a clear instructions file, is often the better habit.

docs.title: Session Log
docs.text:
A session log is the recorded history of a session: the prompts, the replies, the tool calls, and the results, in order. It answers the question "what actually happened?" after the fact, without relying on anyone's memory or on the agent's own summary. You can use it to find where a wrong turn began, to count tokens for cost, or to check whether a claimed test run really occurred.

A worked example: the agent's report says "all tests pass." You open the session log and look for the test command. If the log shows the command ran and printed 94 passing tests, the claim is supported. If the log shows no test command at all, the claim has no evidence behind it. The log turns an assertion into something you can verify.

Question Where to look What did I ask for? The prompts in the session log What did the agent actually run? The tool calls in the session log What did it report, and did the log support it? Compare the final report with the tool results How many tokens did the session use? The usage record for the session (Chapter 11)

docs.title: AI Hallucination
docs.text:
An AI hallucination is output from an AI model that is false or unsupported but presented fluently and confidently. In code, a hallucination might be a function name that does not exist, an option a library never had, or a claim about how a system behaves. The model is not lying; it is continuing text plausibly, and a plausible-looking name is easy to produce.

A worked example, with illustrative details: an agent writes a call to a clipboard function called copyImageToClipboard() and reports that the feature is done. The name reads naturally, but that function does not exist in the macOS system libraries. The compiler rejects it, which is the good outcome: a loud failure. The dangerous cases are hallucinations that compile and run but do the wrong thing, such as a hotkey that appears registered but never fires. The case study contains an honest example of that risk: one early hotkey failure was never explained.

Hallucinations are more likely when a request asks for something obscure, very recent, or very specific, because the model has less to draw on and fills the gap with a plausible guess. They are also more likely when the agent cannot run anything to check. The remedies follow from the causes. Prefer agents that can build and test. Ask for evidence, such as the actual command output. And treat any detail that you cannot see running, like a specific function name or option, as a claim to verify.

docs.title: Overconfident Reporting
docs.text:
Overconfident reporting is when an agent describes its work as done, tested, or working more strongly than the evidence supports. The words are cheerful and complete ("The feature is implemented and verified"), but nothing shows the verifying took place. It is a close cousin of hallucination, and it is easy to miss because a confident summary sounds like a result.

A worked example: an agent writes a delay feature and reports, "Delayed capture works correctly." What did it check? If it ran an automated test that captures after a one-second delay and compared the timing, that is evidence. If it only wrote the code and re-read it, the sentence is a hope. Several acceptance tests in the ScreenGrab case study still had to be run by hand, because only a person at the keyboard could see whether the real screen grab behaved.

The following MicroSim lets you practice the habit this chapter recommends: separating what an agent claims from what it showed. Each claim in a short report comes with the evidence the agent provided, and you decide whether the claim is supported.

docs.title: Diagram: Claim and Evidence Checker
docs.text:
Claim and Evidence Checker

Type: microsim sim-id: agent-claim-evidence-checker Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-sciences/tree/main/docs/sims/evidence-loop-authoring Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge whether each of 8 claims in an illustrative agent report is supported or unsupported by the evidence shown with it, with at least 7 correct.

Prerequisites: AI hallucination, overconfident reporting, human review, session log (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 claims the learner commits "Supported" or "Unsupported" after reading the evidence panel. A judgment is correct when it matches the "Correct judgment" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct. Reading the evidence without committing a judgment is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) A confident, detailed report is a verified report. (2) Code that was written has been run. (3) A passing test of one thing confirms a different claim.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating requires applying a criterion to a case. The criterion here is "does the evidence shown match the claim?", and eight short cases with contrasting evidence make the learner apply it repeatedly rather than recite it.

Content:

All reports and evidence are illustrative and the sim labels them "illustrative, not from a real session".

# Agent claim Evidence shown Correct judgment Why (shown as feedback) 1 "All 94 tests pass." Test run output: "94 passed, 0 failed" Supported The output shows the test command ran and counts match the claim 2 "All tests pass." None. The log contains no test command Unsupported No evidence that tests were run 3 "The app builds cleanly." Build output ending in "error: cannot find 'copyImageToClipboard' in scope" Unsupported The build output shows an error, which contradicts the claim 4 "Delayed capture waits 3 seconds." Unit test of the delay timer: "delay = 3.0 s, passed" Supported A passing test targets exactly this claim 5 "The hotkey works on every Mac." The author tried the hotkey once on one Mac Unsupported One trial on one machine does not support "every Mac" 6 "The README explains installation." The README file opened, with an "Install" section listing the install command Supported The file was opened and the section exists 7 "The screen recording permission is handled." Code reviewed, never run; no permission prompt appeared in testing Unsupported Written code that was never run does not show the permission flow works 8 "The clipboard contains the captured image." The author pasted into an image viewer and the grab appeared Supported A person checked the real result directly

Provenance: Illustrative scenarios written for this chapter. The test count 94 comes from the course description section "How the first version was built". The definitions come from this chapter, sections "AI Hallucination", "Overconfident Reporting" and "Session Log".

Rules: Claims appear in the order of the table. A claim is "Supported" only when the evidence shown directly tests that same claim and the result matches it. Evidence that is absent, contradicts the claim, tests something else, or covers a narrower case than the claim makes it "Unsupported".

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads claim 1 and its evidence panel.
  2. The learner chooses Supported or Unsupported and confirms the choice.
  3. The sim shows whether the judgment was correct, with the Why text.
  4. The learner repeats for claims 2 through 8, then sees a summary of correct judgments and the two rules of thumb: "Evidence must test the same claim" and "Written is not run".

Feedback: Eight claims, fixed order, one attempt each. The correct judgment and Why text appear immediately after each confirmation. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. The summary shows the claims judged wrongly with their Why text.

Starting State: Claim 1 and its evidence are shown with the question "Does the evidence support the claim?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that there are 8 claims, that the test count in the example is 94, and that mastery is 7 of 8.

Skepticism Gets Easier

If asking for evidence feels awkward with a tool that sounds so sure, that is normal. You already do this with a new coworker's first report. Start with one habit: for every "it works," ask "where is the output that shows it?"

docs.title: Putting the Pieces Together
docs.text:
Generative AI produces content from learned patterns. An LLM is the text engine behind it, trained to continue text plausibly. An AI coding agent wraps an LLM with tools so it can plan, write source code, run commands, and report. You steer it with prompts, refine with prompt iteration, set its boundaries with permissions and an instructions file, and check its work through human review, with the session log as the record.

Piece Job in one phrase Generative AI Creates new content from learned patterns Large language model Predicts text one token at a time AI coding agent Plans, uses tools, and reports on multi-step software tasks Prompt and prompt iteration Steers the work and refines it in rounds Permissions and instructions file Set the limits and standing rules Human review and session log Verify the claims against evidence

You Can Read an Agent Now

You can now explain what a coding agent does at each stage, name the points where a person must stay in the loop, and tell a supported claim from an overconfident one. That is the foundation for deciding, in the next chapter, whether to buy, subscribe, or generate.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Generative AI and Coding Agents
docs.text: Test your understanding of generative AI, large language models, prompts, AI coding agents, human review, sessions, and the ways an agent can be wrong with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is an AI coding agent?
docs.text:
1. A chat window that answers one question and stops
  2. A search engine that finds existing programs
  3. A program that uses an LLM to carry out multi-step software tasks, reading files, running commands, and checking results
  4. A compiler that translates source code into an app
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An agent keeps going where a plain chat stops: it reads your files, decides what to do, edits files, runs commands, observes the results, and tries again. The LLM is the reasoning engine, and the agent supplies the hands. Option A describes an LLM chat, and option D describes a compiler, which Chapter 9 covers. Option B describes search, which only finds what already exists.

Concept Tested: AI Coding Agent

See: AI Coding Agents

docs.title: 2. What is an agent instructions file?
docs.text:
1. A text file in a project that tells the agent how to behave there, which the agent reads at the start of each session
  2. A log of every command the agent has run
  3. The compiled version of the application
  4. A list of the user's passwords for the agent to use
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The instructions file holds build commands, style rules, and things never to do, so you state a rule once instead of repeating it in every prompt. In this book's project, CLAUDE.md contains one line pointing to AGENTS.md, which holds the rules every coding agent must follow. Option B describes a session log, and option C describes the built product. Option D is not what such a file is for.

Concept Tested: Agent Instructions File

See: Agent Instructions File

docs.title: 3. What is a session log?
docs.text:
1. A list of the features requested in the first prompt
  2. The agent's own summary of what it believes it accomplished
  3. A calendar of when a subscription renews
  4. The recorded history of a session: the prompts, replies, tool calls, and results, in order
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A session log answers "what actually happened?" without relying on anyone's memory or the agent's own summary. You can use it to find where a wrong turn began, count tokens, or check whether a claimed test run occurred. Option B is exactly what the log lets you verify, since a summary is a claim and the log is the evidence. Options A and C describe unrelated records.

Concept Tested: Session Log

See: AI Sessions and Session Logs

docs.title: 4. Why is a large language model weak at knowing whether its own output is true?
docs.text:
1. It cannot produce fluent text
  2. It was trained to continue text plausibly, not to check facts
  3. It has no training data about code
  4. It always refuses to answer questions about facts
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An LLM generates its answer one token at a time, choosing likely continuations from patterns in its training text. That makes it strong at fluent text and regular code, but plausibility is not correctness. It can use only what is in the current conversation plus what it absorbed in training, and running the code to confirm it works is a separate step. Options A and C are the opposite of its strengths, and D is false.

Concept Tested: Large Language Model

See: Large Language Models

docs.title: 5. What is the main practical difference between an LLM chat and an AI coding agent?
docs.text:
1. An agent makes changes directly in your files, can run the code, and reacts to errors on its own, while a chat gives text you copy and paste
  2. A chat can run commands, but an agent cannot
  3. A chat produces code, but an agent only produces documentation
  4. They differ only in the color of the interface
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. In a chat you receive text, then do the work yourself and paste results back. An agent, like a friend hired to sit at your desk, opens the project, makes the change, runs the build, and sees the result. The chapter's example is a build that fails on a misspelled variable, which the agent reads, fixes, and rebuilds without being asked. Option B reverses the two, and options C and D are incorrect.

Concept Tested: AI Coding Agent

See: AI Coding Agents

docs.title: 6. How do clarifying questions help keep a generated tool small?
docs.text:
1. They make the agent write code more slowly
  2. They remove the need to review the output
  3. Each answer can rule out whole features, such as choosing clipboard only, which avoids file saving, a folder setting, and a format option
  4. They require the user to write the full specification first
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Clarifying questions settle choices the request left open, and choosing the smaller option removes features that would otherwise be generated, tested, and maintained. In the ScreenGrab session, four multiple-choice questions let the author pick options instead of writing long answers. Option B is wrong because human review is still required, and options A and D misstate the purpose of the questions.

Concept Tested: Clarifying Questions

See: Clarifying Questions

docs.title: 7. An agent's report says "all tests pass." What should you look for in the session log to support that claim?
docs.text:
1. The agent's confident wording in the final report
  2. The number of lines of code in the project
  3. The length of the conversation
  4. A test command that actually ran and printed passing results
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The log turns an assertion into something verifiable. If it shows the test command ran and printed, for example, 94 passing tests, the claim is supported. If the log shows no test command, the claim has no evidence behind it. Option A is the claim itself, not evidence. Options B and C do not show that tests ran. This habit is the antidote to overconfident reporting.

Concept Tested: Session Log

See: AI Sessions and Session Logs

docs.title: 8. The agent proposes saving screen grabs to a folder, and you reply, "No file saving; the image goes to the clipboard only." What practice is this?
docs.text:
1. Agent planning
  2. Prompt iteration, which refines a prompt in rounds using what each result shows
  3. An AI hallucination
  4. A permission check
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Prompt iteration treats the first answer as a draft and the second prompt as an edit. Here a single sentence made the result smaller and closer to the goal. The chapter notes that a short prompt iterated three times often beats a long prompt written once. Agent planning (A) is the agent's own step of ordering actions. A hallucination (C) is false output, and a permission check (D) asks you to approve an action.

Concept Tested: Prompt Iteration

See: Prompt Iteration

docs.title: 9. Which permission setting does the chapter suggest for deleting files or running commands outside the project folder?
docs.text:
1. Allow without asking, because the agent is fast
  2. Allow only on the first day of a project
  3. Always ask, because the actions are hard to reverse and outside the task
  4. Never allow reads of project files
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's sample setup allows reading files freely, asks at first before edits and then relaxes once you trust the plan, allows the documented build and test commands, and always asks before deleting files or running commands outside the project. Reading changes nothing, and project edits can be undone under version control, but deletions are hard to reverse. Tighter permissions mean more interruptions and more safety.

Concept Tested: Agent Permissions

See: Agent Permissions

docs.title: 10. Why is a hallucination that compiles and runs more dangerous than one the compiler rejects?
docs.text:
1. A compiled hallucination can do the wrong thing silently, such as a hotkey that appears registered but never fires, while a rejected one fails loudly
  2. A rejected hallucination deletes the project
  3. Compilers cannot detect any hallucination
  4. Compiled hallucinations always run faster
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A call to a nonexistent function such as copyImageToClipboard() is rejected by the compiler, which is the good outcome because the failure is visible. The dangerous cases produce no error but behave wrongly, and the case study contains an unexplained early hotkey failure as an example. Remedies include preferring agents that can build and test, asking for actual command output, and verifying details you cannot see running.

Concept Tested: AI Hallucination

See: AI Hallucination

docs.title: References: Generative AI and Coding Agents
docs.text:
1. Large language model - Wikipedia - Explains how language models are trained and used to generate text and code, including limits such as hallucination. Foundation for what a coding agent is built on.

  2. Generative artificial intelligence - Wikipedia - Surveys systems that generate text, code, and images from prompts, with history and risks. Places coding agents within the wider field this chapter introduces.

  3. Intelligent agent - Wikipedia - Defines an agent as an entity that perceives its environment and takes actions toward goals. Supplies the vocabulary behind the chapter's read-edit-run stages of a coding agent.

  4. Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach - Stuart Russell and Peter Norvig - Pearson - Russell and Norvig organized the field around the rational agent: percepts, actions, environment, and performance measure. That unifying frame makes a coding agent's loop easy to describe precisely.

  5. Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI - Ethan Mollick - Portfolio - Mollick popularized the jagged frontier, where AI excels at some tasks and fails unpredictably at others, and the practice of staying a human in the loop. Anchors the chapter's advice on oversight.

  6. Building Effective Agents - Anthropic - Distinguishes workflows from agents and describes patterns such as prompt chaining and tool use. Gives a practitioner's account of how coding agents are structured.

  7. Claude Code Overview - Anthropic Docs - Documents a terminal coding agent that reads files, runs commands, and edits code. A concrete example of the agent workflow described in the chapter.

  8. Claude Code: Best Practices for Agentic Coding - Anthropic - Shares tested habits for directing a coding agent: explore, plan, then implement, with checks along the way. Illustrates where a person must stay in the loop.

  9. Prompt Engineering Overview - Anthropic Docs - Describes how to state goals, give context, and iterate on prompts. Shows how the quality of instructions shapes what a coding agent produces.

  10. Vibe coding - Simon Willison - Separates careless vibe coding from responsible AI-assisted programming where the developer reviews and understands the result. Useful for telling supported claims from overconfident ones.

docs.title: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software
Summary
docs.text: With costs and coding agents both in hand, this chapter frames the central choice of the book: buy, subscribe, or generate. It introduces personal software, the difference between disposable and long-lived tools, and the risks and support responsibility that come with owning what you generate. After this chapter, you will be able to describe all three options and the responsibilities each one carries.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 9 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Build-Or-Buy Decision 22 Buy Option 4 Subscribe Option 4 Personal Software 21 Disposable Software 1 Long-Lived Software 1 Risks Of Ownership 6 Support Responsibility 1 Generate Option 9

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
  • Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
  • Chapter 4: Total Cost of Ownership
  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents

Three Doors, Not Two

You now know what bloat costs and what a coding agent can do, so it is time to choose. By the end of this chapter you will be able to look at any paid tool you use and name three ways out, along with what each one asks of you. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: The Build-or-Buy Decision
docs.text:
A build-or-buy decision is the choice between making a tool yourself and paying someone else for one. Businesses have faced this choice for as long as there has been software: build an in-house system, or buy a product. For individuals, "build" used to be unrealistic. Writing even a small application took weeks of study and practice, so almost everyone bought.

Generative AI changes the price of building, and that is why this book exists. When a short request and a few answers can produce a working app in about 36 minutes, as the ScreenGrab case did, "build" becomes a real option for ordinary users. The decision also gains a third branch. Earlier chapters distinguished two ways of paying for existing software, a one-time license and a subscription. Adding generation gives three options in total:

  • Buy: pay once for a product and keep using it.
  • Subscribe: pay repeatedly for a product you rent.
  • Generate: describe what you need and have an AI coding agent build it for you.

A worked example sets up the rest of the chapter. The ScreenGrab story began with a utility that cost $9 once and ran on all of the author's computers. Over the years it gained features, and it now requires an annual fee of $30 per computer. The author faced the decision directly: keep paying $90 a year for three computers, hunt for a smaller product, or generate a tool with just two features. The sections below describe each option, and the decision explorer later in the chapter lets you practice choosing.

The Decision Is Not Free Versus Paid

Notice that generating is not the "free" door. It costs tokens, time, and ongoing care. The useful question is not which option is cheapest in the first month, but which one fits the job over the whole time you will use it.

docs.title: The Buy Option
docs.text:
The buy option means paying a one-time price for software and then using that version for as long as it works for you. This is the perpetual license model from Chapter 3. You pay once, you own the right to run that version, and the vendor's incentive is to earn the money at the moment of sale.

Buying has real strengths. The cost is known in advance and does not recur. Someone else wrote, tested, and packaged the product, so you receive something that has been exercised by many users. If the tool is stable and does what you need, the cost per year of use falls every year you keep it.

The weaknesses are the ones this book has been tracing. A bought product still arrives with the vendor's full feature set, including the 95% of features most users never touch. A one-time license may not cover major new versions, and a vendor that depends on new sales has a reason to keep adding features so that you upgrade. Some products have also stopped offering one-time purchases at all.

A worked example from the case: the original utility at $9 was an excellent buy. It did its job, it ran on every computer the author owned, and it cost less than a coffee for several years of use. The buy option worked well until the product changed its pricing model.

Aspect Buy option Cost pattern One payment up front Who maintains it The vendor, until you stop upgrading Features you get The vendor's whole feature set Main risk Version lock-in or a product that stops being sold this way

docs.title: The Subscribe Option
docs.text:
The subscribe option means paying a recurring fee, monthly or yearly, for continued access to software. Chapter 3 explained how this changes a vendor's incentives: because revenue depends on renewals, the vendor must keep showing you new value, and "new value" often arrives as new features.

Subscriptions have genuine benefits. Updates, security fixes, and support are normally included. The up-front cost is low. For software that must track a changing outside world, such as tax rules or an online service, a vendor who keeps it current is doing real work that you would otherwise do yourself.

The cost of that convenience compounds. A subscription never finishes. If the fee is per computer, it multiplies with every machine you own. And if you stop paying, you may lose access to the tool, sometimes including the files it created in its own format.

The worked example is the ScreenGrab utility today. At $30 per computer per year, three computers cost $90 a year, which is $450 over five years. The same job cost $9 before. Nothing about the job changed. What changed is the payment model and the number of features the author is paying for but not using.

Aspect Subscribe option Cost pattern Recurring, often per computer Who maintains it The vendor, for as long as you pay Features you get The vendor's whole feature set, growing over time Main risk Paying indefinitely for features you never use

docs.title: The Generate Option
docs.text:
The generate option means describing the tool you want and having an AI coding agent build it. You pay no license fee, since the code is yours. You do pay in tokens, which are the units an AI service charges for, and in your own time to specify, review, and test the result.

The ScreenGrab case gives concrete numbers, drawn from the course description. The author needed only two features: grab a region, and grab a region after a delay, with the image going to the clipboard. The first version was built and installed in about 36 minutes and cost about $6 in estimated API cost. The whole session, including hotkey testing, took about 70 active minutes and cost about $14. That figure is less than one-sixth of a single year's $90 in fees.

Those costs are estimates, and they cover the code only. They exclude the author's own time and later maintenance. The table below puts the three options side by side using the case study's figures, and its last column shows what each figure leaves out.

Option Cost in the case study What the figure leaves out Buy (original utility) $9 once Anything the vendor later added or charged Subscribe (current utility) $90 a year for three computers; $450 over five years The features that go unused Generate (ScreenGrab) About $14 for the whole session The author's time, later maintenance, and testing effort

Cheap to Build Is Not Cheap to Own
