A $14 build can tempt you to stop counting. Before you call generation the winner, add the line the table leaves blank: your time to specify and check the tool, and the upkeep afterward. Chapter 4's total cost of ownership is the tool for doing that sum honestly.

docs.title: Personal Software
docs.text:
Personal software is software made for one person, or a very small group, to meet their own needs rather than the needs of a market. It does not need a sales page, support desk, or thousands of users. It needs to do one job for its owner.

Personal software is not new. People have always written spreadsheets with formulas, macros in a word processor, and little shell scripts. What is new is that someone with no programming experience can produce something larger, such as a native application, by describing it in plain language. The audience for this course, technically curious users who pay for software they barely use, is exactly the group for whom this option has just opened.

The defining feature is the size of the audience. A commercial product must serve millions of different users, so it accumulates features to cover all their needs, which is the root of bloat. Personal software serves one user, so it can be exactly the size of that person's job. The ScreenGrab app has two features because the person it was built for needed two.

A worked example: suppose you need a tool that renames photo files from a trip using the date in each file. A commercial photo manager offers hundreds of features and a subscription. A personal tool does one thing, you describe it in a sentence, and the agent produces it. You are the only user, so you decide what "works" means, and you can test it on your own files.

The trade is that a personal tool has no vendor behind it. No one else found the bugs, wrote the documentation, or waits to answer your questions. Everything the vendor provided as part of the price is now your job.

docs.title: Disposable Software
docs.text:
Disposable software is a tool made for a single occasion and thrown away when the job is done. A script that converts one folder of files, or a page that formats one event's name tags, are typical examples. Because it will be used once, it needs little polish, no installer, and no long-term maintenance.

A worked example: you have 40 scanned receipts named by the scanner with meaningless numbers, and you want each file renamed by its date. You describe that single job, the agent writes a short script, you run it once, check a few results, and delete the script. The total effort is minutes, and nothing remains to maintain.

Generative AI is especially suited to disposable software, because the cost of creating it can be lower than the cost of finding and learning a product for the same one-off job.

docs.title: Long-Lived Software
docs.text:
Long-lived software is a tool you expect to keep using for months or years, across operating system updates and changing needs. A screen grab utility used every day for years falls here. It needs a real installer, clear documentation, tests, and a plan for fixing problems, because you will return to it when something changes.

The distinction matters for the decision. The same generated app can be a bargain as a disposable tool and a burden as a long-lived one, because the long-lived version brings the maintenance and verification costs that the disposable version avoids. Ask early how long you expect to use the tool, and plan accordingly.

Disposable software Long-lived software Expected use Once or a few times Months or years Polish needed Little Installer, README, tests Maintenance None; discard it Ongoing Example Convert one folder of files A daily screen grab tool

docs.title: Risks of Ownership
docs.text:
The risks of ownership are the problems that come with being the owner of software that no vendor stands behind. When you buy or subscribe, a company carries most of these risks. When you generate, they move to you.

The main risks are:

  • Defects: the generated code may contain bugs, some of which only appear in rare situations.
  • Unverified behavior: a tool can look right and still fail in cases nobody tried.
  • Platform changes: an operating system update can break a tool that worked yesterday.
  • Disappearing knowledge: you may forget how the tool was built, and the agent that built it does not remember.
  • Security: a tool with access to your screen or files must not do more than you intended.

The ScreenGrab case study shows these risks plainly, not as hypotheticals. One early hotkey failure was never explained. Several acceptance tests still have to be run by hand. A later fix was needed for Macs that have only the Command Line Tools installed. None of these ruined the project, and all of them are the kind of event a vendor would normally absorb. Chapters 12 to 14 return to testing, bugs, and maintenance in depth.

A worked example of risk in practice: the author installs the app and the hotkey works on the machine where it was built. On a second computer the app builds but the hotkey does nothing. Someone must diagnose it, and that someone is the owner. With a purchased product, you would file a support request. With your own tool, you open the session log, ask the agent to investigate, and test the fix yourself.

docs.title: Support Responsibility
docs.text:
Support responsibility is the duty to answer for the software when it breaks: to diagnose it, fix it, and keep it working. With bought or subscribed software this duty sits with the vendor. With generated software it sits with you.

That does not mean you must become a programmer. It means you must be willing to keep the project folder, keep the instructions file and README current, and run a coding agent when something needs fixing. If you will not do that, the generate option is a poor choice for a long-lived tool, however cheap the build was.

Ask Who Answers the Phone

Before you generate anything meant to last, finish this sentence: "When this breaks, I will ___." If you cannot fill the blank with a plan, choose buy or subscribe, or accept that the tool will be disposable.

docs.title: Practicing the Decision
docs.text: The decision explorer below gives you eight short scenarios. For each, you choose buy, subscribe, or generate, and the explorer explains the reasoning. The scenarios are illustrative, and they use the ideas from this chapter: how long the tool will be used, who maintains it, and what happens when it breaks.

docs.title: Diagram: Buy, Subscribe, or Generate Decision Explorer
docs.text:
Buy, Subscribe, or Generate Decision Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: buy-subscribe-generate-decision-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/information-systems/tree/main/docs/sims/build-buy-saas-decision Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: recommend Learning Objective: The learner will recommend buy, subscribe, or generate for each of 8 scenarios, justified by how long the tool will be used and who supports it, with at least 6 correct.

Prerequisites: build-or-buy decision, buy option, subscribe option, generate option, disposable software, long-lived software, risks of ownership, support responsibility (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each scenario the learner commits one of three recommendations. A recommendation is correct when it matches the "Best option" column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 8 correct. Opening the three option summaries is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Generating is always the cheapest choice. (2) A subscription is always a bad deal. (3) A one-time purchase never needs any further thought.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating means judging against criteria. The scenarios vary the criteria (duration, support, regulation, verification) so the learner must weigh them instead of memorizing a single rule.

Content:

The three options, shown as reference summaries the learner can open at any time:

Option One-sentence summary Buy Pay once and keep using that version; the vendor maintains it until you stop upgrading Subscribe Pay repeatedly; the vendor maintains it and keeps it current for as long as you pay Generate Have an AI coding agent build exactly what you need; you pay tokens and time, and you carry support responsibility

The eight scenarios, in order. All are illustrative:

# Scenario Best option Why (shown as feedback) 1 You must convert one folder of files to a different format this afternoon, and never again. Generate One-off job: disposable software has no maintenance cost, and no product is worth learning for one use 2 A 200-person company needs payroll software that must follow tax rules that change every year. Subscribe The outside rules change constantly, and the vendor's yearly updates and support are the real product 3 A $9 one-time utility does exactly your job on all your computers and has not changed in years. Buy A stable one-time purchase already fits; keep it, since the cost per year keeps falling 4 Your screen grab tool costs $30 per computer per year on 3 computers, and you use 2 of its features. Generate You can name the 2 features, the fee compounds ($90 a year), and a small tool is easy to test 5 A clinic must store patient records and follow privacy law, and no staff member can verify security. Subscribe The vendor carries compliance, security, and support, which the clinic cannot verify itself 6 You need name tags formatted for one event next weekend. Generate A single-occasion job suits disposable software, with no upkeep afterward 7 A $40 one-time-license drawing app does everything you need on one computer and rarely changes. Buy A stable tool with a fixed price and no recurring cost; generating adds work for no gain 8 You need one job done on two computers, the only product charges $15 per computer per year, and you can describe the job in two sentences and have time to test it. Generate A short specification and time to verify make generating practical, and the fee recurs forever

Counts: Generate is the best option in 4 scenarios (1, 4, 6, 8), Subscribe in 2 (2, 5), and Buy in 2 (3, 7).

Provenance: Scenarios are illustrative and written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". The $9, $30, $90 figures in scenarios 3 and 4 come from the course description section "How a simple tool became a subscription". The option summaries come from this chapter.

Rules: Each scenario has exactly one best option. The learner chooses exactly one of three options per scenario. No arithmetic is required of the learner. A scenario is correct only when the chosen option equals the Best option column.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1 and may open the three option summaries.
  2. The learner picks one of Buy, Subscribe, or Generate and confirms the choice.
  3. The sim shows whether the choice was correct and the Why text, and the learner moves to the next scenario.
  4. After scenario 8, the sim shows the score and lists the scenarios answered incorrectly with their Why text. The learner should notice that the best option depends on duration and support more than on price alone.

Feedback: Eight scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: " and the Why text. Incorrect: the best option and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 6 or more shows "You can weigh the three options"; a lower score invites a restart.

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with the three option summaries closed and the question "Which option fits this job best?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states three options (buy, subscribe, generate), the figures $9, $30 per computer per year, $90 a year, $450 over five years, about $6 for the first build, about $14 for the whole session, and about 70 active minutes. The explorer has 8 scenarios and mastery is 6 of 8.

You Can Name Every Door

You can now describe buy, subscribe, and generate, say how personal, disposable, and long-lived software differ, and name who answers when a generated tool breaks. Next, you will learn how to write the specification that keeps a generated tool small.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software
docs.text: Test your understanding of the buy, subscribe, and generate options, personal and disposable software, and the risks of ownership with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What does the generate option mean?
docs.text:
1. Paying a one-time price for a product and keeping that version
  2. Paying a recurring fee for continued access to a product
  3. Downloading a free alternative from an open-source project
  4. Describing the tool you want and having an AI coding agent build it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. With the generate option you pay no license fee because the code is yours, but you do pay in tokens and in your own time to specify, review, and test the result. Option A is the buy option, option B is the subscribe option, and option C is a different route that the chapter does not call generation. In the ScreenGrab case, the first version was built and installed in about 36 minutes.

Concept Tested: Generate Option

See: The Generate Option

docs.title: 2. What is disposable software?
docs.text:
1. A tool sold with a limited license that expires
  2. A tool made for a single occasion and thrown away when the job is done
  3. A tool whose source code is hidden from the user
  4. A tool that deletes the user's files after use
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Disposable software, such as a script that converts one folder of files, needs little polish, no installer, and no long-term maintenance because it will be used once. Generative AI suits it especially well, because creating it can cost less than finding and learning a product for the same one-off job. Options A, C, and D describe licensing, proprietary code, and destructive behavior, none of which defines disposable software.

Concept Tested: Disposable Software

See: Disposable Software

docs.title: 3. Who holds the support responsibility for a generated tool?
docs.text:
1. The owner, who must diagnose it, fix it, and keep it working
  2. The vendor of the AI coding agent
  3. The maker of the operating system
  4. No one, because generated software never breaks
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Support responsibility is the duty to answer for software when it breaks. With bought or subscribed software it sits with the vendor, and with generated software it sits with you. That does not require becoming a programmer, but it does mean keeping the project folder, instructions file, and README current and running a coding agent when something needs fixing. If you will not do that, generation is a poor choice for a long-lived tool.

Concept Tested: Support Responsibility

See: Support Responsibility

docs.title: 4. Why can personal software be exactly the size of its owner's job, while commercial software accumulates features?
docs.text:
1. Personal software is always written in a simpler language
  2. Commercial software is required by law to include extra features
  3. A commercial product must serve millions of different users and covers all their needs, while personal software serves one user
  4. Personal software cannot have any bugs
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The defining feature of personal software is the size of its audience. A product that serves a market accumulates features to cover everyone's needs, which the chapter calls the root of bloat. Software for one person can do one job, which is why ScreenGrab has two features: the person it was built for needed two. Options A, B, and D are not claims the chapter makes.

Concept Tested: Personal Software

See: Personal Software

docs.title: 5. What is the main weakness of the buy option, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. You still receive the vendor's whole feature set, and a one-time license may not cover major new versions
  2. The cost recurs every year
  3. You can never use the software after paying
  4. The vendor has no incentive to sell it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A bought product arrives with the vendor's full feature set, including the 95% of features most users never touch. A one-time license may not cover major new versions, and a vendor that depends on new sales has a reason to keep adding features so you upgrade. Some products have also stopped offering one-time purchases. Option B describes the subscribe option, and options C and D are false.

Concept Tested: Buy Option

See: The Buy Option

docs.title: 6. Why can the same generated app be a bargain as disposable software but a burden as long-lived software?
docs.text:
1. Long-lived software must be written in a different language
  2. Disposable software is always more secure
  3. The long-lived version brings maintenance and verification costs that the disposable version avoids
  4. Long-lived software cannot be generated by an agent
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A tool used once needs little polish and no upkeep, so the cheap build is nearly the whole cost. A tool you expect to use for months or years needs an installer, documentation, tests, and a plan for fixing problems, because you will return to it when the operating system or your needs change. This is why the chapter says to ask early how long you expect to use the tool.

Concept Tested: Long-Lived Software

See: Long-Lived Software

docs.title: 7. You have 40 scanned receipts with meaningless file names and want each renamed by its date, once. Which option and kind of software fit best?
docs.text:
1. Subscribe to a photo manager and keep it for years
  2. Buy a large commercial photo suite
  3. Wait for a vendor to add the feature
  4. Generate a disposable script, run it once, check a few results, and delete it
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This matches the chapter's receipt example: describe the single job, let the agent write a short script, run it, spot-check results, and delete it. The total effort is minutes and nothing remains to maintain. Options A and B pay for large feature sets and ongoing costs for a one-off job, and option C leaves the job undone. Generation is especially suited to one-off tasks because creating the tool can cost less than learning a product.

Concept Tested: Disposable Software

See: Disposable Software

docs.title: 8. The whole ScreenGrab session cost about $14, while the subscription costs $90 a year for three computers. How do the two compare?
docs.text:
1. The session cost more than one year of fees
  2. The session cost less than one-sixth of one year's fees
  3. The session cost about half of one year's fees
  4. The two cost exactly the same
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Dividing $14 by $90 gives about 0.16, which is less than one-sixth. The chapter then adds a caution: the $14 is an estimate that covers the code only, and it excludes the author's own time, later maintenance, and testing effort. So the comparison supports generating as a promising option, but it does not settle the question until those costs are counted.

Concept Tested: Generate Option

See: The Generate Option

docs.title: 9. You install a generated app, and on a second computer the app builds but the hotkey does nothing. According to the chapter, what is the right way to respond?
docs.text:
1. File a support request with the vendor and wait
  2. Delete the app and subscribe to a commercial one
  3. Open the session log, ask the agent to investigate, and test the fix yourself
  4. Assume the hotkey works and ignore the problem
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. With a purchased product you would file a support request, but with your own tool someone must diagnose the problem, and that someone is the owner. The chapter's approach is to use the session log and the coding agent to investigate, then verify the fix yourself. There is no vendor behind a personal tool, so option A has no one to contact, and options B and D avoid the responsibility rather than meet it.

Concept Tested: Risks Of Ownership

See: Risks of Ownership

docs.title: 10. Why does the chapter warn that the $14 generate figure should be read with care?
docs.text:
1. The figure is exact and needs no qualification
  2. It covers the code only and leaves out the author's time, later maintenance, and testing effort
  3. It was measured on a competitor's product
  4. It includes five years of subscription fees
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The chapter's side-by-side table lists what each figure leaves out: the buy figure omits later vendor charges, the subscribe figure omits the unused features, and the generate figure omits time, upkeep, and testing. Reading the costs together with their omissions is the analytical skill the chapter builds. Chapter 4's total cost of ownership puts those omitted items back into one number.

Concept Tested: Generate Option

See: The Generate Option

docs.title: References: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software
docs.text:
1. Commercial off-the-shelf - Wikipedia - Describes buying ready-made software or hardware instead of building custom solutions, with typical advantages and risks. Supplies the buy side of the classic make-or-buy frame the chapter extends.

  2. Situated software - Wikipedia - Describes software made for a specific small group and context, not for scale. Names the category into which personal and disposable tools fall.

  3. End-user development - Wikipedia - Covers methods that let non-professional programmers create their own software. Background for the rise of personal software built by the people who use it.

  4. The Cathedral and the Bazaar - Eric S. Raymond - O'Reilly - Raymond opened with the claim that every good work of software starts by scratching a developer's own itch. That origin story is the intellectual ancestor of building a personal tool for one need.

  5. Software Engineering at Google - Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck, and Hyrum Wright - O'Reilly - The authors define software engineering as programming integrated over time. That framing clarifies why long-lived software costs more than a disposable script and who answers when it breaks.

  6. Hyrum's Law - Hyrum Wright - States that with enough users, every observable behavior of a system will be depended on by somebody. Explains why long-lived software is costly to change and why a personal tool never faces this burden.

  7. An App Can Be a Home-Cooked Meal - Robin Sloan - Sloan tells how he built a small app for family use and compares it to cooking at home. A warm, concrete account of the personal-software motive.

  8. Home-Cooked Software and Barefoot Developers - Maggie Appleton - Appleton examines how AI lets non-programmers build software for their own communities, and the risks of unmaintained tools. Connects generation tools to the maintenance question.

  9. In Defense of Not-Invented-Here Syndrome - Joel on Software - Spolsky argues that building core functions yourself can beat buying when the dependency is central. Supplies the pro-build argument the chapter weighs against buying.

  10. Vibe coding - Simon Willison - Separates careless vibe coding from responsible AI-assisted programming where the developer reviews the result. Frames the accountability question when a generated personal tool breaks.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter begins the build sequence with the step that does the most to limit cost: deciding what to leave out. It moves from user needs to functional and non-functional requirements, scope boundaries, non-goals, acceptance criteria, and the minimal specification, using ScreenGrab's region selection, delayed capture, and clipboard output as the running example. After this chapter, you will be able to write a minimal specification for a small tool and explain why its omissions matter.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score User Need 141 Requirements 140 Functional Requirement 91 Non-Functional Requirement 41 Scope Boundaries 6 Non-Goals 5 Explicit Assumptions 1 Default Behavior 1 Acceptance Criteria 49 Software Specification 40 Minimal Specification 4 Specification Review 1 Screen Capture 25 Screen Grab Tool 20 Region Selection 9 Delayed Capture 4 Clipboard Output 4

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
  • Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule
  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents

The Cheapest Place to Cut

A feature you never ask for is a feature the agent never writes, never tests, and never breaks. In this chapter you will learn to write the short document that makes those omissions explicit. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: The Running Example: Screen Capture
docs.text:
Screen capture is the act of recording what is currently displayed on a computer screen as a picture. The result is an image file or an image held in memory, such as on the clipboard. People use it constantly: to show a colleague an error message, to save a receipt on a web page, or to put a chart from one program into a report. A single still picture is called a screenshot. The capture can cover the whole screen, one window, or a chosen rectangle, and the picture contains only what was visible at that instant: it cannot include anything hidden behind another window or below the edge of the display. Recording the screen as moving video is a different job that needs different tools, and this chapter leaves it out on purpose.

A screen grab tool is a program whose job is to perform screen capture on demand. You trigger it with a menu or a keyboard shortcut, it takes the picture, and it puts the result somewhere useful. Commercial screen grab tools tend to grow far beyond that. Typical additions include drawing and annotation, capturing a scrolling web page, recording video, cloud storage and sharing links, text recognition, and team accounts. Each addition is a software feature in the sense of Chapter 1, and each one adds code, tests, and decisions. A screen grab tool is therefore a good teaching case for this course: the core job is tiny and well understood, while the feature list around it can grow without limit. Because most readers have used one, you can judge each requirement in this chapter against your own experience.

A worked example anchors the chapter. The ScreenGrab author used a paid tool and needed exactly two things from it: grab a region of the screen, and grab a region after a delay, with the image going to the clipboard. Every other feature in the product was something the author paid for and did not use. The rest of this chapter turns that observation into a document an AI coding agent can build from.

Feature in a typical commercial tool Needed by the author? Grab a region of the screen Yes Grab a region after a delay Yes Put the image on the clipboard Yes Annotate or draw on the image No Record video No Capture a scrolling page No Upload and share through a cloud account No

docs.title: User Need
docs.text:
A user need is a problem a person has or a result a person wants, stated without choosing how to achieve it. It describes the goal, not the product. This connects directly to the job to be done from Chapter 1: the need is the job.

The difference between a need and a feature is easy to miss, so it deserves a careful look. "I need a screenshot app with a toolbar" names a solution. "I need to paste a picture of part of my screen into an email" names a need. The second statement leaves room for many solutions, including a very small one. The first statement already contains a toolbar, and an agent will faithfully build it.

To find the real need behind a request, keep asking what the person is trying to do and why. A worked example shows the chain for the ScreenGrab author:

  1. "I want a screenshot tool." What for?
  2. "To show someone part of what is on my screen." What do you do with the picture?
  3. "I paste it into a message or document." Do you need the file afterward?
  4. "No, the paste is the end of it."

The chain turns a vague wish into a precise need: put a picture of a chosen part of the screen on the clipboard, and nothing else. It also produced a cut: the author did not need to save files, so the tool will not save files.

A reliable way to write a need is to use a fixed sentence shape: "A person who is doing X needs to Y so that Z." For the author: "A person writing a message needs to put a picture of part of the screen into it so that the reader sees exactly what the writer sees." The shape forces you to name who is acting, what they need, and why. If you cannot fill in the "so that", you have probably written a feature instead of a need. Try the shape on a paid tool you use: a few honest minutes with it usually reveals that your real need is much smaller than the product.

Statement Need or solution? Why "Paste part of my screen into an email" Need States the result, not the means "Give me a toolbar with arrows and highlights" Solution Prescribes a feature "Share captures through a link" Solution Prescribes a method of sharing "Show a colleague an error message quickly" Need States the purpose and leaves the method open

Ask for the Result, Not the Gadget

Think of the need as the destination and every feature as a possible vehicle. Name the destination first, and the agent is free to pick the smallest vehicle that gets you there. Name the vehicle first, and you get the whole garage.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
Requirements are the specific statements of what a software product must do or must be, derived from the user need. If the need is the goal, the requirements are the checklist the finished tool must satisfy. A good requirement is clear, so that two readers understand it the same way. It is necessary, so that removing it would fail the need. And it is testable, so that someone can show whether it was met.

Requirements matter more when an AI agent builds the software, because the agent reads them literally and does not ask for the meaning behind a word. A human developer might notice that "support images" probably means common formats. An agent may choose any reading, or all of them. Precise requirements are cheap to write and reduce the amount the agent must guess, and each guess is a place where unwanted features or unwanted behavior can enter.

Each requirement should also trace back to the need. Ask of every line, "Which part of the need does this serve?" A requirement that serves no part of the need is a candidate for deletion, and that question is the single most effective way to keep a specification minimal. The table below applies the three tests to one requirement as it improves.

Version Clear? Necessary? Testable? "The tool should be good at capturing." No: "good" means different things Unknown No "The tool shall capture images in several formats." Partly: which formats? No: the need ends at the clipboard No: "several" has no count "The tool shall place the captured region on the clipboard as an image." Yes Yes: the need is to paste it elsewhere Yes: paste and look

A worked example shows the traceability in action. The author lists a candidate requirement, "remember the last selected region." Tracing it back, no part of the need (grab a region, grab after a delay, copy to the clipboard) calls for it. It goes on the non-goals list. Requirements that survive this question are few, and that is what keeps the generated tool small.

A worked example from the ScreenGrab need produces three requirements: the user can select a region of the screen; the user can start a capture with a delay; the captured image is placed on the clipboard. Notice what is absent. Nothing is said about annotation, file formats, or sharing, because the need did not call for them.

Requirements fall into two families, described next. The table below previews them in one line each, after which the following sections explain each family with examples.

Family Answers the question ScreenGrab example Functional What does the tool do? Copy the selected region to the clipboard Non-functional How well, or under what limits, does it do it? Complete a grab in under one second

docs.title: Functional Requirements
docs.text:
A functional requirement states a specific behavior or function the software must provide: an action the user takes and the response the tool gives. Functional requirements are usually written as short sentences with the verb "shall", as in "The tool shall copy the captured image to the clipboard". The word "shall" marks something required, as opposed to something merely nice.

Good functional requirements describe observable behavior. You should be able to picture the user doing something and the tool responding. Compare two versions of the same requirement.

Weak Strong "The tool handles region selection." "The tool shall let the user select a rectangular region of the screen by dragging with the mouse." "The tool supports a delay." "The tool shall let the user start a capture that waits for a chosen number of seconds before the picture is taken." "The tool works with the clipboard." "The tool shall place the captured image on the system clipboard so that it can be pasted into other applications."

The weak versions sound reasonable but leave the agent to guess what "handles", "supports", and "works with" mean. The strong versions can each be checked by a person at a keyboard in under a minute.

A complete functional requirement covers four things: what triggers the behavior, what the tool does, what the user sees or gets, and what happens when something goes wrong. The last one is easy to forget. For F2, the clipboard requirement, the error case might read: "If the screen cannot be read, the tool shall show a message and shall leave the clipboard unchanged." Without that line, the agent decides what a failure looks like, and the only way to learn its choice is to hit the failure.

A worked example lists an illustrative set of functional requirements for a ScreenGrab-style minimal tool, each with an identifier so later documents can refer to it:

ID Functional requirement F1 The tool shall let the user select a rectangular region of the screen by dragging with the mouse. F2 The tool shall place the captured region on the clipboard as an image. F3 The tool shall let the user start a capture that waits a chosen number of seconds before the picture is taken. F4 The tool shall let the user cancel a selection in progress by pressing the Escape key. F5 The tool shall start a region selection when the user presses the Control-Shift-4 hotkey.

The first three come directly from the author's two needs. F4 and F5 are the small additions that make the tool usable: a way out of a mistake, and a quick way to start. The case study confirms that grabs from both the menu and the Control-Shift-4 hotkey were seen working.

docs.title: Non-Functional Requirements
docs.text:
A non-functional requirement states a quality the software must have or a limit it must respect, instead of a specific behavior. It describes how well the tool does its job, or the conditions it works under. Common families are speed, reliability, size, privacy, security, ease of installation, and the platforms it must run on.

Non-functional requirements are the ones most often left out, and then they are filled in by guess. If you do not say the tool must be small, the agent may add libraries that make it large. If you do not say it must not send data anywhere, you have not forbidden it. Vague quality words do no work: "fast", "secure", and "lightweight" cannot be checked. A usable non-functional requirement has a number, a named limit, or a clear yes or no.

Non-functional requirements also shape the design more than most people expect. A functional requirement tells the builder what to add, while a non-functional requirement tells the builder how to add it. "No third-party libraries" rules out a whole family of shortcuts, and "installable by running one script" forces the project to include an installer. Chapter 8 follows these choices into the design. Each non-functional line is cheap to write and sometimes expensive to satisfy, so keep the list short and include only the qualities you would actually check.

Quality Vague version Checkable version (illustrative) Speed "It should be fast." "A grab shall complete within 1 second of the user releasing the mouse button." Dependencies "Keep it lightweight." "The tool shall use no third-party libraries." Installation "Easy to install." "The tool shall be installable by running one script." Platform "Works on Macs." "The tool shall run on macOS." Privacy "Respect my data." "The tool shall not send captured images off the computer."

The no-dependencies line is a real feature of the case study: the generated app uses no third-party dependencies. The other numbers in the table are illustrative examples of how to phrase a requirement, not measured results from ScreenGrab.

Beware the Quality Words

Words like "fast," "simple," and "secure" feel like requirements but carry none, because nobody can check them. They tempt you because they are quick to write. Replace each one with a number, a limit, or a yes-or-no statement before the agent sees it.

docs.title: Scope Boundaries
docs.text:
Scope boundaries are the lines that separate what a project includes from what it does not. The scope is the set of things the tool will do; the boundary is the edge. Without a boundary, a project drifts, because every new idea seems small on its own, and no single addition looks like the one that made the tool big. This drift is feature creep from Chapter 1, and in an AI-assisted project it happens quickly, since adding a feature is only one more sentence away.

Boundaries work best when written as concrete, checkable lines. "A small tool" is a hope, while "region capture, delayed capture, clipboard output, and nothing else" is a boundary. A worked example: midway through a project you think, "It would be nice to save a copy of each grab." Checking the boundary gives an immediate answer. File saving is not in the scope, so adding it means changing the scope on purpose, with its cost visible, not letting it slip in.

Inside the scope Outside the scope Select a region by dragging Whole-window or scrolling capture Capture after a delay Video recording Image placed on the clipboard Saving to files, sharing, cloud upload Start by menu or hotkey Editing or annotating the picture

docs.title: Non-Goals
docs.text:
Non-goals are explicit statements of what the project will not do. They are the written form of the omissions. Where the scope lists what is in, the non-goals list the tempting things that are out. They are valuable for a reason specific to AI agents: an agent that is not told "no editing" may reasonably decide that a screenshot tool should have editing, because most screenshot tools do.

Writing a non-goal costs one line, and it prevents an entire feature from being generated, tested, and maintained. Non-goals also settle arguments later: when a new idea arrives, you check the list instead of debating it. A worked example of three non-goals for ScreenGrab:

  1. The tool will not edit or annotate captured images.
  2. The tool will not save captures to files or upload them anywhere.
  3. The tool will not record video.

Each of these cuts directly against the typical commercial feature list in the table at the start of the chapter. This is the 95/5 rule from Chapter 2 put to use: the features most users never open are the ones to name as non-goals.

Write the 'No' Lines First

Before you list a single feature, write three or four non-goals for the features you know a similar product has. It takes two minutes, and the agent treats them as firm limits instead of suggestions.

docs.title: Explicit Assumptions
docs.text: Explicit assumptions are the conditions a specification takes for granted and states openly, such as the platform the tool runs on or how the user will use it. Writing them down matters because an unstated assumption is invisible until it fails. ScreenGrab assumes a Mac running a recent version of macOS and one user capturing one display at a time. If either is false, the specification needs to change, and stating them makes that visible. A worked example: the author later runs the tool on a second computer with two displays. Because the assumption of one display at a time was written down, the problem is easy to place: the tool did what it was specified to do, and the assumption has stopped holding. The decision then is clear, either extend the specification or accept the limit.

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
Default behavior is what the tool does when the user has not chosen anything. A delay needs a default: if the user starts a delayed capture without picking a number, the tool must do something specific. Naming the default in the specification, for example "the delay defaults to 3 seconds", removes a question the agent would otherwise answer by guessing, and the tool behaves predictably on first use. Defaults are cheap decisions with a large effect, because most people never change a setting they were not asked to choose.

The sorter below lets you practice telling these four kinds of statement apart. The twelve illustrative statements are ones a ScreenGrab-style specification might contain, and you place each one in a category.

docs.title: Diagram: Requirement Type Sorter
docs.text:
Requirement Type Sorter

Type: microsim sim-id: requirement-type-sorter Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of 12 specification statements as a functional requirement, a non-functional requirement, a non-goal, or an assumption, with at least 10 correct.

Prerequisites: functional requirement, non-functional requirement, non-goal, explicit assumption (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each of the 12 statements to exactly one of four categories and confirms the assignment. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Category" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct. Reading the category definitions is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A statement about what the tool will not do is a functional requirement. (2) A quality such as speed or size is a feature. (3) An assumption is a requirement the tool must satisfy.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying requires the learner to decide which defining property a statement has (behavior, quality, exclusion, or condition), which shows whether the four concepts are distinguished, not just recited.

Content:

The four categories and their definitions, available to the learner at any time:

Category Definition Functional requirement A specific behavior the tool must provide Non-functional requirement A quality the tool must have or a limit it must respect Non-goal Something the tool deliberately will not do Assumption A condition taken for granted and stated openly

The twelve statements, in this order. All are illustrative statements for a ScreenGrab-style tool:

# Statement Category Why (shown as feedback) 1 The tool shall let the user drag a rectangle over any part of the screen. Functional requirement It describes a behavior the user performs and the tool responds to 2 The tool shall copy the captured image to the clipboard. Functional requirement It is an action the tool performs 3 A grab shall complete within 1 second of the user releasing the mouse button. Non-functional requirement It sets a speed limit, a quality of how well the behavior happens 4 The tool shall not include image editing or annotation. Non-goal It names a capability deliberately left out 5 The tool shall start a capture after a delay that the user chooses. Functional requirement It describes a behavior the user can trigger 6 The tool shall use no third-party libraries. Non-functional requirement It is a limit on how the tool is built, not a behavior 7 Cloud sharing is out of scope. Non-goal It states something deliberately excluded 8 The user has a Mac running a recent version of macOS. Assumption It states a condition taken for granted, not something the tool does 9 The tool shall be installable by running one script. Non-functional requirement It is a quality of installation, not a feature the user operates 10 The user captures only one display at a time. Assumption It is a condition the specification relies on 11 The tool shall let the user cancel a selection by pressing Escape. Functional requirement It describes a user action and the tool's response 12 Video recording is not part of this tool. Non-goal It excludes a capability explicitly

Category counts: Functional requirement 4 (statements 1, 2, 5, 11), Non-functional requirement 3 (3, 6, 9), Non-goal 3 (4, 7, 12), Assumption 2 (8, 10).

Provenance: Statements are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". Category definitions come from this chapter, sections "Functional Requirements", "Non-Functional Requirements", "Non-Goals" and "Explicit Assumptions".

Rules: Each statement belongs to exactly one category. A statement is correct only when the learner's category equals the Category column. Statements appear in the order of the table. A statement already answered cannot be changed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads statement 1 and may open the category definitions.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four categories and confirms.
  3. The sim shows whether the choice is correct, with the Why text, and the next statement appears.
  4. After statement 12, a summary shows the score and the statements answered wrongly, with their Why text. The learner should notice that exclusions and conditions are easy to confuse with requirements.

Feedback: Twelve statements, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: " and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct category and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 12" is shown. A final score of 10 or more shows "You can separate the four kinds of statement"; a lower score invites a restart.

Starting State: Statement 1 is shown with the four categories unselected and the question "What kind of statement is this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states four categories, twelve statements, and mastery at 10 of 12, with category counts of 4, 3, 3 and 2.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria
docs.text:
Acceptance criteria are specific, testable conditions that a requirement must meet for the work to count as done. A requirement says what the tool should do. An acceptance criterion says how you will know that it does. Where requirements can sometimes remain broad, acceptance criteria must be concrete enough that two people running the same check reach the same verdict.

The shape that works well is a trio of parts. State the starting situation, the action, and the observable result. Using the format "Given a situation, when the user acts, then this result is observed", a criterion for requirement F2 reads: "Given that the user has dragged a region and released the mouse, when the capture completes, then pasting into an image viewer shows a picture of exactly that region."

A worked example gives criteria for three of the ScreenGrab requirements:

Requirement Acceptance criterion F1 Region selection Given the tool is running, when the user presses the hotkey and drags from one point to another, then a rectangle between those points is selected. F3 Delayed capture Given a delay of 5 seconds is chosen, when the user starts the capture, then the picture is taken between 4.9 and 5.1 seconds later. F4 Cancel Given a selection is in progress, when the user presses Escape, then no capture is made and the clipboard is unchanged.

Write at least one criterion for every functional requirement, and no criterion that does not trace back to a requirement. That one-to-one habit keeps the checklist short and complete. A worked example for F5, the hotkey: "Given the app is running and another application is in front, when the user presses Control-Shift-4, then a region selection starts." The criterion names the situation, the action, and the observable result.

Notice that each criterion names something a person can see or measure. They also give the later chapters their target: Chapter 12 turns criteria like these into automated tests, and the case study notes that several acceptance tests still had to be run by hand.

Not every criterion is testable, and the difference is the point of the next MicroSim. Before using it, recall the test of testability: could two different people run the check and agree on the result? "It should be fast" fails that test, while "completes within 1 second" passes.

docs.title: Diagram: Acceptance Criteria Testability Judge
docs.text:
Acceptance Criteria Testability Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: acceptance-criteria-testability-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: assess Learning Objective: The learner will assess whether each of 8 acceptance criteria is testable, by deciding if two people running the same check would reach the same verdict, with at least 7 correct.

Prerequisites: acceptance criteria, functional requirement, non-functional requirement (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of 8 criteria the learner commits "Testable" or "Not testable". A judgment is correct when it matches the "Verdict" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct. Viewing the repair suggestion for a criterion after judging is feedback, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A criterion that sounds positive and professional is a testable one. (2) A criterion with the word "all" or "gracefully" is stricter and so better. (3) Only numbers make a criterion testable.

Instructional Rationale: Assessing needs a criterion applied to cases. The criterion is "would two people agree?", and the mix of testable and untestable examples, including one testable criterion with no number, prevents the shortcut of looking for digits.

Content:

The eight criteria, in this order. All are illustrative:

# Criterion Verdict Why (shown as feedback) Repair, shown when Not testable 1 The tool should be fast. Not testable "Fast" has no limit, so two people could disagree A grab completes within 1 second of releasing the mouse button 2 After the user drags a region and releases the mouse, the clipboard holds an image of exactly that region. Testable A person can paste and compare the picture with the region (not needed) 3 The tool is easy to use. Not testable "Easy" depends on the person A new user starts a region capture using only the hotkey, with no instructions 4 With a 5-second delay set, the capture happens between 4.9 and 5.1 seconds after the user starts it. Testable It gives a measurable window (not needed) 5 Pressing Escape during selection ends the capture and leaves the clipboard unchanged. Testable It has a clear action and an observable result, though it needs no number (not needed) 6 The tool handles errors gracefully. Not testable "Gracefully" and "errors" are undefined When the screen cannot be read, the tool shows a message and does not change the clipboard 7 The app works with all Macs. Not testable "All" cannot be checked The app runs on the macOS versions named in the specification 8 Pressing Control-Shift-4 while a web browser is the frontmost app starts a region selection. Testable A person can try it and see whether a selection starts (not needed)

Verdict counts: Testable 4 (criteria 2, 4, 5, 8), Not testable 4 (criteria 1, 3, 6, 7).

Provenance: Criteria are illustrative and written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". The Control-Shift-4 hotkey and the delay idea come from the course description section "The Story". The testability test comes from this chapter, section "Acceptance Criteria".

Rules: A criterion is Testable only when two people running the same check would agree on the result, regardless of whether it contains a number. Criteria appear in the order of the table. The repair text is shown only after a Not testable criterion has been judged.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads criterion 1.
  2. The learner chooses Testable or Not testable and confirms.
  3. The sim shows whether the judgment is correct and the Why text; for a Not testable criterion it also shows the repair.
  4. The learner continues through criterion 8 and then sees the score. The learner should notice that criterion 5 is testable without containing a number.

Feedback: Eight criteria, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: " and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct verdict, the Why text, and any repair. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 7 or more shows "You can judge testability"; a lower score invites a restart.

Starting State: Criterion 1 is shown with the question "Would two people running the same check reach the same verdict?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the test of testability as "two different people run the check and agree on the result", gives 5 seconds with a 4.9 to 5.1 second window, and says the sim has 8 criteria with mastery at 7 of 8.

docs.title: Software Specification
docs.text:
A software specification is a written description of what a piece of software must do and be, assembled from the requirements, boundaries, assumptions, and acceptance criteria. It is the document a builder works from. In traditional projects a specification could run to hundreds of pages. In an AI-assisted project it is the main thing you hand the agent, and its quality sets the ceiling on what the agent can deliver.

A worked example shows the stakes. Compare two ways of asking for the same tool. The first is a single line: "Make a screenshot app." The second is the minimal specification in this chapter. From the first, an agent will probably produce a tool with a file menu, an editor, and a settings window, because that is what screenshot apps usually have. From the second, it produces the two features and the clipboard. The case study's documents, the specification, the design, and the README, together came to about 1,340 lines, a small part of the 5,200-line project but the part that decided what the other 3,860 lines would be.

A specification does four jobs at once. It tells the builder what to make. It tells the builder what not to make. It gives the reviewer a checklist to compare the result against. And it is a record, so months later someone can learn why the tool behaves as it does, even if that someone is you.

The parts fit together in a simple order, and each answers one question. The table below summarizes the parts that the chapter has already explained.

Part Question it answers ScreenGrab example User need Why does this tool exist? Paste a picture of part of my screen into a message Scope and non-goals What is in and out? Region and delayed capture in; editing, saving, video out Functional requirements What does it do? F1 to F5 Non-functional requirements How well, within what limits? No third-party libraries; one-script install Assumptions and defaults What is taken for granted, and what happens untouched? A Mac; the delay defaults to 3 seconds Acceptance criteria How will we know it works? The Given, when, then checks

docs.title: Minimal Specification
docs.text:
A minimal specification is a software specification that includes only what the user needs and states what is left out. It is short by design, because every line in it creates work for the agent and every omission removes work. It is not a vague specification: a minimal specification is exact about the few things it contains, and just as exact about the things it excludes.

The case study shows how this pays. The generated app came to about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files. A more generous specification would have produced more code, more tests, and more places for bugs. Chapter 2's 95/5 rule predicted this: if 95% of users use only 5% of the features, a tool built for one user's 5% can be a small fraction of the size.

Here is a complete minimal specification for a ScreenGrab-style tool, short enough to read in a minute. It is illustrative of the form; the precise numbers marked "illustrative" are examples of how to state a limit.

Section Content Need Paste a picture of a chosen part of the screen into other applications. In scope Select a region by dragging. Capture after a chosen delay. Place the image on the clipboard. Start by menu or hotkey. Non-goals No editing or annotation. No saving, sharing, or upload. No video. Assumptions A Mac with a recent macOS. One display captured at a time. Functional requirements F1 to F5, as listed earlier. Non-functional requirements No third-party libraries. Installable by running one script. A grab completes within 1 second (illustrative). Defaults The delay defaults to 3 seconds (illustrative). Acceptance criteria One Given, when, then check per functional requirement.

docs.title: Specification Review
docs.text:
Specification review is the step where a person reads the specification before any code is generated, looking for missing, vague, or unwanted items. It is the cheapest review in the whole project, because correcting a sentence costs seconds and correcting generated software costs hours. A good review asks three questions of every line: is it needed, is it testable, and is anything missing that the agent would otherwise guess?

A worked example: reading the draft, the reviewer notices that F3 says "a chosen number of seconds" but gives no limits. What happens if the user chooses 0, or 5,000? Adding "at least 1 second and at most 10 seconds" closes the gap in one line. The same pass finds a requirement for "saving a recent history", which serves no part of the need and is cut. The reviewer can be the author, another person, or the agent itself asked to list ambiguities, though the final judgment stays with a person.

docs.title: Region Selection, Delayed Capture and Clipboard Output
docs.text: The three ScreenGrab features are small enough to specify fully. Each one is a worked example of the ideas above, and each reveals a small decision the specification must settle.

docs.title: Region Selection
docs.text:
Region selection is the user's act of choosing which rectangular part of the screen to capture, usually by dragging the mouse from one corner to the opposite corner. It is the heart of the tool and the feature most users reach for first.

A specification for it must settle details the word "select" hides. Which corner does the drag start from, and does dragging up and to the left work as well as dragging down and to the right? What happens if the rectangle has no area because the user clicked without dragging? How does the user abandon a selection? The worked example below answers each with a requirement:

Question Answer in the specification Drag direction Any direction produces the same rectangle between the start and end points Click without dragging No capture is made Abandoning a selection Pressing Escape cancels it (F4) What is captured Exactly the pixels inside the rectangle

Each answer is something an agent would otherwise decide for itself. Region selection is also where the tool's hardest platform problems begin, such as keeping the screen still while you drag, which Chapter 8 takes up as freeze-frame selection. Stating them keeps the behavior predictable and gives the later tests something exact to check.

docs.title: Delayed Capture
docs.text:
Delayed capture is a screen capture that takes the picture a set number of seconds after the user starts it. The delay lets the user prepare the screen first, for example by opening a menu that closes when the mouse moves, which would be impossible to photograph in a single immediate step.

A specification for it must say how the delay is chosen, what the range is, what the default is, and what happens during the wait. The worked example, with illustrative values, shows what a precise answer looks like:

Question Answer in the specification (illustrative) How is the delay chosen? The user picks a whole number of seconds before starting What are the limits? At least 1 second and at most 10 seconds What is the default? 3 seconds What happens during the delay? The tool waits; the user can set up the screen; no picture is taken until the delay ends Does selection happen before or after the delay? The user selects the region first, then the delay begins

The last line illustrates why details matter. A specification that omits it leaves the agent to choose between two quite different behaviors, and only one of them matches the author's habit.

docs.title: Clipboard Output
docs.text:
Clipboard output means delivering the captured image to the system clipboard, the shared holding area behind Copy and Paste, so that the user can paste it directly into another application. The case study's specification makes the clipboard the only destination, which is itself a cut: no folders, no file names, no format menus.

The decision is a good illustration of omission paying off. Saving to a file would require decisions about where, under what name, in which format, and what to do if the file already exists. Each decision is a requirement, a test, and a possible bug. By choosing the clipboard alone, the specification avoids all of them. The worked example below states the requirement and its criterion:

Item Statement Requirement F2 The tool shall place the captured region on the clipboard as an image. Acceptance criterion Given a completed capture, when the user pastes into an image viewer, then a picture of exactly the selected region appears. Explicit non-goal The tool does not save the image to a file.

You Can Write the Short Version

You can now turn a user need into functional and non-functional requirements, draw the scope with non-goals, write testable acceptance criteria, and assemble a minimal specification for a tool like ScreenGrab. Next, you will see how a specification becomes a design that fits a real platform.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Requirements and Minimal Specifications
docs.text: Test your understanding of user needs, requirements, scope boundaries, acceptance criteria, and minimal specifications with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a user need?
docs.text:
1. A problem a person has or a result a person wants, stated without choosing how to achieve it
  2. A list of features the product must include
  3. A description of how the code is organized
  4. A promise the vendor makes in its marketing
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A need describes the goal, not the product, and it connects to the job to be done from Chapter 1. "I need to paste a picture of part of my screen into an email" is a need, while "I need a screenshot app with a toolbar" already names a solution that an agent will faithfully build. Option B describes requirements or features, and option C describes design.

Concept Tested: User Need

See: From User Need to Requirements

docs.title: 2. What are non-goals in a specification?
docs.text:
1. Goals that the team failed to reach
  2. Goals that only the vendor cares about
  3. Explicit statements of what the project will not do
  4. Features scheduled for a later release
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Non-goals are the written form of omissions, listing the tempting things that are out of scope. They matter especially with AI agents, because an agent that is not told "no editing" may reasonably decide that a screenshot tool should have editing, since most do. A non-goal costs one line and prevents a whole feature from being generated, tested, and maintained.

Concept Tested: Non-Goals

See: Non-Goals

docs.title: 3. What are acceptance criteria?
docs.text:
1. The legal terms a user accepts during installation
  2. The list of platforms the software supports
  3. The marketing claims the vendor approves
  4. Specific, testable conditions that a requirement must meet for the work to count as done
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A requirement says what the tool should do, and an acceptance criterion says how you will know that it does. The chapter recommends the "Given a situation, when the user acts, then this result is observed" shape. Two people running the same check must reach the same verdict. Option A describes an end user license agreement from Chapter 3, which is a different kind of acceptance.

Concept Tested: Acceptance Criteria

See: Acceptance Criteria

docs.title: 4. Which of these is a non-functional requirement?
docs.text:
1. "The tool shall copy the captured image to the clipboard."
  2. "A grab shall complete within 1 second of the user releasing the mouse button."
  3. "The tool shall let the user cancel a selection with the Escape key."
  4. "The tool shall start a region selection when the user presses Control-Shift-4."
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A non-functional requirement states a quality or limit, such as speed, size, privacy, or platform, rather than a specific behavior. The time limit describes how well the tool does its job. The other three options each state an action and the tool's response, which makes them functional requirements. The chapter notes that usable non-functional requirements need a number, a named limit, or a clear yes or no.

Concept Tested: Non-Functional Requirement

See: Non-Functional Requirements

docs.title: 5. Why do precise requirements matter even more when an AI agent builds the software?
docs.text:
1. Agents cannot read text
  2. Agents refuse to build anything from short requirements
  3. Agents charge extra for each requirement
  4. The agent reads requirements literally and fills any gaps with its best guess, which is usually the most common feature set
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A human developer might infer that "support images" means common formats, but an agent may choose any reading or all of them. Each guess is a place where unwanted features or behavior can enter. Precise requirements are cheap to write and reduce the amount the agent must guess. A good requirement is clear, necessary, and testable, and every line should trace back to the need.

Concept Tested: Requirements

See: Requirements

docs.title: 6. Why does the chapter ask you to write explicit assumptions?
docs.text:
1. An unstated assumption is invisible until it fails, while a stated one makes the cause of a problem easy to place
  2. Assumptions are legally required in every specification
  3. Assumptions make the tool run faster
  4. Assumptions replace the need for acceptance criteria
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. ScreenGrab assumes a Mac running a recent macOS and one user capturing one display at a time. When the author later runs the tool on a second computer with two displays, the written assumption makes the problem easy to place: the tool did what it was specified to do, and the assumption has stopped holding. Options B, C, and D make claims the chapter does not support.

Concept Tested: Explicit Assumptions

See: Explicit Assumptions

docs.title: 7. A colleague asks, "Give me a toolbar with arrows and highlights." How should you classify this statement?
docs.text:
1. A user need, because it states a result
  2. An acceptance criterion, because it can be tested
  3. A solution, because it prescribes a feature instead of stating a goal
  4. A non-functional requirement, because it concerns appearance
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's table sorts "Give me a toolbar with arrows and highlights" as a solution because it prescribes a feature. By contrast, "Show a colleague an error message quickly" is a need because it states the purpose and leaves the method open. To find the real need, keep asking what the person is trying to do and why, as in the four-question chain for the ScreenGrab author.

Concept Tested: User Need

See: From User Need to Requirements

docs.title: 8. Which statement is the most checkable version of the vague request "Keep it lightweight"?
docs.text:
1. "The tool should feel small."
  2. "The tool shall use no third-party libraries."
  3. "The tool should be efficient."
  4. "The tool should be fast and secure."
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Vague quality words such as "fast," "secure," and "lightweight" cannot be checked. A usable non-functional requirement has a number, a named limit, or a clear yes or no, and the zero-dependency line is a yes or no that a reviewer can verify by inspecting the project. The other options repeat vague words. This line is also a real feature of the ScreenGrab case study.

Concept Tested: Non-Functional Requirement

See: Non-Functional Requirements

docs.title: 9. While drafting a specification you think of "remember the last selected region." Tracing it back, no part of the need calls for it. What should you do?
docs.text:
1. Add it as a functional requirement because it is convenient
  2. Add it as a non-functional requirement
  3. Leave it out silently and say nothing
  4. Place it on the non-goals list
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Every requirement should trace back to the need, and one that serves no part of it is a candidate for deletion. Writing it down as a non-goal is better than silence, because the list settles later arguments and prevents an agent from adding the feature on its own. This question is described as the single most effective way to keep a specification minimal.

Concept Tested: Scope Boundaries

See: Setting Boundaries

docs.title: 10. Why does choosing the clipboard as the only output avoid so much work?
docs.text:
1. Saving a file would require decisions about where, under what name, in which format, and what to do if the file exists, and each decision is a requirement, a test, and a possible bug
  2. Clipboard output is the only output macOS allows
  3. The clipboard requires no testing
  4. Files cannot hold images
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The specification makes the clipboard the only destination, which is itself a cut: no folders, no file names, no format menus. Each avoided decision removes a requirement, a test, and a place for bugs. This is omission paying off, and the explicit non-goal "the tool does not save the image to a file" keeps an agent from adding it back. Options B, C, and D are not true.

Concept Tested: Clipboard Output

See: Region Selection, Delayed Capture and Clipboard Output

docs.title: References: Requirements and Minimal Specifications
docs.text:
1. Requirements analysis - Wikipedia - Describes eliciting, analyzing, and documenting what a system must do. Establishes the process the chapter shrinks into a minimal specification.

  2. Non-functional requirement - Wikipedia - Explains qualities such as performance, security, and usability that constrain how a system behaves. Covers the non-functional side of the chapter's requirements split.

  3. Minimum viable product - Wikipedia - Defines the smallest version of a product that delivers value and supports learning. Parallels the chapter's aim of the smallest specification that keeps a tool small.

  4. User Stories Applied: For Agile Software Development - Mike Cohn - Addison-Wesley - Cohn popularized the As a, I want, so that story template and the INVEST checklist for good stories. His format turns a user need into a short, testable requirement.

  5. Specification by Example - Gojko Adzic - Manning - Adzic advocated using concrete examples as the shared specification and as executable acceptance tests. His approach clarifies how acceptance criteria stay testable instead of vague.

  6. User Stories - Mountain Goat Software - Cohn's own introduction to writing stories, with templates and advice on keeping them small. A free primary source for the story format used in this chapter.

  7. Given When Then - Martin Fowler - Explains the Given, When, Then structure for describing behavior as an example. A compact model for writing the acceptance criteria this chapter requires.

  8. Painless Functional Specifications, Part 1: Why Bother? - Joel on Software - Spolsky makes the case for a short, readable specification before coding and shows what it saves. Supports the chapter's claim that a minimal spec pays for itself.

  9. YAGNI - Martin Fowler - Explains the You Aren't Gonna Need It rule against building features before they are needed. Shows how non-goals protect scope in a minimal specification.

  10. User Stories and Story Examples - Atlassian - Shows how teams write, size, and organize user stories with examples. A practical complement for students drafting their first requirement statements.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter shows how a specification becomes a design that fits a real platform. It covers design decisions and trade-offs, prototypes and feasibility checks, third-party dependencies, and zero-dependency design, then applies them to ScreenGrab's menu bar app, global hotkey, screen recording permission, and freeze-frame selection. No Swift or macOS experience is assumed. After this chapter, you will be able to read a design document and judge the trade-offs behind its decisions.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 17 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Software Design 31 Design Document 1 Design Decision 11 Design Trade-Off 2 Platform Constraints 15 Prototype 3 Technical Feasibility Check 1 Agent Experiments 1 Programming Language Choice 1 Third-Party Dependency 3 Zero-Dependency Design 1 Native Application 11 Menu Bar App 6 Global Hotkey 5 Hotkey Conflict 1 Screen Recording Permission 4 Freeze-Frame Selection 4

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat
  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 7: Requirements and Minimal Specifications

From the What to the How

The specification said what the tool does. Now someone has to decide how, and every choice either keeps the shell light or loads it down. By the end of this chapter you will be able to read a design and tell which choices earned their place. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: What Design Is
docs.text:
Software design is the stage between the specification and the code where you decide how the software will be organized and built to meet the requirements. The specification says what the tool must do. The design says what pieces it will have, how they fit together, which technologies it will use, and how it will cope with the limits of the machine it runs on.

An analogy helps. A homeowner's request is "a kitchen where two people can cook at once". That is the specification. The design is the floor plan: where the stove, the sink, and the counters go, and why. Nobody can build a kitchen from the request alone, and nobody wants to discover the floor plan problems after the walls are up. The same holds for software, and it matters even more when an AI agent writes the code, because the agent will make design choices whether or not you do. If you leave the design unstated, the agent picks the common one.

Design works at three levels, from broad to narrow. At the broadest level, you choose the shape of the product: a menu bar utility, a window application, or a command-line program. In the middle, you choose the main pieces and how they talk to each other. At the narrowest level, you choose details such as the data each piece passes along. For a two-feature tool, most of the value is at the first two levels. A worked example: deciding "this is a menu bar utility with a hotkey, a capture step, and a clipboard step" settles more than any single line of code will, and it can be read and challenged in a minute.

docs.title: Design Document
docs.text:
A design document is a written record of the design: the main pieces, the technology choices, and the reasons behind them. It is read by the builder before coding starts, and by the reviewer afterward. In the ScreenGrab case the specification, design, and README together came to about 1,340 lines, and the design document is the middle piece of that set.

A short design document for a tool like this might contain a list of components, the decisions made with their reasons, the platform limits that shaped them, and the risks that remain. It is worth writing even for a small tool, because the agent can generate it from the specification in minutes and you can review it in a few more. A design document is also a safeguard: a year from now, it explains why the tool is built the way it is.

docs.title: Design Decisions and Trade-Offs
docs.text:
A design decision is a specific choice among alternatives about how the software will be built. Which language will it be written in? Will it have a window or live in the menu bar? Will it use a library or write the feature itself? Each decision should be recorded with the options considered and the reason for the choice.

A design trade-off is the cost that comes with a choice: gaining one quality means giving up another. There is almost never a free option. A worked example is the decision to write the clipboard feature yourself or to rely on a third-party library. The library saves effort now but adds an outside piece that must be kept up to date. Writing it yourself costs a little time now but nothing later.

Decision You gain You give up Use a library for a feature Less code to write and test An outside piece to update and trust Write the feature yourself Full control, nothing external More code in your own tool Add a settings window User choice More code, more tests, more things that can break Keep one fixed behavior Simplicity Flexibility

A design decision recorded without its trade-off is only half useful. When the reason is lost, a later reader cannot tell whether the choice still makes sense after circumstances change.

Every Choice Has a Price Tag

Think of each design decision as a purchase: what do you get, and what do you pay? A design that lists only the benefits has hidden the bill. When you read a design document, look for the "gives up" half.

docs.title: Platform Constraints
docs.text:
Platform constraints are the rules and limits that the operating system and its environment impose on any software that runs there. A platform is the base that software is built on, such as macOS, Windows, or a web browser. The platform decides what an application may do on its own, what needs the user's permission, and what the system reserves for itself.

Platform constraints matter more for a screen grab tool than for most small programs, because capturing the screen touches things the system guards closely. Software that can see everything on your display could also spy on it, so macOS puts several gates in the way. A worked example of the constraints that shaped ScreenGrab, each explained in its own section below:
