Constraint What the platform requires Effect on the design Screen recording permission The user must grant the app permission before it can capture the screen The design must ask for permission and handle a refusal Global hotkeys The system decides which shortcuts an app may claim The design must pick a shortcut and cope with a conflict Application packaging macOS expects a particular structure for an app and a signature on it The design must include a build and install step (Chapter 9) Supported system versions Newer macOS versions change what is allowed The design states which versions it targets

The lesson is that a specification can be perfectly reasonable and still be hard to build on a particular platform. Design is where that collision is found. It is far cheaper to find it in a document than in a failed build.

docs.title: Programming Language Choice
docs.text: Programming language choice is the decision about which language the software will be written in. The choice is shaped by the platform. For a macOS application, the platform's own language is Swift, which gives direct access to every system feature. The case study's app is written in Swift, in about 2,000 lines across 19 files. A good habit is to let the agent propose a language, then ask it to justify the choice against the specification, because a language is hard to change once thousands of lines depend on it. Other options exist, such as wrapping a web page in a cross-platform shell, but they carry more weight and less system integration. You do not need to know Swift to follow this book. You only need to see that the language is a design decision with a reason attached.

docs.title: Native Application
docs.text:
A native application is software built with the platform's own tools and libraries, so that it runs directly on the operating system, not inside another layer such as a web browser. A native macOS app behaves like the other Mac apps: it starts quickly, uses the system's own controls, and can reach system features such as the menu bar and the clipboard without a go-between.

The alternative is a cross-platform application, which is written once and run on several systems, usually by including a large runtime that brings its own copy of a browser engine. The trade-off is clear. Cross-platform saves work if you need to support many systems, but it makes the application larger and slower to start and gives up some system integration.

A worked example for ScreenGrab: the tool is for Macs only, as the specification's assumption states. Nothing is gained from supporting other systems, so the native choice costs nothing and wins on size and integration. This ties to the install size and idle resource use that Chapter 1 named as parts of bloat. The case study's generated app came to about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, small enough that the whole program fits in a few files you could read in an afternoon.

Native application Cross-platform application Built with The platform's own tools A shared runtime plus the app's code Size and start-up Small and quick Larger and slower System features Direct access Through an extra layer Best when One platform is enough Many platforms must be served

docs.title: Third-Party Dependency
docs.text: A third-party dependency is a piece of code written by someone else that your software relies on, such as a library you include so that you do not have to write a feature yourself. Dependencies are normal in modern software and often a good idea. They also carry costs: you must keep them updated, you inherit their bugs, and any security flaw in them becomes a flaw in your tool. A worked example: a library for copying images could save an hour of writing, but it arrives with its own updates, its own bugs, and the chance that its maker stops maintaining it. Each of those becomes your problem on the day you depend on it. Dependencies are a trade-off, not a mistake, and the decision should be made on purpose.

docs.title: Zero-Dependency Design
docs.text:
A zero-dependency design is a design that uses only what the platform already provides, with no third-party code at all. The ScreenGrab app takes this route: the case study records the generated app as having no third-party dependencies. The benefit is a short list of things that can go wrong. There is nothing to update, nothing for a vendor to abandon, and nothing outside the code that you must trust.

The cost is that you write, or have the agent write, features a library would have supplied. For a tool with two features this cost is small. That is why the zero-dependency choice fits a minimal specification so well: the smaller the tool, the cheaper it is to own all of it. In Chapter 14 you will see the maintenance payoff.

docs.title: Checking the Design Before Building It
docs.text: A design can look sound on paper and still fail on the real platform. Three cheap activities find those failures early.

docs.title: Prototype
docs.text: A prototype is a quick, rough version of part of the software, built to test an idea, not to be kept. A prototype may have no polish and no tests. Its job is to answer a question. Because an AI agent can write small programs in minutes, prototypes cost very little in this approach, so there is rarely a reason to guess when you can try. A worked example: to test whether a menu bar app can show a menu, a prototype might be a single file that puts an icon in the menu bar with one item that prints a message. If it works, you keep the knowledge and discard the file. The word "throwaway" is the point: do not let a prototype quietly become the product, because it was built without the tests and care the real tool needs.

docs.title: Technical Feasibility Check
docs.text: A technical feasibility check is a test of whether something the design depends on can actually be done on the target platform. It is the question "can this work at all?" asked before committing to the rest of the build. For ScreenGrab, the riskiest assumptions are that an app living in the menu bar can respond to a global hotkey, and that it can capture the screen once the user grants permission. If either were impossible, the whole design would need to change. The answer is usually yes or no, and either answer is useful. A "no" saves you from building on something that cannot work, and a "yes" lets you proceed with less worry. Feasibility checks should be done in order of risk, starting with the item that would hurt most if it failed.

docs.title: Agent Experiments
docs.text:
Agent experiments are small trials that you ask the coding agent to run to answer a design question, such as "write a ten-line program that registers this hotkey and prints a message when it fires, then run it." The agent writes it, runs it, and reports what happened. Because the output is visible, you can see the answer for yourself rather than trust a description. Experiments turn a risky guess into a known result for a few cents of tokens.

A worked example ties the three together. The author's design depends on a global hotkey. Before building the whole app, the agent builds a tiny prototype that only registers the hotkey and prints a line when it is pressed. Running it is a feasibility check, and the agent doing so is an agent experiment. If nothing prints, the problem is found in minutes, not after the other 1,990 lines exist. The case study is candid that one early hotkey failure was never explained, which is a reminder that even this practice does not remove every surprise.

Test the Scary Part First

List the two or three things in your design that you are least sure the platform allows, and ask the agent to prototype only those. Do it before it writes the rest, so a bad surprise costs minutes, not a rebuild.

docs.title: ScreenGrab's Design Choices
docs.text: The next four sections apply the ideas above to the four features of the platform that shape ScreenGrab. Each is a platform constraint, a design decision, and a trade-off at once.

docs.title: Menu Bar App
docs.text:
A menu bar app is an application that lives in the strip of icons at the top of the macOS screen and has no regular window or Dock icon of its own. You click its icon to open a small menu, and otherwise it stays out of sight. Many small Mac utilities work this way, because it keeps them always available and almost invisible.

The choice fits a screen grab tool for three reasons. The tool is used for seconds at a time, so a full window would be wasted. It must be ready at once, so it should stay running in the background. And it should not clutter the screen it is about to photograph. The case study confirms that grabs from the menu were seen working, which means the menu is one of the two ways to start a capture. The usual trade-off is that a menu bar app can show very little: there is no room for a rich window, so everything must fit in a short menu. For a tool whose whole interface is "start a grab" and perhaps "quit," that limit costs nothing.

Aspect Menu bar app Regular window app Visible presence A small icon in the menu bar A window and a Dock icon Good for Quick utilities used for seconds Tasks that need a workspace Cost Cannot show much; settings are cramped Takes space and attention Fit for ScreenGrab Strong: always ready, out of the way Poor: nothing to display

docs.title: Global Hotkey
docs.text:
A global hotkey is a keyboard shortcut that works no matter which application is in front. Most shortcuts only work inside the program you are using, such as Command-C to copy. A global hotkey is registered with the system, which then reports the key press to your app even when you are working in another one.

A global hotkey suits a screen grab tool because the moment you want a grab is when another program is on screen, not your tool. The ScreenGrab design uses Control-Shift-4. The case study records grabs from the Control-Shift-4 hotkey as seen working. It also records that an early hotkey failure was never explained, so the hotkey is a good example of a platform feature that is easy to describe and harder to make reliable.

Global hotkeys connect to platform constraints in two ways. The system controls which shortcuts an app may claim, and some ways of watching the keyboard require the user to grant extra permission. A worked example of the design reasoning: the team wants the shortcut to work from any app, which requires a global registration. They want to avoid a permission prompt that has nothing to do with screen capture, so they prefer a mechanism that does not need one. Each of those is a design decision with a trade-off, and each belongs in the design document.

docs.title: Hotkey Conflict
docs.text: A hotkey conflict happens when two programs, or the system and a program, both want the same shortcut. Only one can win, and the other silently does nothing. macOS already uses Command-Shift-3, 4, and 5 for its own built-in screenshots, so a custom tool that claimed Command-Shift-4 would collide with the system. Choosing a combination the system does not use, such as Control-Shift-4, avoids this. A conflict is a good reason to make the shortcut a recorded design decision and to expect to change it if it clashes with another program on a user's machine. A worked example of the symptom: the user presses the hotkey and nothing happens, with no error message. That silence is typical of a conflict, which is why the troubleshooting list for any hotkey tool should begin with "is another program using this shortcut?" A clear design might also let the user change the shortcut, though that adds a feature, so a minimal tool may simply document the one it chose.

docs.title: Screen Recording Permission
docs.text:
Screen recording permission is the macOS setting that lets an app capture the contents of the screen. By default an app cannot see other programs' windows. The user must open the system's privacy settings and allow the app. Without the permission, a capture may produce an image missing the other windows, so the picture looks wrong while nothing reports an error.

The permission is a platform constraint that shapes the user's first experience. The design must decide how the app finds out whether it has permission, how it asks, and what it says when the answer is no. A worked example of the experience: the user installs the app, presses the hotkey, and nothing useful appears. Without a design for the permission, the tool seems broken. With one, the app notices that permission is missing and explains the single setting to change.

A Blank Picture Is Not a Bug in Your Code

If a first capture shows a wallpaper or only one window, suspect the permission before you suspect the code. The fix is in the system's privacy settings, not in the app. Put that check first in your testing, and put the message in the app so the next user does not have to guess.

docs.title: Freeze-Frame Selection
docs.text:
Freeze-frame selection is a way of choosing a screen region by first capturing the whole screen as a still picture, then letting the user drag a rectangle over that still picture. The final capture is cut out of the frozen image, not taken from the live screen.

The design solves three problems that live selection has. The screen can change while the user drags, because a clock ticks, a video plays, or a notification arrives, and the result would differ from what the user saw when they started. The selection outline itself could end up in the picture. And a menu that closes when the mouse moves can be captured only if the picture is taken before the pointer reaches it. Freezing the screen first makes the picture match what the user saw at the instant they started.

The cost is that the tool must capture the full screen before the user selects anything, which makes the screen recording permission essential, and it must display the frozen picture as an overlay. A worked comparison:

Live selection Freeze-frame selection Picture taken After the drag, from the live screen Before the drag, then cropped Moving content May change during the drag Fixed at the moment of the hotkey Selection outline in the picture A risk Never, since the picture predates the outline Needs Less Full-screen capture first

Platform Words Are Just Words

If terms like "global hotkey" and "permission" feel like a foreign language, remember that you only need the idea behind each one: where it lives, what it asks of the user, and what it costs. You have already used all of them as a user. This chapter just shows you the other side of the screen.

docs.title: Reading a Design by Its Trade-Offs
docs.text: The component map below shows how the choices fit together. Before you use it, here is one more term: a component is a distinct part of the software with a single job. Seven components make up the simplified picture, and the map follows one immediate grab from the hotkey press to the clipboard. It is a teaching simplification, not a listing of the actual source files.

docs.title: Diagram: ScreenGrab Component Map
docs.text:
ScreenGrab Component Map

Type: graph-model sim-id: screengrab-component-map Library: vis-network Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: explain Learning Objective: The learner will explain the order in which seven components handle one immediate screen grab, by choosing the next component correctly in at least 5 of 6 steps.

Prerequisites: menu bar app, global hotkey, screen recording permission, freeze-frame selection, clipboard output, component (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: At each of six steps the learner commits the next component in the path before it is revealed. A choice is correct when it matches the "Next component" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Clicking a component to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The picture is taken after the user finishes dragging. (2) The permission is checked only once at install time and then never matters. (3) The menu bar icon does the capturing.

Instructional Rationale: Predicting the next component forces the learner to reason from each component's job to the sequence, which shows the design is understood as a flow and not as a list of parts.

Content:

The seven components (the nodes), each with the description shown when the learner opens it. The map is a simplified, illustrative teaching model of the design described in this chapter.

# Component Description shown 1 Global hotkey Listens for Control-Shift-4 from any application and starts a grab 2 Menu bar item Shows the icon in the menu bar and offers a menu command that starts a grab; it does not capture anything itself 3 Permission check Confirms that screen recording permission has been granted; if not, tells the user what to change 4 Screen freeze Captures the whole screen as a still picture at the moment of the grab 5 Selection overlay Shows the still picture and lets the user drag a rectangle over it 6 Crop Cuts the chosen rectangle out of the still picture 7 Clipboard Receives the cropped image so that it can be pasted

The connections (the edges), shown as the path of one immediate grab: Global hotkey to Permission check; Menu bar item to Permission check; Permission check to Screen freeze; Screen freeze to Selection overlay; Selection overlay to Crop; Crop to Clipboard.

Six prediction steps, in this order:

Step Component shown Choices Next component Why (shown as feedback) 1 Global hotkey Permission check; Crop; Clipboard Permission check Nothing can be captured until permission is confirmed 2 Permission check Selection overlay; Screen freeze; Clipboard Screen freeze With permission confirmed, the whole screen is captured as a still 3 Screen freeze Crop; Selection overlay; Global hotkey Selection overlay The still picture is displayed so the user can drag over it 4 Selection overlay Clipboard; Crop; Screen freeze Crop The chosen rectangle is cut from the still picture 5 Crop Clipboard; Permission check; Menu bar item Clipboard The cropped image is delivered to the clipboard 6 Menu bar item Permission check; Selection overlay; Clipboard Permission check The menu command starts the same path, so it also goes through the permission check first

Provenance: Component names and the order come from this chapter, sections "Menu Bar App", "Global Hotkey", "Screen Recording Permission", "Freeze-Frame Selection" and "Clipboard Output" (Chapter 7). The map is a simplified teaching model, and the sim labels it "simplified and illustrative, not the source code layout".

Rules: The path has exactly one correct next component at each step. The two start points (Global hotkey and Menu bar item) merge at Permission check. Choices are shown in the fixed order of the table.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the seven components and may open any one to read its description.
  2. The learner starts the six prediction steps. At each step the current component is highlighted and the learner chooses the next one from three choices.
  3. After each choice the sim reveals the correct next component, draws the connection, and shows the Why text.
  4. After step 6, the full path is shown, and the learner should notice that two different starts share the same path.

Feedback: Six steps, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: " and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct component and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 6" is shown. A final score of 5 or 6 shows "You can trace a grab"; a lower score invites a restart.

Starting State: The seven components are shown with no connections drawn, and the question is "What happens first when the user presses the hotkey?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states seven components, six prediction steps, mastery at 5 of 6, and the hotkey Control-Shift-4.

The second practice activity moves from structure to judgment. Reading a design well means asking, for each decision, which option best serves what the specification values. The judge below gives eight decisions with a stated priority and two options each.

docs.title: Diagram: Design Trade-Off Judge
docs.text:
Design Trade-Off Judge

Type: microsim sim-id: design-trade-off-judge Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge which of two options best serves a stated priority in each of 8 design decisions, with at least 6 correct.

Prerequisites: design decision, design trade-off, third-party dependency, zero-dependency design, native application, menu bar app, global hotkey, hotkey conflict, screen recording permission, freeze-frame selection, prototype (all defined in this chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each decision the learner commits one of two options. A choice is correct when it matches the "Better option" column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 8 correct. Reading the trade-off summary of an option before choosing is exploration.

Misconceptions: (1) Using a library is always better because it is less work. (2) The most feature-rich option is the best design. (3) A design decision has a right answer apart from the priority it serves.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating means choosing against a criterion. Each decision states its criterion as a priority, so the learner must connect a trade-off to what the specification values instead of picking the option that sounds more impressive.

Content:

The eight decisions, in this order. All are illustrative and based on the ScreenGrab design described in the chapter.

# Decision Stated priority Option 1 Option 2 Better option Why (shown as feedback) 1 How to read the screen's pixels No third-party libraries; easy to maintain Use the platform's own capture capability Add a third-party capture library Option 1 It meets the no-libraries priority and leaves nothing outside to update 2 How the tool presents itself Always ready; no window clutter A regular app with a window and a Dock icon A menu bar app Option 2 A menu bar app is always available and stays out of the way 3 How to start a capture while another app is in front Works from any application A shortcut that works only while the tool's own window is in front A global hotkey Option 2 Only a global hotkey is reported to the tool when another app is in front 4 How to pick the region The picture matches what the user saw when starting Let the user drag over the live screen Freeze the screen first, then drag over the still picture Option 2 A frozen picture cannot change during the drag 5 Which shortcut to choose Avoid clashing with the system Reuse Command-Shift-4 Choose a combination the system does not already use Option 2 Command-Shift-4 is already a built-in macOS screenshot shortcut, which would conflict 6 How to learn whether hotkeys work for a background app Find problems early and cheaply Build the whole app, then test the hotkey Write a tiny prototype that only registers the hotkey and prints a message Option 2 A prototype answers the risky question in minutes before the rest is built 7 How to build for a Mac-only tool Small size; fits the system A native application A cross-platform shell wrapping a web page Option 1 Native is smaller and integrates directly, and no other platform is needed 8 What to do when screen recording permission is missing Avoid blank pictures without explanation Capture anyway and hope the picture is right Detect the missing permission and tell the user what to change Option 2 Without the permission, captures can look wrong with no error, so the user needs a message

Counts: Option 1 is better in 2 decisions (1 and 7), Option 2 is better in 6 decisions (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8).

Provenance: Decisions are illustrative and based on this chapter's sections. The Command-Shift-4 system shortcut is a standard macOS feature described in the section "Hotkey Conflict". The sim labels the scenarios "illustrative".

Rules: Each decision has exactly one better option given its stated priority. Option order is as in the table. Stating the priority is part of each decision. A decision cannot be re-answered.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads decision 1, its stated priority, and the two options.
  2. The learner chooses Option 1 or Option 2 and confirms.
  3. The sim shows whether the choice is correct and the Why text, then moves on.
  4. After decision 8, the sim shows the score and, for each decision answered wrongly, the priority it served. The learner should notice that the right answer follows the priority.

Feedback: Eight decisions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" and the Why text. Incorrect: the better option and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 6 or more shows "You can judge a design"; a lower score invites a restart.

Starting State: Decision 1 is shown with its priority and two options, and the question "Which option better serves the priority?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that Command-Shift-3, 4 and 5 are macOS's built-in screenshot shortcuts, that ScreenGrab uses Control-Shift-4, and that the app uses no third-party dependencies. The judge has 8 decisions with mastery at 6 of 8.

You Can Read a Design

You can now read a design document, name the trade-off behind each decision, and explain why ScreenGrab is a native, menu bar, zero-dependency app with a global hotkey, a permission check, and freeze-frame selection. Next, you will watch that design become running code.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Software Design and Platform Constraints
docs.text: Test your understanding of design decisions, platform constraints, dependencies, feasibility checks, and the ScreenGrab design choices with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a zero-dependency design?
docs.text:
1. A design that has no requirements
  2. A design that depends on a single large library
  3. A design that uses only what the platform already provides, with no third-party code
  4. A design that needs no operating system
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. ScreenGrab takes this route, and the case study records the generated app as having no third-party dependencies. The benefit is a short list of things that can go wrong: nothing to update, nothing for a vendor to abandon, and nothing outside the code that you must trust. The cost is writing features a library would have supplied, which is small for a two-feature tool.

Concept Tested: Zero-Dependency Design

See: Dependencies

docs.title: 2. What is a global hotkey?
docs.text:
1. A keyboard shortcut registered with the system that works no matter which application is in front
  2. A shortcut that works only inside one program
  3. A key combination that restarts the computer
  4. A shortcut shared by all programs at once
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Most shortcuts, such as Command-C, only work inside the program you are using. A global hotkey is registered with the system, which reports the key press to your app even when you work in another one. That suits a screen grab tool because the moment you want a grab is when another program is on screen. ScreenGrab uses Control-Shift-4.

Concept Tested: Global Hotkey

See: Global Hotkey

docs.title: 3. What is screen recording permission?
docs.text:
1. A license that allows an app to be sold
  2. A setting that lets an app record video only
  3. A fee charged for each screenshot
  4. The macOS setting that lets an app capture the contents of the screen
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. By default an app cannot see other programs' windows, so the user must allow it in the system's privacy settings. Without the permission, a capture may produce an image missing the other windows, so the picture looks wrong while nothing reports an error. The design must decide how the app learns whether it has permission, how it asks, and what it says when the answer is no.

Concept Tested: Screen Recording Permission

See: Screen Recording Permission

docs.title: 4. What is a design trade-off?
docs.text:
1. A discount offered when two products are bought together
  2. The cost that comes with a choice, where gaining one quality means giving up another
  3. A disagreement between the designer and the user
  4. A choice that has no downsides
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. There is almost never a free option. Using a library gains less code to write and test but gives up an outside piece to update and trust. Writing the feature yourself gives control and nothing external but adds more code to your own tool. The chapter advises recording each design decision with its trade-off, because without the reason a later reader cannot tell whether the choice still makes sense.

Concept Tested: Design Trade-Off

See: Design Decisions and Trade-Offs

docs.title: 5. Why does freeze-frame selection capture the whole screen before the user drags a rectangle?
docs.text:
1. To make the final image larger
  2. To avoid needing screen recording permission
  3. So the final picture matches what the user saw at the instant they started, unaffected by moving content or the selection outline
  4. To save memory
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. With live selection, the screen can change while the user drags, the selection outline might appear in the picture, and a menu that closes when the mouse moves may be lost. Freezing the screen first fixes all three problems, because the final capture is cut from the frozen image. The cost is that the full-screen capture happens first, which makes screen recording permission essential. Option B is therefore the opposite of the truth.

Concept Tested: Freeze-Frame Selection

See: Freeze-Frame Selection

docs.title: 6. What is the main trade-off between a native application and a cross-platform application?
docs.text:
1. Cross-platform saves work when many systems must be served but is larger, slower to start, and has less direct system integration
  2. Native applications cannot use the clipboard
  3. Cross-platform applications are always smaller
  4. Native applications require a web browser
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A native app is built with the platform's own tools, so it starts quickly, uses system controls, and reaches features such as the menu bar and clipboard directly. A cross-platform app usually includes a large runtime that brings its own browser engine. Because ScreenGrab is for Macs only, the native choice costs nothing and wins on size and integration, which connects to Chapter 1's install size and idle resource use.

Concept Tested: Native Application

See: Native Application

docs.title: 7. Your design depends on a global hotkey, and you are unsure it will work. What is the cheapest sensible first step?
docs.text:
1. Build the entire app and hope the hotkey works
  2. Remove the hotkey from the design without testing
  3. Ask users to guess whether it works
  4. Ask the agent to build a tiny prototype that only registers the hotkey and prints a line when pressed
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. This is both a technical feasibility check and an agent experiment: a small throwaway test answers whether the design can work at all, for a few cents of tokens. If nothing prints, you find the problem in minutes instead of after the other 1,990 lines exist. The chapter also candidly notes that one early hotkey failure in the case study was never explained, so even this practice does not remove every surprise.

Concept Tested: Technical Feasibility Check

See: Checking the Design Before Building It

docs.title: 8. A user presses a custom hotkey and nothing happens, with no error message. According to the chapter, which cause is typical of this symptom?
docs.text:
1. A native application
  2. A hotkey conflict, where another program or the system already claims the same shortcut
  3. A zero-dependency design
  4. Too many acceptance criteria
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. When two programs, or the system and a program, want the same shortcut, only one wins and the other silently does nothing. macOS already uses Command-Shift-3, 4, and 5 for built-in screenshots, which is why ScreenGrab chose Control-Shift-4. The silence is the telltale sign, and the chapter suggests recording the shortcut as a design decision you expect to change if it clashes on a user's machine.

Concept Tested: Hotkey Conflict

See: Hotkey Conflict

docs.title: 9. A user installs the app, presses the hotkey, and the captured image is missing other programs' windows. What is the most likely platform constraint at work?
docs.text:
1. The screen recording permission has not been granted
  2. The delay is set too short
  3. The clipboard is full
  4. The app uses too many libraries
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Without screen recording permission, a capture may omit other programs' windows, and the picture looks wrong while nothing reports an error. The chapter says a design without a permission plan makes the tool seem broken, while a good design notices that permission is missing and explains the single setting to change. Options B, C, and D do not explain missing windows.

Concept Tested: Screen Recording Permission

See: Screen Recording Permission

docs.title: 10. Why is the menu bar app form a strong fit for ScreenGrab?
docs.text:
1. It lets the app show a rich workspace window
  2. It guarantees the tool never has bugs
  3. The tool is used for seconds at a time, must be ready at once, and should not clutter the screen it is about to photograph
  4. It removes the need for a hotkey
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A menu bar app lives in the strip of icons at the top of the screen with no regular window or Dock icon, so it is always available and nearly invisible. The usual trade-off, that it can show very little, costs nothing when the whole interface is "start a grab" and perhaps "quit." A regular window app would take space and attention for a tool with nothing to display.

Concept Tested: Menu Bar App

See: Menu Bar App

docs.title: References: Software Design and Platform Constraints
docs.text:
1. Software design - Wikipedia - Defines software design as the process of turning requirements into a plan for implementation, including structure and interfaces. Frames the design document the chapter teaches readers to interpret.

  2. AppKit - Wikipedia - Describes Apple's framework for building macOS graphical applications, including windows, menus, and events. Background for the native, menu bar design decisions in ScreenGrab.

  3. Screenshot - Wikipedia - Explains how screen captures are produced and the operating-system facilities involved. Grounds the chapter's discussion of capture permissions and freeze-frame selection.

  4. A Philosophy of Software Design - John Ousterhout - Yaknyan Press - Ousterhout's central idea is the deep module, with a simple interface hiding substantial functionality, as the weapon against complexity. His vocabulary helps readers judge whether a design stays small.

  5. Fundamentals of Software Architecture - Mark Richards and Neal Ford - O'Reilly - The authors' first law states that everything in software architecture is a trade-off. That principle underlies the chapter's habit of naming the trade-off behind each design decision.

  6. Human Interface Guidelines - Apple Developer - Apple's official design guidance for macOS apps, covering menu bar extras, windows, and system conventions. Explains why a platform-native design feels consistent to users.

  7. NSStatusItem - Apple Developer Documentation - Reference for the menu bar item class used to place an app in the system status bar. Concrete documentation for the menu bar design choice.

  8. ScreenCaptureKit - Apple Developer Documentation - Documents Apple's framework for capturing screen content, including permission requirements. Shows the platform constraint behind the chapter's permission check. Read it alongside the design's permission check.

  9. Documenting Architecture Decisions - Michael Nygard - Introduces the architecture decision record, a short note capturing context, decision, and consequences. A template for recording the trade-offs a design document explains.

  10. Architecture Decision Records - ADR GitHub Organization - Collects ADR templates, tools, and examples from many teams. Gives students ready formats for documenting the design choices they read in this chapter.

docs.title: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
Summary
docs.text: This chapter follows the design into running software. It covers code generation, compiler errors, the developer toolchain, build and installer scripts, rollback and uninstall, code signing, the README, and the Git workflow that records each step. It closes by assembling the ScreenGrab case study from the specification through the first install. After this chapter, you will be able to describe every stage of the AI-assisted build process and direct an agent through them.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Code Generation 3 Compiler Errors 4 Build Script 10 Developer Toolchain 3 Installer Script 4 Install Rollback 1 Uninstall Process 1 README File 4 Version Control 14 Git Repository 13 Git Commit 5 Git Push And Pull 4 Code Signing 2 Ad-Hoc Signing 1 ScreenGrab Case Study 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 7: Requirements and Minimal Specifications
  • Chapter 8: Software Design and Platform Constraints

From Paper to Running Program

You have a specification and a design, which means the hard thinking is done. Now watch an agent turn them into an app you can click, and learn the handful of scripts and habits that make the result repeatable. Grab only what you need!

docs.title: Code Generation
docs.text:
Code generation is the step where the AI coding agent writes the source code from the specification and the design. The agent reads the documents, decides which files are needed, and writes them. This is the step most people picture when they imagine AI building software, and it is the shortest part of the work in terms of your effort. Your effort went into the earlier steps, which determine what the agent writes.

The quality of generated code depends heavily on what came before. A precise specification with clear non-goals produces a small, focused program. A vague one produces something that guesses. In the ScreenGrab case, the app came to about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files with no third-party dependencies, because the specification asked for two features and the design chose to use only what the platform provides.

Generated code is a first draft, not a finished product. It has to be compiled, tested, and reviewed, and the sections below describe the loop that does that.

docs.title: The Developer Toolchain
docs.text:
A developer toolchain is the set of programs that turn source code into a running application and that support the work around it: the compiler, a linker that joins the pieces, build tools, and a debugger. On macOS the toolchain is supplied by Apple's developer tools, which come in two forms. Xcode is the full development environment. The Command Line Tools are a smaller package with just the compiler and related programs and no graphical environment.

The distinction matters in the case study. A later fix was needed for Macs that have only the Command Line Tools. The case study does not say more than that, but it illustrates the general lesson: a build depends on the toolchain, and different machines may have different ones. The toolchain should be named in the README so that the next user knows what to install. A worked example of checking: the command swift --version prints the compiler's version if the toolchain is installed, and an error if it is not. An installer script can run that one command first and stop with a clear message when it fails.

docs.title: Compiler Errors
docs.text:
A compiler is the program that translates source code, which people can read, into the machine instructions the computer runs. When the compiler finds something it cannot translate, it stops and prints a compiler error: a message that names the file, the line, and the reason. Compiler errors are not failures of the project. They are the compiler doing its job, and they are one of the most useful safety nets in the whole process, because the problem is found before the program ever runs.

Before the example, here is how to read the message format: first the file name, then the line number and column where the problem was found, then the word "error", then a plain description. A worked example, with illustrative content:

CaptureController.swift:42:17: error: cannot find 'captureRegion' in scope

This says that on line 42 of the file CaptureController.swift, the code uses a name, captureRegion, that does not exist anywhere the compiler can see. The most likely causes are a misspelled name, or a name the agent assumed but never defined, which is a form of the hallucination described in Chapter 5.

With an agent, the usual cycle is quick. The agent builds the project, reads the errors, edits the files, and builds again. You do not need to understand each error, but you do need to know the cycle exists and that a clean build is only the first checkpoint: code that compiles can still do the wrong thing. A clean build says the code is well-formed, not that the code is right. Tests, covered in Chapter 12, address that gap.

A Wall of Red Text Is Normal

The first build of generated code often prints a screen of errors, and that can feel like failure. It is not: the agent reads those same messages and fixes them, usually in a loop of a few tries. Your job is only to notice if the same error keeps coming back, and then to ask the agent what it has tried.

docs.title: Build Script
docs.text:
A build script is a short program that carries out every step needed to turn the source code into a finished application, in a fixed order, with one command. Without one, a person must remember a dozen separate commands and run them correctly each time. With one, building is repeatable: the same command gives the same result on any machine that has the toolchain.

Before the example, here are the pieces. The first line tells the system to run the file with the Bash shell. The command set -e tells the script to stop at the first error, instead of pressing on and producing a broken result. The swift build line compiles the code. The codesign line signs the finished app, a step explained later in this chapter. This is a simplified illustration of the idea, not the project's actual script.

#!/bin/bash
set -e
swift build -c release
cp .build/release/ScreenGrab ScreenGrab.app/Contents/MacOS/
codesign --force --sign - ScreenGrab.app

The script is five lines, but it already shows the value. If you change a file next month, you do not have to remember how the app is assembled. You run one command. The case study's install and build scripts came to about 500 lines, which is a measure of how much real-world detail a robust version includes: checking that the toolchain is present, handling errors with clear messages, and tidying up.

A Script Is a Recipe You Can Rerun

Notice that the build script moves knowledge out of your head and into a file. A step done by hand is done once, while a step in a script is done the same way every time, by you, by the agent, or by a stranger who downloads the project.

docs.title: Installer Script
docs.text:
An installer script is a program that takes the built application and puts it in place on a computer so that it can be used. For ScreenGrab, that means building the app, signing it, copying it to the Applications location, and starting it. The point of an installer script is that a user types one command and does not need to know the steps.

The script is also where many practical problems live. Does the folder already exist? Is an older version still running? Does the user have the tools? A good installer checks these and says what is wrong in plain words. A worked example of the contrast: a poor installer fails with a cryptic message, while a good one prints "The Swift toolchain was not found. Install the Command Line Tools and run this again." The second saves the user, which may be you in a year, an hour of searching.

The case study shows the pattern: the author asked for the app to be installed with a README, and the first install was done within about 36 minutes of the first prompt. A later fix was needed for Macs with only the Command Line Tools, which is the kind of environment difference an installer must anticipate.

docs.title: Install Rollback
docs.text: Install rollback is the ability to undo a failed or unwanted installation and return to the state before it began. If the installer replaces a working older version and then fails halfway, a rollback restores the older version, so the user is not left with nothing. The usual technique is to keep a backup copy of what is being replaced, install the new version, test that it starts, and only then discard the backup. A rollback matters most for a tool you depend on every day. A worked example for ScreenGrab: the installer finds an older version, copies it aside, installs the new build, and launches it. If the launch fails, the installer puts the older copy back and prints the reason, so the hotkey that worked yesterday still works today.

docs.title: Uninstall Process
docs.text: An uninstall process is the set of steps that removes the application and anything it created, leaving the computer as it was. A tool you can install but not remove is a liability. A good uninstall script deletes the app and its settings files. It also tells the user about anything it cannot remove itself, such as the permission granted in the system's privacy settings, which belongs to the user and which the user must take back. Writing the uninstall script at the same time as the installer keeps the tool honest about what it leaves behind. A worked example of the list it should work through: stop the running app, delete the app from the Applications location, delete any settings file it wrote, and print a reminder to remove the screen recording permission. The reminder is part of the process because the script cannot do that last step for you.

docs.title: Code Signing
docs.text: Code signing is the process of attaching a digital signature to an application, which lets the operating system verify who made it and that it has not been changed since. macOS checks signatures and refuses to run, or warns about, software that is unsigned. It is a platform constraint of the kind Chapter 8 described, and a build script must handle it. Signing also protects against tampering: if a signed app's files are altered after signing, the system can detect that the signature no longer matches. For a downloaded app from a stranger, that check is a real safeguard, and for your own build it is mostly a requirement to satisfy.

docs.title: Ad-Hoc Signing
docs.text:
Ad-hoc signing is code signing without an identity: the app is signed, which satisfies the system's requirement that the code carry a signature, but the signature names no developer and is not backed by a paid developer account. It is the right level for a personal tool that you build and run on your own computers. It does not give strangers any reason to trust the app, and it is why a downloaded personal tool may need extra steps before the system will run it.

A related point: because an ad-hoc signature is tied to the exact build, rebuilding the app can change how the system recognizes it. The practical result may be that you have to grant a permission such as screen recording again. If a permission seems to vanish after a rebuild, this is a likely cause.

Code signing with a developer identity Ad-hoc signing Needs A developer account Nothing beyond the toolchain Tells the system Who made the app Only that the code is signed Good for Distributing to other people A personal tool on your own computers Cost A recurring account fee None

docs.title: The README
docs.text:
A README file is a plain-text document, stored at the top of the project, that explains what the tool is, what it needs, how to install it, and how to use it. It is the first thing a visitor to the project reads. For a personal tool it is also the note you leave for your future self, who will have forgotten everything.

A useful README for ScreenGrab answers five questions in order: what does this do, what does it need before it can be installed, how do I install it, how do I use it, and how do I remove it. It also lists the non-goals, so nobody asks for a feature the tool deliberately omits. A worked example of its skeleton:

Section One line of content What it does Grabs a region of the screen, optionally after a delay, and puts it on the clipboard Requirements A Mac with the Swift toolchain installed Install Run the installer script Use Press Control-Shift-4 or use the menu bar icon Uninstall Run the uninstall script, then remove the permission in system settings Not included Editing, saving, sharing, video

The case study counted the specification, the design, and the README together at about 1,340 lines. An agent writes a README well when it has the specification and the scripts in front of it, but you should still follow it once to confirm that the steps really work.

docs.title: Version Control
docs.text:
Version control is a system that records every change made to a project over time, so that you can see what changed, when, and why, and return to any earlier state. Without it, the only protection against a bad edit is a hope that you remember what the file used to say. With it, a mistake costs a few seconds.

Version control matters even more with an AI agent. An agent can change many files in one go, and it can make mistakes confidently. A complete history lets you compare the new version against the old, see exactly what the agent altered, and roll back if the result is worse. It makes bold edits safe.

A worked example: you ask the agent to add a settings window to ScreenGrab, and the result is larger, slower, and breaks the hotkey. Without history, you would be trying to remember what the project looked like an hour ago. With history, you ask Git to show the changes since your last snapshot, see that the agent added dozens of lines you never asked for, and return to the earlier state with one command. This is the same habit of leaving things out that the earlier chapters taught, applied to code that has already been written: if it should not be there, take it out.

docs.title: Git Repository
docs.text:
Git is the most widely used version control system, and a Git repository is a project folder that Git is tracking, together with its stored history. A repository holds the files as they are now and every earlier recorded version. Creating one is a single command in the project folder, and from then on Git can tell you what has changed.

A worked example of the first steps: in the project folder you run git init to start tracking, then git status to see which files Git has noticed. A new project shows every file as untracked, meaning Git sees them but has not yet recorded them. After the first commit, git status reports a clean state, and from then on it lists only what has changed since. A repository also keeps a list of files to ignore, such as the compiled app, because those can be rebuilt from the source and do not belong in the history.

A repository can be purely local, on your own computer, or it can have a copy on a hosting service such as GitHub, which provides a backup and a way to share the project. Chapter 14 covers sharing a tool as open source.

docs.title: Git Commit
docs.text:
A Git commit is a saved snapshot of the project at a moment in time, together with a message that says what changed and why. Commits are the steps of the history. Each one can be inspected, compared with the one before, or returned to.

Before the example, here is what the commands do. The git add command chooses which changed files go into the next snapshot. The git commit command saves the snapshot, with the text after -m as its message. The git log command lists the history, one line per commit when --oneline is added.

git add .
git commit -m "Add delayed capture with a default of 3 seconds"
git log --oneline

A good message names the change and the reason in a sentence. "Add delayed capture" is useful; "update" is not. A commit should also hold one logical change, so that if it turns out to be wrong, it can be undone without disturbing anything else.

Commit Before You Ask for the Next Thing

Before you send the agent off to change something, commit what you have. If the next change goes wrong, one command takes you back to a known good version.

docs.title: Git Push and Pull
docs.text:
Git push sends your commits from your computer to a remote copy of the repository, such as one on GitHub. Git pull brings commits from the remote copy down to your computer. Together they keep copies in step. Push makes your work backed up and shareable. Pull lets another computer, or another person, receive it.

This matters for a personal tool across several machines. The author has three main computers. After building the tool on one, a push and a pull on each of the others puts the same source on all three, and the same installer script builds it there. That is cheaper and clearer than copying files by hand.

Two cautions keep push and pull safe. First, pull before you push when you work on more than one machine, so that you start from the latest version. Second, if two machines changed the same lines, Git cannot decide which version wins and asks you to resolve the conflict. With a one-person project that rarely happens, which is another small benefit of a personal tool.

Command What it does When you use it git commit Saves a snapshot locally After each logical change git push Sends commits to the remote copy When you want a backup or to share git pull Fetches commits from the remote copy Before you start work on another machine

docs.title: The ScreenGrab Case Study
docs.text: The ScreenGrab case study is the real build that this book follows: a paid screen grab tool replaced by a generated app that does only what its one user needs. The work moved through a set order of specification, design, code, tests, and installer. The arrangement below lets you rehearse that order.

docs.title: Diagram: AI-Assisted Build Stage Sequencer
docs.text:
AI-Assisted Build Stage Sequencer

Type: microsim sim-id: ai-assisted-build-stage-sequencer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/prompt-architecture-builder Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: list Learning Objective: The learner will list the five stages of the ScreenGrab build in their correct order, given five unordered cards that each show a stage and its output, within two attempts.

Prerequisites: minimal specification, design document, code generation, installer script, README file (all defined in this chapter or earlier chapters above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner arranges five cards in a sequence and submits it. The sequence is correct when it matches the "Position" column in Content exactly. Mastery is a correct sequence on the first or second submission.

Misconceptions: (1) Code is written first and the specification is written afterward to describe it. (2) Tests are optional extras added at the end of a project. (3) The installer comes before the code that it installs.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level recall of a sequence is best exercised by reconstructing the sequence from cards, because the learner must retrieve the order from memory instead of recognizing it in a list. Showing each card's output gives the learner a meaningful clue.

Content:

The five cards, shown in a scrambled initial order (Installer, Code, Specification, Tests, Design). Each card shows its stage name and its output:

Position Stage Output shown on the card Why it comes here (shown as feedback) 1 Specification A minimal specification of what the tool does and does not do Everything else is built from what the tool is supposed to do 2 Design A design document of components, decisions, and trade-offs The design turns the requirements into a plan that fits the platform 3 Code About 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files Code is written from the design 4 Tests About 1,370 lines, with 94 automated tests Tests check the code against the specification 5 Installer Install and build scripts of about 500 lines, plus a README The installer packages code that already exists and has been checked

Provenance: Stage order and the numbers on the cards come from the course description section "How the first version was built" and from this chapter's section "The ScreenGrab Case Study".

Rules: The correct sequence is exactly Specification, Design, Code, Tests, Installer. Two submissions are allowed. A submission is correct only if all five positions match.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the five cards in the scrambled order and the instruction "Put the build in the order it happened."
  2. The learner rearranges the cards into a sequence and submits it.
  3. If the sequence is wrong, the sim tells the learner how many cards are in the right position and allows one more attempt. If it is right, the sim shows the Why text for each position.
  4. After the second attempt or a correct sequence, the sim shows the correct order with the Why text for each card.

Feedback: Two attempts. After the first incorrect submission: "n of 5 cards are in the right position. Try once more." After the second incorrect submission, or after a correct one: the correct order and the Why text for each position. A correct submission shows "You can list the build stages".

Starting State: The five cards in the scrambled order and the question "Which stage came first?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states that the work moved through the order specification, design, code, tests, and installer, with about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, about 1,370 test lines with 94 tests, and about 500 lines of scripts.

The first install produced the following, in the author's numbers. Before the table, note that each row counts lines of text in different kinds of files, which is why the totals matter: they show where the effort went.

Result at first install Amount App code about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, with no third-party dependencies Tests about 1,370 lines, with 94 automated tests Install and build scripts about 500 lines Specification, design, and README about 1,340 lines Total about 5,200 lines

The timeline matters as much as the size. The app was built and installed about 36 minutes after the first prompt. The first real screen grab came at about 44 minutes. The whole session, including hotkey testing, took about 70 active minutes. The estimated API cost was about $6 for the build and about $14 for the whole session, figures that exclude generating this textbook, the author's own time, and later maintenance. Chapter 11 breaks these numbers into tokens.

One observation deserves attention: the app code is less than half of the total. The tests are more than two-thirds as long as the app, and the documents and scripts together are longer than the tests. That proportion is typical of software that is meant to be relied on. The chart below lets you work with it directly.

docs.title: Diagram: ScreenGrab First Install Size Breakdown
docs.text:
ScreenGrab First Install Size Breakdown

Type: chart sim-id: screengrab-first-install-size-breakdown Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare the four parts of the ScreenGrab first install by line count and share of the total, answering at least 3 of 4 comparison questions correctly.

Prerequisites: lines of code, source code, installer script, README file, specification (all defined in this chapter or earlier chapters above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: After viewing the chart in both modes, the learner answers four comparison questions, each with a fixed answer. An answer is correct when it matches the "Correct answer" column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct. Switching modes and hovering are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Most of the project is the app code. (2) Tests are a small add-on. (3) Specifications and documents are negligible in size.

Instructional Rationale: Analyzing means breaking a whole into parts and relating them. Comparing parts by both absolute count and share, and then answering questions that require relating two parts, shows whether the learner has absorbed the structure.

Content:

The chart shows four bars. Values are the rounded figures from the chapter, and the sim labels them "approximate, from the course description". The mode toggle switches between "Lines" and "Share of total (%)".

Part Lines Share of total (%) App code (Swift, 19 files) 2,000 38 Tests (94 automated tests) 1,370 26 Install and build scripts 500 10 Specification, design, and README 1,340 26

Shares are computed from the four rounded values, whose sum is 5,210, and rounded to the nearest whole percent. The chapter's stated total is "about 5,200 lines".

The four comparison questions, in order:

# Question Choices Correct answer Why (shown as feedback) 1 Which part is the largest? App code; Tests; Install and build scripts; Specification, design, and README App code At 2,000 lines it exceeds every other part 2 About what share of the lines are tests? 10%; 26%; 38%; 50% 26% 1,370 of 5,210 is about 26% 3 How do the test lines compare with the app code lines? About one-third; About two-thirds; About equal; About double About two-thirds 1,370 divided by 2,000 is about 0.69 4 Which is larger, the install and build scripts or the specification, design, and README? Scripts; Specification, design, and README; Equal Specification, design, and README 1,340 lines is more than twice the 500 lines of scripts

Provenance: The four values come from the course description section "How the first version was built". Shares and ratios are computed from them as stated in Rules.

Rules: Share = part lines divided by 5,210, times 100, rounded to the nearest whole percent. Ratio of tests to app code = 1,370 divided by 2,000. The toggle changes only the displayed axis and values, not the order of the bars. Each question has exactly one correct choice.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner views the chart in Lines mode and hovers each bar to see its value.
  2. The learner switches to Share mode and sees the percentages.
  3. The learner answers the four questions in order, choosing one answer each.
  4. After the fourth question, the sim shows the score and the explanations for any missed. The learner should notice that the app code is the largest part but under 40% of the whole.

Feedback: Four questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct answer and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 4" is shown. A final score of 3 or 4 shows "You can read the breakdown"; a lower score invites a second look at the chart.

Starting State: The chart in Lines mode with all four bars visible and the question "Where did the lines go?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states the four values 2,000, 1,370, 500 and 1,340, the total of about 5,200 lines, 19 files, and 94 tests, and says the app code is less than half of the total.

The case study also records what did not go perfectly, and an honest account must include it. One early hotkey failure was never explained. Several acceptance tests still have to be run by hand, because only a person at the keyboard can see whether a real screen grab behaved. A later fix was needed for Macs with only the Command Line Tools. The installed app has been seen working from both the menu and the Control-Shift-4 hotkey. The current version is open source under the MIT License.

Installed Is Not the Same as Verified

When the installer prints "success," it means the steps ran, not that the tool does its job on your machine. Press the hotkey and make a real grab yourself, then paste it. Do the check on each computer where you install it, because the toolchain and permissions can differ.

The pieces in this chapter fit together as a chain, in which each stage leaves something the next one needs. The table below summarizes the chain, using only terms defined above.

Stage What it leaves behind What protects you Code generation Source files Compiler errors that catch malformed code Build script A finished app One repeatable command Signing A signed app The system's signature check Installer script An installed app Rollback if the install fails README Instructions A reader who can follow them Git commit and push A recorded history and a backup The ability to undo Uninstall script A clean removal A tool you can leave

You Can Direct the Whole Build

You can now describe every stage from generated code to a running install: compiling and its errors, build and installer scripts with rollback and uninstall, signing, the README, and the Git commits that record each step. Next, you will learn what all of this cost in tokens.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
docs.text: Test your understanding of code generation, compiling, build and installer scripts, code signing, the README, version control, and the ScreenGrab case study with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a build script?
docs.text:
1. A document that lists the features the app must have
  2. A short program that carries out every step needed to turn source code into a finished application, in a fixed order, with one command
  3. A message the compiler prints when it finds an error
  4. A copy of the app stored on a remote server
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Without a build script a person must remember a dozen separate commands and run them correctly each time. With one, building is repeatable: the same command gives the same result on any machine with the toolchain. A script that begins with set -e stops at the first error rather than producing a broken result. Option A describes a specification, and option C describes a compiler error.

Concept Tested: Build Script

See: Build Script

docs.title: 2. What is ad-hoc signing?
docs.text:
1. Signing an app with a paid developer identity so strangers can trust it
  2. Leaving an app completely unsigned
  3. Signing the README file
  4. Code signing without an identity: the app carries a signature, but it names no developer and is not backed by a paid developer account
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Ad-hoc signing satisfies the system's requirement that the code carry a signature. It is the right level for a personal tool you build and run on your own computers, and it costs nothing beyond the toolchain. It gives strangers no reason to trust the app, so a downloaded personal tool may need extra steps before the system will run it. Option A describes signing with a developer identity.

Concept Tested: Ad-Hoc Signing

See: Ad-Hoc Signing

docs.title: 3. What is a Git commit?
docs.text:
1. A saved snapshot of the project at a moment in time, together with a message that says what changed and why
  2. A command that sends changes to a remote server
  3. A command that fetches changes from a remote server
  4. A list of files Git should ignore
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Commits are the steps of the history, and each can be inspected, compared with the one before, or returned to. A good message names the change and the reason, so "Add delayed capture" is useful and "update" is not. A commit should hold one logical change so it can be undone without disturbing anything else. Options B and C describe push and pull, and option D describes an ignore list.

Concept Tested: Git Commit

See: Git Commit

docs.title: 4. What is the purpose of install rollback?
docs.text:
1. To make the installer run faster
  2. To remove the application permanently after use
  3. To undo a failed or unwanted installation and restore the state before it began, such as bringing back an older working version
  4. To hide the installer from the user
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. If an installer replaces a working older version and then fails halfway, a rollback restores the older version so the user is not left with nothing. The usual technique is to keep a backup of what is being replaced, install the new version, test that it starts, and only then discard the backup. Rollback matters most for a tool you depend on every day. Option B describes the uninstall process.

Concept Tested: Install Rollback

See: Install Rollback

docs.title: 5. The build finishes with no compiler errors. What can you conclude?
docs.text:
1. The code is well-formed, but it can still do the wrong thing, so tests are still needed
  2. The code is correct and ready to ship
  3. The code has no hallucinations
  4. The tool meets every acceptance criterion
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A clean build says the code is well-formed, not that it is right. Compiler errors are a useful safety net because they catch problems before the program runs, but code that compiles can still behave incorrectly, as with a hotkey that never fires. Chapter 12 addresses that gap with tests. Options B, C, and D claim more than a clean build can show.

Concept Tested: Compiler Errors

See: Compiling and Its Errors

docs.title: 6. Why does version control matter even more when an AI agent changes the code?
docs.text:
1. Agents cannot write files without Git
  2. Version control makes the agent faster
  3. Agents never make mistakes
  4. An agent can change many files at once and make mistakes confidently, so history lets you see exactly what changed and roll back
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In the chapter's example, an agent adds a settings window that makes the app larger and slower and breaks the hotkey. With history you ask Git to show the changes since your last snapshot, see the dozens of lines you never asked for, and return to the earlier state with one command. This makes bold edits safe, and it applies the book's habit of leaving things out to code already written.

Concept Tested: Version Control

See: Version Control

docs.title: 7. The compiler prints CaptureController.swift:42:17: error: cannot find 'captureRegion' in scope. What does this tell you?
docs.text:
1. The file CaptureController.swift does not exist
  2. On line 42 of that file, the code uses a name the compiler cannot find, likely a misspelling or a name the agent assumed but never defined
  3. The app has been successfully signed
  4. The installer failed to copy the app
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The message format gives the file name, then the line and column, then the word "error," then a plain description. A name that does not exist anywhere the compiler can see is most often a misspelling or a name the agent assumed, which is a form of the hallucination from Chapter 5. The agent usually reads such errors, edits the file, and builds again, so you need not understand each one.

Concept Tested: Compiler Errors

See: Compiler Errors

docs.title: 8. After you rebuild the app, a permission such as screen recording seems to vanish. What is the likely cause?
docs.text:
1. The README was edited
  2. Git removed the permission during the commit
  3. An ad-hoc signature is tied to the exact build, so rebuilding can change how the system recognizes the app and you may need to grant the permission again
  4. The compiler deleted the privacy settings
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter notes that because an ad-hoc signature is tied to the exact build, a rebuild can change how the system recognizes the app. The practical result may be that screen recording must be granted again. This is a platform constraint of the kind Chapter 8 described. The other options attribute the change to tools that do not touch system privacy settings.

Concept Tested: Ad-Hoc Signing

See: Ad-Hoc Signing

docs.title: 9. The author has three computers and builds the tool on one of them. What workflow does the chapter suggest for getting the same source onto the others?
docs.text:
1. Copy the files by hand each time
  2. Push the commits to a remote copy such as GitHub, then pull on each other machine and run the installer script there
  3. Rebuild the tool from scratch on each machine with a new prompt
  4. Email the compiled app to each machine
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Push sends commits to a remote repository for backup and sharing, and pull brings them down to another computer. The same installer script then builds the tool there. The chapter advises pulling before you push when working on several machines, so you start from the latest version. This is cheaper and clearer than copying files by hand and avoids regenerating the code.

Concept Tested: Git Push and Pull

See: Git Push and Pull

docs.title: 10. In the first install, the app code was about 2,000 lines out of about 5,200 total. What does this proportion suggest?
docs.text:
1. Software meant to be relied on carries substantial tests, scripts, and documents around the code, so the app code is less than half of the total
  2. The agent wasted most of its effort
  3. The tests were unnecessary
  4. The project was poorly specified
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The tests came to about 1,370 lines, the scripts about 500, and the specification, design, and README about 1,340. The chapter calls this proportion typical of software that is meant to be relied on. It also explains why the 1,340 lines of documents matter: they decided what the other 3,860 lines would be. Options B, C, and D misread the numbers.

Concept Tested: ScreenGrab Case Study

See: The ScreenGrab Case Study

docs.title: References: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
docs.text:
1. Compiler - Wikipedia - Explains how compilers translate source code into executable form, including the kinds of errors they report. Background for the chapter's treatment of compile errors during generation.

  2. Build automation - Wikipedia - Describes scripting and tooling that make builds repeatable. Supports the chapter's emphasis on build and installer scripts with rollback. Read it with the installer and uninstall scripts.

  3. Code signing - Wikipedia - Covers cryptographic signing of software to establish origin and integrity. Foundation for the chapter's discussion of ad-hoc signing on macOS.

  4. The C Programming Language - Brian W. Kernighan and Dennis M. Ritchie - Prentice Hall - Kernighan and Ritchie began with the hello, world program as the first thing a reader compiles and runs. That minimal write-build-run loop became the standard way to teach any toolchain.

  5. The Pragmatic Programmer (20th Anniversary Edition) - David Thomas and Andrew Hunt - Addison-Wesley - Hunt and Thomas advocate tracer bullets, automating everything, and keeping all work under version control. Their rules justify the scripted build, install, and commit habits in this chapter.

  6. Pro Git - Scott Chacon and Ben Straub - The free, official Git book, covering commits, branches, and history. Explains the version control commands that record each step of a generated build.

  7. Conventional Commits - Conventional Commits - Specifies a lightweight convention for commit messages that makes history readable. A model for the commit messages that document each generation step.

  8. Notarizing macOS Software Before Distribution - Apple Developer Documentation - Describes Apple's notarization and signing requirements for distributed apps. Shows what ad-hoc signing leaves out for apps shared beyond one machine.

  9. Getting Started with Swift - Swift.org - Official tutorials for building Swift packages from the command line with swift build. Matches the build workflow used to compile the tool in this chapter.

  10. Make a README - Make a README - Gives a section-by-section template for a useful README. Supports the chapter's guidance on documenting install and uninstall steps for a generated tool.

docs.title: Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing
Summary
docs.text: This chapter opens up the unit that AI work is billed in. It explains the token, the context window, input and output tokens, prompt caching, cache writes, reads, and expiration, then shows how token pricing and model capability tiers combine in model selection. After this chapter, you will be able to list the token types that determine API cost and explain why each is priced differently.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Token 106 Input Tokens 45 Output Tokens 14 Context Window 32 Prompt Caching 31 Cache Write Tokens 14 Cache Read Tokens 14 Cache Expiration 2 Token Pricing 13 Model Capability Tiers 2 Model Selection 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents

A Price Tag on Every Word

The ScreenGrab build cost about $14, and by the end of this chapter you will know exactly which parts of that bill came from where. You will be able to read a usage report the way you read a grocery receipt. Grab only what you need!

Chapter 5 described a coding agent as a loop: it reads, it thinks, it writes, and it runs your tools. This chapter looks at the same loop through the billing meter. Every step of that loop is counted in one unit, and the price of that unit changes depending on what the step was doing. Once you can read that meter, the $6 and $14 figures in the ScreenGrab story stop being magic numbers and become arithmetic you can check.

docs.title: The Token
docs.text:
A token is the smallest piece of text that a language model reads or writes. It is not quite a word and not quite a letter. Before a model sees your request, a program called a tokenizer chops the text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary of common fragments. Short common words such as "the" or "need" are usually one token. Long or rare words are split into several pieces. Punctuation, spaces, digits, and code symbols also count.

A widely used rule of thumb for English prose is that one token is about four characters, or about three-quarters of a word. That rule is only an average. The exact split depends on the model's tokenizer, so two vendors can count the same sentence differently. The splits in this chapter are illustrative: they show the pattern, not any one vendor's exact output.

Tokens matter for three reasons. They are the unit of billing, because vendors charge per million tokens. They are the unit of limits, because a model can only hold a fixed number of tokens at once, a limit we meet shortly as the context window. And they are the unit of time, because a model produces its answer one token after another, so longer answers take longer.

Here is how the pattern looks on five short texts. The "four-character estimate" column divides the character count by four.

Text Characters Illustrative split Tokens Four-character estimate Grab only what you need! 24 Grab / only / what / you / need / ! 6 6.0 ScreenGrab 10 Screen / Grab 2 2.5 Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious 34 Super / cal / if / rag / il / istic / exp / ial / id / ocious 10 8.5 swift build -c release 22 swift / build / - / c / release 5 5.5 1,150,000 9 1 / , / 150 / , / 000 5 2.25
