Ordinary English lands close to the rule. A rare word costs somewhat more. Numbers and symbols cost the most, because each digit group and each comma is its own piece. This matters in a coding session, where much of the text is code, file paths, and numbers.

Think in Tokens, Not Words

A model never sees your sentence; it sees a numbered list of fragments. Every price in this chapter is a price per fragment, so counting fragments is the first step of every cost estimate.

docs.title: Worked example: tokens in a small program
docs.text:
ScreenGrab has about 2,000 lines of Swift in its app code. If a line of Swift averages roughly 10 tokens (an illustrative figure, since code varies), the finished app code is about 20,000 tokens. Yet the first install stage in the course description used about 206,000 output tokens. The gap is not waste. Output tokens also include the agent's reasoning, the tests, the scripts, the specification, the README, and every draft that was rewritten. The finished files are only a fraction of what the model wrote on the way there.

Try the estimate yourself before the sim reveals the answers.

docs.title: Diagram: Token Split Explorer
docs.text:
Token Split Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: token-split-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/interactive-tokenizer-explorer Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: compare Learning Objective: The learner will compare their predicted token count with the illustrative split for each of five short texts, and identify the one text that the four-characters-per-token rule underestimates by more than 50%.

Prerequisites: token, tokenizer, four-characters-per-token rule of thumb (all defined in the section "The Token" above).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the five texts, the learner commits a predicted token count before the split is revealed. After all five reveals, the learner answers "Which text did the four-character rule underestimate by more than 50%?" The answer is correct when it names the text in row 5 of the Content table. Reading the reveal and hovering over pieces are exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) One word is always one token. (2) The four-character rule works equally well for every kind of text. (3) Every tokenizer splits text the same way.

Instructional Rationale: Predicting before the reveal makes the learner commit to a mental model of tokens, and the reveal creates the mismatch that corrects it. Comparing prediction to split for five contrasting kinds of text lets the learner see where the rule holds and where it fails.

Content:

All token splits below are illustrative and the sim must label them "illustrative: real tokenizers differ".

# Text shown Characters Illustrative pieces Tokens Four-character estimate Reason shown after reveal 1 Grab only what you need! 24 Grab, " only", " what", " you", " need", ! 6 6.0 Common words are one token each, so the rule fits ordinary English. 2 ScreenGrab 10 Screen, Grab 2 2.5 A joined name splits at its natural word boundary. 3 Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious 34 Super, cal, if, rag, il, istic, exp, ial, id, ocious 10 8.5 A rare long word breaks into many short pieces. 4 swift build -c release 22 swift, " build", " -", c, " release" 5 5.5 Command-line text splits at spaces and symbols. 5 1,150,000 9 1, ",", 150, ",", 000 5 2.25 Digits and separators each become their own piece, so the rule underestimates numbers.

Provenance: The five texts are chosen by the chapter author. The pieces and counts are illustrative, not the output of a named tokenizer. The characters and four-character estimates are computed from the Rules.

Rules: Four-character estimate = characters / 4, shown to two decimals. A prediction is an integer from 1 to 40 (min 1, max 40, step 1, default 5). A prediction is "close" when |prediction - tokens| <= 2. The rule underestimates a text when tokens > 1.5 x estimate. Only row 5 meets this (5 > 1.5 x 2.25 = 3.375); row 3 does not (10 < 12.75).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads text 1 and sets a predicted token count.
  2. The learner presses Reveal. The text is shown split into its pieces, with the true token count, the four-character estimate, and whether the prediction was close.
  3. The learner repeats for texts 2 to 5 in order. A revealed split stays visible and cannot be re-predicted.
  4. After the fifth reveal, a table of all five rows appears and the learner picks the text that the rule underestimates by more than 50%.
  5. The learner should notice that the rule is good for ordinary English and poor for numbers.

Feedback: Five predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. After each reveal the sim states "Close" or "Off by N tokens" and shows the Reason text for that row. The final question allows two attempts. Correct: "Row 5: digit groups and commas each count as a token." Incorrect: "Compare tokens with the estimate in each row; the rule underestimates when tokens exceed 1.5 times the estimate." After the second wrong attempt the correct row is revealed. A score shows "Predictions close: n of 5".

Starting State: Text 1 is shown with the prediction at 5. The question on screen is "How many tokens will this take?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states one token is about four characters or three-quarters of a word. The chapter's table lists the same five texts with the same counts: 6, 2, 10, 5, 5.

docs.title: Input Tokens
docs.text:
Input tokens are all the tokens you send to the model on a request. That sounds like "my question", but in a coding session the question is a tiny part of it. Each request carries the whole working context again. A model has no memory between requests, so the agent must resend everything the model needs to continue the job.

In a coding session, the input includes several layers that the following table separates. The first two layers do not change from turn to turn, and the last three grow as the session proceeds.

Layer of input What it holds Changes between turns? Instructions The agent's system prompt and your project rules, such as the CLAUDE.md file No Tool definitions Descriptions of what the agent may do: read a file, run a command No Conversation history Every earlier request and reply in the session Grows each turn File contents Source files the agent has read Grows as it reads more Tool results Compiler errors, test output, command output Grows each turn

Two of these layers are bigger than they look. The instructions and tool definitions together can run to thousands of tokens before you type a word. File contents also stay: if the agent reads a 500-line Swift file at roughly 10 tokens a line (an illustrative figure), that adds about 5,000 tokens, and those 5,000 tokens ride along in the history on every later turn, whether or not the agent still needs the file.

Because history is resent on every turn, input does not grow in a straight line. If each turn adds 2,000 tokens, the history after turn \( n \) holds \( 2000n \) tokens, and the total sent over \( n \) turns is the sum of those histories.

docs.title: Total Input Sent Over a Session
docs.text:
\[ T_{\text{sent}} = \sum_{k=1}^{n} (a \cdot k) = a \cdot \frac{n(n+1)}{2} \]

where:

  • \( T_{\text{sent}} \) is the total input tokens sent across the whole session
  • \( a \) is the number of tokens added per turn
  • \( n \) is the number of turns
  • \( k \) is the turn number

docs.title: Worked example: a 40-turn session
docs.text:
Set \( a = 2000 \) and \( n = 40 \). Then \( T_{\text{sent}} = 2000 \times 40 \times 41 / 2 = 1{,}640{,}000 \) tokens. At $5 per million input tokens, the plain cost is \( 1.64 \times 5 \) = $8.20. The conversation itself ends at only \( 2000 \times 40 = 80{,}000 \) tokens, so the agent has paid to send about 20 times the final conversation. This is the problem prompt caching exists to solve, and the next sections show how it solves it.

The Hidden Re-Send

It is easy to think a long session costs "what I typed". It costs what was resent, every turn. If a session feels expensive, look at how large the history has become before you blame the last question, and start a fresh session when the old context no longer helps.

docs.title: Output Tokens
docs.text:
Output tokens are the tokens the model writes in reply. In a coding session that means code, tests, shell commands, edits, and the model's visible reasoning. Output tokens are the most expensive kind. In the price table used by this book, output costs four times as much as a plain input token, and 100 times as much as a cached read.

Output also includes the model's reasoning when the tool shows or bills it, so a hard problem can produce thousands of output tokens before a single line of code appears. Output is expensive because it is slow and sequential. A model processes input in parallel, but it must produce output one token at a time, each token depending on the one before. That uses the vendor's computing hardware far longer per token.

docs.title: Worked example: what 206,000 output tokens cost
docs.text: In the first stage of the ScreenGrab build, the agent wrote about 206,000 output tokens. At $20 per million, that is \( 0.206 \times 20 \) = $4.12. The same stage used only about 500,000 new tokens in total, so output was roughly 41% of the new tokens but about 74% of the stage's spend ($4.12 of $5.59, counting the other 294,000 new tokens at $5 per million). Writing is the costly activity, which is why concise specifications (Chapter 7) that keep the agent from writing unneeded code save real money.

docs.title: The Context Window
docs.text:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens a model can consider at one time. It holds the input and the output together. Think of it as the model's desk: everything on the desk is visible, and nothing off the desk exists. Depending on the model, windows range from tens of thousands of tokens to over a million. Vendors raise these limits regularly, so check the current figure for the model you use.

When the history gets close to the limit, a coding agent usually compacts it: it asks the model to write a summary, then continues from the summary instead of the full history. Compaction keeps the session alive and shrinks later input, but the summary is lossy, and the summarizing step itself costs input and output tokens. The window matters to cost in two ways. First, when the history approaches the limit the agent must drop or summarize earlier material, and details can be lost. Second, a bigger window invites bigger prompts, and bigger prompts mean more input tokens on every turn.

docs.title: Worked example: how full is the desk?
docs.text: Using the 40-turn session above, the history after turn 40 holds 80,000 tokens plus the fixed instructions and tool definitions. If those add 20,000 tokens, the context holds 100,000 tokens. In a model with a 200,000-token window that is half full. Another 40 turns at the same pace would add 80,000 more, reaching 180,000 and leaving almost no room for the next answer. A long session therefore has a natural limit even before cost becomes a problem.

docs.title: Prompt Caching
docs.text:
Prompt caching lets the vendor keep the already-processed beginning of a prompt, so that the next request which starts with the same material does not pay full price to process it again. The cache is matched from the start of the prompt, so it works on a prefix: the stable material at the front.

Think of Pinch moving house. Without caching, you pack and unpack the whole shell every morning. With caching, the shell stays packed and you only carry in what changed since yesterday.

docs.title: Worked example: 40 turns over 100,000 tokens
docs.text:
Suppose a 100,000-token project context is sent on each of 40 turns. Without caching, each turn pays the input price, so the cost is \( 40 \times 100{,}000 = 4{,}000{,}000 \) tokens, or 4 million tokens at $5 per million, which is $20.00. With caching, the first turn writes the context to the cache and the other 39 turns read it, at prices set out in the next two sections. The total falls to $1.28, a saving of about 94%.

Keep the Front of the Prompt Still

A cache matches from the first token onward, so changing something near the start of a prompt makes everything after it a miss. Keep stable material, such as rules and tool lists, at the front, and put the changing material at the end. If your reads suddenly drop to zero, look for an edit near the top.

docs.title: Cache Write Tokens
docs.text:
Cache write tokens are the input tokens the vendor stores in the cache the first time it sees them. A write is the setup cost: you pay to process and keep the material so that later requests can reuse it. Some vendors charge a premium for writes over the plain input price. This book's estimates follow the course description and price writes the same as plain input, at $5 per million, which keeps the arithmetic simple.

Some vendors charge a premium for writes. As a hypothetical, with a 25% premium the first-turn write above would cost $0.625 instead of $0.50, a difference of about 12 cents on a $1.28 total, so the saving stays large. Every turn also writes. The new request and the new reply added since the last turn were not in the cache, so they are written for the first time and become part of the cached prefix for the next turn.

docs.title: Worked example: the first turn
docs.text: In the 100,000-token project context example, the first turn writes 100,000 tokens. At $5 per million that costs \( 0.1 \times 5 \) = $0.50. That $0.50 is the entire up-front price of the cache. If the session ends after one turn, caching has saved nothing and cost nothing extra in this book's price model; the benefit only starts on turn two.

docs.title: Cache Read Tokens
docs.text:
Cache read tokens are the input tokens served from the cache instead of being processed again. A read is the cheap part of caching. In this book's price table, a cache read costs $0.20 per million tokens, which is one twenty-fifth of the $5 plain input price.

A read is cheap because the vendor stores the work it already did on that prefix and reuses it, instead of computing it again. The discount is steep: \( 1 - 0.20/5 = 96\% \) off the plain input price. In a long coding session, cache reads dominate the token count by a wide margin. The whole ScreenGrab session used about 18.9 million cache reads but only about 1.15 million new tokens. Reads are numerous because the growing history is read again on nearly every turn.

docs.title: Worked example: the 39 reads
docs.text: Continue the example above. Turns 2 to 40 each read the 100,000-token context from the cache, which is 39 reads and 3.9 million tokens. At $0.20 per million, that costs \( 3.9 \times 0.20 \) = $0.78. Add the $0.50 write from turn one, and the total is $1.28. Compare the growing-history example from the Input Tokens section: with caching, the 80,000 tokens written cost $0.40 and the earlier history read again costs 1.56 million tokens times $0.20 per million, or $0.31, for a total of about $0.71 against $8.20 uncached.

docs.title: Cache Expiration
docs.text:
Cache expiration is the rule that a cached prefix is discarded if it is not used within a time limit. A typical default lifetime is a few minutes, and each read usually renews it, but exact limits and options differ by vendor and change over time. If you step away from a session for longer than the lifetime, the next request pays to write the context again. This is why a burst of fast work is cheaper than the same work spread across a day.

Check the Cache Line

After a long pause, look at the next usage report. If cache reads are near zero and cache writes jumped, the cache expired and you paid to rebuild it. Finish a chunk of related work in one sitting to avoid that.

docs.title: Token Pricing
docs.text:
Token pricing is the vendor's published price per million tokens for each token type. Four token types matter for estimating cost: output, plain input, cache writes, and cache reads. The prices below are the ones the course description uses for Claude Opus 5.5, with writes priced the same as plain input. These are the book's assumptions, and vendors change prices, so always check the current price page before you plan a real project.

Token type Price per million tokens Relative to plain input Output $20.00 4 times Plain input and cache write $5.00 1 time Cache read $0.20 one twenty-fifth

The cost of a request is the sum over the token types of each count times its price.

docs.title: Cost of a Request
docs.text:
\[ C = \frac{N_{\text{out}} \cdot p_{\text{out}} + N_{\text{new}} \cdot p_{\text{in}} + N_{\text{read}} \cdot p_{\text{read}}}{1{,}000{,}000} \]

where:

  • \( C \) is the cost in dollars
  • \( N_{\text{out}} \) is the number of output tokens
  • \( N_{\text{new}} \) is the number of new input tokens, including cache writes
  • \( N_{\text{read}} \) is the number of cache read tokens
  • \( p_{\text{out}} = 20 \), \( p_{\text{in}} = 5 \) and \( p_{\text{read}} = 0.20 \) are the prices in dollars per million tokens

docs.title: Worked example: the whole session
docs.text:
The ScreenGrab session had 325,000 output tokens, 825,000 other new tokens (1.15 million new minus 325,000 output), and 18.9 million cache reads. Then \( C = (325{,}000 \times 20 + 825{,}000 \times 5 + 18{,}900{,}000 \times 0.20) / 1{,}000{,}000 = 6.50 + 4.13 + 3.78 \) = $14.41, which the course description rounds to about $14.

The next sim lets you change the context size and number of turns and see how the totals move.

docs.title: Diagram: Prompt Cache Cost Calculator
docs.text:
Prompt Cache Cost Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: prompt-cache-cost-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/tool-use-loop-cost Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the cost of repeating a fixed context over several turns with and without prompt caching, to within $0.01.

Prerequisites: input tokens, cache write tokens, cache read tokens, token pricing (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For three challenge scenarios, the learner types the cost with caching and the cost without caching before the sim shows its values. An answer is correct when it is within $0.01 of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 scenarios with both answers correct. Changing the free-exploration inputs is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Caching makes every request cheaper, including the first. (2) Cache reads cost the same as plain input. (3) A single-turn request benefits from caching.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so the learner commits numbers before seeing the model result. Free exploration afterward lets the learner see the break-even behavior that the third scenario hints at.

Content:

Prices (per million tokens, from the section "Token Pricing"): plain input $5.00, cache write $5.00, cache read $0.20.

The fixed context is resent every turn. The learner can adjust:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Context size 10,000 200,000 10,000 100,000 tokens Number of turns 1 100 1 40 turns

Challenge scenarios, in order:

# Context (tokens) Turns Cost without caching Cost with caching Feedback when wrong 1 100,000 40 $20.00 $1.28 Without: 40 x 100,000 = 4 million tokens x $5 = $20.00. With: one write ($0.50) plus 39 reads of 100,000 tokens x $0.20 per million ($0.78) = $1.28. 2 50,000 10 $2.50 $0.34 Without: 10 x 50,000 = 500,000 tokens x $5 per million = $2.50. With: write $0.25 plus 9 reads of 50,000 tokens ($0.09) = $0.34. 3 200,000 1 $1.00 $1.00 With one turn there is only a write and no reads, and a write costs the same as plain input here, so caching saves nothing.

Provenance: Prices are the Claude Opus 5.5 figures stated in docs/course-description.md and the chapter section "Token Pricing". The sim must label them "book assumptions: check current vendor pricing". Scenario values are computed from the Rules.

Rules: Cost without caching = turns x context x 5 / 1,000,000. Cost with caching = context x 5 / 1,000,000 + (turns - 1) x context x 0.20 / 1,000,000. Costs are shown in dollars rounded to two decimals. Only the fixed context is modeled; new tokens added per turn and output are ignored. The saving is shown as a percentage, (without - with) / without, which is 0% when turns = 1.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1 (context and turns) and types the cost without caching and the cost with caching.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows both model values and the worked calculation next to the learner's numbers.
  3. After all three scenarios, free exploration unlocks and the learner changes context size and turns. Both costs and the percentage saving update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that the saving is zero at one turn and rises toward 96% as turns grow.

Feedback: Three scenarios, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: with caching $X, without $Y." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that scenario. After the second wrong attempt the model values and worked calculation are shown and the scenario counts as missed. A running count "Scenarios correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with two empty answer boxes. The question on screen is "What does 40 turns over a 100,000-token context cost, with and without a cache?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's worked example states $20.00 without caching, $1.28 with caching, a $0.50 write, a $0.78 read cost, and a saving of about 94% for 100,000 tokens over 40 turns.

docs.title: Model Capability Tiers
docs.text: Model capability tiers are the levels a vendor offers within one family of models, typically a large, a medium, and a small model. Larger models reason better on hard problems and cost more per token. As an illustration only, a small model might cost one-fifth of the largest model per token, with the medium model in between; check each vendor's price page for real ratios. Smaller models are faster and cheaper but make more mistakes on complex work. The ScreenGrab session shows both ends: it started on the cheaper Sonnet 5.5 and the cost estimate applies Opus 5.5 prices.

docs.title: Model Selection
docs.text:
Model selection is the choice of which tier to use for which job. A sound habit is to start with the cheapest tier that could plausibly do the work, and move up only when it fails. Switching tiers mid-session has a catch: a cache belongs to one model, so a switch means the new model writes the context again. Use a larger model for the design, the tricky debugging, and the review. Use a smaller one for routine edits and boilerplate.

You Can Read the Meter

You can now separate tokens into output, new input, cache writes, and cache reads, and say why each is priced differently. That is the whole toolkit for estimating the cost of an AI session, and Chapter 11 puts it to work on ScreenGrab.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
• A token is a text fragment of about four characters, and it is the unit of billing, limits, and time.
  • Input is resent on every turn, so total input grows much faster than the conversation itself.
  • Output is the most expensive token type, at four times plain input in this book's price table.
  • Prompt caching pays a one-time write and then cheap reads, which saved about 94% in the 40-turn example.
  • Caches expire, so keep related work together and keep the front of the prompt stable.
  • Choose the cheapest model tier that can do the job.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing
docs.text: Test your understanding of tokens, the context window, prompt caching, token pricing, and model selection with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a token?
docs.text:
1. A software license key
  2. A complete sentence of text
  3. The smallest piece of text that a language model reads or writes, from a fixed vocabulary of common fragments
  4. A single letter of the alphabet
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A token is not quite a word and not quite a letter. A tokenizer splits text into pieces, so short common words are usually one token while rare words are split into several. A rule of thumb for English is about four characters per token. Tokens are the unit of billing, limits, and time, and exact splits vary by vendor.

Concept Tested: Token

See: The Token

docs.title: 2. What is the context window?
docs.text:
1. The maximum number of tokens a model can consider at one time, holding input and output together
  2. The window in which a cache entry stays valid
  3. The user interface of a coding agent
  4. The time limit for a single answer
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The chapter compares it to the model's desk: everything on the desk is visible and nothing off it exists. When history nears the limit, an agent usually compacts it by asking the model to write a summary, which is lossy and itself costs tokens. Option B describes cache expiration, which is a time limit rather than a size limit. Options C and D are not what the term means.

Concept Tested: Context Window

See: The Context Window

docs.title: 3. In this book's price table, how does the price of a cache read compare with plain input?
docs.text:
1. Four times as much
  2. The same
  3. Half as much
  4. One twenty-fifth as much, or $0.20 per million tokens against $5.00
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A cache read costs $0.20 per million tokens, a 96% discount from the $5 plain input price. The vendor stores the work already done on that prefix and reuses it. Option A is the ratio of output to plain input. Because the growing history is read again on nearly every turn, cache reads dominate the token count: the ScreenGrab session used about 18.9 million of them.

Concept Tested: Cache Read Tokens

See: Cache Read Tokens

docs.title: 4. Why are output tokens the most expensive token type?
docs.text:
1. Because vendors dislike long answers
  2. Because the model must produce output one token at a time, each depending on the one before, which uses hardware far longer per token
  3. Because output tokens are stored in the cache
  4. Because output always contains personal data
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A model processes input in parallel but writes output sequentially. In the book's table, output costs $20 per million, four times plain input and 100 times a cache read. Output includes code, tests, commands, and visible reasoning, so concise specifications that keep the agent from writing unneeded code save real money.

Concept Tested: Output Tokens

See: Output Tokens

docs.title: 5. Why does the total input sent over a coding session grow much faster than the conversation itself?
docs.text:
1. The model forgets earlier turns, so the user retypes them
  2. Tokens grow longer over time
  3. The model has no memory between requests, so the whole working context is resent on every turn
  4. Vendors add hidden text to each request
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Each request carries instructions, tool definitions, conversation history, file contents, and tool results again. If each turn adds 2,000 tokens, the total sent over 40 turns is 2,000 × 40 × 41 ÷ 2 = 1,640,000 tokens, about 20 times the final 80,000-token conversation. This is the problem prompt caching exists to solve.

Concept Tested: Input Tokens

See: Input Tokens

docs.title: 6. What does cache expiration imply for how you should work?
docs.text:
1. A burst of fast work is cheaper than the same work spread across a day, because a cache unused past its lifetime must be written again
  2. Caches never expire, so you can step away freely
  3. Longer breaks always make sessions cheaper
  4. Expiration only affects output tokens
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A cached prefix is discarded if it is not used within a time limit, typically a few minutes, and each read usually renews it. If you step away longer than the lifetime, the next request pays to write the context again. Exact limits differ by vendor and change over time, so check current documentation. Options B, C, and D contradict this behavior.

Concept Tested: Cache Expiration

See: Cache Expiration

docs.title: 7. A session adds 2,000 tokens per turn for 40 turns, and the full history is resent each turn. About how many input tokens are sent in total?
docs.text:
1. 80,000
  2. 800,000
  3. 164,000
  4. 1,640,000
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Use T = a × n(n+1) ÷ 2 with a = 2,000 and n = 40: 2,000 × 40 × 41 ÷ 2 = 1,640,000 tokens. At $5 per million, that costs $8.20 without caching. Option A is only the final conversation size, 2,000 × 40. The gap between 80,000 and 1,640,000 shows why total input grows faster than a straight line.

Concept Tested: Input Tokens

See: Input Tokens

docs.title: 8. A 100,000-token context is sent on each of 40 turns with no caching, at $5 per million input tokens. What is the cost?
docs.text:
1. $1.28
  2. $20.00
  3. $0.50
  4. $8.20
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Forty turns of 100,000 tokens is 4,000,000 tokens, and at $5 per million that is $20.00. With caching, the first turn writes the context for $0.50 and the other 39 turns read it at $0.20 per million, for $0.78, a total of $1.28, a saving of about 94%. Option A is the cached total, and option D belongs to the growing-history example.

Concept Tested: Prompt Caching

See: Prompt Caching

docs.title: 9. The first stage of the ScreenGrab build wrote about 206,000 output tokens at $20 per million. What did that output cost?
docs.text:
1. About $4.12
  2. About $41.20
  3. About $1.03
  4. About $0.41
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Convert 206,000 tokens to 0.206 million and multiply by $20: 0.206 × 20 = $4.12. This is the cost formula from the chapter applied to the output term alone. Options B, C, and D come from misplacing the decimal point or using the wrong price. Note that the output total is far larger than the roughly 20,000 tokens in the finished app, because output includes reasoning, tests, scripts, and rewritten drafts.

Concept Tested: Token Pricing

See: Token Pricing

docs.title: 10. In the first build stage, output was about 41% of the new tokens but about 74% of the spend. What best explains this gap?
docs.text:
1. Output tokens are served from the cache
  2. Input tokens are free
  3. Output costs four times as much per token as plain input, so a smaller share of tokens produces a larger share of cost
  4. The vendor charges a flat fee per stage
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. At $20 per million, output tokens carry 4 times the price of plain input at $5 per million, so $4.12 of the stage's $5.59 came from output. Writing is the costly activity, which is why a concise specification pays off. Option A is wrong because output tokens cannot be read from a cache, and options B and D contradict the book's pricing model.

Concept Tested: Output Tokens

See: Output Tokens

docs.text:
1. Byte-pair encoding - Wikipedia - Explains the subword algorithm many language models use to split text into tokens. Shows why token counts differ from word counts, the basis of token pricing.

  2. Cache (computing) - Wikipedia - Describes how caches store results to speed repeated access, including hits, misses, and expiration. Provides the general concept behind prompt caching's write-once, read-cheaply pattern.

  3. Large language model - Wikipedia - Covers tokenization, context windows, and inference in language models. Background for why input and output tokens are priced separately. Read it to see why long prompts cost more.

  4. Speech and Language Processing - Daniel Jurafsky and James H. Martin - Prentice Hall (3rd ed. draft online) - Jurafsky and Martin give a clear, worked treatment of tokenization and byte-pair encoding with small examples. Their step-by-step merges make the token concept concrete.

  5. Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach - John L. Hennessy and David A. Patterson - Morgan Kaufmann - Hennessy and Patterson's average memory access time formula weighs hit time against miss penalty. The same hit-versus-miss reasoning, an analogy only, clarifies when a prompt cache pays off.

  6. Prompt Caching - Anthropic Docs - Official documentation of cache writes, cache reads, lifetimes, and pricing multipliers. The primary source for the caching mechanics and savings in this chapter.

  7. Token Counting - Anthropic Docs - Explains how to count the tokens in a request before sending it. Lets students check the token figures behind any cost estimate.

  8. Models Overview - Anthropic Docs - Lists available model tiers with capabilities and pricing. Supports the chapter's advice to choose the cheapest tier that can do the job.

  9. Summary of the Tokenizers - Hugging Face - Compares byte-pair, WordPiece, and SentencePiece tokenization with examples. Shows that tokenizers differ, so token counts vary by model. Read it before comparing token counts between tools.

  10. Let's Build the GPT Tokenizer - Andrej Karpathy - A two-hour video that builds a byte-pair tokenizer from scratch and explains its quirks. Gives students an intuition for why tokens behave oddly.

docs.title: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost
Summary
docs.text: This chapter applies token pricing to the real ScreenGrab session. It separates wall-clock time from active working time, makes estimation assumptions explicit, and works through API cost estimates, subscription usage windows, cost per line of code, and session cost breakdowns. After this chapter, you will be able to estimate a session's API cost from its token counts and identify which activities used the most tokens.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 11 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Wall-Clock Time 3 Active Working Time 1 Time To First Install 1 Usage Measurement 12 Estimation Assumptions 11 API Cost Estimate 10 Subscription Usage Window 2 Cost-Weighted Tokens 1 Cost Per Line Of Code 1 Session Cost Breakdown 3 Token-Heavy Activities 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
  • Chapter 10: Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing

Check the Receipt

A claim like "it only cost $6" is worth exactly as much as the arithmetic behind it. In this chapter you will rebuild that number from raw token counts, and then see which part of the session did the spending. Grab only what you need!

Chapter 10 gave you the price list. This chapter shows you how to use it on a real session. The goal is a habit: whenever someone reports what an AI build cost or how long it took, you can ask what was measured, what was assumed, and whether the arithmetic holds.

docs.title: Measuring Time
docs.text:
Time can be measured two ways, and the ScreenGrab story uses both, so it pays to keep them apart.

Wall-clock time is the elapsed real time on the clock, from a starting event to an ending event, including every pause. If you start a session at 9:00 and the app is installed at 9:36, the wall-clock time is 36 minutes, even if you spent ten of those minutes making coffee.

Active working time is the time the agent or the person was actually working, with idle gaps removed. It is always less than or equal to wall-clock time. The ScreenGrab session ran for about 70 active minutes, counted this way.

Time to first install is the wall-clock time from the first prompt to a working installed app. For ScreenGrab that was about 36 minutes. It is the number most useful to a would-be builder, because it answers "how long until I have something I can use?" The first real screen grab came about 44 minutes after the first prompt.

The three measures fit on one timeline of the ScreenGrab session, with every figure from the course description:

Moment Minutes from first prompt Measure App built and installed about 36 Time to first install (wall-clock) First real screen grab about 44 Wall-clock Session complete not reported as wall-clock About 70 active minutes

Wall-clock numbers are what you would see on a stopwatch from the first prompt. The active-time figure removes idle gaps, so it is the one to use if you ask how much working time a similar build takes.

Putting time and output together gives a rate. The first install produced about 5,200 lines in about 36 minutes, which is roughly 144 lines per minute. No human types that fast, but a rate like this says nothing about quality, which is the subject of Chapters 12 and 13.

docs.title: Usage Measurement
docs.text:
Usage measurement is the practice of recording how many tokens of each type a session used. Coding agents keep a usage record for each request, listing input tokens, output tokens, cache writes, and cache reads. Summing the records over a session gives the totals that the cost formula needs.

Different tools label the totals differently, so read the labels before you use them. The course description reports "new tokens, including output", which means output is counted inside the new-token figure. To price the rest at the plain input price, you subtract output from the new tokens.

docs.title: Worked example: reading the totals
docs.text:
For the whole ScreenGrab session the record shows about 1.15 million new tokens including output, about 325,000 output tokens, and about 18.9 million cache reads. Subtracting gives the other new tokens: \( 1{,}150{,}000 - 325{,}000 = 825{,}000 \). Those are the tokens that were not output and were not read from the cache, which means they were sent for the first time and written to the cache. If you forget the subtraction and price all 1.15 million new tokens as plain input and then also add output, you count the output twice.

Don't Count Output Twice

A usage report that says "new tokens, including output" has already folded output into the total. Subtract the output tokens first, then price the remainder as input, or your estimate comes out too high. Check by confirming that your three counts add up to the report's total.

docs.title: Estimation Assumptions
docs.text:
An estimation assumption is any choice you make to turn measured usage into a dollar figure when the measurement alone does not say. Every cost estimate hides some. A trustworthy estimate lists them. These are the assumptions behind the $6 and $14 figures:

  • All tokens are priced at Claude Opus 5.5 rates: $20 per million output, $0.20 per million cache reads, and $5 per million for everything else.
  • All other new tokens are treated as cache writes at $5 per million, the same as plain input.
  • The session actually started on the cheaper Sonnet 5.5, so applying Opus prices probably overstates cost.
  • The session ran on a subscription, so no API bill was ever sent. The estimate is "what it would have cost at API prices".
  • The figures cover the code only. They exclude generating this textbook, the author's time, and later maintenance.
  • Token counts are rounded to "about" values.

Assumptions can push the answer in either direction, and it helps to check how much they matter.

docs.title: Worked example: how much does one assumption move the answer?
docs.text: Suppose a vendor charged 25% more for cache writes than for plain input, which is a hypothetical for this exercise. The 825,000 other new tokens would cost \( 825{,}000 \times 6.25 / 1{,}000{,}000 \) = $5.16 instead of $4.13, a difference of about $1.03 on a $14.41 total, or about 7%. The headline stays near $14 to $15, which tells you that this particular assumption is not the one that matters most. The price tier is: Sonnet pricing would lower the whole figure far more.

docs.title: API Cost Estimate
docs.text:
An API cost estimate is the dollar cost a session would have had if it had been billed per token by the vendor's programming interface. Chapter 10 gave the formula. Apply it to each token type and add the results.

The course description reports three stages of the ScreenGrab session. This table sets out the token counts again, then the arithmetic for the "other new" tokens (new tokens minus output).

Stage New tokens (incl. output) Output Other new Cache reads Built and installed 500,000 206,000 294,000 3.8 million First real grab 573,000 238,000 335,000 6.3 million Whole session 1,150,000 325,000 825,000 18.9 million

docs.title: Worked example: the "built and installed" stage
docs.text:
Output: \( 206{,}000 \times 20 / 1{,}000{,}000 \) = $4.12 (output at $20 per million). Other new: \( 294{,}000 \times 5 / 1{,}000{,}000 \) = $1.47. Cache reads: \( 3{,}800{,}000 \times 0.20 / 1{,}000{,}000 \) = $0.76. The total is \( 4.12 + 1.47 + 0.76 \) = $6.35, which the course description rounds to about $6. Repeating the steps for the other two rows gives about $7.70 for the first real grab (reported as about $8) and about $14.41 for the whole session (reported as about $14).

Use the next sim to check your own arithmetic against these rows and then try different prices.

docs.title: Diagram: Session Cost Estimator
docs.text:
Session Cost Estimator

Type: microsim sim-id: session-cost-estimator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/openai-token-usage-anatomy Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the estimated API cost of each of the three ScreenGrab session stages from its token counts and the stated prices, to within $0.02.

Prerequisites: output tokens, other new tokens, cache read tokens, token pricing, API cost estimate (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each of the three stages, the learner types the total estimated cost before the sim shows its value. An answer is correct when it is within $0.02 of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the prices in free exploration is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The "new tokens" figure excludes output. (2) Cache reads, being most of the tokens, must be most of the cost. (3) All tokens in a session are priced the same.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so the learner commits a number before the result is shown. The what-if exploration afterward lets the learner see how sensitive the total is to each price.

Content:

Token counts per stage (from the chapter section "API Cost Estimate"):

# Stage New tokens including output Output tokens Cache reads 1 Built and installed 500,000 206,000 3,800,000 2 First real grab 573,000 238,000 6,300,000 3 Whole session 1,150,000 325,000 18,900,000

Default prices in dollars per million tokens: output 20.00, other new tokens 5.00, cache reads 0.20. Adjustable prices for free exploration:

Price Min Max Step Default Unit Output 5.00 30.00 1.00 20.00 dollars per million tokens Other new tokens 1.00 10.00 1.00 5.00 dollars per million tokens Cache reads 0.05 1.00 0.05 0.20 dollars per million tokens

Challenge answers at the default prices:

# Output cost Other new cost Cache read cost Total Feedback when wrong 1 $4.12 $1.47 $0.76 $6.35 Other new = 500,000 - 206,000 = 294,000 tokens x $5 per million = $1.47. Add output $4.12 and reads $0.76. 2 $4.76 $1.68 $1.26 $7.70 Other new = 573,000 - 238,000 = 335,000 tokens x $5 per million = $1.675, shown as $1.68. Add output $4.76 and reads $1.26. 3 $6.50 $4.13 $3.78 $14.41 Other new = 1,150,000 - 325,000 = 825,000 tokens x $5 per million = $4.125, shown as $4.13. Add output $6.50 and reads $3.78.

Provenance: Token counts and default prices are from docs/course-description.md and the chapter section "API Cost Estimate". The sim must label the prices "book assumptions: check current vendor pricing". Costs are computed from the Rules.

Rules: Other new tokens = new tokens including output - output tokens. Cost per type = tokens x price / 1,000,000. Total = sum of the three. Amounts are rounded half up to the nearest cent for display, and the total is computed before rounding (stage 2 is 7.695, shown $7.70; stage 3 is 14.405, shown $14.41).

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads the token counts for stage 1 and types the total estimated cost.
  2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the three component costs and the total beside the learner's answer.
  3. The learner repeats for stages 2 and 3 in order.
  4. After stage 3, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes any of the three prices and all three stage totals update at once.
  5. The learner should notice that changing the output price moves the total more than changing the cache read price, even though cache reads are far more numerous.

Feedback: Three stages, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: about $X." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that stage. After the second wrong attempt the model total and worked calculation are shown and the stage counts as missed. A running count "Stages correct: n of 3" is shown.

Starting State: Stage 1 is shown with the token counts and an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What would this stage have cost at API prices?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states about $6.35 for built and installed (reported as about $6), about $7.70 for the first real grab (reported as about $8), and about $14.41 for the whole session (reported as about $14), using $20, $5, and $0.20 per million.

docs.title: Subscription Usage Window
docs.text:
A subscription usage window is a block of time, often five hours, during which a flat-fee plan lets you use a limited amount of AI work before it pauses you. Instead of sending a bill per token, the plan meters usage against the window and resets it. The ScreenGrab build ran on such a plan, and the course description reports that it used about 5% of one five-hour window.

That 5% is a reported observation, not a conversion. Plans do not publish how they weigh output against cache reads, so you cannot reliably turn 5% into dollars. What you can say is that the whole first build fit inside a small fraction of one window.

docs.title: Cost-Weighted Tokens
docs.text:
Cost-weighted tokens are a session's tokens converted to a common unit by weighting each type by its price relative to output. Using the book's prices, output has weight 1, other new tokens have weight 0.25 (because $5 is a quarter of $20), and cache reads have weight 0.01.

For the whole session: \( 325{,}000 \times 1 + 825{,}000 \times 0.25 + 18{,}900{,}000 \times 0.01 = 325{,}000 + 206{,}250 + 189{,}000 = 720{,}250 \) output-equivalent tokens. That is about 3.6% of the 20.05 million raw tokens, and it equals the cost divided by the output price: \( 14.405 / 20 = 0.72025 \) million. Raw token counts overstate what a session "weighs"; cost-weighted tokens do not. The weights come from the price list, so if prices change the weights change, and the unit is only comparable between sessions priced the same way.

docs.title: Cost Per Line of Code
docs.text:
Cost per line of code divides the session's cost by the number of lines it produced. The result is a rough yardstick, not a quality measure. With about 5,200 lines at first install, the build stage cost \( 6.35 / 5{,}200 \) = $0.0012 per line, or about 0.12 cents. The whole session works out at \( 14.405 / 5{,}200 \) = $0.0028 per line, about 0.28 cents.

Cost per line is useful for comparison across your own sessions, and misleading across projects, because a line of test code and a line of installer script are not the same effort. Treat this with care. Lines include tests, scripts, and documents, not only the 2,000 lines of Swift, and a cheap line that is wrong costs more than an expensive one that is right.

docs.title: Session Cost Breakdown
docs.text:
A session cost breakdown divides a session's total cost among its token types, so you can see which type drives the bill. The table below puts the token shares next to the cost shares for the whole session, so you can compare them.

Token type Tokens Share of tokens Cost Share of cost Output 325,000 1.6% $6.50 45.1% Other new (writes) 825,000 4.1% $4.13 28.6% Cache reads 18,900,000 94.3% $3.78 26.2% Total 20,050,000 100% $14.41 about 100% (shares are rounded)

Cache reads are 94% of the tokens but only 26% of the cost. Output is under 2% of the tokens and 45% of the cost. A chart of tokens alone would send you looking in the wrong place.

Count and Cost Are Different Rulers

Look at the two share columns. The biggest slice by count is the smallest slice by cost, which is why the question "what used the most tokens?" and the question "what cost the most?" can have different answers.

Try the comparison yourself before the chart reveals it.

docs.title: Diagram: Token Share Versus Cost Share Chart
docs.text:
Token Share Versus Cost Share Chart

Type: chart sim-id: token-share-versus-cost-share Library: Chart.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/cross-vendor-token-drift Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish the token type that has the largest share of tokens from the token type that has the largest share of cost in the whole ScreenGrab session, and select each correctly on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: output tokens, other new tokens, cache read tokens, session cost breakdown (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: Before the chart is revealed, the learner answers two questions: "Which token type is the largest share of tokens?" and "Which token type is the largest share of cost?" An answer is correct when it matches the Content table (cache reads for tokens, output for cost). Mastery is both correct on the first attempt. Hovering over bars after the reveal is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The type with the most tokens must cost the most. (2) Output is a small part of a session's cost because there is little of it.

Instructional Rationale: Predicting before the reveal commits the learner to the intuition that count equals cost, and the two-bar comparison then breaks it. Analyze-level work asks the learner to separate two measures that look alike.

Content:

Whole-session figures (from the chapter section "Session Cost Breakdown"):

Token type Tokens Share of tokens (%) Cost ($) Share of cost (%) Output 325,000 1.6 6.50 45.1 Other new (writes) 825,000 4.1 4.13 28.6 Cache reads 18,900,000 94.3 3.78 26.2

The chart shows two stacked bars of 100%: one for token share and one for cost share. Hovering over a segment shows the type, its tokens or cost, and its share. A note states that cost uses the book's assumed prices ($20, $5, and $0.20 per million tokens).

Question feedback:

# Question Correct answer Feedback when wrong 1 Which token type is the largest share of tokens? Cache reads Cache reads are 18.9 million of 20.05 million tokens, or 94.3%, because the growing history is re-read on almost every turn. 2 Which token type is the largest share of cost? Output Output is only 1.6% of tokens but 45.1% of cost, because each output token costs $20 per million, 100 times a cache read.

Provenance: Token counts and prices are from docs/course-description.md. Shares and costs are computed from the Rules and match the chapter table.

Rules: Share of tokens = type tokens / 20,050,000. Cost = tokens x price / 1,000,000, with prices $20, $5, and $0.20 per million. Share of cost = type cost / 14.405. Shares are shown to one decimal, so they may sum to 99.9% or 100.0%.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner chooses an answer to question 1 and then to question 2, before any chart is shown.
  2. The learner presses Reveal. The two stacked bars appear, with correct and incorrect answers marked.
  3. The learner hovers over each segment to read its tokens, cost, and share.
  4. The learner should notice that the cache read segment is largest in the token bar and smallest in the cost bar.

Feedback: Two questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [type]." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that question. The correct answers are revealed together with the chart. A score "Questions correct: n of 2" is shown.

Starting State: The two questions are shown with three answer choices each and no chart. The prompt on screen is "Which kind of token is the biggest? Which kind costs the most?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states cache reads are 94.3% of tokens and 26.2% of cost, output is 1.6% of tokens and 45.1% of cost, and the whole session costs about $14.41.

docs.title: Token-Heavy Activities
docs.text:
Token-heavy activities are the kinds of work that consume the most tokens, and they differ by token type. Writing large amounts of code, tests, and documents drives output tokens. Reading many files or long command output drives new input tokens. Long sessions with a large history drive cache reads, because each step re-reads the whole context.

ScreenGrab shows the pattern. In the first 36 minutes the agent produced about 5,200 lines and used 206,000 output tokens and 3.8 million cache reads. In the rest of the session, which covered further testing and hotkey checks, output rose by only 119,000 tokens, yet cache reads rose by 15.1 million and the estimated cost by about $8.06. About 80% of all cache reads, and 56% of the cost, came after the app was installed. Checking the software was not free, because every check re-read a large context.

Restart a Bloated Session

When a task is finished and the next one is unrelated, begin a fresh session. The new session starts with a small history, so its cache reads stay small. Carry over only the notes you need.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
An estimate is only as good as its stated assumptions, and a cost figure is only as good as the usage record behind it. Wall-clock time, active working time, and time to first install each answer a different question, so say which one you mean. Chapter 12 turns from what the session cost to whether the software it produced actually works.

You Can Audit an AI Bill

You can now turn a usage record into a dollar estimate, state the assumptions behind it, and say which activity drove the spending. That is the skill that lets you question any "it only cost" claim, including the ones in this book.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost
docs.text: Test your understanding of wall-clock and active time, estimation assumptions, API cost estimates, cost-weighted tokens, and session cost breakdowns with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is wall-clock time?
docs.text:
1. The elapsed real time on the clock from a starting event to an ending event, including every pause
  2. The time the agent spent writing code, with idle gaps removed
  3. The time a cache entry remains valid
  4. The time the compiler takes to build the app
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. If a session starts at 9:00 and the app is installed at 9:36, the wall-clock time is 36 minutes even if ten of those minutes went to making coffee. Option B describes active working time, which is always less than or equal to wall-clock time. The chapter urges you to say which of the time measures you mean, because each answers a different question.

Concept Tested: Wall-Clock Time

See: Measuring Time

docs.title: 2. In the ScreenGrab case, what was the time to first install?
docs.text:
1. About 70 minutes
  2. About 44 minutes
  3. About 36 minutes
  4. About 5 minutes
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Time to first install is the wall-clock time from the first prompt to a working installed app, and for ScreenGrab it was about 36 minutes. It is the most useful number for a would-be builder because it answers how long until you have something usable. The first real screen grab came about 44 minutes after the first prompt, and the whole session took about 70 active minutes.

Concept Tested: Time To First Install

See: Measuring Time

docs.title: 3. What is an estimation assumption?
docs.text:
1. A guarantee from the vendor about future prices
  2. Any choice you make to turn measured usage into a dollar figure when the measurement alone does not say
  3. A measurement taken directly from the usage record
  4. A rounding rule for token counts only
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Every cost estimate hides some assumptions, and a trustworthy estimate lists them. The chapter's list includes pricing all tokens at Opus 5.5 rates, treating other new tokens as cache writes, noting that the session ran on a subscription, and excluding the textbook, the author's time, and maintenance. Option C describes a measured fact, not an assumption.

Concept Tested: Estimation Assumptions

See: Estimation Assumptions

docs.title: 4. The chapter tests a hypothetical 25% premium on cache writes and finds the total barely moves. Which assumption does it say matters more?
docs.text:
1. The rounding of token counts
  2. The number of files in the project
  3. The color theme of the editor
  4. The price tier, since Sonnet pricing would lower the whole figure far more than a write premium
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A 25% write premium would add about $1.03 to a $14.41 total, roughly 7%. The session actually started on the cheaper Sonnet 5.5, but the estimate applies Opus 5.5 prices, so the headline probably overstates cost. Checking how far each assumption moves the answer tells you which ones to examine first. Options A, B, and C are not discussed as significant drivers.

Concept Tested: Estimation Assumptions

See: Estimation Assumptions

docs.title: 5. The first build used about 5% of one five-hour subscription usage window. Why can't you reliably convert that 5% into dollars?
docs.text:
1. Plans do not publish how they weigh output against cache reads, so the percentage is an observation, not a conversion
  2. Because five hours is too short to measure
  3. Because subscription plans have no usage limits
  4. Because the percentage is always exactly $14
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A subscription usage window is a block of time, often five hours, during which a flat-fee plan lets you do a limited amount of work. The 5% is a reported observation. What you can say is that the whole first build fit in a small fraction of one window. Option C is false, since the window itself is a usage limit, and option D confuses an observation with a price.

Concept Tested: Subscription Usage Window

See: Subscription Usage Window

docs.title: 6. Why are cost-weighted tokens a better yardstick than raw token counts?
docs.text:
1. They are always larger numbers
  2. They weight each token type by its price relative to output, so cheap cache reads do not make a session look heavier than it is
  3. They ignore output tokens entirely
  4. They do not depend on prices
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. With the book's prices, output has weight 1, other new tokens 0.25, and cache reads 0.01. The ScreenGrab session's 20.05 million raw tokens weigh only 720,250 output-equivalent tokens, about 3.6%. The weights come from the price list, so if prices change the weights change, and the unit is comparable only between sessions priced the same way. Option D is therefore false.

Concept Tested: Cost-Weighted Tokens

See: Cost-Weighted Tokens

docs.title: 7. The usage record shows about 1.15 million new tokens including output and about 325,000 output tokens. How many other new tokens should be priced at the plain input rate?
docs.text:
1. 1,150,000
  2. 325,000
  3. 825,000
  4. 1,475,000
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Because the new-token figure already includes output, subtract: 1,150,000 − 325,000 = 825,000. These are tokens sent for the first time and written to the cache. If you price all 1.15 million new tokens as plain input and then add output separately, you count the output twice. Reading the labels before using the totals avoids that error.

Concept Tested: Usage Measurement

See: Usage Measurement

docs.title: 8. In the "built and installed" stage, output cost $4.12 and other new tokens cost $1.47. The stage had 3.8 million cache reads at $0.20 per million. What is the total cost?
docs.text:
1. $5.59
  2. $4.12
  3. $14.41
  4. $6.35
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Cache reads cost 3.8 × $0.20 = $0.76. Adding $4.12 + $1.47 + $0.76 gives $6.35, which the course description rounds to about $6. Option A is the sum without cache reads, and option C is the whole-session total. The chapter's table repeats the same method for the other two rows, getting about $7.70 for the first real grab and about $14.41 for the whole session.

Concept Tested: API Cost Estimate

See: API Cost Estimate

docs.title: 9. The whole session cost about $14.405 and produced about 5,200 lines. What is the approximate cost per line of code?
docs.text:
1. About $0.28
  2. About $0.0028
  3. About $0.00028
  4. About $2.77
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Dividing $14.405 by 5,200 lines gives about $0.0028 per line, or 0.28 cents. The chapter warns that this is a rough yardstick: it is useful for comparing your own sessions but misleading across projects, since test lines and installer-script lines are not the same effort, and a cheap line that is wrong costs more than an expensive one that is right.

Concept Tested: Cost Per Line Of Code

See: Cost Per Line of Code

docs.title: 10. Cache reads were 94% of the session's tokens but only 26% of its cost, while output was under 2% of the tokens and 45% of the cost. What does this show?
docs.text:
1. Output tokens are the cheapest token type
  2. A chart of tokens alone would be a good guide to cost
  3. Token share and cost share can differ sharply, so a token-only chart would send you looking in the wrong place
  4. Cache reads should be eliminated entirely
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Because output costs 100 times as much per token as a cache read, a tiny share of tokens can dominate the bill. The chapter also shows that about 80% of cache reads and 56% of the cost came after the app was installed, because every check re-read a large context. So testing is not free, and a cost breakdown by token type tells you where to look.

Concept Tested: Session Cost Breakdown

docs.title: References: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost
docs.text:
1. Software development effort estimation - Wikipedia - Reviews methods for estimating how long and how costly software work will be, and why estimates miss. Frames the chapter's careful, assumption-labeled estimates.

  2. Software metric - Wikipedia - Defines measures of software and its development process and cautions against misuse. Supports the chapter's rule that a number needs a stated assumption.

  3. Telemetry - Wikipedia - Explains automatic collection and transmission of measurements from remote systems. Background for the usage records from which session costs are computed.

  4. How to Measure Anything - Douglas W. Hubbard - Wiley - Hubbard teaches that measurement means reducing uncertainty, not reaching certainty, and uses calibrated estimates and Fermi-style decomposition. This is the right mindset for pricing an AI session from imperfect records.

  5. Software Estimation: Demystifying the Black Art - Steve McConnell - Microsoft Press - McConnell popularized the cone of uncertainty and the habit of giving estimate ranges instead of single numbers. His advice shapes how this chapter states cost with assumptions.

  6. Manage Costs Effectively - Anthropic Docs - Explains how Claude Code reports session cost and token usage, and ways to reduce spending. A primary source for reading a real session's usage record.

  7. Monitoring Usage - Anthropic Docs - Describes the telemetry metrics Claude Code can export, such as token counts and cost. Shows where the numbers behind a session estimate come from.

  8. ccusage - GitHub - An open-source command line tool that reads local usage logs and reports tokens and estimated cost by day and session. A concrete example of auditing an AI bill.

  9. Evidence Based Scheduling - Joel on Software - Spolsky shows how to turn a developer's past estimate accuracy into probability ranges. Illustrates using recorded data to question time claims.

  10. Pricing - Anthropic - Lists current per-token prices for each model tier. The input rates needed to convert a usage record into dollars. Use them with a usage record to estimate dollars.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter takes up the question of whether generated software actually works. It defines software verification and testing, then covers automated, unit, and integration tests, coverage, isolation, side effects, stubs, simulated input, and off-screen rendering, followed by the manual, acceptance, and smoke tests a person has to run. After this chapter, you will be able to tell which kinds of behavior a given test can confirm.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 14 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Software Verification 43 Software Testing 38 Automated Test 14 Unit Test 5 Integration Test 1 Test Coverage 1 Test Isolation 3 Test Side Effects 1 Stubbed Dependency 1 Simulated Input Events 1 Off-Screen Rendering 1 Manual Testing 11 Acceptance Test 5 Smoke Test 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 7: Requirements and Minimal Specifications
  • Chapter 8: Software Design and Platform Constraints

Did Anyone Actually Check That?

An AI agent can write 5,200 lines in 36 minutes, and every line looks confident. This chapter teaches you to tell the difference between "the agent says it works" and "something checked that it works". Grab only what you need, and check what you grab!

Chapter 9 ended with ScreenGrab installed and running. That is not the same as ScreenGrab working. Generated code is fast to produce and easy to trust, and the cheapest moment to catch a mistake is before you depend on the tool. This chapter gives you the vocabulary for the checking, using the real test suite from the ScreenGrab project as the running example.

docs.title: Software Verification
docs.text:
Software verification is the activity of gathering evidence that software meets its stated requirements. It asks one question: did we build the thing we said we would build? The evidence can come from several sources. A program can run automatically and compare results with expected values. A person can use the software and watch what happens. A reviewer can read the code. A script can inspect the installed app.

Verification differs from asking whether the requirements were the right ones. That second question belongs to the specification work of Chapter 7. Verification takes the requirements as given and checks the software against them.

Four methods produce evidence, and a project usually needs more than one. Testing runs the software and compares results with expectations. Inspection reads the code or the configuration without running it. Demonstration uses the software by hand and watches. Analysis reasons from known facts, such as a timing calculation. This chapter concentrates on testing, but the weak links are usually found by demonstration.

The word evidence matters. A requirement such as "pressing Esc during a grab cancels it and leaves the clipboard unchanged" is verified only when something has observed that behavior. Saying "the agent wrote the cancel code" is a claim, not evidence. Good evidence has four properties:

  • It was observed, not assumed from reading code.
  • It can be repeated by someone else following the same steps.
  • It was recorded, with the output or log line kept.
  • It is dated and names the setup it ran on.

docs.title: Worked example: one requirement, three kinds of evidence
docs.text:
Take that Esc requirement. The ScreenGrab project gathers evidence three ways, and each one proves something different.

Evidence What it observes What it cannot show An automated test of the grab coordinator using fake parts After a cancel, no image was delivered and the stored clipboard was untouched That the real overlay window receives a real Esc key press An automated test of the overlay view with a synthesized key event The view reports "cancel" when it is sent an Esc event That macOS delivers a physical key press to the view Manual acceptance test AC-5: start a grab, press Esc The real overlay disappears, and the real clipboard still has its old content Anything about a different Mac, a different display, or the next release

No single row is enough. Together they form a chain from the logic down to the real screen. Verification is the work of building that chain and knowing where its weak links are.

The table above is also a map of this chapter. The first two rows are automated tests and the third is a manual one. The sections that follow explain each kind, and Chapter 13 explains how to report which links in the chain you actually have.

docs.title: Software Testing
docs.text:
Software testing is one method of verification: running the software with chosen inputs and comparing what it does with what was expected. Every test has the same three-part shape, often called arrange, act, assert.

  1. Arrange: set up the starting situation and the inputs.
  2. Act: run the one piece of behavior under test.
  3. Assert: state the expected result and fail if the actual result differs.

The next snippet shows that shape in a real ScreenGrab test. Before you read it, here is what it does. The function selectionRect turns two points, where a drag started and ended, into a rectangle, and it clamps the rectangle so it cannot extend past the edge of the display (bounds). The test arranges a 400 by 300 display, drags from (350, 250) to far past the corner at (900, 900), and asserts that the result stops at the display edge.

private let bounds = CGRect(x: 0, y: 0, width: 400, height: 300)

@Test func clampsToDisplayEdges() {
    // Act: a drag that runs far past the bottom-right corner
    let rect = SelectionGeometry.selectionRect(
        from: CGPoint(x: 350, y: 250), to: CGPoint(x: 900, y: 900), within: bounds)
    // Assert: the selection stops at the display edge
    #expect(rect == CGRect(x: 350, y: 250, width: 50, height: 50))
}

Where does the expected value come from? It must come from the requirement, not from the code. If you ask an agent to write a test by running the code and copying down whatever it prints, the test passes by construction and proves nothing. A useful test fails when the code is wrong, and a failure looks like this (simplified):

Expectation failed: (rect -> CGRect(x: 350, y: 250, width: 550, height: 650))
  == CGRect(x: 350, y: 250, width: 50, height: 50)

The message shows that the clamp did not happen: the rectangle ran past the edge of the 400 by 300 display. A reader can see at once which behavior broke. A test is an executable claim about behavior. When it passes, you know that this input produced that output, once, on this machine. It says nothing about inputs the test did not try. That is the central limit of testing: tests show the presence of confirmed behavior, not the absence of mistakes.

A Test Is a Claim With a Receipt

Notice that a passing test confirms exactly one thing: the one case it ran. When you read "94 tests pass", ask which behaviors those 94 claims are about, and which behaviors have no claim at all.

The next sections define each kind of test, and a sorting exercise at the end of the chapter lets you check that you can tell them apart.

docs.title: Automated Tests
docs.text:
An automated test is a test that a program runs and judges by itself, with no person watching. You start the whole suite with one command and read a pass or fail result. ScreenGrab's suite runs through swift test, and the project script src/scripts/test.sh wraps it for machines that have only the Command Line Tools.

Automated tests have three strengths. They are fast, so you can rerun them after every change. They are repeatable, so a failure points at a change, not at a different mood or a different mouse movement. And they are cheap to run again, so a bug fixed once stays fixed (Chapter 13 returns to this).

They also have a firm limit. An automated test can only confirm what a program can observe. A program cannot easily press a physical key, feel whether a crosshair looks right, or ask the operating system's permission dialog for consent. Those need a person.

docs.title: Worked example: what ScreenGrab's 94 tests cover
docs.text: ScreenGrab has 94 automated tests spread across five test files. They cover the selection geometry, the image encoder, file naming, hotkey records and settings, the grab state machine, and how the overlay view draws and responds. The project's design document lists them by area and says what each verifies. That list shows an important rule: the tests are strongest where behavior is pure logic, and they get weaker as the code gets closer to the real screen and the real keyboard.

docs.title: Unit Tests
docs.text:
A unit test checks one small piece of logic in isolation, such as a single function or class. The piece under test is the "unit". Unit tests are the fastest and most precise kind. When one fails, you know which function broke.

ScreenGrab's design deliberately separated its pure logic from its window-handling code so that the logic could be unit tested. Geometry conversion, file naming, delay limits, and hotkey validation are all pure logic. The clampsToDisplayEdges test above is a unit test. Code is easy to unit test when it takes its inputs as parameters and returns a result, and hard when it reaches out to the clock, the disk, or the screen. That is why the file naming function receives an "exists" check as a parameter, rather than looking at the real disk: a test can pass in a check that always says "the name is taken" and verify the " (2)" suffix without creating any file.

docs.title: Worked example: a unit test with a table of cases
docs.text: One ScreenGrab test checks that a drag in any of the four directions gives the same rectangle. It runs the same assertion on four start and end pairs: down and right, up and left, and the two diagonals. Each pair must produce the rectangle starting at (10, 20) with width 100 and height 50. This is a common unit-testing habit. Choose the cases that could plausibly fail, such as each direction, a minimum size, or an edge, and run them as a list rather than writing one case and hoping.

docs.title: Integration Tests
docs.text: An integration test checks that several parts work correctly together. Where a unit test isolates one function, an integration test wires real parts to each other and checks the combined result. For example, ScreenGrab's crop-accuracy test builds an image where each pixel has a known color, passes it through the real geometry and cropping functions, and checks the exact pixels that come out, including at 2 times Retina scale. That test would not catch an error inside one function alone, but it would catch two correct functions that disagree about points versus pixels.

docs.title: Test Coverage
docs.text:
Test coverage is the proportion of the code, or of the requirements, that a test suite exercises. Code coverage is usually reported as the percentage of lines run during the tests. High coverage means few lines are untested. It does not mean the tests are good: a test can run a line without checking its result. Treat coverage as a way to find the code nobody tested, not as proof that the tested code is right.

Coverage Is Not Correctness

A suite can run every line and still check nothing, because running a line is not the same as asserting its result. Ask the agent which assertion protects each requirement, and treat a line with no assertion as untested.

docs.title: Test Isolation
docs.text: Test isolation means each test runs independently of the others and of the outside world, so that one test's outcome cannot depend on another's. Isolated tests can run in any order and a failure points at one cause. The usual tools are a fresh setup for each test and private copies of anything shared, such as settings or the clipboard.

docs.title: Test Side Effects
docs.text:
Test side effects are changes a test makes outside itself: files written, settings changed, the clipboard overwritten, windows shown. Side effects are a hazard because they make tests depend on each other and can damage the machine under test. ScreenGrab's tests show the care this needs.

The tests use a private named pasteboard, so they never touch your real clipboard. Preferences are held in an in-memory object, because a real suite leaves a settings file in the user's library after every run, even after cleanup. The automated tests need no permissions and put nothing on the visible screen.

docs.title: Stubbed Dependencies
docs.text:
A stubbed dependency is a stand-in for a part that the code under test relies on, supplied by the test so that the real part is not needed. A stub returns fixed answers. Its more elaborate cousin, a fake, also records what it was asked. The reason to use them is to cut off the parts of the world that are slow, risky, or impossible to automate.

ScreenGrab's grab coordinator depends on a screen capturer, a permission checker, a countdown, a selector, and an output. The tests replace each with a fake, so every cell of the coordinator's state table can be exercised without a real display or a permission prompt. The installer tests do the same with shell commands: rollback was tested with a stubbed mv, and the permission-reset flow with stubbed tccutil and defaults, so no real settings changed.

docs.title: Simulated Input Events
docs.text: Simulated input events are keyboard and mouse events that a test builds by hand and sends to a view, in place of a person's real input. ScreenGrab's overlay tests synthesize mouse drags and Esc presses and check that the view reports the right selection or a cancel. The limit is stated in the design document: a test can send a made-up event to the view, but it cannot prove that macOS delivers a physical key press, because producing a real one from a program needs Accessibility permission. Even the hotkey test builds a Carbon hotkey event by hand and checks everything after the key press itself.

docs.title: Off-Screen Rendering
docs.text:
Off-screen rendering draws a view into a bitmap in memory instead of onto the display, so a test can inspect the pixels. ScreenGrab's tests render the selection overlay this way and check three things: the area outside the selection is dimmed, the selection itself is not, and the image is the right way up. No window appears, and no screen-recording permission is needed. One test does order a window far off-screen, because only a window that is ordered in has real backing stores for its layers. Pixel checks like these catch drawing errors that a logic test cannot see.

Fake the World, Not the Logic

When you ask an agent for tests, tell it to replace the clipboard, the clock, and the screen with stand-ins, and to leave your own logic real. A test that fakes the logic it is supposed to check proves nothing.

docs.title: Manual Testing
docs.text:
