Manual testing is checking software by using it as a person would, and observing the result yourself. It is the only way to confirm what a program cannot observe: what real hardware and a real operating system do, and what a human can see and feel.

Automated and manual testing complement each other, as the table below shows.

Automated test Manual test Who runs it A program, in seconds A person, in minutes Repeatable on every change Yes Only if someone does the work Can press a real key, or grant a real permission No, in general Yes Can judge how a screen looks and feels Only by pixel checks Yes Risk Misses what it cannot observe Skipped, forgotten, or done differently each time

docs.title: Worked example: what ScreenGrab needs a person for
docs.text: The design document says plainly what automation cannot reach: real ScreenCaptureKit output, on-screen overlay behavior, the live crosshair, and pasting into real applications. It adds that a real key press cannot be simulated without Accessibility access, so hotkey delivery has to be tried by hand. Each of these is a manual test, and each needs a note of who ran it and when. A manual test without a record is only a memory. The cost is also real: ScreenGrab's 34 acceptance tests take a person a good while, which is why they get skipped, and why the verification status of Chapter 13 exists to say which have been run.

docs.title: Acceptance Tests
docs.text: An acceptance test is a check, defined in advance from the requirements, that decides whether the software is good enough to accept. Each one has an ID, a scenario, an expected result, and the requirements it covers. They are often run by hand. ScreenGrab's specification lists 34, named AC-1 to AC-34.

docs.title: Worked example: reading one acceptance test
docs.text: Take AC-5 from the specification: "Start a grab, press Esc. Expected: the overlay disappears and the clipboard still has its previous content. Covers FR-2.5 and FR-9.2." The table row links a scenario to numbered requirements. A table of this kind is called a traceability matrix: it traces each requirement to the tests that cover it. For example, requirement FR-2.5 (cancel a grab with Esc or a right click) is covered by AC-5 and AC-7. That link lets you ask two useful questions: is every requirement covered by at least one acceptance test, and has each acceptance test actually been run? Chapter 13 shows why the second question is the one that gets skipped.

docs.title: Smoke Tests
docs.text:
A smoke test is a quick set of checks that the software starts and its most basic parts are alive. The name comes from hardware: power it on and see whether smoke comes out. A smoke test does not prove the software correct. It proves that it is worth testing further.

ScreenGrab's smoke checks run against the installed app and trigger no permission prompt. One confirms that the app runs with no Dock icon (lsappinfo reports it as a background app). Another confirms that a second launch exits and leaves the first process running. A third reports idle CPU and memory, which came out at 0.0% CPU and about 25 MB.

docs.title: Diagram: Which Test Can Confirm This
docs.text:
Now you have the vocabulary. Try classifying twelve real ScreenGrab behaviors.

Which Test Can Confirm This

Type: microsim sim-id: which-test-can-confirm-this Library: p5.js Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of twelve ScreenGrab behaviors as confirmable by a unit test, an integration test, a smoke test, or a manual acceptance test, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: automated test, unit test, integration test, smoke test, manual testing, acceptance test (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns each behavior to one of four test kinds. An assignment is correct when it matches the answer column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt per item. Reading the reasons after answering is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Automated tests can confirm everything about the software. (2) Passing unit tests mean the real screen behaves correctly. (3) A smoke test proves the software is correct.

Instructional Rationale: Classification requires the learner to reason about what a check can observe, which is the Understand-level skill of sorting examples under a concept. Immediate reasons after each answer let the learner repair the wrong rule at once.

Content:

The four kinds of test: Unit test, Integration test, Smoke test, Manual acceptance test.

# Behavior to confirm Correct kind Why (shown as feedback) 1 A drag from bottom-right to top-left gives the same rectangle as top-left to bottom-right Unit test It is pure logic in one function, so it can be checked in isolation. 2 A synthetic image with known pixel colors is cropped through the real geometry and cropping functions, and the output pixels match exactly at 2 times scale Integration test Several real parts must agree about points and pixels. 3 Two grabs in the same second are saved with the second named with " (2)" Unit test File naming is pure logic with an injected "exists" check. 4 A hotkey that another app has already registered is reported as a conflict Integration test It calls the real operating system registration and checks the combined result. 5 Pressing the real Control-Shift-4 keys starts a grab while another app is in front Manual acceptance test A program cannot send a real key press without Accessibility permission. 6 The pasted image in a Keynote or Pages document is exactly the selected region at the expected size Manual acceptance test It needs a real other application and a person to judge the result. 7 The installed app runs with no Dock icon Smoke test A quick check of the installed app, with no permission prompt. 8 The selection overlay, rendered off-screen, dims outside the selection and leaves the selection undimmed Integration test The view and its drawing code are tested together, through pixels. 9 After Screen Recording permission is revoked, a grab shows an alert with a button to open System Settings and copies no image Manual acceptance test It needs the real operating-system permission, which a program cannot grant or revoke. 10 A delay of 99 seconds is clamped to the allowed maximum Unit test Delay clamping is a pure function of its input. 11 The app idles at about 0% CPU Smoke test A quick ps check of the installed app, with no permission prompt. 12 With two displays of different pixel density, the captured pixels match the highlighted area on both Manual acceptance test It needs two real displays and a person to compare.

Provenance: Items come from the ScreenGrab design document section 10 and specification section 10 (acceptance tests AC-3, AC-4, AC-9, and AC-21), and from the chapter's examples. Item 10's maximum is illustrative; the sim must label item 10 "illustrative value".

Rules: Four answer choices per item. An item is correct when the chosen kind equals the Correct kind. The score counts correct first answers only. The order is fixed as listed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads behavior 1 and chooses one of the four kinds.
  2. The sim immediately shows correct or incorrect and the Why text.
  3. The learner moves to the next behavior. An answered item cannot be changed.
  4. After item 12, the sim shows the score and a table grouping the 12 behaviors by correct kind.
  5. The learner should notice that the manual group is the one that touches real keys, real permissions, and real displays.

Feedback: Twelve items, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [kind]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 12" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" shown when n >= 10.

Starting State: Behavior 1 is shown with four unselected choices. The question on screen is "Which kind of test could confirm this?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states ScreenGrab has 94 automated tests and 34 acceptance tests (AC-1 to AC-34), and that the smoke checks report about 0.0% CPU and about 25 MB at idle.

docs.title: Diagram: ScreenGrab Grab Flow Test Coverage
docs.text:
The sorter classifies single behaviors. This second diagram follows one whole grab from key press to paste and shows where each kind of check applies.

ScreenGrab Grab Flow Test Coverage

Type: workflow sim-id: grab-flow-test-coverage Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Analyze Bloom Verb: distinguish Learning Objective: The learner will distinguish the steps of a ScreenGrab grab that an automated test can confirm from the steps that only a person can confirm, by marking all 7 steps and matching the Content table on at least 6 of 7.

Prerequisites: automated test, simulated input events, stubbed dependency, off-screen rendering, manual testing (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner opens each step, commits "automated can confirm" or "only a person can confirm" before the answer is shown, and finishes with at least 6 of 7 matching the Content table. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) If most steps are automated, the whole flow is verified. (2) The key press itself is covered by the hotkey tests.

Instructional Rationale: Walking the flow in order shows that automation covers the middle of the chain but not its two ends, the real key press and the real pasted result. Committing a judgment per step makes the learner perform the distinguishing, not just read it.

Content:

The flow has 7 steps in this order, shown as a flowchart. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the step's description, then two buttons for the learner's judgment, then the answer and reason.

# Step Description Answer Reason 1 Press the hotkey A person presses Control-Shift-4 in another app. Only a person can confirm A program cannot send a real key press without Accessibility permission. 2 Hotkey reaches the app The registered hotkey event is delivered to ScreenGrab's handler. Automated can confirm A test builds a Carbon hotkey event by hand and checks the handler receives the right action. 3 Coordinator starts the grab The state machine moves from idle to selecting. Automated can confirm Tested with fakes for every dependency. 4 Screen is captured The real display is captured to a frozen still image. Only a person can confirm It needs the real Screen Recording permission and a real display. 5 User drags a selection The overlay shows and the drag chooses a region. Automated can confirm Synthesized mouse events and off-screen rendering check selection and drawing. 6 Image is cropped and copied The region is cropped, encoded, and written to the clipboard. Automated can confirm Tested with known pixels and a private named pasteboard. 7 Image is pasted into another app The user pastes into Preview, Keynote, or Pages. Only a person can confirm It needs a real other application and a person to judge size and orientation.

An edge label on every arrow states what is passed on: "key event", "action", "frozen image", "selection", "cropped PNG and TIFF", "clipboard contents".

Provenance: From the ScreenGrab design document sections 7 and 10 and specification section 10. The step descriptions are the chapter author's summary of those sections.

Rules: There are 7 steps and each has one answer. The learner's final score is the number of steps where the committed judgment matches the Answer column. Mastery when score >= 6.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner clicks step 1. The information box shows the description and two buttons.
  2. The learner chooses a judgment. The answer and reason appear, and the step is marked answered.
  3. The learner repeats for steps 2 to 7 in any order.
  4. When all 7 are answered, the sim shows the score and highlights the steps that need a person.
  5. The learner should notice that the first, fourth, and last steps cannot be fully confirmed by automation.

Feedback: Seven steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite" plus the Reason. The score "Matched: n of 7" is shown after step 7, with "Mastery" when n >= 6.

Starting State: The flow is shown with no steps answered. The question on screen is "At which steps does a person have to look?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a real key press, the real screen capture, and the real paste need a person, and that the hotkey test builds the event by hand and checks everything after the key press.

You Can Read a Test Suite

You can now name what unit, integration, smoke, and acceptance tests each confirm, and spot the behaviors that automation cannot reach. That is the skill that separates "the tests pass" from "it works".

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Software Testing: Automated and Manual
docs.text: Test your understanding of verification, automated and manual tests, unit and integration tests, stubs, acceptance tests, and smoke tests with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a unit test?
docs.text:
1. A test that checks the whole installed app on a real screen
  2. A test that checks one small piece of logic in isolation, such as a single function or class
  3. A test that a person runs by hand to judge how the screen looks
  4. A test that confirms the software starts
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Unit tests are the fastest and most precise kind, because when one fails you know which function broke. ScreenGrab's design deliberately separated pure logic, such as geometry conversion, file naming, delay limits, and hotkey validation, from window-handling code so that the logic could be unit tested. Option A describes manual or acceptance testing, and option D describes a smoke test.

Concept Tested: Unit Tests

See: Unit Tests

docs.title: 2. What is a smoke test?
docs.text:
1. A test of how well the software handles overheating hardware
  2. A complete proof that the software is correct
  3. A test that measures code coverage
  4. A quick set of checks that the software starts and its most basic parts are alive
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The name comes from hardware: power it on and see whether smoke comes out. A smoke test does not prove the software correct, only that it is worth testing further. ScreenGrab's smoke checks confirm the app runs with no Dock icon, that a second launch exits and leaves the first process running, and that idle use is about 0.0% CPU and about 25 MB of memory.

Concept Tested: Smoke Tests

See: Smoke Tests

docs.title: 3. What are test side effects?
docs.text:
1. Benefits a test brings to unrelated code
  2. Warnings printed by the compiler
  3. Changes a test makes outside itself, such as writing files, changing settings, or overwriting the clipboard
  4. Errors in the specification
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Side effects are a hazard because they make tests depend on each other and can damage the machine under test. ScreenGrab's tests use a private named pasteboard so they never touch your real clipboard, and they hold preferences in an in-memory object because a real suite would leave a settings file in the user's library. The automated tests need no permissions and show nothing on the visible screen.

Concept Tested: Test Side Effects

See: Test Side Effects

docs.title: 4. Why must a test's expected value come from the requirement rather than from running the code and copying its output?
docs.text:
1. A test built from the code's own output passes by construction and proves nothing
  2. Requirements are always shorter than code
  3. The compiler refuses to accept copied values
  4. Copied values make tests run slower
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. If you ask an agent to run the code and write down whatever it prints, the test cannot fail when the code is wrong. A useful test fails when the code is wrong, and the failure message should show which behavior broke. The chapter's clamping example shows a rectangle running past the display edge. Tests show the presence of confirmed behavior, not the absence of mistakes.

Concept Tested: Software Testing

See: Software Testing

docs.title: 5. What can an automated test generally not confirm that a manual test can?
docs.text:
1. Whether a function returns the right value
  2. What real hardware and a real operating system do, such as delivering a physical key press or granting a real permission
  3. Whether the code compiles
  4. Whether a file name is formatted correctly
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. An automated test can only confirm what a program can observe. A program cannot easily press a physical key, feel whether a crosshair looks right, or ask the operating system's permission dialog for consent. The design document says a real key press cannot be simulated without Accessibility access. Options A, C, and D are things automation does well.

Concept Tested: Manual Testing

See: Manual Testing

docs.title: 6. Why does high test coverage not prove that the tests are good?
docs.text:
1. Coverage numbers are always inaccurate
  2. High coverage always means perfect software
  3. Coverage only measures documentation
  4. A test can run a line without checking its result, so coverage shows only which code nobody tested
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Test coverage is the proportion of code or requirements a suite exercises, usually reported as the percentage of lines run. A line that runs but is never checked counts as covered. The chapter advises using coverage to find code that nobody tested, not as proof that the tested code is right. Option B is the misconception the chapter warns against.

Concept Tested: Test Coverage

See: Test Coverage

docs.title: 7. You want to test ScreenGrab's grab coordinator without a real display or a permission prompt. What technique does the chapter describe?
docs.text:
1. Replace the screen capturer, permission checker, countdown, selector, and output with stubs or fakes supplied by the test
  2. Run the test only on a machine with Xcode
  3. Skip the test and rely on the agent's report
  4. Grant every permission in advance
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A stubbed dependency is a stand-in for a part the code relies on, returning fixed answers, and a fake also records what it was asked. Using them, every cell of the coordinator's state table can be exercised without a real display. The installer tests do the same with shell commands, such as a stubbed mv for rollback and stubbed tccutil and defaults for the permission reset.

Concept Tested: Stubbed Dependencies

See: Stubbed Dependencies

docs.title: 8. An automated test sends a synthesized Esc event to the overlay view, and the view reports "cancel." What additional evidence is needed to show that pressing the real Esc key cancels a real grab?
docs.text:
1. Another identical automated test
  2. A higher coverage percentage
  3. A manual acceptance test such as AC-5, in which a person starts a grab, presses Esc, and observes the overlay disappear and the clipboard unchanged
  4. A longer README
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The synthesized-event test shows the view reacts to an Esc event, but it cannot prove that macOS delivers a physical key press to the view. The chapter's three rows of evidence form a chain from logic down to the real screen, and the manual test is the link that observes the real behavior. Repeating a test of the same kind, as in option A, adds no new kind of evidence.

Concept Tested: Acceptance Tests

See: Acceptance Tests

docs.title: 9. How does a traceability matrix help you judge whether testing is complete?
docs.text:
1. It counts how many lines of code each developer wrote
  2. It lists the files in the project
  3. It measures how fast the tests run
  4. It traces each requirement to the tests that cover it, so you can ask whether every requirement has at least one acceptance test
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. In ScreenGrab's specification, requirement FR-2.5, cancelling a grab with Esc or a right click, is covered by acceptance tests AC-5 and AC-7. The link lets you ask whether every requirement is covered by at least one test and whether every test traces to a requirement. The 34 acceptance tests are named AC-1 to AC-34, and several still have to be run by hand.

Concept Tested: Acceptance Tests

See: Acceptance Tests

docs.title: 10. ScreenGrab's 94 automated tests are strongest where behavior is pure logic and weaker closer to the real screen and keyboard. What is the underlying reason?
docs.text:
1. The design separated pure logic so it could be tested in isolation, while real screen capture, key delivery, and permissions need a real system or a person
  2. The agent wrote lazier tests for the screen code
  3. Pure logic is harder to test than window code
  4. Tests cannot check logic
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Logic that takes inputs as parameters and returns results is easy to unit test, while code that reaches out to the clock, the disk, or the screen is hard. The design document says real ScreenCaptureKit output, on-screen overlay behavior, the live crosshair, and pasting into real applications are beyond automation. Those are covered by manual tests, which need a record of who ran them and when.

Concept Tested: Automated Tests

See: Automated Tests

docs.title: References: Software Testing: Automated and Manual
docs.text:
1. Software testing - Wikipedia - Surveys testing levels, methods, and goals, from unit tests to acceptance tests. Gives the overview that organizes this chapter. Read it before the specific test types.

  2. Unit testing - Wikipedia - Explains testing of individual units in isolation, with benefits and limits. Supports the chapter's account of what unit tests confirm.

  3. Smoke testing (software) - Wikipedia - Describes quick, shallow checks that confirm a build basically works. Defines the smoke test the chapter places between integration and acceptance.

  4. Test Driven Development: By Example - Kent Beck - Addison-Wesley - Beck popularized the red, green, refactor cycle: write a failing test, make it pass, then clean up. His worked examples show tests as a design tool, not an afterthought.

  5. The Art of Software Testing - Glenford J. Myers - Wiley - Myers framed testing as executing a program with the intent of finding errors, and cataloged systematic test-case design. That mindset separates 'the tests pass' from 'it works'.

  6. The Practical Test Pyramid - Martin Fowler (Ham Vocke) - Shows how to balance many fast unit tests, fewer integration tests, and very few end-to-end tests. Explains why the chapter's test layers differ in cost and confidence.

  7. Test Sizes - Google Testing Blog - Classifies tests as small, medium, or large by resources and speed rather than by label. A clear way to reason about what automation can run quickly.

  8. Unit Test - Martin Fowler - Explains the two meanings of unit test, solitary and sociable, and why definitions vary. Helps students read claims about test suites carefully.

  9. Test Coverage - Martin Fowler - Argues that coverage numbers reveal untested code but do not prove quality. Reinforces the chapter's caution about behaviors automation cannot reach.

  10. XCTest - Apple Developer Documentation - Reference for Apple's testing framework for Swift and Objective-C projects. Shows how automated tests are written for a macOS tool.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter deals with what happens when software fails and how to report its status honestly. It covers bug reproduction, root cause analysis, environment-specific bugs, regression tests, and the unexplained failure from the ScreenGrab session, then the limits of automated tests, evidence-based reporting, and verification status. After this chapter, you will be able to write a verification plan that separates automated tests from checks a person must run.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 10 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Software Bug 7 Bug Reproduction 3 Root Cause Analysis 2 Unexplained Failure 1 Environment-Specific Bug 1 Regression Test 1 Limits Of Automated Tests 4 Evidence-Based Reporting 5 Verification Status 4 Verification Plan 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
  • Chapter 12: Software Testing: Automated and Manual

Honest Software Reports

The most useful sentence in software is "I checked, and here is how". In this chapter you will learn to write status reports that say exactly what was verified, what was not, and what nobody can explain yet. Grab only what you need, including only the claims you can back up!

The ScreenGrab session did not end with a clean sweep. One early hotkey failure was never explained, several acceptance tests still have to be run by hand, and a later fix was needed for Macs that have only the Command Line Tools. This chapter uses those loose ends as teaching material, because real projects always have them. What separates a trustworthy report from a misleading one is not the absence of loose ends but whether they are written down.

docs.title: Software Bugs
docs.text:
A software bug is a difference between what the software does and what its requirements, or its user's reasonable expectation, say it should do. A bug is not the same as a crash. A tool that runs smoothly and copies the wrong region is buggy. A bug can live in the code, in a missing requirement, in a wrong assumption about the platform, or in the way pieces fit together.

AI-generated code has bugs for the same reasons human code does, plus one more: the agent may write confident code against a requirement you never actually stated. The cheapest defense is the one from Chapter 7, which is a clear specification. The second defense is the testing in Chapter 12.

docs.title: Worked example: a hypothetical Retina bug
docs.text:
This example is hypothetical, built from a risk the ScreenGrab specification lists: coordinate conversion between points and pixels. On a Retina display, one point is two pixels. Suppose a grab of a region 490 points wide and 285 points tall came out as an image 490 by 285 pixels, when the correct size is 980 by 570 pixels. Compare expected and actual:

Expected Actual Image size 980 by 570 pixels 490 by 285 pixels Appearance when pasted Sharp, at the size on screen Blurry or half size

The difference is the bug. The next sections follow what you do with it.

docs.title: Bug Reproduction
docs.text:
Bug reproduction is the act of making a bug happen again on demand, using a written recipe. A bug you can reproduce is a bug you can fix and test. A bug you cannot reproduce can only be guessed at. A good recipe has four parts: the starting state, the exact steps, the expected result, and the actual result, plus the environment (operating system version, hardware, and app version).

For the hypothetical Retina bug the recipe reads: start on a 2 times display; press Control-Shift-4; drag over a region 490 by 285 points; release; paste into Preview using File, New from Clipboard; expect 980 by 570 pixels; actually get 490 by 285. Anyone with a Retina display can follow it.

docs.title: Root Cause Analysis
docs.text:
Root cause analysis is the search for the underlying reason a bug happens, rather than the nearest visible symptom. Fixing the symptom, for example by doubling the output size, can hide the problem and break other cases. The usual method is to keep asking why until you reach a cause that, if removed, makes the bug impossible.

For the Retina example: why was the image half size? Because the crop used point values as pixel values. Why? Because the scale factor was not applied. Why not? Because that conversion was done in two places and one place skipped it. The root cause is the duplicated conversion, and the fix is a single tested conversion function, which is exactly what the ScreenGrab design records as its mitigation for this risk.

docs.title: Environment-Specific Bugs
docs.text:
An environment-specific bug appears only on some setups, such as a particular operating system version, hardware, tool installation, or shell. These bugs are the reason "it works on my machine" is not evidence. The ScreenGrab project recorded two real ones.

The first was the Command Line Tools issue. A later fix was needed for Macs with only the Command Line Tools and no full Xcode. The design document explains the cause: the Command Line Tools ship the Swift Testing framework but not XCTest, and, depending on the Swift version, the build tool may not find the framework, its macro plugin, or a library loaded at run time. The test script therefore passes all three locations explicitly.

The second was a shell quirk. In non-interactive zsh scripts, plain log runs a shell built-in, not the system log command, because /etc/zshrc disables that built-in only for interactive shells. Scripts must call /usr/bin/log by its full path.

It Worked on My Machine Is Not a Report

Software that passes on the machine that built it can fail on a clean one. Whenever you report a result, record the operating system version and the tools installed, and test the install on a machine that has only what a real user would have.

docs.title: Regression Tests
docs.text:
A regression test is a test added after a bug is fixed, which fails if the bug ever returns. The word regression means going backwards: a fixed behavior breaking again after a later change. AI agents change code often and quickly, so a fix without a regression test is a fix that may quietly undo itself.

The steps are simple. Write the test from the reproduction recipe. Run it against the broken code and watch it fail. Apply the fix. Watch the test pass. The first step, seeing it fail, matters, because a test that never failed has not shown that it can catch the bug. ScreenGrab's test that repeated partial redraws do not stack up dimming in the overlay layer is the kind of check that is normally added once such a bug has been seen.

docs.title: The Unexplained Failure
docs.text:
An unexplained failure is a failure that was observed but that nobody can account for, usually because it could not be reproduced and not enough evidence was captured when it happened. ScreenGrab has one. An early report said the Control-Shift-4 hotkey did nothing. Later a real key press worked at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, confirmed by the log. The design document does not claim the earlier problem is fixed. It says the earlier failure is unexplained: the earlier processes logged no hotkey activity, with the same code and the shortcut registered, and neither Secure Input nor the frontmost app was recorded at those moments.

The right response is to leave it open and write down what to capture next time. Calling it fixed because it later worked would be a false claim, since nothing was changed that could account for the difference.

Unexplained Is a Valid Status

Notice that "I do not know why it failed" is more useful than "it must have been a glitch". The first tells the next person what to measure. The second hides the risk.

docs.title: Diagram: Bug Investigation Workflow
docs.text:
The steps in this chapter form a sequence with one important branch: what happens when the bug cannot be reproduced. The next diagram lets you walk it.

Bug Investigation Workflow

Type: workflow sim-id: bug-investigation-workflow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Remember Bloom Verb: identify Learning Objective: The learner will identify what each of the seven steps of a bug investigation produces, answering at least 6 of 7 correctly.

Prerequisites: software bug, bug reproduction, root cause analysis, unexplained failure, regression test (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each step, the learner picks which of three outputs the step produces, before the correct output is shown. A pick is correct when it matches the Output column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) A bug that cannot be reproduced can be closed as fixed. (2) Fixing the visible symptom is the same as fixing the root cause. (3) A fix is finished when the code changes.

Instructional Rationale: Remember-level recall of the sequence benefits from touching each step and committing an answer. The branch on "can it be reproduced?" shows that the process has an honest exit for unexplained failures.

Content:

The diagram is a flowchart with seven steps and one decision. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the step's description and three possible outputs. The learner picks one.

# Step Description Correct output Wrong outputs shown Reason 1 Observe the failure Notice a difference between expected and actual behavior A written observation of expected versus actual A fixed bug; a new feature You cannot work on a bug nobody has written down. 2 Try to reproduce it Follow the recipe on the original setup A recipe that makes the bug happen on demand A passing test; a release Reproduction is a recipe, not a fix. 3 Decision: reproducible? If yes continue to step 4. If no, record an unexplained failure A yes or no, with the environment noted A root cause; a regression test The answer decides whether the investigation can continue. 4 Record an unexplained failure State what was seen, what was known, and what to capture next time A written note of known facts and missing facts A claim that the bug is fixed; a deleted report Honest reporting beats a false fix. 5 Find the root cause Ask why until removing the cause makes the bug impossible A named underlying cause A workaround; a bigger test suite The cause, not the symptom, is what you fix. 6 Fix and add a regression test Change the code and write a test that fails before the fix A fix plus a test that failed first and now passes A new bug report; a README change A fix without a test may silently return. 7 Re-verify and report Run the full checks and record the evidence A status report with dated evidence A guess that it is fixed; a deleted test A claim needs a receipt.

Edge labels: "reproduced" from step 3 to step 5, "cannot reproduce" from step 3 to step 4. Step 4 leads to a final node "wait for new evidence" whose information box reads "Capture the frontmost app, the log, and the settings the next time it happens".

Provenance: Steps follow the chapter sections "Bug Reproduction", "Root Cause Analysis", "Regression Tests" and "The Unexplained Failure". The step descriptions are the chapter author's wording.

Rules: Seven steps, each with exactly one correct output. The score is the number of correct picks. Mastery when score >= 6. The order of the three choices for each step is shuffled once per visit.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner clicks a step. An information box shows the description and three outputs.
  2. The learner picks one output. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the Reason.
  3. The learner opens the remaining steps in any order until all seven are answered.
  4. The learner should notice that step 3 sends the process down one of two paths, and that both paths end in written evidence.

Feedback: Seven steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite: this step produces [correct output]" plus the Reason. The score "Correct: n of 7" is shown after the last step.

Starting State: The flowchart is shown with no step answered. The question on screen is "What does each step of a bug investigation produce?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter lists reproduction recipes with four parts plus the environment, root cause by asking why, a regression test that must be seen to fail before the fix, and an unexplained failure branch.

docs.title: Limits of Automated Tests
docs.text:
The limits of automated tests are the kinds of fact that a program cannot confirm, no matter how many tests it runs. Chapter 12 covered what tests can see. These limits are the other side of that coin, and the ScreenGrab record names several.

  • A real physical key press needs Accessibility permission to simulate, so hotkey delivery has to be tried by hand.
  • Real screen capture needs the Screen Recording permission, which a person grants.
  • Pasting into real applications, and judging how the result looks, needs a person.
  • Behavior on hardware the author does not own, such as the Intel half of the universal build, cannot be seen from one machine.
  • A stubbed test shows the code handles the stub's answers, not what the real tool does.
  • A test only covers the cases its author thought of, and a generated test suite shares the blind spots of the generated code.

docs.title: Worked example: 94 passing tests and an open question
docs.text: With all 94 automated tests passing, ScreenGrab's hotkey still had an open question, since a program could not press the key. The tests exercised everything after the press, including a hand-built hotkey event reaching the handler. They could not show that the keyboard produced that event. The gap was closed only when a person pressed the keys and the log showed the result. A test result and a verification result are different things.

docs.title: Evidence-Based Reporting
docs.text: Evidence-based reporting is the practice of stating each claim about software together with the evidence for it, so a reader can judge how far to trust it. A claim without evidence is an opinion. A good evidence note includes what was checked, how, when, on what setup, and what was not checked. The last item is the one most often missing, and it is the one that stops a reader from over-trusting the rest.

docs.title: Worked example: rewriting a vague claim
docs.text:
The vague claim: "Hotkeys work." Here is the same claim rewritten to the standard of the ScreenGrab design document:

  • Control-Shift-4 with a real key press worked at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, confirmed by the log.
  • An earlier report of it failing is unexplained.
  • Control-Shift-5 with a real key press, and Control-Shift-4 with VS Code in front, have not yet been run.

The second version is longer and less comforting, and far more useful. A reader knows what is safe to rely on, what is risky, and what to check next.

Add a Date, a Setup, and a Source

When an agent says "verified", ask three things: when, on what setup, and what output proves it. If it cannot give all three, change the claim to "not yet verified".

docs.title: Verification Status
docs.text:
A verification status is a label attached to one claim that says how well it has been verified. Using a small fixed set of labels keeps reports honest and quick to scan. This book uses four.

Status Meaning Verified automatically A test or script confirmed it, with output on record Verified by hand A person confirmed it, with a dated note or log line Not yet run No check has been done Claim exceeds evidence The claim says more than the evidence shows

docs.title: Worked example: reading ScreenGrab's status table
docs.text:
The design document ends its testing chapter with a status table. Read through the labels above, its rows sort like this.

Claim from the design document Status 94 automated tests pass Verified automatically Installer rollback after a failed swap works (with a stubbed move command) Verified automatically Smoke checks pass, with 0.0% CPU and about 25 MB at idle Verified automatically A real 980 by 570 grab pasted into another app with correct orientation and colors Verified by hand Control-Shift-4 works with a real key press Verified by hand The x86_64 half of the universal build works Not yet run Control-Shift-5 works with a real key press Not yet run Countdown cancel paths, Preferences recording, timings, multiple displays Not yet run

The fourth label, "claim exceeds evidence", has no rows in the real table, because the author wrote the claims carefully. It is the label you apply when you meet a sentence such as "ScreenGrab works" resting on 94 passing tests.

Now judge ten claims yourself.

docs.title: Diagram: Verification Status Classifier
docs.text:
Verification Status Classifier

Type: microsim sim-id: verification-status-classifier Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/unicorns/tree/main/docs/sims/claim-verification-tree Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge the verification status of each of ten ScreenGrab claims from the evidence offered for it, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: automated test, manual testing, evidence-based reporting, verification status, the four status labels (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns one of the four status labels to each claim. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct status in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt per item. Reading the reasons after answering is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Passing automated tests verify the whole product. (2) A later success explains an earlier failure. (3) A claim with no evidence is false rather than unverified.

Instructional Rationale: Judging requires applying criteria to evidence, which is the Evaluate-level skill. Ten mixed cases make the learner apply the same four criteria repeatedly, and each reason models the correct justification.

Content:

The four labels: Verified automatically, Verified by hand, Not yet run, Claim exceeds evidence.

# Claim Evidence offered Correct status Why (shown as feedback) 1 94 automated tests pass A test run reports 94 of 94 passing Verified automatically A program ran the tests and the output is on record. 2 ScreenGrab works The 94 automated tests pass Claim exceeds evidence The tests cover logic, not the real key press, capture permission, or paste. 3 Control-Shift-4 starts a grab A real key press at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, confirmed in the log Verified by hand A person pressed the keys and the log recorded the result. 4 Control-Shift-5 starts a delayed grab None yet Not yet run No check has been done. 5 The earlier Control-Shift-4 failure is fixed The key later worked, and nothing was changed Claim exceeds evidence The cause is unknown, so a later success does not show it is fixed. 6 The Intel (x86_64) half of the universal app works The build contains the x86_64 slice, but it was never run Not yet run Containing the code is not the same as running it. 7 The app idles at about 0.0% CPU and 25 MB A smoke check using ps on macOS 26.6.2 Verified automatically A script measured it and the output is on record. 8 The installer rolls back after a failed swap A test with a stubbed move command Verified automatically A test confirmed the flow, with the stub noted. 9 A real grab pastes with correct orientation and colors A 980 by 570 grab was pasted into another app and checked Verified by hand A person made the grab and looked at the pasted result. 10 The countdown cancel paths work None yet Not yet run These need a person and have not been run.

Provenance: Claims and evidence are from section 10.4 "Verification status" of the ScreenGrab design document. Items 2 and 5 are claims the chapter author wrote to illustrate the fourth label; the sim must label them "constructed example".

Rules: Four answer choices per item. An item is correct when the chosen label equals the Correct status. The score counts first answers only. The order is fixed as listed.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads claim 1 and the evidence offered.
  2. The learner chooses one of the four labels.
  3. The sim shows correct or incorrect and the Why text. An answered item cannot be changed.
  4. After claim 10, the sim shows the score and a table of the ten claims grouped by status.
  5. The learner should notice that "Not yet run" is a different label from "Claim exceeds evidence".

Feedback: Ten items, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [status]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" when n >= 8.

Starting State: Claim 1 is shown with its evidence and four unselected labels. The question on screen is "How well is this claim verified?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's status table lists these labels and states that the Intel half has not been run, Control-Shift-5 has not been run, Control-Shift-4 worked at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, and the earlier failure is unexplained.

docs.title: Verification Plans
docs.text:
A verification plan is a written list of the checks that will establish a piece of software's status, naming for each one the requirement it covers, who or what runs it, and how it is judged. Its main job is to separate the checks a program can run from the checks a person must run, so that nothing falls into the gap between them.

A plan for ScreenGrab's hotkey requirements might look like this.

Requirement Check Run by Pass rule Status Hotkey is registered and conflicts are reported Registration and conflict tests Automated Tests pass Verified automatically Hotkey event reaches the handler with the right action Hand-built Carbon event test Automated Tests pass Verified automatically A real Control-Shift-4 press starts a grab AC-3 with the log checked Person Log shows the grab started Verified by hand A real Control-Shift-5 press starts a delayed grab AC-11 Person HUD counts down, grab completes Not yet run Hotkey works with VS Code in front AC-3 with VS Code frontmost Person Grab starts Not yet run

The capstone in Chapter 15 asks you to write one of these for your own tool. Fill the "Run by" column first. Anything that says Person is work that no agent can do for you.

You Can Back Up a Claim

You can now investigate a bug from reproduction to regression test, name the limits of automated tests, label a claim's verification status, and write a plan that hands the human checks to a human. Chapter 14 looks at what comes after the first install.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans
docs.text: Test your understanding of bug reproduction, root cause analysis, regression tests, the limits of automated tests, evidence-based reporting, and verification status with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a regression test?
docs.text:
1. A test that measures how fast the software runs
  2. A test added after a bug is fixed, which fails if the bug ever returns
  3. A test written before any code exists
  4. A test that confirms the software starts
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Regression means going backwards: a fixed behavior breaking again after a later change. Because AI agents change code often and quickly, a fix without a regression test may quietly undo itself. The steps are to write the test from the reproduction recipe, watch it fail against the broken code, apply the fix, and watch it pass. Option D describes a smoke test.

Concept Tested: Regression Tests

See: Regression Tests

docs.title: 2. What is bug reproduction?
docs.text:
1. Copying a bug into another program on purpose
  2. Writing a report that describes the bug in general terms
  3. Fixing the bug by editing the code
  4. Making a bug happen again on demand using a written recipe
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. A bug you can reproduce is a bug you can fix and test, while one you cannot reproduce can only be guessed at. A good recipe has the starting state, the exact steps, the expected result, and the actual result, plus the environment: operating system version, hardware, and app version. The chapter's Retina example gives a recipe that anyone with a 2 times display can follow.

Concept Tested: Bug Reproduction

See: Bug Reproduction

docs.title: 3. What is root cause analysis?
docs.text:
1. The search for the underlying reason a bug happens, rather than the nearest visible symptom
  2. A review of the license terms
  3. A count of how many users reported the bug
  4. A comparison of two vendors' prices
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Fixing the symptom, such as doubling the output size, can hide the problem and break other cases. The method is to keep asking why until you reach a cause that, if removed, makes the bug impossible. In the hypothetical Retina example, the chain ends at a scale conversion that was done in two places, with one skipping the scale factor.

Concept Tested: Root Cause Analysis

See: Root Cause Analysis

docs.title: 4. ScreenGrab's early hotkey failure was never explained, though a real key press later worked. Why does the chapter say not to call it fixed?
docs.text:
1. Because hotkeys can never work reliably
  2. Because the later success proves nothing about any hotkey
  3. Because nothing was changed that could account for the difference, so calling it fixed would be a false claim
  4. Because the log was deleted
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. An unexplained failure is one that was observed but cannot be accounted for, usually because it could not be reproduced and not enough evidence was captured. The right response is to leave it open and write down what to capture next time. The later success, confirmed by the log, is real evidence for that moment, but it does not explain the earlier failure. Options A and D are not claims the chapter makes.

Concept Tested: Unexplained Failure

See: The Unexplained Failure

docs.title: 5. Why is "it works on my machine" not evidence, according to the chapter?
docs.text:
1. Because all machines are identical
  2. Because an environment-specific bug appears only on some setups, such as a particular OS version, hardware, tool installation, or shell
  3. Because the author's machine is always broken
  4. Because evidence must come from a vendor
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. ScreenGrab recorded two real examples. Macs with only the Command Line Tools ship the Swift Testing framework but not XCTest, so the test script passes three locations explicitly. And in non-interactive zsh scripts, plain log runs a shell built-in, so scripts must call /usr/bin/log by its full path. Behavior on hardware the author does not own cannot be seen from one machine.

Concept Tested: Environment-Specific Bugs

See: Environment-Specific Bugs

docs.title: 6. All 94 of ScreenGrab's automated tests passed, yet the hotkey still had an open question. What does the chapter conclude?
docs.text:
1. A test result and a verification result are different things, because a program could not press the physical key
  2. The tests were written incorrectly
  3. Automated tests are useless
  4. The hotkey needs no verification
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The tests exercised everything after the press, including a hand-built hotkey event reaching the handler, but they could not show that the keyboard produced that event. The gap closed only when a person pressed the keys and the log showed the result. A stubbed test shows the code handles the stub's answers, not what the real tool does. Option C overstates the point, since the tests remain valuable.

Concept Tested: Limits Of Automated Tests

See: Limits of Automated Tests

docs.title: 7. Which verification status applies to the claim "Control-Shift-5 works with a real key press," for which no check has been done?
docs.text:
1. Verified automatically
  2. Verified by hand
  3. Claim exceeds evidence
  4. Not yet run
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The chapter uses four labels: verified automatically, verified by hand, not yet run, and claim exceeds evidence. In ScreenGrab's status table, the Control-Shift-5 press, the x86_64 half of the universal build, and several countdown and multi-display checks are all "not yet run." Writing that label plainly tells a reader what is risky and what to check next.

Concept Tested: Verification Status

See: Verification Status

docs.title: 8. When writing a regression test for a fixed bug, which step shows that the test can actually catch the bug?
docs.text:
1. Deleting the test after the fix
  2. Writing the test after the fix without running it
  3. Running the test against the broken code and watching it fail before applying the fix
  4. Running the test only on a machine that never had the bug
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. A test that never failed has not shown it can catch the bug. The sequence is to write the test from the reproduction recipe, run it against the broken code and see it fail, apply the fix, and see it pass. This is the habit that keeps a fix from quietly undoing itself when an agent changes the code again.

Concept Tested: Regression Tests

See: Regression Tests

docs.title: 9. In the hypothetical Retina bug, the crop used point values as pixel values because the scale conversion was done in two places and one skipped it. What is the fix the chapter describes?
docs.text:
1. Double the output size at the end
  2. Tell users to avoid Retina displays
  3. Remove the crop feature
  4. Replace the duplicated conversion with a single tested conversion function
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Root cause analysis points at the duplicated conversion, not at the half-size image. Doubling the output (option A) would fix one symptom and risk breaking other cases. A single tested function removes the possibility of one place skipping the scale factor, which is the mitigation the ScreenGrab design records for this risk. A regression test can then guard it.

Concept Tested: Root Cause Analysis

See: Root Cause Analysis

docs.title: 10. A report says "ScreenGrab works," and its only support is 94 passing automated tests. Which verification status label fits best?
docs.text:
1. Claim exceeds evidence
  2. Verified by hand
  3. Not yet run
  4. Verified automatically for the whole claim
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. The sentence "ScreenGrab works" says far more than passing tests show: real key presses, real screen capture, pasting into real applications, and other hardware were not covered by those tests. The chapter says this fourth label has no rows in the real table because the author wrote claims carefully, and it is the label to apply to a sweeping sentence like this one. A better claim lists what was checked and what was not.

Concept Tested: Evidence-Based Reporting

See: Verification Status

docs.title: References: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans
docs.text:
1. Debugging - Wikipedia - Covers the process of finding and resolving defects, with common techniques and tools. Frames the reproduction-to-regression-test path taught in the chapter.

  2. Regression testing - Wikipedia - Explains rerunning tests to confirm that changes did not break existing behavior. Supports the chapter's rule that every fixed bug earns a regression test.

  3. Verification and validation - Wikipedia - Distinguishes building the product right from building the right product. Underpins the chapter's labeling of a claim's verification status. It separates a passing check from a verified claim.

  4. Why Programs Fail: A Guide to Systematic Debugging - Andreas Zeller - Morgan Kaufmann - Zeller treats debugging as scientific method and introduced delta debugging to isolate failure causes automatically. His TRAFFIC steps give a repeatable path from report to fix.

  5. Debugging: The 9 Indispensable Rules - David J. Agans - AMACOM - Agans distilled debugging into memorable rules such as make it fail and quit thinking and look. Their plain wording makes disciplined reproduction easy for beginners.

  6. How to Report Bugs Effectively - Simon Tatham - A classic guide to writing bug reports with exact steps, expected results, and actual results. Teaches the evidence a reader needs to reproduce a problem.

  7. Bug Writing Guidelines - Mozilla - Mozilla's guidance on summaries, reproducible steps, and attachments for bug reports. A real project's standard for evidence in a report.

  8. How to Create a Minimal, Reproducible Example - Stack Overflow - Explains how to shrink a failing case to the smallest code that still shows the problem. A practical method for the reproduction step of investigation.

  9. Effective Troubleshooting - Google SRE Book - Describes a hypothetico-deductive method for diagnosing failures: observe, hypothesize, test. Models the evidence-first investigation the chapter teaches. Read it before debugging a failure you cannot yet explain.

  10. Claude Code: Best Practices for Agentic Coding - Anthropic - Recommends giving an agent ways to verify its work, such as tests and screenshots. Supports the chapter's point that generated claims need independent evidence.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text: This chapter looks past the first install. It covers technical debt, operating system compatibility, toolchain changes, and patch releases, then the open source path: licenses including MIT and Creative Commons, public repositories, forks, pull requests, community contribution, and documentation for others. After this chapter, you will be able to assess the long-term cost of maintaining a personal tool and prepare one for sharing.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 15 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Technical Debt 1 Operating System Compatibility 1 Toolchain Changes 1 Patch Release 1 Open Source Software 13 Open Source License 5 Permissive License 4 MIT License 3 Creative Commons License 1 Public Repository 7 Forking 4 Pull Request 3 Community Contribution 2 Long-Term Stewardship 1 Documentation For Others 3

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
  • Chapter 4: Total Cost of Ownership
  • Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents
  • Chapter 6: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software
  • Chapter 8: Software Design and Platform Constraints
  • Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
  • Chapter 13: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans

The Shell You Carry Next Year

Building a tool is a weekend. Keeping it working is a decade, and a tool you share can have help carrying it. By the end of this chapter you will be able to estimate that decade honestly and publish your tool so others can pick it up. Grab only what you need!

The ScreenGrab story so far has an end that looks like a beginning: the app is installed and working. Chapter 4 taught you that the purchase price is only part of the cost of ownership, and the same is true of a tool you generate. The $6 build is the cheap part. This chapter covers the cost that arrives later, and the option that spreads it across other people: open source.

docs.title: Technical Debt
docs.text:
Technical debt is the future cost created by choosing a quick or incomplete solution now. Like financial debt it accrues interest: every later change takes longer because of the shortcut. In a personal tool, typical debts are undocumented workarounds, code that only the original agent session understood, and dependencies that stop being updated.

ScreenGrab keeps its debt low on purpose. It has no third-party dependencies, so there are no outside libraries to fall behind. The pure logic is separated from the window code and covered by tests. Screen capture is isolated behind one type, so a change in Apple's capture technology touches one file. These choices cost a little at design time and save more in maintenance.

Debt Has Interest

Think of a shortcut as a loan. The code ships today, and every later change pays a little interest. A tool you will keep for years should borrow less than a throwaway you will delete on Friday.

docs.title: Operating System Compatibility
docs.text:
Operating system compatibility is the ability of the software to keep working as the operating system changes. A tool that depends on system behavior is at the mercy of each new release. The ScreenGrab specification names two examples.

First, macOS ties the Screen Recording permission to the app's code signature. An app signed ad hoc gets a new identity whenever its code changes, so the permission must be granted again after such a rebuild. The scripts accept a stable signing identity to avoid this. Second, since macOS 15 the system periodically asks the user to re-confirm Screen Recording access for apps that capture the screen. That is outside the app's control, so the README documents it.

docs.title: Toolchain Changes
docs.text: Toolchain changes are updates to the compilers, build tools, and test frameworks that turn your source code into a running app. A toolchain change can break a tool that never changed. ScreenGrab shows this in miniature: it builds with the Swift tools that come with Command Line Tools, and the design document notes that, depending on the Swift version, the build may not find the testing framework, its macro plugin, or a run-time library. The test script passes all three locations, which is a fix for exactly this kind of drift. Managing the risk takes three habits: write down the tool versions you built with, rebuild occasionally rather than only when something breaks, and keep the build in a script rather than in your memory.

docs.title: Patch Releases
docs.text: A patch release is a small new version that fixes a defect without adding features. Version numbers often follow the pattern major, minor, patch. A fix for a bug moves the last number, for example from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 (a hypothetical example). A patch release tells users that updating is low risk. For a personal tool, a patch release is also a record that lets you tell which build is installed on which computer.

docs.title: Worked example: a year of maintenance
docs.text:
The estimate below is illustrative. It uses invented hours, not measurements, to show how to think about the cost. Suppose one macOS update a year forces a compatibility fix, and one toolchain update a year forces a build fix. The table lists the hours and the cost if an AI session does the work at the ScreenGrab session rate of about $14 per session.

Task per year Illustrative hours of your time Illustrative AI cost Read release notes, test the app on the new macOS 1 $0 Compatibility fix with an agent 1 $14 Toolchain fix with an agent 1 $14 Rebuild, reinstall on three computers, re-grant permission 1 $0 Total 4 hours $28

At a value of $50 an hour for your time, which you should replace with your own, four hours is $200. Added to $28, that is about $228 a year, more than the $90 a year in subscription fees that the tool replaces. The illustration is deliberately not flattering: ownership cost is mostly your time. It also shows why sharing the work matters, which the rest of the chapter explains.

docs.title: Open Source Software
docs.text:
Open source software is software whose source code is available to everyone and whose license gives everyone the right to use, study, change, and share it. The Open Source Initiative's definition adds that an open source license must allow free redistribution, must include the source code, must allow derived works, and must not discriminate against people or fields of use. Open source does not mean free of support or free of effort, only free of permission barriers. Two things must both be true: you can see the code, and the license says you may use it. Code on a public web page with no license is visible but not open source, because nobody is granted permission.

ScreenGrab is open source. The code is public, and the MIT License grants everyone the right to use, change, and share the app, including commercially. That is how a $0 option exists for anyone who wants the app without the fee or the build.

docs.title: Worked example: what open source does to the cost table
docs.text: Return to the $90 a year of fees. For a reader who simply installs the finished open source app, the money cost is $0 and the build time is the time to run the installer. For a reader who wants changes, the cost is the time to fork and edit. For the author, the cost of building was $14 in tokens, and sharing adds the time to prepare and document the project. Open source does not remove the cost of the work. It lets many people share one copy of that cost.

docs.title: Open Source Licenses
docs.text:
An open source license is the legal document that gives others permission to use, change, and share your code, and sets any conditions. Without one, the law's default is that nobody except the author may copy or change the work, even if it is posted publicly. The license is what makes sharing real. Most licenses have the same three parts: a grant that says what you may do, conditions that say what you must do in return, and a disclaimer that says the software comes without warranty. Licenses also interact. If your tool includes a library under a copyleft license, that license can apply to your tool as well, which is another reason ScreenGrab's lack of dependencies is convenient.

Licenses fall into two broad families, defined next, and a few terms help read them. Distribute means to give copies to others. A derivative work is a new work built from the original, such as a changed copy.

No License Means No Permission

A public repository without a license file is not open source, because others have no legal right to reuse your code. Before you announce your tool, add a LICENSE file to the top folder, and check that the copyright line has your name and year.

docs.title: Permissive Licenses
docs.text: A permissive license places very few conditions on reuse. Others may use, change, and even sell your code, usually as long as they keep your copyright notice. The other family is the copyleft license, such as the GNU General Public License, which adds a condition: if someone distributes a changed version, they must release it under the same license. Common permissive licenses are MIT, the BSD licenses, and Apache 2.0, which also grants a patent license. Permissive licenses suit tools you want used widely with no strings. Copyleft licenses suit projects whose authors want improvements to stay open.

docs.title: Worked example: two ways to license the same tool
docs.text: Suppose a company wants to put ScreenGrab into a commercial product. Under a permissive license, it may do so if it keeps the copyright and license notice. Under a copyleft license, it would have to publish its changed version's source under the same license. Neither choice is better in general. The author's goal decides: ScreenGrab is meant to give people a free tool with no strings, so a permissive license fits.

docs.title: The MIT License
docs.text: The MIT License is a short, popular permissive license. It grants everyone permission to use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and sell copies of the software. It has two conditions: include the copyright notice and the permission notice in all copies, and accept that the software comes with no warranty. ScreenGrab's LICENSE file reads "MIT License, Copyright (c) 2026 Dan McCreary". The whole license is about twenty lines, which is part of why people choose it. Its warranty disclaimer matters to a personal-tool author: if your tool misbehaves on someone else's machine, the license says you are not liable for it.

docs.title: Creative Commons Licenses
docs.text:
A Creative Commons license is one of a family of licenses designed for creative works such as text, images, and music, not for software code. Each license is a combination of conditions: BY means credit the author, NC means non-commercial use only, SA means share adaptations under the same license. This book's text is licensed CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, while its code is MIT.

Note that a license with the NC condition restricts commercial use, so it is generally not considered an open source license, although it still allows free sharing and adapting. Use Creative Commons for writing and images, and an open source license for code.

One Folder, Two Licenses

If your project has both code and prose, say so in plain words. Put the code license in a LICENSE file and write one sentence in the README, such as "The text is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0". Readers will not have to guess.

Try matching licenses to scenarios before moving on.

docs.title: Diagram: Open Source License Matcher
docs.text:
Open Source License Matcher

Type: microsim sim-id: open-source-license-matcher Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/search-microsims/tree/main/docs/sims/cc-license-chooser Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: apply Learning Objective: The learner will apply the conditions of five license choices to choose the license that fits each of eight scenarios, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

Prerequisites: open source license, permissive license, copyleft, MIT License, Creative Commons license, the BY, NC and SA conditions (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: The learner assigns one of five license choices to each of eight scenarios. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct choice in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt per scenario. Reading the reasons is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Any Creative Commons license is also an open source license. (2) A public repository with no license can be reused freely. (3) Copyleft and permissive licenses place the same conditions on reuse.

Instructional Rationale: Applying the conditions to concrete scenarios shows that license choice depends on what the author wants others to be able to do. Eight scenarios cover each choice at least once and force the learner to apply the conditions rather than recall names.

Content:

The five choices: MIT License, Copyleft license (such as the GNU General Public License), CC BY 4.0, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, No license (all rights reserved).

# Scenario Correct choice Why (shown as feedback) 1 Source code of a small utility. Anyone may use it for any purpose, including commercially. They only need to keep your credit. MIT License MIT is permissive and asks only for the copyright notice. 2 Source code where anyone who distributes an improved version must also release its source. Copyleft license (such as the GNU General Public License) Copyleft requires changed versions to carry the same license. 3 Chapters of a book that may be shared and adapted with credit, not used commercially, with adaptations under the same terms. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 BY gives credit, NC bars commercial use, SA keeps adaptations under the same terms. 4 A collection of diagrams that anyone, including companies, may reuse with credit. CC BY 4.0 BY alone requires only credit and allows commercial reuse. 5 A personal script on your own laptop that you never share. No license (all rights reserved) Nobody else needs permission, so no license is needed. 6 Short code samples in a textbook that readers may paste into their own commercial apps. MIT License Code samples suit a permissive code license. 7 Photos on a website that may be reused commercially if the photographer is credited. CC BY 4.0 Photos are creative works, and BY allows commercial reuse with credit. 8 Lesson plans that teachers may remix, provided remixes carry the same terms and are not resold. CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 NC bars resale and SA keeps remixes under the same terms.

Provenance: The license conditions are from the chapter sections "Permissive Licenses", "The MIT License" and "Creative Commons Licenses". Scenarios are written by the chapter author.

Rules: Five answer choices per scenario. A scenario is correct when the chosen license equals the Correct choice. The score counts first answers only. The order is fixed as listed. The sim states that it is an educational exercise and not legal advice.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads scenario 1 and chooses one of five licenses.
  2. The sim shows correct or incorrect and the Why text. An answered scenario cannot be changed.
  3. The learner moves through scenarios 2 to 8 in order.
  4. After scenario 8, the sim shows the score and a table of the eight scenarios grouped by license.
  5. The learner should notice that the Creative Commons choices are used for text and images, and the other choices for code.

Feedback: Eight scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [license]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 8" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" when n >= 7.

Starting State: Scenario 1 is shown with five unselected license choices. The question on screen is "Which license fits what this author wants?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states ScreenGrab's code is under the MIT License, this book's text is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and a license with the NC condition is generally not considered open source.

docs.title: Public Repositories
docs.text: A public repository is a project folder, with its full change history, hosted where anyone can see it. ScreenGrab lives at github.com/dmccreary/macos-screen-grab. Making it public is what turns a license into something people can use.

docs.title: Worked example: a pre-publication checklist
docs.text:
Before making a repository public, check these items one at a time.

  1. A LICENSE file is in the top folder.
  2. A README explains what the tool does and how to install it.
  3. No passwords, keys, tokens, or personal data are in the files or in the history.
  4. Paths on your own computer, such as your home folder name, are removed or made generic.
  5. The build and the tests run on a clean machine from the instructions alone.

Item 3 is the dangerous one. A secret deleted in a later change is still in the history that anyone can read.

History Remembers Secrets

Removing a password from a file does not remove it from earlier versions, and a public repository exposes all of them. Search the files and the history before you publish, and if a key was ever committed, treat it as leaked and replace it.

docs.title: Forking
docs.text: Forking is making your own copy of someone else's repository under your own account. The copy keeps its link to the original, so you can bring in later updates. A fork is the normal way to change a project you do not own. Over time the original moves on, so a fork has to bring in the original's updates (often called syncing with upstream) or it drifts apart. With a permissive license, the fork keeps the original copyright notice and adds its own changes under its own name. You edit your copy freely, without asking permission and without affecting the original.

docs.title: Worked example: a fork for a different shortcut
docs.text: Suppose a reader prefers Control-Option-S for a grab and wants it as the default. They fork ScreenGrab, change the default in their copy, and build and install their fork. Their fork is now theirs to maintain. Because the license is MIT, they need no permission. If the change would help everyone, they can offer it back to the original, using a pull request.

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
A pull request is a proposal to merge changes from one branch or fork into another repository. It shows the differences, collects comments, and lets the owner accept or decline. Owners review pull requests because a change from a stranger, or from an AI agent, needs checking just as any code does. A good pull request is small, explains why, and includes the evidence from Chapter 13. Review matters most when the author is an AI agent, because the reviewer must check that the change does what it claims and nothing more. The owner may also decline, and a declined pull request is not an insult: the proposal may simply not fit the project's purpose.

The next diagram follows one contribution from discovery to merge, and asks where the code changes at each step.

docs.title: Diagram: Fork and Pull Request Flow
docs.text:
Fork and Pull Request Flow

Type: workflow sim-id: fork-and-pull-request-flow Library: Mermaid Status: Specified Bloom Level: Understand Bloom Verb: classify Learning Objective: The learner will classify each of the six steps of a contribution by where code changes (the contributor's fork, the original repository, or nowhere), with at least 5 of 6 correct.

Prerequisites: public repository, forking, pull request, community contribution (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For each step, the learner picks one of three places before the answer is shown. A pick is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Forking changes the original repository. (2) Opening a pull request changes the original code. (3) The contributor can merge their own change into someone else's project.

Instructional Rationale: Classifying where code changes at each step corrects the most common confusion, that a fork or a pull request alters the original. Committing an answer before the reveal makes the learner reason about ownership instead of reading it.

Content:

The diagram is a flowchart with six steps in order. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the description and three choices: "Contributor's fork", "Original repository", "Nowhere (no code changes)".

# Step Description Answer Reason 1 Find the public repository A contributor reads the code and the LICENSE file of a public repository Nowhere (no code changes) Reading changes nothing. 2 Fork it The contributor makes their own copy under their own account Contributor's fork The new copy is created in the contributor's account; the original is untouched. 3 Change and test the fork The contributor edits the copy and runs the tests Contributor's fork All edits happen in the copy. 4 Open a pull request The contributor proposes the changes to the owner Nowhere (no code changes) A pull request is a proposal; no code moves yet. 5 The owner reviews The owner reads the differences, asks questions, and requests changes Nowhere (no code changes) Review is discussion; the original code is unchanged. 6 The owner merges The owner accepts the proposal and brings the changes in Original repository Only the owner's decision changes the original.

Edge labels: "copy" from step 2 to step 3, "propose" from step 3 to step 4, "feedback" from step 5 back to step 3, "accept" from step 5 to step 6.

Provenance: From the chapter sections "Public Repositories", "Forking" and "Pull Requests". Step descriptions are the chapter author's wording.

Rules: Six steps, each with one correct answer. The score is the number of correct picks. Mastery when score >= 5. The order of the three choices is the same for every step.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner clicks a step. An information box shows the description and three choices.
  2. The learner picks one choice. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the Reason.
  3. The learner opens the remaining steps in any order until all six are answered.
  4. The learner should notice that only the final step changes the original repository.

Feedback: Six steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Answer]" plus the Reason. The score "Correct: n of 6" is shown after the last step.

Starting State: The flowchart is shown with no step answered. The question on screen is "At which step does the original project actually change?"
