Chapter Anchors: The chapter states a fork is a copy under the contributor's own account, a pull request is a proposal, and the owner decides whether to merge.

docs.title: Community Contribution
docs.text: A community contribution is any help given to a project by people other than its original author: a bug report, a fix, a doc improvement, a test on another machine. Contributions are not only code. Bug reports with the reproduction recipe from Chapter 13 are valuable, as are documentation fixes and translations. For a personal tool the most valuable contribution is often a test report from a machine the author does not own, such as the Intel half of ScreenGrab's universal build that nobody has run yet.

docs.title: Long-Term Stewardship
docs.text: Long-term stewardship is the ongoing responsibility for keeping a shared project healthy: reviewing contributions, making patch releases, answering issues, and, when the time comes, handing it over or retiring it with a clear note. Sharing a tool creates this duty. Typical duties are to reply to issues within a stated time, tag patch releases, and keep the dependency list short. It is fine to say in the README that a project is a personal tool with no support promised. Being clear about it is part of being a good steward.

docs.title: Documentation for Others
docs.text:
Documentation for others is written material that lets a stranger install, use, and change your tool without asking you. You wrote the tool, so you do not need a README to use it, which is why it gets skipped. For ScreenGrab the set includes a README with install steps, a specification of what it does, and a design document that explains why. A reader should be able to go from zero to a working install by following the README alone.

You Know the Long Game

You can now estimate the yearly cost of keeping a tool alive, choose between permissive, copyleft, and Creative Commons licensing, and prepare a repository for strangers. Chapter 15 puts every number in this book to work on a decision of your own.

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: Maintenance and Open Source Sharing
docs.text: Test your understanding of technical debt, compatibility, patch releases, open source licenses, forks, pull requests, and stewardship with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a patch release?
docs.text:
1. A major version that adds many new features
  2. A new product sold under a different name
  3. A small new version that fixes a defect without adding features
  4. A license change that removes source code access
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Version numbers often follow the pattern major, minor, patch, and a bug fix moves the last number, for example from 1.0.0 to 1.0.1 (a hypothetical example). A patch release tells users that updating is low risk. For a personal tool it is also a record that lets you tell which build is installed on which computer.

Concept Tested: Patch Releases

See: Patch Releases

docs.title: 2. What is a Creative Commons license designed for?
docs.text:
1. Creative works such as text, images, and music, not software code
  2. Compiled applications only
  3. Operating systems
  4. Hardware designs only
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Creative Commons licenses combine conditions: BY means credit the author, NC means non-commercial use only, and SA means share adaptations under the same license. This book's text is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, while its code is MIT. A license with the NC condition restricts commercial use, so it is generally not considered open source. Use Creative Commons for writing and images, and an open source license for code.

Concept Tested: Creative Commons License

See: Creative Commons Licenses

docs.title: 3. How does a permissive license differ from a copyleft license?
docs.text:
1. Permissive licenses forbid all reuse
  2. Copyleft licenses allow reuse without any conditions
  3. They are identical in every respect
  4. A permissive license places very few conditions on reuse, while copyleft requires distributed changes to be released under the same license
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Under a permissive license such as MIT, BSD, or Apache 2.0, others may use, change, and even sell your code, usually if they keep your copyright notice. Under a copyleft license such as the GNU General Public License, someone who distributes a changed version must release it under the same license. Neither is better in general, and the author's goal decides.

Concept Tested: Permissive License

See: Permissive Licenses

docs.title: 4. How does open source change the cost of the work of building a tool?
docs.text:
1. It removes the cost of the work entirely
  2. It does not remove the cost of the work, but lets many people share one copy of that cost
  3. It makes the work more expensive for every user
  4. It transfers all costs to the vendor
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A reader who only installs the finished app pays $0 in money and the time to run the installer. A reader who wants changes pays the time to fork and edit. The author paid $14 in tokens, and sharing adds time to prepare and document the project. Open source does not mean free of support or effort, only free of permission barriers.

Concept Tested: Open Source Software

See: Open Source Software

docs.title: 5. While preparing to make a repository public, you find a password that was deleted from the files in an earlier commit. What does the chapter say about this?
docs.text:
1. It is safe, because deleted content is gone forever
  2. It is safe, because only the owner can read the history
  3. It is dangerous, because a secret deleted in a later change is still in the history that anyone can read
  4. It is only a problem for private repositories
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The pre-publication checklist lists a LICENSE file, a README, no passwords, keys, tokens, or personal data in the files or the history, generic paths, and a build that runs on a clean machine from the instructions alone. The chapter calls the secrets item the dangerous one, because the full change history is published with a public repository.

Concept Tested: Public Repositories

See: Public Repositories

docs.title: 6. A reader prefers Control-Option-S as the default shortcut and wants a version of ScreenGrab with that change. What does the chapter suggest?
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository, change the default in the copy, and build it, then offer the change back with a pull request if it would help everyone
  2. Ask the author to rewrite the app
  3. Edit the original repository directly without permission
  4. Buy a commercial replacement
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. A fork is your own copy of someone else's repository under your own account, and it keeps its link to the original so you can sync later updates. Because the license is MIT, no permission is needed. The fork is then yours to maintain, and a pull request can propose the change back. Option C is not possible without write access, and a stranger's change should be reviewed anyway.

Concept Tested: Forking

See: Forking

docs.title: 7. The chapter's illustrative year of maintenance totals 4 hours of your time plus $28 in agent sessions. At $50 an hour, how does the yearly ownership cost compare with the $90 subscription it replaces?
docs.text:
1. It is far below the subscription at about $28
  2. It is about equal at $90
  3. It is $14 per year
  4. It is about $228, higher than the subscription, because ownership cost is mostly your time
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. Four hours at $50 is $200, and adding $28 gives about $228 a year, more than the $90 in fees. The chapter calls the illustration deliberately unflattering: the hours are invented, and you should substitute your own time value. It shows that the token bill is the cheap part, and it motivates sharing the work, since open source spreads the maintenance across more people.

Concept Tested: Maintenance Cost

See: Patch Releases

docs.title: 8. Why does ScreenGrab accumulate so little technical debt?
docs.text:
1. It was never tested
  2. It has no third-party dependencies, separates pure logic from window code with tests, and isolates screen capture behind one type
  3. It is updated hourly by a vendor
  4. It relies on many outside libraries that update themselves
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Technical debt is the future cost of a quick or incomplete solution, and like financial debt it accrues interest because every later change takes longer. ScreenGrab's design choices cost a little at design time and save more in maintenance. With no outside libraries there is nothing to fall behind, and a change in Apple's capture technology touches only one file.

Concept Tested: Technical Debt

See: Technical Debt

docs.title: 9. Why must the Screen Recording permission often be granted again after rebuilding an ad-hoc signed app?
docs.text:
1. macOS ties the permission to the app's code signature, and an ad-hoc signed app gets a new identity whenever its code changes
  2. Rebuilding deletes all system settings
  3. The permission expires every hour
  4. The compiler removes it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. This is an operating system compatibility issue. The scripts accept a stable signing identity to avoid it. A second issue is outside the app's control: since macOS 15, the system periodically asks the user to re-confirm Screen Recording access for apps that capture the screen, so the README documents it. Options B, C, and D invent mechanisms that the chapter does not describe.

Concept Tested: Operating System Compatibility

See: Operating System Compatibility

docs.title: 10. The author wants ScreenGrab to be a free tool with no strings, even if a company later embeds it in a commercial product. Which license choice best fits that goal?
docs.text:
1. A copyleft license, so the company must release its changes
  2. A Creative Commons NC license, so commercial use is banned
  3. A permissive license such as MIT, which allows commercial use if the notice is kept
  4. No license, so nobody can copy it
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The chapter's company example shows that under a permissive license it may embed the code if it keeps the copyright and license notice, while a copyleft license would force it to publish its changed source. ScreenGrab is meant to give people a free tool with no strings, and the MIT License fits that goal. Without any license, the law's default is that nobody except the author may copy or change the work.

Concept Tested: Permissive License

See: Permissive Licenses

docs.title: References: Maintenance and Open Source Sharing
docs.text:
1. Open-source software - Wikipedia - Describes software with source code released under licenses permitting use and modification, with history and models. Gives the sharing context for the chapter.

  2. Copyleft - Wikipedia - Explains licenses that require derivative works to stay under the same terms. Defines one side of the permissive-versus-copyleft choice. Compare it with permissive licenses before choosing one.

  3. Creative Commons license - Wikipedia - Covers the family of licenses for sharing creative works with defined permissions. Supports the chapter's guidance on licensing text and images alongside code.

  4. Producing Open Source Software - Karl Fogel - O'Reilly - Fogel wrote the standard guide to running an open-source project, from first release to handling newcomers, and made it freely available. It shows how to prepare a repository for strangers.

  5. Working in Public: The Making and Maintenance of Open Source Software - Nadia Eghbal - Stripe Press - Eghbal's taxonomy of federations, clubs, stadiums, and toys shows how a project's audience drives maintainer workload. It explains the real, ongoing cost of sharing code.

  6. Open Source Guides - GitHub - Practical guides for starting, running, and sustaining open-source projects. Helps students prepare a repository and set expectations as maintainers. Read the sections on maintainers first.

  7. Choose a Creative Commons License - Creative Commons - An interactive tool that picks a license based on how you want others to reuse your work. A hands-on step in the chapter's licensing guidance.

  8. Keep a Changelog - Olivier Lacan - Proposes a simple format for recording notable changes in each release. A low-effort habit that reduces maintenance cost for users and maintainers.

  9. Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 - Semantic Versioning - Specifies a major, minor, patch numbering scheme that signals the impact of changes. Gives a shared language for releases in a maintained tool.

  10. Licensing a Repository - GitHub Docs - Explains how to add a license file to a repository and what happens without one. A necessary step before sharing generated code.

docs.title: The Final Decision and the Capstone Project
Summary
docs.text: This final chapter puts the book's analysis to work on a tool you choose. It covers cost per feature used, cost comparisons, the cost of generating software, decision criteria, and the decision matrix, then guides you through the capstone: specify, generate, and test a replacement for a paid tool and publish the cost comparison. After this chapter, you will be able to decide whether to buy, subscribe to, or generate a tool, with verification and maintenance taken into account.

docs.title: Concepts Covered
docs.text:
This chapter covers the following 8 concepts from the learning graph:

Concept Concept Impact Score Cost Per Feature Used 1 Cost Comparison 3 Cost Of Generating Software 5 Decision Criteria 4 Decision Matrix 3 Sharing A Personal Tool 2 Replacement Tool Capstone 2 Published Cost Comparison 1

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
This chapter builds on concepts from:

  • Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule
  • Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives
  • Chapter 4: Total Cost of Ownership
  • Chapter 6: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software
  • Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code
  • Chapter 11: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost
  • Chapter 12: Software Testing: Automated and Manual
  • Chapter 13: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans
  • Chapter 14: Maintenance and Open Source Sharing

Your Turn to Pick the Shell

You have the whole toolkit now: the 95/5 rule, token arithmetic, tests, evidence, and licenses. In this chapter you use it on a tool you pay for, and decide with numbers whether to keep paying. Grab only what you need!

The book has followed one case. A utility that cost $9 grew into a $30 per computer per year subscription, and a custom replacement was generated for about $6 to build and about $14 for the whole session. This chapter turns that story into a method you can run on your own tools, and ends with a project that makes you run it.

docs.title: Cost per Feature Used
docs.text: Cost per feature used is what you pay, in a given period, divided by the number of features you actually use. It exposes bloat in a way the sticker price hides. A $90 yearly fee sounds modest, but it is a different number once you divide by what you get.

docs.title: Worked example: ScreenGrab's two features
docs.text: The author used two features: grab a region, and grab a region after a delay. The subscription costs $90 a year across three computers, so the cost per feature used is \( 90 / 2 \) = $45 per feature per year, or \( 450 / 2 \) = $225 per feature over five years. The generated tool costs about $14 once, or \( 14 / 2 \) = $7 per feature. Cost per feature used is a rough yardstick and ignores maintenance, but it names the question: what am I paying for that I never touch?

docs.title: Cost Comparisons
docs.text: A cost comparison puts two or more options on the same footing: the same time horizon, the same number of computers, and the same list of what is and is not counted. The common mistakes are comparing a one-time price with an annual one, and leaving out the costs that are hardest to count. Chapter 4 showed the subscription side. The next section builds the generated side. Two more rules keep a comparison fair: state the date you checked each price, because subscription prices change, and show the comparison at more than one horizon, because a generated tool's up-front cost is paid once while a subscription's cost keeps growing. At one year the subscription is $90 and the generated tool's build is $14; at five years the subscription is $450.

docs.title: The Cost of Generating Software
docs.text:
The cost of generating software is everything it takes to get a working, trusted, kept-alive tool from an AI agent, not only the token bill. It has four parts, and three of them are not on the usage report.

  • Build tokens: about $6 for ScreenGrab's first install, and about $14 for the whole session (Chapter 11).
  • Your time: the active minutes you spend directing the agent, about 70 for the session.
  • Verification: the hand checks that no agent can do for you (Chapters 12 and 13).
  • Maintenance: operating system and toolchain upkeep, year after year (Chapter 14).

The break-even depends mostly on the last two, and the next table shows how. It models five years with a three-computer subscription of \( 3 \times 30 \times 5 \) = $450. The generated option costs the $14 build plus five years of maintenance, where each year costs your hours times your time value, plus $14 per agent session. The scenarios below are illustrative.

Scenario Maintenance hours a year Time value per hour Agent sessions a year Five-year cost Subscribe not applicable not applicable not applicable $450 Generate, hobbyist 2 $0 1 $84 Generate, light upkeep 1 $50 1 $334 Generate, Chapter 14's estimate 4 $50 2 $1,154

The three generated rows give three different answers. The result is not that generating always wins or always loses. It is that the answer depends on how much upkeep the tool needs and what your time is worth, and ScreenGrab's design choices (no dependencies, isolated platform code) push toward the light end. At $50 an hour with one session a year, generating stays cheaper only while upkeep is below about 1.5 hours a year.

Don't Price Your Time at Zero by Accident

Leaving your own hours out makes generating look free. Decide on a time value, even a low one, and put the hours in the table. If the answer only works at zero, say so in your report.

Check your arithmetic with the calculator before moving on.

docs.title: Diagram: Subscribe or Generate Cost Calculator
docs.text:
Subscribe or Generate Cost Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: subscribe-or-generate-cost-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/cost-attribution-rollup Bloom Level: Apply Bloom Verb: calculate Learning Objective: The learner will calculate the five-year cost of a three-computer subscription and of three generated-tool scenarios, each to within $1.

Prerequisites: cost comparison, cost of generating software, subscription fee, maintenance (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: For the four challenge rows, the learner types the five-year cost before the sim shows its value. An answer is correct when it is within $1 of the model value. Mastery is 4 of 4 correct. Changing the inputs in free exploration is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) Generating is always cheaper than subscribing. (2) The token bill is the whole cost of a generated tool. (3) The time horizon does not affect the comparison.

Instructional Rationale: Apply-level calculation needs a check, so the learner commits a number before the model value is shown. Free exploration then lets the learner find the break-even point that the chapter's text states.

Content:

Model inputs and their ranges:

Quantity Min Max Step Default Unit Computers 1 10 1 3 computers Annual fee per computer 0 100 5 30 dollars Years 1 10 1 5 years Build cost 0 50 1 14 dollars Maintenance hours per year 0 10 0.5 1 hours Time value 0 150 10 50 dollars per hour Agent sessions per year 0 5 1 1 sessions Cost of one agent session 0 50 1 14 dollars

Challenge rows, in order, with years = 5, computers = 3, fee = 30, and build cost = 14:

# Row Maintenance hours per year Time value Agent sessions per year Correct five-year cost Feedback when wrong 1 Subscribe not applicable not applicable not applicable $450 3 computers x $30 x 5 years = $450. 2 Generate, hobbyist 2 $0 1 $84 $14 build + 5 x (2 x $0 + 1 x $14) = $14 + $70 = $84. 3 Generate, light upkeep 1 $50 1 $334 $14 + 5 x (1 x $50 + $14) = $14 + $320 = $334. 4 Generate, Chapter 14's estimate 4 $50 2 $1,154 $14 + 5 x (4 x $50 + 2 x $14) = $14 + 5 x $228 = $1,154.

Provenance: The $30 fee, 3 computers, and $14 session cost are from docs/course-description.md. The maintenance hours, time value, and number of sessions are illustrative and the sim must label them "illustrative". Costs are computed from the Rules.

Rules: Subscribe cost = computers x fee x years. Generate cost = build cost + years x (maintenance hours x time value + sessions x session cost). The break-even maintenance hours per year, shown in exploration only when time value > 0, = ((subscribe cost - build cost) / years - sessions x session cost) / time value, shown to two decimals; at the default inputs it is 1.46 hours. When the generated cost is less than the subscribe cost, the sim shows "Generate is cheaper by $X"; when equal or greater, "Subscribe is cheaper by $X" (or "equal").

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner reads row 1 and types its five-year cost, then presses Check.
  2. The sim shows the model value and the worked calculation. The learner repeats for rows 2 to 4 in order.
  3. After row 4, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes any input and both five-year costs and the cheaper option update at once.
  4. The learner should notice that raising maintenance hours or time value moves the winner from Generate to Subscribe.

Feedback: Four rows, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: $X." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that row. After the second wrong attempt the model value and the worked calculation are shown and the row counts as missed. A running count "Rows correct: n of 4" is shown.

Starting State: Row 1 (Subscribe) is shown with an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What does the subscription cost over five years?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter's table states $450 for the subscription and $84, $334, and $1,154 for the three generated scenarios, and says generating stays cheaper only while upkeep is below about 1.5 hours a year at $50 an hour with one session a year.

docs.title: Decision Criteria
docs.text:
Decision criteria are the factors you use to choose, written down before you compare options so that the numbers do not pick for you. Cost is only one. For a buy, subscribe, or generate choice, these are the criteria this book supports:

  • Cost over your horizon: the cost comparison above, with its assumptions stated.
  • Fit: how much of the product you actually use (the 95/5 rule).
  • Verification effort: how much checking you must do yourself.
  • Maintenance load: the upkeep you will carry.
  • Risk if it fails: what breaks, or what data is lost, when the tool is wrong.

Add a sixth when it applies: Continuity, meaning what happens if the vendor changes the price or the tool is discontinued. Write the criteria and their importance before you look at prices, because it is easy to rationalize a choice afterward.

docs.title: Worked example: ScreenGrab against the criteria
docs.text: Cost over five years favors generating in the light-upkeep case. Fit favors generating strongly, since two features are used. Verification effort favors subscribing, because a vendor tests its product and ScreenGrab still has acceptance tests nobody has run. Maintenance favors subscribing. Risk is low for both, since a failed screen grab loses nothing. The criteria point both ways, which is why a decision matrix is worth building.

docs.title: The Decision Matrix
docs.text: A decision matrix scores each option on each criterion, multiplies by the importance weight of that criterion, and adds the results. The highest total wins. It does not replace judgment. It forces you to write your weights down and shows how much the answer depends on them.

docs.title: Worked example: a five-criterion matrix
docs.text:
Scores run from 1 (poor) to 5 (good), and weights from 1 (minor) to 5 (critical). The scores below are one person's illustrative judgment.

Criterion Weight Subscribe score Generate score Cost over five years 5 2 5 Fit to what I use 4 2 5 Verification effort 3 5 2 Maintenance load 3 5 2 Risk if it fails 2 4 3 Weighted total (maximum 85) 56 63

Subscribe: \( 5 \times 2 + 4 \times 2 + 3 \times 5 + 3 \times 5 + 2 \times 4 = 56 \). Generate: \( 5 \times 5 + 4 \times 5 + 3 \times 2 + 3 \times 2 + 2 \times 3 = 63 \). Generating leads by 7 points. A margin that small deserves a robustness check, which is what the sim below does.

docs.title: Diagram: Weighted Decision Matrix Explorer
docs.text:
Weighted Decision Matrix Explorer

Type: microsim sim-id: weighted-decision-matrix-explorer Library: p5.js Status: Specified Template: https://github.com/dmccreary/3d-printing-course/tree/main/docs/sims/concept-selection-matrix Bloom Level: Evaluate Bloom Verb: judge Learning Objective: The learner will judge how robust the winner of a weighted decision matrix is by finding which single-criterion weight changes flip the winner, answering both evaluation questions correctly.

Prerequisites: decision criteria, decision matrix, weight, score (all defined in the chapter above this block).

Evidence of Mastery: After exploring, the learner answers two questions: "By how many points does the leading option win at the default weights?" and "For how many of the five criteria does changing that weight alone (to any whole number from 1 to 5) flip the winner?" Answers are correct when they match the Content (7 points; 2 criteria). Dragging weights is exploration, not evidence.

Misconceptions: (1) The option with the higher total is obviously right. (2) Every criterion can change the outcome equally. (3) Weights are facts rather than judgments.

Instructional Rationale: Evaluating a choice means testing it against alternative judgments. Letting the learner change weights one at a time exposes which criteria carry the result, and the two questions ask the learner to state a judgment about robustness.

Content:

Criteria, fixed scores (1 to 5, higher is better), and default weights:

Criterion Default weight Subscribe score Generate score Cost over five years 5 2 5 Fit to what I use 4 2 5 Verification effort 3 5 2 Maintenance load 3 5 2 Risk if it fails 2 4 3

Each weight can be changed: min 1, max 5, step 1, unit points. Defaults sit on the grid. At the defaults, Subscribe totals 56, Generate totals 63, and the maximum possible total is 85.

Weight changes of a single criterion (all others at default). Totals are weight x score summed over the five criteria:

Criterion changed New weight Subscribe total Generate total Winner Cost over five years 1 48 43 Subscribe Cost over five years 2 50 48 Subscribe Cost over five years 3 52 53 Generate Fit to what I use 1 50 48 Subscribe Fit to what I use 2 52 53 Generate Verification effort 5 66 67 Generate Maintenance load 5 66 67 Generate Risk if it fails 5 68 72 Generate

The table lists the boundary cases. Every other single-weight change from 1 to 5 also leaves Generate ahead.

Question feedback:

# Question Correct answer Feedback when wrong 1 By how many points does the leading option win at default weights? 7 Generate 63 minus Subscribe 56 = 7. 2 For how many criteria does changing that weight alone flip the winner? 2 Only Cost (weight 1 or 2) and Fit (weight 1) flip the winner; changing Verification, Maintenance, or Risk alone does not.

Provenance: Criteria and scores are the chapter's worked example and are illustrative; the sim must label them "illustrative judgments". Totals are computed from the Rules.

Rules: Total for an option = sum over criteria of weight x score. The leader is the option with the strictly higher total; equal totals show "tie". The single-criterion flip count is found by trying every whole weight from 1 to 5 for one criterion at a time with the others at default. Cost flips at weights 1 and 2, Fit flips at weight 1, and Verification, Maintenance, and Risk never flip. The sim computes every total from the formula.

Learner Activity:

  1. The learner sees the matrix at default weights with both totals.
  2. The learner changes any weight. Both totals, the margin, and the leader update at once.
  3. The learner resets the weights with a Reset action, which returns all five to default.
  4. When ready, the learner answers question 1 and question 2.
  5. The learner should notice that most weights can change a lot without changing the winner, and a few cannot.

Feedback: Two questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second wrong attempt the answer is revealed. A count "Questions correct: n of 2" is shown.

Starting State: The matrix is shown at default weights. The question on screen is "Is Generate's lead solid, or does it depend on one weight?"

Chapter Anchors: The chapter states totals of 56 for Subscribe and 63 for Generate, a margin of 7 points, and a maximum of 85.

docs.title: Sharing a Personal Tool
docs.text: Sharing a personal tool means preparing it so that strangers can use it safely: a license, a README, honest statements about verification status, and a clear note about support. Chapter 14 covered the mechanics. The decision question is whether sharing is worth the effort. A shared tool needs, at a minimum, a license, a README that gives the verification status honestly, and a statement of what support you offer. Sharing turns your maintenance into a community's, and it gives you a way to find bugs on machines you do not own. It also creates the duty of stewardship, so decide in advance how much support you will promise.

docs.title: The Replacement Tool Capstone
docs.text:
The replacement tool capstone is the course project: pick a paid tool you use, build your own minimal replacement, test it, and publish what it cost. You do the same work that this book followed, in your own domain. The steps are:

  1. Choose a paid tool whose price bothers you, and record what you pay today.
  2. Log the features you use for a week, and list them. Expect the 95/5 rule.
  3. Write a minimal specification with an explicit list of what is left out (Chapter 7).
  4. Design within platform limits (Chapter 8), then generate, build, and install (Chapter 9).
  5. Measure the session: wall-clock time, active time, tokens by type, and an estimated cost (Chapter 11).
  6. Test and verify: automated tests where a program can check, and a written verification plan for what you must check by hand (Chapters 12 and 13).
  7. Decide: run the cost comparison and decision matrix above, including maintenance (Chapter 14).
  8. Publish the result, as the next section describes.

Pick a Small Tool First

Choose a tool where you can name the features you use in one sentence and test them yourself without special hardware. A tool with two features is a good first capstone; a tool with twenty is a second project.

docs.title: The Published Cost Comparison
docs.text:
A published cost comparison is a public write-up of your capstone's costs and decision, in a form that a stranger can check. It makes the work useful to others and keeps you honest. It should include:

Section What it contains The tool and its price Product, plan, price, date checked, and where you checked it Features used and left out The list from your week-long log Generated tool Lines of code, token counts by type, estimated cost, time to first install, and the estimation assumptions Verification status A table that uses the four labels from Chapter 13 Maintenance estimate Hours and costs, labeled as an estimate Comparison and decision Multi-year cost, your decision matrix with weights, and the verdict What is not counted Your time, if you left it out, and anything else excluded

You Finished the Whole Book

You can now count what a tool costs per feature used, price a generated alternative honestly, verify it, decide with a weighted matrix, and publish the evidence. You came in knowing that software bloats, and you leave knowing what to do about it. Grab only what you need!

See Annotated References

docs.title: Quiz: The Final Decision and the Capstone Project
docs.text: Test your understanding of cost per feature used, decision criteria, decision matrices, the cost of generating software, and the capstone with these review questions.

docs.title: 1. What is a decision matrix?
docs.text:
1. A list of every feature a product offers
  2. A table that scores each option on each criterion, multiplies by the criterion's importance weight, and adds the results
  3. A schedule of software releases
  4. A record of the commands an agent ran
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. The highest weighted total wins, but the matrix does not replace judgment. It forces you to write your weights down and shows how much the answer depends on them. In the chapter, scores run from 1 to 5 and weights from 1 to 5, so a five-criterion matrix has a maximum of 85. Options A, C, and D describe different documents.

Concept Tested: Decision Matrix

See: The Decision Matrix

docs.title: 2. Which parts of the cost of generating software do NOT appear on the token usage report?
docs.text:
1. Output tokens and cache reads
  2. Build tokens only
  3. Plain input tokens
  4. Your time, verification, and maintenance
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The cost of generating software has four parts: build tokens (about $6 for the first install and about $14 for the session), your time (about 70 active minutes), verification (hand checks no agent can do), and maintenance (operating system and toolchain upkeep every year). Three of the four are not on the usage report, and the break-even depends mostly on the last two.

Concept Tested: Cost Of Generating Software

See: The Cost of Generating Software

docs.title: 3. Why does the chapter say to write your decision criteria and their importance before you look at prices?
docs.text:
1. It is easy to rationalize a choice afterward, so deciding what matters first stops the numbers from picking for you
  2. Prices are never available in advance
  3. Criteria cannot be changed after prices are known
  4. Vendors require it
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Decision criteria are the factors you use to choose, written down before you compare options. The chapter's criteria are cost over your horizon, fit, verification effort, maintenance load, and risk if it fails, with continuity as a sixth when it applies. Writing weights first keeps a preferred option from quietly reshaping the criteria. Options B, C, and D make claims that the chapter does not support.

Concept Tested: Decision Criteria

See: Decision Criteria

docs.title: 4. Why do the criteria for ScreenGrab point in both directions, making a decision matrix worth building?
docs.text:
1. All criteria favor subscribing
  2. All criteria favor generating
  3. Cost and fit favor generating, while verification effort and maintenance favor subscribing, so no single criterion settles the choice
  4. The criteria cannot be scored
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. Cost over five years favors generating in the light-upkeep case, and fit favors it strongly since only two features are used. Verification and maintenance favor subscribing because a vendor tests its product, while ScreenGrab still has acceptance tests nobody has run. Risk is low for both, since a failed grab loses nothing. With mixed signals, weights decide the outcome.

Concept Tested: Decision Criteria

See: Decision Criteria

docs.title: 5. The subscription costs $90 a year, and you use two of its features. What is the cost per feature used per year?
docs.text:
1. $45
  2. $90
  3. $7
  4. $225
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Dividing $90 by 2 features gives $45 per feature per year, or $225 per feature over five years ($450 ÷ 2, which is option D's five-year figure). The generated tool at about $14 once comes to $7 per feature. The measure is rough and ignores maintenance, but it names the useful question: what am I paying for that I never touch?

Concept Tested: Cost Per Feature Used

See: Cost per Feature Used

docs.title: 6. A decision matrix has three criteria weighted 5, 4, and 3. An option scores 3, 5, and 2 on them in that order. What is its weighted total?
docs.text:
1. 38
  2. 41
  3. 47
  4. 10
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. Multiply each score by its weight and add: 5 × 3 + 4 × 5 + 3 × 2 = 15 + 20 + 6 = 41. Option D is the sum of the scores alone, which ignores weights. The chapter's worked matrix uses the same method, with a subscribe total of 56 and a generate total of 63, a seven-point margin that deserves a robustness check.

Concept Tested: Decision Matrix

See: The Decision Matrix

docs.title: 7. In the chapter's scenarios, generating with 4 maintenance hours a year at $50 an hour and 2 agent sessions a year costs $1,154 over five years, against $450 for the subscription. What does this show?
docs.text:
1. Generating is always cheaper
  2. Token costs dominate the total
  3. The subscription is always a bad choice
  4. Maintenance time dominates, so the answer depends on how much upkeep the tool needs and what your time is worth
Show Answer

The correct answer is D. The generated rows give three different answers: $84 for a hobbyist who values time at zero, $334 for light upkeep, and $1,154 at four hours a year. At $50 an hour with one session a year, generating stays cheaper only while upkeep is below about 1.5 hours a year. Tokens of $14 per session are small next to the value of your hours.

Concept Tested: Cost Comparisons

See: The Cost of Generating Software

docs.title: 8. In the chapter's matrix, generate scores 63 and subscribe scores 56. Why does this seven-point margin deserve a robustness check?
docs.text:
1. Seven points is always decisive
  2. Scores can never change
  3. The scores are one person's illustrative judgment, so small changes in weights or scores could reverse the result
  4. Matrices are only valid when totals are equal
Show Answer

The correct answer is C. The matrix does not replace judgment. It exposes how much the answer depends on the weights you wrote down. A small margin built on subjective scores may flip if cost matters a little less or verification matters a little more. The chapter's weighted decision matrix explorer exists to test exactly this sensitivity before you act on the verdict.

Concept Tested: Decision Matrix

See: The Decision Matrix

docs.title: 9. You are designing the published cost comparison for your own capstone so that a stranger can check it. Which design is best?
docs.text:
1. A short paragraph saying the new tool is cheaper
  2. A write-up with the price and date checked, the feature log, lines of code and token counts by type, time to first install, estimation assumptions, a verification-status table, a labeled maintenance estimate, the decision matrix, and a list of what is not counted
  3. Only a screenshot of the finished app
  4. Only the token bill
Show Answer

The correct answer is B. A published cost comparison should be checkable: product, plan, price, date checked, and where; the week-long feature log; lines of code, token counts by type, estimated cost, and time to first install; verification status using the four labels; a maintenance estimate labeled as an estimate; multi-year cost and the weighted matrix; and what is not counted. Naming exclusions keeps the work honest and useful to others.

Concept Tested: Published Cost Comparison

See: The Published Cost Comparison

docs.title: 10. A reader claims, "Generating always beats subscribing, because a $14 session is far less than a $90 fee." What is the best critique?
docs.text:
1. The claim leaves out your time, verification, and yearly maintenance, which can outweigh the token bill, so the result depends on upkeep and what an hour is worth
  2. The claim is correct, because token cost is the only cost
  3. The claim fails because subscriptions are always cheaper
  4. The claim cannot be evaluated because costs are secret
Show Answer

The correct answer is A. Comparing one session to one year's fee is the kind of mismatch the chapter warns about: a cost comparison needs the same time horizon, the same number of computers, and the same list of what is counted. Once your hours, hand verification, and upkeep are included, the generated option can cost more than the subscription, as in the $1,154 scenario. The honest conclusion is conditional, not universal.

Concept Tested: Cost Comparisons

See: Cost Comparisons

docs.title: References: The Final Decision and the Capstone Project
docs.text:
1. Decision matrix - Wikipedia - Describes scoring options against weighted criteria to choose among alternatives. The method behind the chapter's weighted decision matrix. Read it before building your own matrix.

  2. Cost-benefit analysis - Wikipedia - Explains comparing the total expected costs and benefits of options, including uncertainty and valuation limits. Supports the chapter's cost-per-feature-used comparison.

  3. Sensitivity analysis - Wikipedia - Covers how varying inputs changes a model's output. Shows students how to test which assumption could flip their buy-or-generate decision.

  4. Thinking, Fast and Slow - Daniel Kahneman - Farrar, Straus and Giroux - Kahneman documented the planning fallacy and the value of taking the outside view over a rosy inside view. Both ideas warn against trusting optimistic cost and time claims.

  5. Decisions with Multiple Objectives - Ralph L. Keeney and Howard Raiffa - Cambridge University Press - Keeney and Raiffa built the formal theory of weighing several objectives with additive value functions. It is the intellectual basis for a weighted decision matrix.

  6. Performing a Project Premortem - Gary Klein, Harvard Business Review - Klein proposes imagining the project has already failed and listing reasons why. A short technique for stress-testing a decision before committing.

  7. The Turing Way: Guide for Reproducible Research - The Turing Way - A community handbook on making results reproducible and shareable. Guides publishing the evidence behind a capstone decision. Its checklists suit a capstone repository.

  8. GitHub Pages Documentation - GitHub Docs - Explains how to publish a static site from a repository. Supports the capstone step of publishing your evidence. It is the free hosting path used for this book.

  9. MkDocs Material: Getting Started - Martin Donath - Shows how to install and configure the documentation framework used to build this book. Helpful for students publishing their own capstone write-up.

  10. Decision Matrix Analysis - Mind Tools - A step-by-step walkthrough of building and weighing a decision matrix with a worked example. A practical template for the final decision.

docs.title: Learning Graph for ScreenGrab: Software Bloat and the Generated Alternative
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

docs.title: Acceptance Criteria Testability Judge
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 7: Requirements and Minimal Specifications.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** acceptance-criteria-testability-judge<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** assess<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will assess whether each of 8 acceptance criteria is testable, by deciding if two people running the same check would reach the same verdict, with at least 7 correct.

**Prerequisites:** acceptance criteria, functional requirement, non-functional requirement (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of 8 criteria the learner commits "Testable" or "Not testable". A judgment is correct when it matches the "Verdict" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct. Viewing the repair suggestion for a criterion after judging is feedback, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A criterion that sounds positive and professional is a testable one. (2) A criterion with the word "all" or "gracefully" is stricter and so better. (3) Only numbers make a criterion testable.

**Instructional Rationale:** Assessing needs a criterion applied to cases. The criterion is "would two people agree?", and the mix of testable and untestable examples, including one testable criterion with no number, prevents the shortcut of looking for digits.

**Content:**

The eight criteria, in this order. All are illustrative:

| # | Criterion | Verdict | Why (shown as feedback) | Repair, shown when Not testable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The tool should be fast. | Not testable | "Fast" has no limit, so two people could disagree | A grab completes within 1 second of releasing the mouse button |
| 2 | After the user drags a region and releases the mouse, the clipboard holds an image of exactly that region. | Testable | A person can paste and compare the picture with the region | (not needed) |
| 3 | The tool is easy to use. | Not testable | "Easy" depends on the person | A new user starts a region capture using only the hotkey, with no instructions |
| 4 | With a 5-second delay set, the capture happens between 4.9 and 5.1 seconds after the user starts it. | Testable | It gives a measurable window | (not needed) |
| 5 | Pressing Escape during selection ends the capture and leaves the clipboard unchanged. | Testable | It has a clear action and an observable result, though it needs no number | (not needed) |
| 6 | The tool handles errors gracefully. | Not testable | "Gracefully" and "errors" are undefined | When the screen cannot be read, the tool shows a message and does not change the clipboard |
| 7 | The app works with all Macs. | Not testable | "All" cannot be checked | The app runs on the macOS versions named in the specification |
| 8 | Pressing Control-Shift-4 while a web browser is the frontmost app starts a region selection. | Testable | A person can try it and see whether a selection starts | (not needed) |

Verdict counts: Testable 4 (criteria 2, 4, 5, 8), Not testable 4 (criteria 1, 3, 6, 7).

**Provenance:** Criteria are illustrative and written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". The Control-Shift-4 hotkey and the delay idea come from the course description section "The Story". The testability test comes from this chapter, section "Acceptance Criteria".

**Rules:** A criterion is Testable only when two people running the same check would agree on the result, regardless of whether it contains a number. Criteria appear in the order of the table. The repair text is shown only after a Not testable criterion has been judged.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads criterion 1.
2. The learner chooses Testable or Not testable and confirms.
3. The sim shows whether the judgment is correct and the Why text; for a Not testable criterion it also shows the repair.
4. The learner continues through criterion 8 and then sees the score. The learner should notice that criterion 5 is testable without containing a number.

**Feedback:** Eight criteria, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <verdict>" and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct verdict, the Why text, and any repair. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 7 or more shows "You can judge testability"; a lower score invites a restart.

**Starting State:** Criterion 1 is shown with the question "Would two people running the same check reach the same verdict?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states the test of testability as "two different people run the check and agree on the result", gives 5 seconds with a 4.9 to 5.1 second window, and says the sim has 8 criteria with mastery at 7 of 8.

docs.title: Claim and Evidence Checker
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** agent-claim-evidence-checker<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-sciences/tree/main/docs/sims/evidence-loop-authoring<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** judge<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge whether each of 8 claims in an illustrative agent report is supported or unsupported by the evidence shown with it, with at least 7 correct.

**Prerequisites:** AI hallucination, overconfident reporting, human review, session log (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of 8 claims the learner commits "Supported" or "Unsupported" after reading the evidence panel. A judgment is correct when it matches the "Correct judgment" column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct. Reading the evidence without committing a judgment is exploration.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A confident, detailed report is a verified report. (2) Code that was written has been run. (3) A passing test of one thing confirms a different claim.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluating requires applying a criterion to a case. The criterion here is "does the evidence shown match the claim?", and eight short cases with contrasting evidence make the learner apply it repeatedly rather than recite it.

**Content:**

All reports and evidence are illustrative and the sim labels them "illustrative, not from a real session".

| # | Agent claim | Evidence shown | Correct judgment | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | "All 94 tests pass." | Test run output: "94 passed, 0 failed" | Supported | The output shows the test command ran and counts match the claim |
| 2 | "All tests pass." | None. The log contains no test command | Unsupported | No evidence that tests were run |
| 3 | "The app builds cleanly." | Build output ending in "error: cannot find 'copyImageToClipboard' in scope" | Unsupported | The build output shows an error, which contradicts the claim |
| 4 | "Delayed capture waits 3 seconds." | Unit test of the delay timer: "delay = 3.0 s, passed" | Supported | A passing test targets exactly this claim |
| 5 | "The hotkey works on every Mac." | The author tried the hotkey once on one Mac | Unsupported | One trial on one machine does not support "every Mac" |
| 6 | "The README explains installation." | The README file opened, with an "Install" section listing the install command | Supported | The file was opened and the section exists |
| 7 | "The screen recording permission is handled." | Code reviewed, never run; no permission prompt appeared in testing | Unsupported | Written code that was never run does not show the permission flow works |
| 8 | "The clipboard contains the captured image." | The author pasted into an image viewer and the grab appeared | Supported | A person checked the real result directly |

**Provenance:** Illustrative scenarios written for this chapter. The test count 94 comes from the course description section "How the first version was built". The definitions come from this chapter, sections "AI Hallucination", "Overconfident Reporting" and "Session Log".

**Rules:** Claims appear in the order of the table. A claim is "Supported" only when the evidence shown directly tests that same claim and the result matches it. Evidence that is absent, contradicts the claim, tests something else, or covers a narrower case than the claim makes it "Unsupported".

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads claim 1 and its evidence panel.
2. The learner chooses Supported or Unsupported and confirms the choice.
3. The sim shows whether the judgment was correct, with the Why text.
4. The learner repeats for claims 2 through 8, then sees a summary of correct judgments and the two rules of thumb: "Evidence must test the same claim" and "Written is not run".

**Feedback:** Eight claims, fixed order, one attempt each. The correct judgment and Why text appear immediately after each confirmation. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. The summary shows the claims judged wrongly with their Why text.

**Starting State:** Claim 1 and its evidence are shown with the question "Does the evidence support the claim?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that there are 8 claims, that the test count in the example is 94, and that mastery is 7 of 8.

docs.title: AI-Assisted Build Stage Sequencer
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** ai-assisted-build-stage-sequencer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-persona-testing/tree/main/docs/sims/prompt-architecture-builder<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Remember<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** list<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will list the five stages of the ScreenGrab build in their correct order, given five unordered cards that each show a stage and its output, within two attempts.

**Prerequisites:** minimal specification, design document, code generation, installer script, README file (all defined in this chapter or earlier chapters above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner arranges five cards in a sequence and submits it. The sequence is correct when it matches the "Position" column in Content exactly. Mastery is a correct sequence on the first or second submission.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Code is written first and the specification is written afterward to describe it. (2) Tests are optional extras added at the end of a project. (3) The installer comes before the code that it installs.

**Instructional Rationale:** Remember-level recall of a sequence is best exercised by reconstructing the sequence from cards, because the learner must retrieve the order from memory instead of recognizing it in a list. Showing each card's output gives the learner a meaningful clue.

**Content:**

The five cards, shown in a scrambled initial order (Installer, Code, Specification, Tests, Design). Each card shows its stage name and its output:

| Position | Stage | Output shown on the card | Why it comes here (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Specification | A minimal specification of what the tool does and does not do | Everything else is built from what the tool is supposed to do |
| 2 | Design | A design document of components, decisions, and trade-offs | The design turns the requirements into a plan that fits the platform |
| 3 | Code | About 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files | Code is written from the design |
| 4 | Tests | About 1,370 lines, with 94 automated tests | Tests check the code against the specification |
| 5 | Installer | Install and build scripts of about 500 lines, plus a README | The installer packages code that already exists and has been checked |

**Provenance:** Stage order and the numbers on the cards come from the course description section "How the first version was built" and from this chapter's section "The ScreenGrab Case Study".

**Rules:** The correct sequence is exactly Specification, Design, Code, Tests, Installer. Two submissions are allowed. A submission is correct only if all five positions match.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees the five cards in the scrambled order and the instruction "Put the build in the order it happened."
2. The learner rearranges the cards into a sequence and submits it.
3. If the sequence is wrong, the sim tells the learner how many cards are in the right position and allows one more attempt. If it is right, the sim shows the Why text for each position.
4. After the second attempt or a correct sequence, the sim shows the correct order with the Why text for each card.

**Feedback:** Two attempts. After the first incorrect submission: "n of 5 cards are in the right position. Try once more." After the second incorrect submission, or after a correct one: the correct order and the Why text for each position. A correct submission shows "You can list the build stages".

**Starting State:** The five cards in the scrambled order and the question "Which stage came first?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the work moved through the order specification, design, code, tests, and installer, with about 2,000 lines of Swift in 19 files, about 1,370 test lines with 94 tests, and about 500 lines of scripts.

docs.title: AI Coding Agent Loop Stepper
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 5: Generative AI and Coding Agents.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** ai-coding-agent-loop-stepper<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/ai-strategy-for-education/tree/main/docs/sims/ai-agent-anatomy<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** explain<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will explain the order of the seven stages an AI coding agent moves through, by predicting the next stage correctly in at least 5 of 6 steps.

**Prerequisites:** AI coding agent, prompt, natural language request, clarifying questions, agent planning, agent tool use, agent permissions, human review (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** At each of six steps the learner commits a prediction of the next stage before it is revealed. A prediction is correct when it matches the "Next stage" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first try. Reading the stage descriptions and pressing Next without predicting is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The agent writes all the code in one step and then stops. (2) The agent never needs the person after the request. (3) The agent's report that work is done proves the work is done.

**Instructional Rationale:** Predicting the next stage forces the learner to rebuild the loop from the meaning of each stage instead of reading a list. The concrete ScreenGrab example visible at every stage keeps the abstract loop tied to a real case.

**Content:**

The seven stages, in order, each shown with its ScreenGrab example:

| # | Stage | What happens | ScreenGrab example (from the chapter) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Request | The person states the goal in a natural language request | A short request for a tool that grabs a region and copies it to the clipboard |
| 2 | Clarifying questions | The agent asks the person to settle open choices | Four multiple-choice questions answered by the author |
| 3 | Plan | The agent lists the steps it intends to take | Specification first, then design, code, tests, installer |
| 4 | Tool use: write | The agent creates or edits files, after a permission check | Writing the Swift source files |
| 5 | Tool use: run | The agent runs commands such as a build or the tests, after a permission check | Building the app and running the automated tests |
| 6 | Report | The agent states what it did and what it believes the result is | A summary that the app was built and installed |
| 7 | Human review | The person checks the report against evidence and decides what happens next | Trying the hotkey and a first real screen grab |

Prediction steps (six): the learner is shown stage N and picks the next stage from three choices: the correct next stage and two other stages from the table.

| Step | Shown stage | Choices | Correct next stage | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Request | Plan; Clarifying questions; Human review | Clarifying questions | The agent settles open choices before it commits to a plan |
| 2 | Clarifying questions | Plan; Report; Request | Plan | With the choices settled, the agent lays out its steps |
| 3 | Plan | Tool use: write; Report; Human review | Tool use: write | Files must exist before anything can be built or tested |
| 4 | Tool use: write | Tool use: run; Request; Plan | Tool use: run | New files are built and tested to see whether they work |
| 5 | Tool use: run | Report; Clarifying questions; Request | Report | After running commands, the agent summarizes the outcome |
| 6 | Report | Human review; Plan; Tool use: write | Human review | A report is a claim, and the person must check it |

**Provenance:** Stage names and definitions come from this chapter, sections "AI Coding Agents", "Prompts and Natural Language Requests", "Human in the Loop" and "Human Review". The ScreenGrab examples come from the course description section "How the first version was built".

**Rules:** The stage order is fixed. Stages 4 and 5 each show a permission check before they run. After stage 7 the sim states that the loop can return to stage 1 with a new or refined prompt. Choices are shown in a fixed order for each step.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees stage 1 with its description and example, and the question "What comes next?"
2. The learner picks one of three choices and locks it in. The sim reveals the correct next stage.
3. The learner moves to the next step and repeats until all six predictions are made.
4. After step 6, a summary lists the seven stages in order and marks the two permission checks and the final human review.

**Feedback:** Six predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. On a correct prediction the sim shows "Correct" with the Why text. On an incorrect prediction it shows the correct stage and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 6" is shown. At the end, 5 or 6 correct displays "You can explain the loop"; fewer than 5 invites a restart.

**Starting State:** Stage 1, Request, is shown with its example and the question "What does the agent do after it receives the request?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that there are seven stages: request, clarifying questions, plan, tool use (write), tool use (run), report, and human review, and that the author answered four multiple-choice questions.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** bloat-feature-growth-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the percentage of an illustrative product's features that a given user never uses, for a given version, to within 1 percentage point.

**Prerequisites:** software feature, feature set, software version, software release cycle (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For 3 challenge cases, the learner enters the unused percentage as a whole number before the sim reveals it. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 1 of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Moving the version control and choosing a user type is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A product that adds features gives every user more value. (2) The share of unused features stays the same as the product grows.

**Instructional Rationale:** Calculating before seeing the answer makes the learner apply the formula to new inputs. Free exploration afterward shows the share of unused features climbing with every version.

**Content:**

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

The number of features in version v is F(v) = 6 + 4 x (v - 1).

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Version v | 1 | 10 | 1 | 1 | version number |

There are three user types. Each has a count of features they want to use.

| User type | Features wanted |
|---|---|
| Author (grab and delayed grab only) | 2 |
| Casual user | 4 |
| Power user | 18 |

A user uses the smaller of the features wanted and F(v).

| # | User type | Version | F(v) | Features used | Model value: unused % | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Author | 10 | 42 | 2 | 95 | Unused = (42 - 2) / 42 = 0.952, which is 95%. |
| 2 | Casual user | 10 | 42 | 4 | 90 | Unused = (42 - 4) / 42 = 0.905, which is 90%. |
| 3 | Power user | 5 | 22 | 18 | 18 | Unused = (22 - 18) / 22 = 0.182, which is 18%. |

**Provenance:** Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter; no real product is measured. The Author row echoes the book's case in which the author needs two features.

**Rules:** Used(v) = min(wanted, F(v)). Unused percentage = 100 x (F(v) - Used(v)) / F(v), rounded to the nearest whole number. Rounding uses half up. When F(v) equals Used(v), unused is 0.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the version control and chooses a user type, and sees the number of features, the number used, and the used and unused shares update.
2. The learner starts the challenges. For each, the sim shows the user type and version, and the learner enters the unused percentage.
3. The learner presses Check and sees the Model value next to their entry.
4. After the third challenge, the learner returns to free exploration and should notice that the Author's unused share rises with every version while the Power user's rises more slowly.

**Feedback:** Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: <value>% of features unused." Incorrect on the first attempt: the Feedback when wrong text without the final number. After the second wrong attempt the Model value is revealed and the challenge counts as missed. A count "Correct: n of 3" is shown.

**Starting State:** Version 1, Author selected, showing 6 features, 2 used, 67% unused. The question on screen is "How much of this product do you use?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that F(v) is 6 at version 1, adds 4 per version, and reaches 42 at version 10; that the author needs 2 features; and that the numbers are illustrative.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat.

Type: chart
**sim-id:** bloat-footprint-comparison<br/>
**Library:** Chart.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** compare<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare the resource footprint of an illustrative full-featured product and an illustrative single-purpose utility on three measures, correctly ranking which measure differs most between them.

**Prerequisites:** resource footprint, install size, idle resource use, single-purpose utility (defined in the chapter section "Resource Footprint" above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** Before the values are revealed, the learner ranks the three measures from the largest to the smallest ratio between the two programs. The ranking is correct when it equals install size, idle memory, background helper processes. Mastery is a correct ranking in one attempt. Hovering bars after the reveal is exploration.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A smaller program is smaller by the same factor on every measure. (2) Install size is the only footprint that matters.

**Instructional Rationale:** Predicting a ranking before the reveal forces the learner to reason about why storage differs more than running cost, which is comparison rather than reading numbers off a chart.

**Content:**

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

| Measure | Unit | Full-featured product | Single-purpose utility | Ratio | Why the ratio is what it is (shown on hover) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Install size | MB | 1200 | 15 | 80 | Storage holds every feature, used or not. |
| Idle memory | MB | 450 | 30 | 15 | Both programs must keep something running to catch a hotkey, so the gap is smaller than for storage. |
| Background helper processes | count | 3 | 1 | 3 | Both need one helper for the hotkey. The full product adds an update checker and a sync agent. |

Ratio = full-featured value divided by single-purpose value.

**Provenance:** Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter. They are not measurements of any real product.

**Rules:** The ratio for each measure is the full-featured value divided by the utility value. Measures are ranked from the largest ratio to the smallest. Ties, if the values were changed, keep the table order.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees the three measure names with the values hidden and orders them from largest to smallest ratio.
2. The learner presses Reveal and sees the grouped bars and the ratios.
3. The learner hovers over a bar and reads the Why text for that measure.
4. The learner should notice that the largest ratio belongs to the measure that costs the user the least each day.

**Feedback:** One attempt at the ranking. Correct: "Correct: storage differs most, helpers least." Incorrect: the correct order is shown with the Why text for the measure the learner placed wrongly. The reveal always happens after the ranking.

**Starting State:** Three measure names are shown with no values. The question on screen is "Which measure differs most between the two programs?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states the six illustrative values 1,200 and 15 MB, 450 and 30 MB, 3 and 1 helpers, and the ratios 80, 15 and 3 times.

docs.title: Software Vocabulary Concept Map
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 1: Software Features and the Anatomy of Bloat.

Type: graph-model
**sim-id:** bloat-software-concept-map<br/>
**Library:** vis-network<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/computer-science/tree/main/docs/sims/oop-benefits-concept-map<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** classify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify six described examples under the correct term among software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, and software release cycle, scoring at least 5 of 6 on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, software release cycle (each defined in the chapter sections "Software, Products, and Features" and "Versions and Release Cycles").

**Evidence of Mastery:** In the matching quiz, the learner picks one of the six terms for each of 6 described examples. An answer is correct when it equals the Correct term column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct on the first attempt. Clicking nodes to read definitions is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Software and software product are the same thing. (2) A feature set is the same as a feature. (3) A version is the same as a release cycle.

**Instructional Rationale:** Classifying a concrete example under an abstract term makes the learner apply the definition instead of recalling its wording, which is the Understand-level behavior. The concept map gives the learner the relationships to reason from.

**Content:**

The map has eight nodes. Clicking a node opens its definition.

| Node | Definition shown on click |
|---|---|
| Software | A set of instructions that tells a computer what to do. |
| Software Product | Software packaged with an installer, documentation, a license, a price, updates, and support. |
| Software Feature | One distinct capability of a product that serves a purpose a user can name. |
| Feature Set | The complete collection of features a product offers. |
| Software Version | A numbered snapshot of a product at one point in time. |
| Software Release Cycle | The schedule on which a vendor publishes new versions. |
| Software Bloat | Growth of a feature set beyond what most users need or use. |
| Single-Purpose Utility | A small tool built to do one job and little else. |

The edges, shown with their labels, are:

| From | Label | To |
|---|---|---|
| Software Product | packages | Software |
| Software Feature | is one part of | Feature Set |
| Feature Set | belongs to | Software Product |
| Software Version | is a snapshot of | Software Product |
| Software Release Cycle | schedules | Software Version |
| Software Bloat | is what an oversized | Feature Set |
| Single-Purpose Utility | keeps a small | Feature Set |

The matching quiz has 6 items in this fixed order. The answer bank is the six terms software, software product, software feature, feature set, software version, and software release cycle.

| # | Description shown | Correct term | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The Swift source files that make up a screen grab app | software | They are instructions for the computer, with no license, price, or support around them. |
| 2 | The app, its installer, its license for three computers, and its update service sold under one name | software product | Software becomes a product when it is packaged with the means to obtain and keep using it. |
| 3 | Grabbing a region of the screen and copying it to the clipboard | software feature | It is one capability a user can name. |
| 4 | All 40 commands in a hypothetical editor's menus, taken together | feature set | It is the complete collection of capabilities, not a single one. |
| 5 | Release 4.2 as published in March | software version | It is a numbered snapshot of the product at one moment. |
| 6 | A new paid release published every fall | software release cycle | It describes the schedule on which versions appear, not any one version. |

**Provenance:** Node definitions come from the chapter sections above. Quiz items 1, 2, 3 and 5 follow the chapter's screen grab example; items 4 and 6 are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

**Rules:** Each quiz item is answered once. An answer is correct when it equals the Correct term for that item. The score is the count of correct answers out of 6. Mastery is a score of at least 5 on the first attempt through the quiz.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner clicks any node to read its definition and sees which nodes it connects to.
2. The learner starts the matching quiz and reads item 1.
3. The learner chooses one of the six terms and sees the feedback at once.
4. The learner continues through items 2 to 6 and sees the final score.

**Feedback:** Six items in fixed order, one attempt each. A correct answer shows "Correct" and the Why text. An incorrect answer shows the Why text for that item and highlights the correct node on the map. The score "n of 6" is shown after the last item, with the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 5.

**Starting State:** The map is shown with no node selected and the quiz not started. The prompt reads "Click a node to see what it means, then test yourself."

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the author's screen grab utility cost $9, that three computers share one license, that a feature set is the complete collection of a product's capabilities, and that the map has six quiz items.
