docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 13: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans.

Type: workflow
**sim-id:** bug-investigation-workflow<br/>
**Library:** Mermaid<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Remember<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** identify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will identify what each of the seven steps of a bug investigation produces, answering at least 6 of 7 correctly.

**Prerequisites:** software bug, bug reproduction, root cause analysis, unexplained failure, regression test (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each step, the learner picks which of three outputs the step produces, before the correct output is shown. A pick is correct when it matches the Output column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 7 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A bug that cannot be reproduced can be closed as fixed. (2) Fixing the visible symptom is the same as fixing the root cause. (3) A fix is finished when the code changes.

**Instructional Rationale:** Remember-level recall of the sequence benefits from touching each step and committing an answer. The branch on "can it be reproduced?" shows that the process has an honest exit for unexplained failures.

**Content:**

The diagram is a flowchart with seven steps and one decision. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the step's description and three possible outputs. The learner picks one.

| # | Step | Description | Correct output | Wrong outputs shown | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Observe the failure | Notice a difference between expected and actual behavior | A written observation of expected versus actual | A fixed bug; a new feature | You cannot work on a bug nobody has written down. |
| 2 | Try to reproduce it | Follow the recipe on the original setup | A recipe that makes the bug happen on demand | A passing test; a release | Reproduction is a recipe, not a fix. |
| 3 | Decision: reproducible? | If yes continue to step 4. If no, record an unexplained failure | A yes or no, with the environment noted | A root cause; a regression test | The answer decides whether the investigation can continue. |
| 4 | Record an unexplained failure | State what was seen, what was known, and what to capture next time | A written note of known facts and missing facts | A claim that the bug is fixed; a deleted report | Honest reporting beats a false fix. |
| 5 | Find the root cause | Ask why until removing the cause makes the bug impossible | A named underlying cause | A workaround; a bigger test suite | The cause, not the symptom, is what you fix. |
| 6 | Fix and add a regression test | Change the code and write a test that fails before the fix | A fix plus a test that failed first and now passes | A new bug report; a README change | A fix without a test may silently return. |
| 7 | Re-verify and report | Run the full checks and record the evidence | A status report with dated evidence | A guess that it is fixed; a deleted test | A claim needs a receipt. |

Edge labels: "reproduced" from step 3 to step 5, "cannot reproduce" from step 3 to step 4. Step 4 leads to a final node "wait for new evidence" whose information box reads "Capture the frontmost app, the log, and the settings the next time it happens".

**Provenance:** Steps follow the chapter sections "Bug Reproduction", "Root Cause Analysis", "Regression Tests" and "The Unexplained Failure". The step descriptions are the chapter author's wording.

**Rules:** Seven steps, each with exactly one correct output. The score is the number of correct picks. Mastery when score >= 6. The order of the three choices for each step is shuffled once per visit.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner clicks a step. An information box shows the description and three outputs.
2. The learner picks one output. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the Reason.
3. The learner opens the remaining steps in any order until all seven are answered.
4. The learner should notice that step 3 sends the process down one of two paths, and that both paths end in written evidence.

**Feedback:** Seven steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite: this step produces [correct output]" plus the Reason. The score "Correct: n of 7" is shown after the last step.

**Starting State:** The flowchart is shown with no step answered. The question on screen is "What does each step of a bug investigation produce?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter lists reproduction recipes with four parts plus the environment, root cause by asking why, a regression test that must be seen to fail before the fix, and an unexplained failure branch.

docs.title: Buy, Subscribe, or Generate Decision Explorer
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 6: Build or Buy and the Rise of Personal Software.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** buy-subscribe-generate-decision-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/information-systems/tree/main/docs/sims/build-buy-saas-decision<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** recommend<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will recommend buy, subscribe, or generate for each of 8 scenarios, justified by how long the tool will be used and who supports it, with at least 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** build-or-buy decision, buy option, subscribe option, generate option, disposable software, long-lived software, risks of ownership, support responsibility (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each scenario the learner commits one of three recommendations. A recommendation is correct when it matches the "Best option" column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 8 correct. Opening the three option summaries is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Generating is always the cheapest choice. (2) A subscription is always a bad deal. (3) A one-time purchase never needs any further thought.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluating means judging against criteria. The scenarios vary the criteria (duration, support, regulation, verification) so the learner must weigh them instead of memorizing a single rule.

**Content:**

The three options, shown as reference summaries the learner can open at any time:

| Option | One-sentence summary |
|---|---|
| Buy | Pay once and keep using that version; the vendor maintains it until you stop upgrading |
| Subscribe | Pay repeatedly; the vendor maintains it and keeps it current for as long as you pay |
| Generate | Have an AI coding agent build exactly what you need; you pay tokens and time, and you carry support responsibility |

The eight scenarios, in order. All are illustrative:

| # | Scenario | Best option | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | You must convert one folder of files to a different format this afternoon, and never again. | Generate | One-off job: disposable software has no maintenance cost, and no product is worth learning for one use |
| 2 | A 200-person company needs payroll software that must follow tax rules that change every year. | Subscribe | The outside rules change constantly, and the vendor's yearly updates and support are the real product |
| 3 | A $9 one-time utility does exactly your job on all your computers and has not changed in years. | Buy | A stable one-time purchase already fits; keep it, since the cost per year keeps falling |
| 4 | Your screen grab tool costs $30 per computer per year on 3 computers, and you use 2 of its features. | Generate | You can name the 2 features, the fee compounds ($90 a year), and a small tool is easy to test |
| 5 | A clinic must store patient records and follow privacy law, and no staff member can verify security. | Subscribe | The vendor carries compliance, security, and support, which the clinic cannot verify itself |
| 6 | You need name tags formatted for one event next weekend. | Generate | A single-occasion job suits disposable software, with no upkeep afterward |
| 7 | A $40 one-time-license drawing app does everything you need on one computer and rarely changes. | Buy | A stable tool with a fixed price and no recurring cost; generating adds work for no gain |
| 8 | You need one job done on two computers, the only product charges $15 per computer per year, and you can describe the job in two sentences and have time to test it. | Generate | A short specification and time to verify make generating practical, and the fee recurs forever |

Counts: Generate is the best option in 4 scenarios (1, 4, 6, 8), Subscribe in 2 (2, 5), and Buy in 2 (3, 7).

**Provenance:** Scenarios are illustrative and written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". The $9, $30, $90 figures in scenarios 3 and 4 come from the course description section "How a simple tool became a subscription". The option summaries come from this chapter.

**Rules:** Each scenario has exactly one best option. The learner chooses exactly one of three options per scenario. No arithmetic is required of the learner. A scenario is correct only when the chosen option equals the Best option column.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads scenario 1 and may open the three option summaries.
2. The learner picks one of Buy, Subscribe, or Generate and confirms the choice.
3. The sim shows whether the choice was correct and the Why text, and the learner moves to the next scenario.
4. After scenario 8, the sim shows the score and lists the scenarios answered incorrectly with their Why text. The learner should notice that the best option depends on duration and support more than on price alone.

**Feedback:** Eight scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <option>" and the Why text. Incorrect: the best option and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 6 or more shows "You can weigh the three options"; a lower score invites a restart.

**Starting State:** Scenario 1 is shown with the three option summaries closed and the question "Which option fits this job best?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states three options (buy, subscribe, generate), the figures $9, $30 per computer per year, $90 a year, $450 over five years, about $6 for the first build, about $14 for the whole session, and about 70 active minutes. The explorer has 8 scenarios and mastery is 6 of 8.

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 8: Software Design and Platform Constraints.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** design-trade-off-judge<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** judge<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge which of two options best serves a stated priority in each of 8 design decisions, with at least 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** design decision, design trade-off, third-party dependency, zero-dependency design, native application, menu bar app, global hotkey, hotkey conflict, screen recording permission, freeze-frame selection, prototype (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each decision the learner commits one of two options. A choice is correct when it matches the "Better option" column in Content. Mastery is 6 of 8 correct. Reading the trade-off summary of an option before choosing is exploration.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Using a library is always better because it is less work. (2) The most feature-rich option is the best design. (3) A design decision has a right answer apart from the priority it serves.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluating means choosing against a criterion. Each decision states its criterion as a priority, so the learner must connect a trade-off to what the specification values instead of picking the option that sounds more impressive.

**Content:**

The eight decisions, in this order. All are illustrative and based on the ScreenGrab design described in the chapter.

| # | Decision | Stated priority | Option 1 | Option 2 | Better option | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | How to read the screen's pixels | No third-party libraries; easy to maintain | Use the platform's own capture capability | Add a third-party capture library | Option 1 | It meets the no-libraries priority and leaves nothing outside to update |
| 2 | How the tool presents itself | Always ready; no window clutter | A regular app with a window and a Dock icon | A menu bar app | Option 2 | A menu bar app is always available and stays out of the way |
| 3 | How to start a capture while another app is in front | Works from any application | A shortcut that works only while the tool's own window is in front | A global hotkey | Option 2 | Only a global hotkey is reported to the tool when another app is in front |
| 4 | How to pick the region | The picture matches what the user saw when starting | Let the user drag over the live screen | Freeze the screen first, then drag over the still picture | Option 2 | A frozen picture cannot change during the drag |
| 5 | Which shortcut to choose | Avoid clashing with the system | Reuse Command-Shift-4 | Choose a combination the system does not already use | Option 2 | Command-Shift-4 is already a built-in macOS screenshot shortcut, which would conflict |
| 6 | How to learn whether hotkeys work for a background app | Find problems early and cheaply | Build the whole app, then test the hotkey | Write a tiny prototype that only registers the hotkey and prints a message | Option 2 | A prototype answers the risky question in minutes before the rest is built |
| 7 | How to build for a Mac-only tool | Small size; fits the system | A native application | A cross-platform shell wrapping a web page | Option 1 | Native is smaller and integrates directly, and no other platform is needed |
| 8 | What to do when screen recording permission is missing | Avoid blank pictures without explanation | Capture anyway and hope the picture is right | Detect the missing permission and tell the user what to change | Option 2 | Without the permission, captures can look wrong with no error, so the user needs a message |

Counts: Option 1 is better in 2 decisions (1 and 7), Option 2 is better in 6 decisions (2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8).

**Provenance:** Decisions are illustrative and based on this chapter's sections. The Command-Shift-4 system shortcut is a standard macOS feature described in the section "Hotkey Conflict". The sim labels the scenarios "illustrative".

**Rules:** Each decision has exactly one better option given its stated priority. Option order is as in the table. Stating the priority is part of each decision. A decision cannot be re-answered.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads decision 1, its stated priority, and the two options.
2. The learner chooses Option 1 or Option 2 and confirms.
3. The sim shows whether the choice is correct and the Why text, then moves on.
4. After decision 8, the sim shows the score and, for each decision answered wrongly, the priority it served. The learner should notice that the right answer follows the priority.

**Feedback:** Eight decisions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" and the Why text. Incorrect: the better option and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 8" is shown. A final score of 6 or more shows "You can judge a design"; a lower score invites a restart.

**Starting State:** Decision 1 is shown with its priority and two options, and the question "Which option better serves the priority?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that Command-Shift-3, 4 and 5 are macOS's built-in screenshot shortcuts, that ScreenGrab uses Control-Shift-4, and that the app uses no third-party dependencies. The judge has 8 decisions with mastery at 6 of 8.

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 14: Maintenance and Open Source Sharing.

Type: workflow
**sim-id:** fork-and-pull-request-flow<br/>
**Library:** Mermaid<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** classify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify each of the six steps of a contribution by where code changes (the contributor's fork, the original repository, or nowhere), with at least 5 of 6 correct.

**Prerequisites:** public repository, forking, pull request, community contribution (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each step, the learner picks one of three places before the answer is shown. A pick is correct when it matches the Answer column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Forking changes the original repository. (2) Opening a pull request changes the original code. (3) The contributor can merge their own change into someone else's project.

**Instructional Rationale:** Classifying where code changes at each step corrects the most common confusion, that a fork or a pull request alters the original. Committing an answer before the reveal makes the learner reason about ownership instead of reading it.

**Content:**

The diagram is a flowchart with six steps in order. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the description and three choices: "Contributor's fork", "Original repository", "Nowhere (no code changes)".

| # | Step | Description | Answer | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Find the public repository | A contributor reads the code and the LICENSE file of a public repository | Nowhere (no code changes) | Reading changes nothing. |
| 2 | Fork it | The contributor makes their own copy under their own account | Contributor's fork | The new copy is created in the contributor's account; the original is untouched. |
| 3 | Change and test the fork | The contributor edits the copy and runs the tests | Contributor's fork | All edits happen in the copy. |
| 4 | Open a pull request | The contributor proposes the changes to the owner | Nowhere (no code changes) | A pull request is a proposal; no code moves yet. |
| 5 | The owner reviews | The owner reads the differences, asks questions, and requests changes | Nowhere (no code changes) | Review is discussion; the original code is unchanged. |
| 6 | The owner merges | The owner accepts the proposal and brings the changes in | Original repository | Only the owner's decision changes the original. |

Edge labels: "copy" from step 2 to step 3, "propose" from step 3 to step 4, "feedback" from step 5 back to step 3, "accept" from step 5 to step 6.

**Provenance:** From the chapter sections "Public Repositories", "Forking" and "Pull Requests". Step descriptions are the chapter author's wording.

**Rules:** Six steps, each with one correct answer. The score is the number of correct picks. Mastery when score >= 5. The order of the three choices is the same for every step.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner clicks a step. An information box shows the description and three choices.
2. The learner picks one choice. The sim marks it correct or incorrect and shows the Reason.
3. The learner opens the remaining steps in any order until all six are answered.
4. The learner should notice that only the final step changes the original repository.

**Feedback:** Six steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Answer]" plus the Reason. The score "Correct: n of 6" is shown after the last step.

**Starting State:** The flowchart is shown with no step answered. The question on screen is "At which step does the original project actually change?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states a fork is a copy under the contributor's own account, a pull request is a proposal, and the owner decides whether to merge.

The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 12: Software Testing: Automated and Manual.

Type: workflow
**sim-id:** grab-flow-test-coverage<br/>
**Library:** Mermaid<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish the steps of a ScreenGrab grab that an automated test can confirm from the steps that only a person can confirm, by marking all 7 steps and matching the Content table on at least 6 of 7.

**Prerequisites:** automated test, simulated input events, stubbed dependency, off-screen rendering, manual testing (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner opens each step, commits "automated can confirm" or "only a person can confirm" before the answer is shown, and finishes with at least 6 of 7 matching the Content table. Opening a step to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) If most steps are automated, the whole flow is verified. (2) The key press itself is covered by the hotkey tests.

**Instructional Rationale:** Walking the flow in order shows that automation covers the middle of the chain but not its two ends, the real key press and the real pasted result. Committing a judgment per step makes the learner perform the distinguishing, not just read it.

**Content:**

The flow has 7 steps in this order, shown as a flowchart. Each step is clickable. Clicking opens an information box with the step's description, then two buttons for the learner's judgment, then the answer and reason.

| # | Step | Description | Answer | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Press the hotkey | A person presses Control-Shift-4 in another app. | Only a person can confirm | A program cannot send a real key press without Accessibility permission. |
| 2 | Hotkey reaches the app | The registered hotkey event is delivered to ScreenGrab's handler. | Automated can confirm | A test builds a Carbon hotkey event by hand and checks the handler receives the right action. |
| 3 | Coordinator starts the grab | The state machine moves from idle to selecting. | Automated can confirm | Tested with fakes for every dependency. |
| 4 | Screen is captured | The real display is captured to a frozen still image. | Only a person can confirm | It needs the real Screen Recording permission and a real display. |
| 5 | User drags a selection | The overlay shows and the drag chooses a region. | Automated can confirm | Synthesized mouse events and off-screen rendering check selection and drawing. |
| 6 | Image is cropped and copied | The region is cropped, encoded, and written to the clipboard. | Automated can confirm | Tested with known pixels and a private named pasteboard. |
| 7 | Image is pasted into another app | The user pastes into Preview, Keynote, or Pages. | Only a person can confirm | It needs a real other application and a person to judge size and orientation. |

An edge label on every arrow states what is passed on: "key event", "action", "frozen image", "selection", "cropped PNG and TIFF", "clipboard contents".

**Provenance:** From the ScreenGrab design document sections 7 and 10 and specification section 10. The step descriptions are the chapter author's summary of those sections.

**Rules:** There are 7 steps and each has one answer. The learner's final score is the number of steps where the committed judgment matches the Answer column. Mastery when score >= 6.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner clicks step 1. The information box shows the description and two buttons.
2. The learner chooses a judgment. The answer and reason appear, and the step is marked answered.
3. The learner repeats for steps 2 to 7 in any order.
4. When all 7 are answered, the sim shows the score and highlights the steps that need a person.
5. The learner should notice that the first, fourth, and last steps cannot be fully confirmed by automation.

**Feedback:** Seven steps, any order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" plus the Reason. Incorrect: "Not quite" plus the Reason. The score "Matched: n of 7" is shown after step 7, with "Mastery" when n >= 6.

**Starting State:** The flow is shown with no steps answered. The question on screen is "At which steps does a person have to look?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states a real key press, the real screen capture, and the real paste need a person, and that the hotkey test builds the event by hand and checks everything after the key press.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** licenses-offer-sorter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/learning-linux/tree/main/docs/sims/open-vs-closed<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** classify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify six described software offers by when payment is made (one time or recurring) and by what is counted (per computer or per user), getting both answers right for at least 5 of 6 offers.

**Prerequisites:** one-time license, subscription license, per-computer licensing, per-user licensing (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each offer, the learner picks a payment pattern and a counting unit. An offer is correct only when both choices equal the Correct values in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 offers correct on the first pass. Reading the definitions is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A one-time price means the license is per computer. (2) A subscription always counts users rather than machines.

**Instructional Rationale:** Placing each offer on two independent dimensions shows the learner that payment timing and counting unit are separate choices, which is the distinction the chapter teaches.

**Content:**

The two choices are payment pattern (One time or Recurring) and counting unit (Per computer or Per user).

| # | Offer shown (all prices illustrative) | Correct payment | Correct counting unit | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pay $9 once and install it on each of your own computers. | One time | Per user | One payment; the license names the person, not the machines. |
| 2 | Pay $30 per year for each computer it is installed on. | Recurring | Per computer | The fee repeats yearly and is multiplied by machines. |
| 3 | Pay $12 per month for each person on a team, on any number of devices. | Recurring | Per user | Monthly payments repeat, and the count is people. |
| 4 | Pay $40 once for each computer; the next major version costs extra. | One time | Per computer | One payment, but each machine needs its own license. |
| 5 | Pay $60 per year per person, with unlimited computers. | Recurring | Per user | The fee repeats yearly and the count is people. |
| 6 | Buy a $25 key that works on one specific computer with no expiry. | One time | Per computer | A single payment with a license tied to one machine. |

**Provenance:** All offers and prices are illustrative and invented for this chapter; the sim labels them illustrative.

**Rules:** Each offer is answered once with two choices. An offer is correct when both choices match. The score is the number of correct offers out of 6. Mastery is a score >= 5.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads offer 1 and picks One time or Recurring.
2. The learner picks Per computer or Per user.
3. The learner presses Check and sees whether each choice was right, with the Why text.
4. The learner moves through offers 2 to 6 and then sees the score.

**Feedback:** Six offers in fixed order, one attempt each. Each choice is marked right or wrong, and the Why text is always shown. The final screen shows "n of 6" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 5.

**Starting State:** Offer 1 is shown with no choices selected. The question on screen is "How is this offer paid, and what is counted?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the book's case has a fee of $30 per computer per year, that three computers cost $90 per year, and that the sorter has 6 offers.

docs.title: Switching Cost Calculator
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** licenses-switching-cost-calculator<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the years needed to recover a switching cost from the annual fee saved, to within 0.1 years, for 3 challenge cases.

**Prerequisites:** switching costs, proprietary file format, vendor lock-in, annual fee (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For 3 challenge cases, the learner types the years to recover the switching cost before the sim shows it. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 0.1 of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the inputs freely is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Switching is free if the new tool is free. (2) Files in an open format cost nothing to move, so lock-in is unrelated to file format.

**Instructional Rationale:** Computing the payback period from the learner's own inputs makes the learner apply the chapter's formula and see how conversion work stretches the recovery time.

**Content:**

All figures are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Files in the vendor's format | 0 | 1000 | 50 | 200 | files |
| Minutes to convert one file | 1 | 10 | 1 | 1 | minutes |
| Value of the learner's time | 10 | 100 | 5 | 40 | dollars per hour |
| Hours to learn the replacement | 0 | 20 | 1 | 4 | hours |
| Annual fee saved | 10 | 300 | 10 | 90 | dollars per year |

Challenge cases, in this order:

| # | Files | Minutes per file | Time value ($/h) | Learning hours | Fee saved ($/yr) | Switching cost ($) | Model value: years |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 200 | 1 | 40 | 4 | 90 | 293.33 | 3.3 |
| 2 | 600 | 2 | 30 | 2 | 90 | 660.00 | 7.3 |
| 3 | 0 | 1 | 40 | 4 | 90 | 160.00 | 1.8 |

Feedback text per case: case 1 "Conversion is 200 x 1 / 60 = 3.33 h = $133.33; learning is $160; total $293.33; 293.33 / 90 = 3.26, which rounds to 3.3." Case 2 "Conversion is 600 x 2 / 60 = 20 h = $600; learning is $60; total $660; 660 / 90 = 7.33, which rounds to 7.3." Case 3 "No files means no conversion cost; learning is $160; 160 / 90 = 1.78, which rounds to 1.8."

**Provenance:** The case 1 numbers are the chapter's worked example. Cases 2 and 3 are illustrative and invented for this chapter.

**Rules:** Conversion cost = files x minutes / 60 x time value. Learning cost = learning hours x time value. Switching cost = conversion cost + learning cost. Years to recover = switching cost / annual fee saved, rounded to 1 decimal place. The annual fee saved is always at least 10, so division by zero cannot occur.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner changes the five inputs and sees the conversion cost, learning cost, switching cost, and years to recover update.
2. The learner starts the challenges; for each, the sim sets the five inputs and hides the result.
3. The learner types the years to recover and presses Check.
4. The learner returns to free exploration and should notice that doubling the file count roughly doubles the conversion cost but not the learning cost.

**Feedback:** Three cases in fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: n years." Incorrect on the first attempt: the matching feedback text without the final number. After the second wrong attempt, the full feedback text and the Model value are shown and the case counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

**Starting State:** The defaults are shown (200 files, 1 minute, $40 per hour, 4 hours, $90 per year) with the result 3.3 years displayed. The question on screen is "How long until switching pays for itself?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's worked example states 200 files, 1 minute each, $40 per hour, 4 hours of learning, a switching cost of $293.33, $90 saved per year, and recovery in 3.26 years.

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 3: Licenses, Subscriptions, and Vendor Incentives.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** licenses-vendor-incentive-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** attribute<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will attribute each of 8 vendor decisions to the pricing model, one-time or subscription, whose incentives make it more likely, scoring at least 7 of 8.

**Prerequisites:** one-time license, subscription license, recurring revenue, upgrade revenue, customer lifetime value, vendor incentives (defined in the chapter section "How Pricing Shapes Vendor Behavior").

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner chooses One-time license or Subscription license for each of 8 decisions. A choice is correct when it equals the Correct model column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first pass. Reading the revenue summaries is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Vendors behave the same way under every pricing model. (2) Subscription pricing only changes how customers pay and not what vendors build.

**Instructional Rationale:** Attributing a decision to an incentive makes the learner trace a cause, which is the Analyze-level act, instead of memorizing which model is better.

**Content:**

The revenue summaries shown before the decisions:

| Model | Where the next dollar comes from | The vendor's strongest incentive |
|---|---|---|
| One-time license | A new buyer or an upgrade purchase | Win new buyers and make upgrades look worth buying |
| Subscription license | A renewal or a higher fee | Prevent cancellation and raise what each customer pays |

The 8 decisions, in this fixed order:

| # | Vendor decision shown | Correct model | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Add a showy feature so owners feel they must buy the next version. | One-time license | Upgrade revenue depends on making the next version look new. |
| 2 | Keep customers satisfied so they renew every year. | Subscription license | Each renewal is the next dollar, so keeping the customer matters. |
| 3 | Charge for each major version. | One-time license | The sale of a version is the revenue event. |
| 4 | Make cancellation steps long and hard to find. | Subscription license | Each canceled customer ends the recurring revenue. |
| 5 | Stop fixing bugs in old versions to push owners to the new one. | One-time license | Owners of old versions pay nothing more until they upgrade. |
| 6 | Raise the annual fee, expecting most customers to renew. | Subscription license | Customers who are locked in may pay more rather than switch. |
| 7 | Compete mainly on the number of new customers won each quarter. | One-time license | Without renewals, revenue depends on new sales. |
| 8 | Add reminders and features that bring users back every week. | Subscription license | Frequent use makes renewal feel worthwhile. |

**Provenance:** All eight decisions are illustrative scenarios invented for this chapter and derived from the incentives defined in the chapter text; the sim labels them illustrative.

**Rules:** Each decision is answered once. The score is the number of correct answers out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads the revenue summaries for the two models.
2. The learner reads decision 1 and chooses a model.
3. The sim shows right or wrong with the Why text.
4. The learner moves through decisions 2 to 8 and then sees the score.

**Feedback:** Eight decisions in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" with the Why text. Incorrect: the correct model and the Why text. The final screen shows "n of 8" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 7.

**Starting State:** Both revenue summaries are visible and decision 1 is shown. The question on screen is "Which pricing model makes this decision more likely?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that 10,000 customers at $30 per year produce about $300,000, that a five-year customer paying $30 per year is worth $150, and that the explorer has 8 decisions.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 14: Maintenance and Open Source Sharing.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** open-source-license-matcher<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/search-microsims/tree/main/docs/sims/cc-license-chooser<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** apply<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will apply the conditions of five license choices to choose the license that fits each of eight scenarios, with at least 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** open source license, permissive license, copyleft, MIT License, Creative Commons license, the BY, NC and SA conditions (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns one of five license choices to each of eight scenarios. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct choice in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt per scenario. Reading the reasons is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Any Creative Commons license is also an open source license. (2) A public repository with no license can be reused freely. (3) Copyleft and permissive licenses place the same conditions on reuse.

**Instructional Rationale:** Applying the conditions to concrete scenarios shows that license choice depends on what the author wants others to be able to do. Eight scenarios cover each choice at least once and force the learner to apply the conditions rather than recall names.

**Content:**

The five choices: MIT License, Copyleft license (such as the GNU General Public License), CC BY 4.0, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, No license (all rights reserved).

| # | Scenario | Correct choice | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Source code of a small utility. Anyone may use it for any purpose, including commercially. They only need to keep your credit. | MIT License | MIT is permissive and asks only for the copyright notice. |
| 2 | Source code where anyone who distributes an improved version must also release its source. | Copyleft license (such as the GNU General Public License) | Copyleft requires changed versions to carry the same license. |
| 3 | Chapters of a book that may be shared and adapted with credit, not used commercially, with adaptations under the same terms. | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | BY gives credit, NC bars commercial use, SA keeps adaptations under the same terms. |
| 4 | A collection of diagrams that anyone, including companies, may reuse with credit. | CC BY 4.0 | BY alone requires only credit and allows commercial reuse. |
| 5 | A personal script on your own laptop that you never share. | No license (all rights reserved) | Nobody else needs permission, so no license is needed. |
| 6 | Short code samples in a textbook that readers may paste into their own commercial apps. | MIT License | Code samples suit a permissive code license. |
| 7 | Photos on a website that may be reused commercially if the photographer is credited. | CC BY 4.0 | Photos are creative works, and BY allows commercial reuse with credit. |
| 8 | Lesson plans that teachers may remix, provided remixes carry the same terms and are not resold. | CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 | NC bars resale and SA keeps remixes under the same terms. |

**Provenance:** The license conditions are from the chapter sections "Permissive Licenses", "The MIT License" and "Creative Commons Licenses". Scenarios are written by the chapter author.

**Rules:** Five answer choices per scenario. A scenario is correct when the chosen license equals the Correct choice. The score counts first answers only. The order is fixed as listed. The sim states that it is an educational exercise and not legal advice.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads scenario 1 and chooses one of five licenses.
2. The sim shows correct or incorrect and the Why text. An answered scenario cannot be changed.
3. The learner moves through scenarios 2 to 8 in order.
4. After scenario 8, the sim shows the score and a table of the eight scenarios grouped by license.
5. The learner should notice that the Creative Commons choices are used for text and images, and the other choices for code.

**Feedback:** Eight scenarios, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [license]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 8" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" when n >= 7.

**Starting State:** Scenario 1 is shown with five unselected license choices. The question on screen is "Which license fits what this author wants?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states ScreenGrab's code is under the MIT License, this book's text is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, and a license with the NC condition is generally not considered open source.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 10: Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** prompt-cache-cost-calculator<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/tool-use-loop-cost<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the cost of repeating a fixed context over several turns with and without prompt caching, to within $0.01.

**Prerequisites:** input tokens, cache write tokens, cache read tokens, token pricing (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For three challenge scenarios, the learner types the cost with caching and the cost without caching before the sim shows its values. An answer is correct when it is within $0.01 of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 scenarios with both answers correct. Changing the free-exploration inputs is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Caching makes every request cheaper, including the first. (2) Cache reads cost the same as plain input. (3) A single-turn request benefits from caching.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so the learner commits numbers before seeing the model result. Free exploration afterward lets the learner see the break-even behavior that the third scenario hints at.

**Content:**

Prices (per million tokens, from the section "Token Pricing"): plain input $5.00, cache write $5.00, cache read $0.20.

The fixed context is resent every turn. The learner can adjust:

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Context size | 10,000 | 200,000 | 10,000 | 100,000 | tokens |
| Number of turns | 1 | 100 | 1 | 40 | turns |

Challenge scenarios, in order:

| # | Context (tokens) | Turns | Cost without caching | Cost with caching | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 100,000 | 40 | $20.00 | $1.28 | Without: 40 x 100,000 = 4 million tokens x $5 = $20.00. With: one write ($0.50) plus 39 reads of 100,000 tokens x $0.20 per million ($0.78) = $1.28. |
| 2 | 50,000 | 10 | $2.50 | $0.34 | Without: 10 x 50,000 = 500,000 tokens x $5 per million = $2.50. With: write $0.25 plus 9 reads of 50,000 tokens ($0.09) = $0.34. |
| 3 | 200,000 | 1 | $1.00 | $1.00 | With one turn there is only a write and no reads, and a write costs the same as plain input here, so caching saves nothing. |

**Provenance:** Prices are the Claude Opus 5.5 figures stated in docs/course-description.md and the chapter section "Token Pricing". The sim must label them "book assumptions: check current vendor pricing". Scenario values are computed from the Rules.

**Rules:** Cost without caching = turns x context x 5 / 1,000,000. Cost with caching = context x 5 / 1,000,000 + (turns - 1) x context x 0.20 / 1,000,000. Costs are shown in dollars rounded to two decimals. Only the fixed context is modeled; new tokens added per turn and output are ignored. The saving is shown as a percentage, (without - with) / without, which is 0% when turns = 1.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads scenario 1 (context and turns) and types the cost without caching and the cost with caching.
2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows both model values and the worked calculation next to the learner's numbers.
3. After all three scenarios, free exploration unlocks and the learner changes context size and turns. Both costs and the percentage saving update at once.
4. The learner should notice that the saving is zero at one turn and rises toward 96% as turns grow.

**Feedback:** Three scenarios, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: with caching $X, without $Y." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that scenario. After the second wrong attempt the model values and worked calculation are shown and the scenario counts as missed. A running count "Scenarios correct: n of 3" is shown.

**Starting State:** Scenario 1 is shown with two empty answer boxes. The question on screen is "What does 40 turns over a 100,000-token context cost, with and without a cache?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's worked example states $20.00 without caching, $1.28 with caching, a $0.50 write, a $0.78 read cost, and a saving of about 94% for 100,000 tokens over 40 turns.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 7: Requirements and Minimal Specifications.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** requirement-type-sorter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** classify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify each of 12 specification statements as a functional requirement, a non-functional requirement, a non-goal, or an assumption, with at least 10 correct.

**Prerequisites:** functional requirement, non-functional requirement, non-goal, explicit assumption (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns each of the 12 statements to exactly one of four categories and confirms the assignment. An assignment is correct when it matches the "Category" column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct. Reading the category definitions is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A statement about what the tool will not do is a functional requirement. (2) A quality such as speed or size is a feature. (3) An assumption is a requirement the tool must satisfy.

**Instructional Rationale:** Classifying requires the learner to decide which defining property a statement has (behavior, quality, exclusion, or condition), which shows whether the four concepts are distinguished, not just recited.

**Content:**

The four categories and their definitions, available to the learner at any time:

| Category | Definition |
|---|---|
| Functional requirement | A specific behavior the tool must provide |
| Non-functional requirement | A quality the tool must have or a limit it must respect |
| Non-goal | Something the tool deliberately will not do |
| Assumption | A condition taken for granted and stated openly |

The twelve statements, in this order. All are illustrative statements for a ScreenGrab-style tool:

| # | Statement | Category | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The tool shall let the user drag a rectangle over any part of the screen. | Functional requirement | It describes a behavior the user performs and the tool responds to |
| 2 | The tool shall copy the captured image to the clipboard. | Functional requirement | It is an action the tool performs |
| 3 | A grab shall complete within 1 second of the user releasing the mouse button. | Non-functional requirement | It sets a speed limit, a quality of how well the behavior happens |
| 4 | The tool shall not include image editing or annotation. | Non-goal | It names a capability deliberately left out |
| 5 | The tool shall start a capture after a delay that the user chooses. | Functional requirement | It describes a behavior the user can trigger |
| 6 | The tool shall use no third-party libraries. | Non-functional requirement | It is a limit on how the tool is built, not a behavior |
| 7 | Cloud sharing is out of scope. | Non-goal | It states something deliberately excluded |
| 8 | The user has a Mac running a recent version of macOS. | Assumption | It states a condition taken for granted, not something the tool does |
| 9 | The tool shall be installable by running one script. | Non-functional requirement | It is a quality of installation, not a feature the user operates |
| 10 | The user captures only one display at a time. | Assumption | It is a condition the specification relies on |
| 11 | The tool shall let the user cancel a selection by pressing Escape. | Functional requirement | It describes a user action and the tool's response |
| 12 | Video recording is not part of this tool. | Non-goal | It excludes a capability explicitly |

Category counts: Functional requirement 4 (statements 1, 2, 5, 11), Non-functional requirement 3 (3, 6, 9), Non-goal 3 (4, 7, 12), Assumption 2 (8, 10).

**Provenance:** Statements are illustrative, written for this chapter, and the sim labels them "illustrative". Category definitions come from this chapter, sections "Functional Requirements", "Non-Functional Requirements", "Non-Goals" and "Explicit Assumptions".

**Rules:** Each statement belongs to exactly one category. A statement is correct only when the learner's category equals the Category column. Statements appear in the order of the table. A statement already answered cannot be changed.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads statement 1 and may open the category definitions.
2. The learner chooses one of the four categories and confirms.
3. The sim shows whether the choice is correct, with the Why text, and the next statement appears.
4. After statement 12, a summary shows the score and the statements answered wrongly, with their Why text. The learner should notice that exclusions and conditions are easy to confuse with requirements.

**Feedback:** Twelve statements, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <category>" and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct category and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 12" is shown. A final score of 10 or more shows "You can separate the four kinds of statement"; a lower score invites a restart.

**Starting State:** Statement 1 is shown with the four categories unselected and the question "What kind of statement is this?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states four categories, twelve statements, and mastery at 10 of 12, with category counts of 4, 3, 3 and 2.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 8: Software Design and Platform Constraints.

Type: graph-model
**sim-id:** screengrab-component-map<br/>
**Library:** vis-network<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** explain<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will explain the order in which seven components handle one immediate screen grab, by choosing the next component correctly in at least 5 of 6 steps.

**Prerequisites:** menu bar app, global hotkey, screen recording permission, freeze-frame selection, clipboard output, component (all defined in this chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** At each of six steps the learner commits the next component in the path before it is revealed. A choice is correct when it matches the "Next component" column in Content. Mastery is 5 of 6 correct. Clicking a component to read its description is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The picture is taken after the user finishes dragging. (2) The permission is checked only once at install time and then never matters. (3) The menu bar icon does the capturing.

**Instructional Rationale:** Predicting the next component forces the learner to reason from each component's job to the sequence, which shows the design is understood as a flow and not as a list of parts.

**Content:**

The seven components (the nodes), each with the description shown when the learner opens it. The map is a simplified, illustrative teaching model of the design described in this chapter.

| # | Component | Description shown |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Global hotkey | Listens for Control-Shift-4 from any application and starts a grab |
| 2 | Menu bar item | Shows the icon in the menu bar and offers a menu command that starts a grab; it does not capture anything itself |
| 3 | Permission check | Confirms that screen recording permission has been granted; if not, tells the user what to change |
| 4 | Screen freeze | Captures the whole screen as a still picture at the moment of the grab |
| 5 | Selection overlay | Shows the still picture and lets the user drag a rectangle over it |
| 6 | Crop | Cuts the chosen rectangle out of the still picture |
| 7 | Clipboard | Receives the cropped image so that it can be pasted |

The connections (the edges), shown as the path of one immediate grab: Global hotkey to Permission check; Menu bar item to Permission check; Permission check to Screen freeze; Screen freeze to Selection overlay; Selection overlay to Crop; Crop to Clipboard.

Six prediction steps, in this order:

| Step | Component shown | Choices | Next component | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Global hotkey | Permission check; Crop; Clipboard | Permission check | Nothing can be captured until permission is confirmed |
| 2 | Permission check | Selection overlay; Screen freeze; Clipboard | Screen freeze | With permission confirmed, the whole screen is captured as a still |
| 3 | Screen freeze | Crop; Selection overlay; Global hotkey | Selection overlay | The still picture is displayed so the user can drag over it |
| 4 | Selection overlay | Clipboard; Crop; Screen freeze | Crop | The chosen rectangle is cut from the still picture |
| 5 | Crop | Clipboard; Permission check; Menu bar item | Clipboard | The cropped image is delivered to the clipboard |
| 6 | Menu bar item | Permission check; Selection overlay; Clipboard | Permission check | The menu command starts the same path, so it also goes through the permission check first |

**Provenance:** Component names and the order come from this chapter, sections "Menu Bar App", "Global Hotkey", "Screen Recording Permission", "Freeze-Frame Selection" and "Clipboard Output" (Chapter 7). The map is a simplified teaching model, and the sim labels it "simplified and illustrative, not the source code layout".

**Rules:** The path has exactly one correct next component at each step. The two start points (Global hotkey and Menu bar item) merge at Permission check. Choices are shown in the fixed order of the table.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees the seven components and may open any one to read its description.
2. The learner starts the six prediction steps. At each step the current component is highlighted and the learner chooses the next one from three choices.
3. After each choice the sim reveals the correct next component, draws the connection, and shows the Why text.
4. After step 6, the full path is shown, and the learner should notice that two different starts share the same path.

**Feedback:** Six steps, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: <component>" and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct component and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 6" is shown. A final score of 5 or 6 shows "You can trace a grab"; a lower score invites a restart.

**Starting State:** The seven components are shown with no connections drawn, and the question is "What happens first when the user presses the hotkey?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states seven components, six prediction steps, mastery at 5 of 6, and the hotkey Control-Shift-4.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 9: Generating, Building, and Installing the Code.

Type: chart
**sim-id:** screengrab-first-install-size-breakdown<br/>
**Library:** Chart.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** compare<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare the four parts of the ScreenGrab first install by line count and share of the total, answering at least 3 of 4 comparison questions correctly.

**Prerequisites:** lines of code, source code, installer script, README file, specification (all defined in this chapter or earlier chapters above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** After viewing the chart in both modes, the learner answers four comparison questions, each with a fixed answer. An answer is correct when it matches the "Correct answer" column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 4 correct. Switching modes and hovering are exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Most of the project is the app code. (2) Tests are a small add-on. (3) Specifications and documents are negligible in size.

**Instructional Rationale:** Analyzing means breaking a whole into parts and relating them. Comparing parts by both absolute count and share, and then answering questions that require relating two parts, shows whether the learner has absorbed the structure.

**Content:**

The chart shows four bars. Values are the rounded figures from the chapter, and the sim labels them "approximate, from the course description". The mode toggle switches between "Lines" and "Share of total (%)".

| Part | Lines | Share of total (%) |
|---|---|---|
| App code (Swift, 19 files) | 2,000 | 38 |
| Tests (94 automated tests) | 1,370 | 26 |
| Install and build scripts | 500 | 10 |
| Specification, design, and README | 1,340 | 26 |

Shares are computed from the four rounded values, whose sum is 5,210, and rounded to the nearest whole percent. The chapter's stated total is "about 5,200 lines".

The four comparison questions, in order:

| # | Question | Choices | Correct answer | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which part is the largest? | App code; Tests; Install and build scripts; Specification, design, and README | App code | At 2,000 lines it exceeds every other part |
| 2 | About what share of the lines are tests? | 10%; 26%; 38%; 50% | 26% | 1,370 of 5,210 is about 26% |
| 3 | How do the test lines compare with the app code lines? | About one-third; About two-thirds; About equal; About double | About two-thirds | 1,370 divided by 2,000 is about 0.69 |
| 4 | Which is larger, the install and build scripts or the specification, design, and README? | Scripts; Specification, design, and README; Equal | Specification, design, and README | 1,340 lines is more than twice the 500 lines of scripts |

**Provenance:** The four values come from the course description section "How the first version was built". Shares and ratios are computed from them as stated in Rules.

**Rules:** Share = part lines divided by 5,210, times 100, rounded to the nearest whole percent. Ratio of tests to app code = 1,370 divided by 2,000. The toggle changes only the displayed axis and values, not the order of the bars. Each question has exactly one correct choice.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner views the chart in Lines mode and hovers each bar to see its value.
2. The learner switches to Share mode and sees the percentages.
3. The learner answers the four questions in order, choosing one answer each.
4. After the fourth question, the sim shows the score and the explanations for any missed. The learner should notice that the app code is the largest part but under 40% of the whole.

**Feedback:** Four questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" and the Why text. Incorrect: the correct answer and the Why text. A running count "Correct: n of 4" is shown. A final score of 3 or 4 shows "You can read the breakdown"; a lower score invites a second look at the chart.

**Starting State:** The chart in Lines mode with all four bars visible and the question "Where did the lines go?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states the four values 2,000, 1,370, 500 and 1,340, the total of about 5,200 lines, 19 files, and 94 tests, and says the app code is less than half of the total.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 11: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** session-cost-estimator<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/openai-token-usage-anatomy<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the estimated API cost of each of the three ScreenGrab session stages from its token counts and the stated prices, to within $0.02.

**Prerequisites:** output tokens, other new tokens, cache read tokens, token pricing, API cost estimate (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the three stages, the learner types the total estimated cost before the sim shows its value. An answer is correct when it is within $0.02 of the model value. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the prices in free exploration is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The "new tokens" figure excludes output. (2) Cache reads, being most of the tokens, must be most of the cost. (3) All tokens in a session are priced the same.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation needs practice with a check, so the learner commits a number before the result is shown. The what-if exploration afterward lets the learner see how sensitive the total is to each price.

**Content:**

Token counts per stage (from the chapter section "API Cost Estimate"):

| # | Stage | New tokens including output | Output tokens | Cache reads |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Built and installed | 500,000 | 206,000 | 3,800,000 |
| 2 | First real grab | 573,000 | 238,000 | 6,300,000 |
| 3 | Whole session | 1,150,000 | 325,000 | 18,900,000 |

Default prices in dollars per million tokens: output 20.00, other new tokens 5.00, cache reads 0.20. Adjustable prices for free exploration:

| Price | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Output | 5.00 | 30.00 | 1.00 | 20.00 | dollars per million tokens |
| Other new tokens | 1.00 | 10.00 | 1.00 | 5.00 | dollars per million tokens |
| Cache reads | 0.05 | 1.00 | 0.05 | 0.20 | dollars per million tokens |

Challenge answers at the default prices:

| # | Output cost | Other new cost | Cache read cost | Total | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | $4.12 | $1.47 | $0.76 | $6.35 | Other new = 500,000 - 206,000 = 294,000 tokens x $5 per million = $1.47. Add output $4.12 and reads $0.76. |
| 2 | $4.76 | $1.68 | $1.26 | $7.70 | Other new = 573,000 - 238,000 = 335,000 tokens x $5 per million = $1.675, shown as $1.68. Add output $4.76 and reads $1.26. |
| 3 | $6.50 | $4.13 | $3.78 | $14.41 | Other new = 1,150,000 - 325,000 = 825,000 tokens x $5 per million = $4.125, shown as $4.13. Add output $6.50 and reads $3.78. |

**Provenance:** Token counts and default prices are from docs/course-description.md and the chapter section "API Cost Estimate". The sim must label the prices "book assumptions: check current vendor pricing". Costs are computed from the Rules.

**Rules:** Other new tokens = new tokens including output - output tokens. Cost per type = tokens x price / 1,000,000. Total = sum of the three. Amounts are rounded half up to the nearest cent for display, and the total is computed before rounding (stage 2 is 7.695, shown $7.70; stage 3 is 14.405, shown $14.41).

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads the token counts for stage 1 and types the total estimated cost.
2. The learner presses Check. The sim shows the three component costs and the total beside the learner's answer.
3. The learner repeats for stages 2 and 3 in order.
4. After stage 3, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes any of the three prices and all three stage totals update at once.
5. The learner should notice that changing the output price moves the total more than changing the cache read price, even though cache reads are far more numerous.

**Feedback:** Three stages, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: about $X." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that stage. After the second wrong attempt the model total and worked calculation are shown and the stage counts as missed. A running count "Stages correct: n of 3" is shown.

**Starting State:** Stage 1 is shown with the token counts and an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What would this stage have cost at API prices?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states about $6.35 for built and installed (reported as about $6), about $7.70 for the first real grab (reported as about $8), and about $14.41 for the whole session (reported as about $14), using $20, $5, and $0.20 per million.

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 15: The Final Decision and the Capstone Project.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** subscribe-or-generate-cost-calculator<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/cost-attribution-rollup<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the five-year cost of a three-computer subscription and of three generated-tool scenarios, each to within $1.

**Prerequisites:** cost comparison, cost of generating software, subscription fee, maintenance (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For the four challenge rows, the learner types the five-year cost before the sim shows its value. An answer is correct when it is within $1 of the model value. Mastery is 4 of 4 correct. Changing the inputs in free exploration is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Generating is always cheaper than subscribing. (2) The token bill is the whole cost of a generated tool. (3) The time horizon does not affect the comparison.

**Instructional Rationale:** Apply-level calculation needs a check, so the learner commits a number before the model value is shown. Free exploration then lets the learner find the break-even point that the chapter's text states.

**Content:**

Model inputs and their ranges:

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Computers | 1 | 10 | 1 | 3 | computers |
| Annual fee per computer | 0 | 100 | 5 | 30 | dollars |
| Years | 1 | 10 | 1 | 5 | years |
| Build cost | 0 | 50 | 1 | 14 | dollars |
| Maintenance hours per year | 0 | 10 | 0.5 | 1 | hours |
| Time value | 0 | 150 | 10 | 50 | dollars per hour |
| Agent sessions per year | 0 | 5 | 1 | 1 | sessions |
| Cost of one agent session | 0 | 50 | 1 | 14 | dollars |

Challenge rows, in order, with years = 5, computers = 3, fee = 30, and build cost = 14:

| # | Row | Maintenance hours per year | Time value | Agent sessions per year | Correct five-year cost | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Subscribe | not applicable | not applicable | not applicable | $450 | 3 computers x $30 x 5 years = $450. |
| 2 | Generate, hobbyist | 2 | $0 | 1 | $84 | $14 build + 5 x (2 x $0 + 1 x $14) = $14 + $70 = $84. |
| 3 | Generate, light upkeep | 1 | $50 | 1 | $334 | $14 + 5 x (1 x $50 + $14) = $14 + $320 = $334. |
| 4 | Generate, Chapter 14's estimate | 4 | $50 | 2 | $1,154 | $14 + 5 x (4 x $50 + 2 x $14) = $14 + 5 x $228 = $1,154. |

**Provenance:** The $30 fee, 3 computers, and $14 session cost are from docs/course-description.md. The maintenance hours, time value, and number of sessions are illustrative and the sim must label them "illustrative". Costs are computed from the Rules.

**Rules:** Subscribe cost = computers x fee x years. Generate cost = build cost + years x (maintenance hours x time value + sessions x session cost). The break-even maintenance hours per year, shown in exploration only when time value > 0, = ((subscribe cost - build cost) / years - sessions x session cost) / time value, shown to two decimals; at the default inputs it is 1.46 hours. When the generated cost is less than the subscribe cost, the sim shows "Generate is cheaper by $X"; when equal or greater, "Subscribe is cheaper by $X" (or "equal").

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads row 1 and types its five-year cost, then presses Check.
2. The sim shows the model value and the worked calculation. The learner repeats for rows 2 to 4 in order.
3. After row 4, free exploration unlocks. The learner changes any input and both five-year costs and the cheaper option update at once.
4. The learner should notice that raising maintenance hours or time value moves the winner from Generate to Subscribe.

**Feedback:** Four rows, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: $X." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that row. After the second wrong attempt the model value and the worked calculation are shown and the row counts as missed. A running count "Rows correct: n of 4" is shown.

**Starting State:** Row 1 (Subscribe) is shown with an empty answer box. The question on screen is "What does the subscription cost over five years?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's table states $450 for the subscription and $84, $334, and $1,154 for the three generated scenarios, and says generating stays cheaper only while upkeep is below about 1.5 hours a year at $50 an hour with one session a year.

docs.title: Break-Even Chart for a Generated Tool
docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 4: Total Cost of Ownership.

Type: chart
**sim-id:** tco-break-even-chart<br/>
**Library:** Chart.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the break-even time between a paid subscription and a generated tool, to within 0.1 year, for 3 values of the generated tool's yearly maintenance time.

**Prerequisites:** break-even point, multi-year cost, maintenance cost, learning cost, total cost of ownership (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For 3 challenge cases, the learner types the break-even time in years before the sim draws the crossing point. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 0.1 of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Moving the maintenance control is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) A generated tool is always cheaper than a subscription. (2) Break-even depends only on the purchase price.

**Instructional Rationale:** Computing the crossing point for different maintenance assumptions shows the learner that the answer is sensitive to one input, which a single TCO figure hides.

**Content:**

Two cumulative cost lines are drawn from year 0 to year 10. All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

| Line | Upfront cost K | Yearly cost S |
|---|---|---|
| Paid subscription | 40 | 110 |
| Generated tool | 54 | 40 x m |

The subscription's upfront cost is 1 hour of learning at $40. Its yearly cost is 3 x 30 = 90 in fees plus 0.5 x 40 = 20 in time. The generated tool's upfront cost is 14 in build cost plus 1 hour of setup at 40. Its yearly cost is m hours of maintenance at $40.

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Generated tool maintenance m | 0 | 4 | 0.5 | 1 | hours per year |

Challenge cases, in this order:

| # | m | Break-even (years) | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | 0.2 | (54 - 40) / (110 - 40 x 1) = 14 / 70 = 0.2 years. |
| 2 | 2 | 0.5 | (54 - 40) / (110 - 40 x 2) = 14 / 30 = 0.47, which rounds to 0.5 years. |
| 3 | 2.5 | 1.4 | (54 - 40) / (110 - 40 x 2.5) = 14 / 10 = 1.4 years. |

**Provenance:** The $30 per computer fee, three computers and the $14 build cost come from the course description and the chapter. The hours and the $40 value of an hour are illustrative assumptions.

**Rules:** Break-even time = (K_generated - K_subscription) / (S_subscription - S_generated), rounded to 1 decimal place, when S_generated < S_subscription. When S_generated >= S_subscription, the lines never cross after year 0 and the sim shows "never cheaper" in place of a time. At m = 2.75 the yearly costs are equal; the control's step grid does not reach 2.75, so the "never cheaper" case is reached at m >= 3.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner moves the maintenance control and sees the generated tool's line change slope and the crossing point move.
2. The learner starts the challenges; for each, the sim sets m and hides the crossing point.
3. The learner types the break-even time and presses Check.
4. The learner returns to free exploration, sets m to 3 or more, and should notice that the generated line never falls below the subscription line.

**Feedback:** Three cases in fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: <value> years." Incorrect on the first attempt: "Not quite. Divide the difference in upfront costs by the difference in yearly costs." After the second wrong attempt the Feedback when wrong text is shown and the case counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

**Starting State:** The two lines are drawn with m = 1 and the crossing point hidden. The question on screen is "When does the generated tool become cheaper?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states a subscription cost of $90 per year in fees, a generated tool cost of $14, an hour valued at $40, and a break-even of about 0.2 years under the chapter's default assumptions.

docs.text: Run MicroSim in Fullscreen

docs.title: Specification
docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 4: Total Cost of Ownership.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** tco-calculator<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/personal-finance/tree/main/docs/sims/total-cost-of-ownership-comparison<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Apply<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** calculate<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will calculate the total cost of ownership of a software path over a chosen number of years, to within $1, for 3 challenge cases.

**Prerequisites:** purchase price, cost per computer, multi-year cost, software maintenance, maintenance cost, learning cost, opportunity cost, total cost of ownership (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For 3 challenge cases, the learner types the TCO before the sim shows it. An entry is correct when it is within +/- 1 dollar of the Model value in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 correct. Changing the inputs freely is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The purchase price is the cost of owning a tool. (2) A tool that costs nothing after purchase has no ownership cost. (3) Time spent has no cost.

**Instructional Rationale:** Applying the formula to concrete cases makes the learner handle each cost item, and free exploration shows how the time estimates dominate the total.

**Content:**

TCO = P + n x f x y + m x r x y + L x r, with the meanings of P, n, f, y, m, r and L given in the chapter. All presets are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative.

| Quantity | Symbol | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Purchase or build cost | P | 0 | 100 | 1 | 14 | dollars |
| Computers | n | 1 | 10 | 1 | 3 | computers |
| Annual fee per computer | f | 0 | 100 | 5 | 0 | dollars per computer per year |
| Years | y | 1 | 10 | 1 | 5 | years |
| Maintenance time | m | 0 | 10 | 0.5 | 1 | hours per year |
| Value of an hour | r | 10 | 100 | 5 | 40 | dollars per hour |
| Learning or setup time | L | 0 | 40 | 0.5 | 1 | hours |

Three presets:

| Preset | P | n | f | y | m | r | L | TCO |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Paid subscription | 0 | 3 | 30 | 5 | 0.5 | 40 | 1 | 590 |
| Original one-time license | 9 | 3 | 0 | 5 | 0 | 40 | 0 | 9 |
| Generated tool | 14 | 3 | 0 | 5 | 1 | 40 | 1 | 254 |

Challenge cases, in this order:

| # | P | n | f | y | m | r | L | Model TCO ($) | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0 | 3 | 30 | 3 | 0.5 | 40 | 1 | 370 | Fees 3 x 30 x 3 = 270; maintenance 0.5 x 40 x 3 = 60; learning 1 x 40 = 40; total 370. |
| 2 | 14 | 3 | 0 | 10 | 1 | 40 | 1 | 454 | Maintenance 1 x 40 x 10 = 400; learning 40; build 14; total 454. |
| 3 | 0 | 1 | 30 | 5 | 0 | 60 | 2 | 270 | Fees 1 x 30 x 5 = 150; learning 2 x 60 = 120; total 270. |

**Provenance:** The preset values P = 14 and the fee of $30 per computer come from the course description. The hours and the value of an hour are illustrative assumptions invented for this chapter.

**Rules:** TCO = P + n x f x y + m x r x y + L x r, rounded to the nearest dollar. All inputs are non-negative. Inputs outside the ranges above are not allowed.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner chooses a preset and sees each cost item and the total.
2. The learner changes any input and sees the items and the total update.
3. The learner starts the challenges; for each, the sim sets the inputs and hides the total.
4. The learner types the TCO, presses Check, and sees the itemized feedback.
5. The learner returns to free exploration and should notice that, for the Generated tool preset, maintenance time moves the total more than the build cost.

**Feedback:** Three cases in fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: $<value>." Incorrect on the first attempt: "Not quite. Add the four cost items." After the second wrong attempt the Feedback when wrong text is shown and the case counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

**Starting State:** The Generated tool preset is shown with a TCO of $254. The question on screen is "What does this tool really cost over five years?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states presets with TCO values of $590, $9 and $254, a value of an hour of $40, a horizon of five years on three computers, and the formula TCO = P + n x f x y + m x r x y + L x r.
