docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 11: Measuring an AI Session: Time and Cost.

Type: chart
**sim-id:** token-share-versus-cost-share<br/>
**Library:** Chart.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/cross-vendor-token-drift<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish the token type that has the largest share of tokens from the token type that has the largest share of cost in the whole ScreenGrab session, and select each correctly on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** output tokens, other new tokens, cache read tokens, session cost breakdown (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** Before the chart is revealed, the learner answers two questions: "Which token type is the largest share of tokens?" and "Which token type is the largest share of cost?" An answer is correct when it matches the Content table (cache reads for tokens, output for cost). Mastery is both correct on the first attempt. Hovering over bars after the reveal is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The type with the most tokens must cost the most. (2) Output is a small part of a session's cost because there is little of it.

**Instructional Rationale:** Predicting before the reveal commits the learner to the intuition that count equals cost, and the two-bar comparison then breaks it. Analyze-level work asks the learner to separate two measures that look alike.

**Content:**

Whole-session figures (from the chapter section "Session Cost Breakdown"):

| Token type | Tokens | Share of tokens (%) | Cost ($) | Share of cost (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Output | 325,000 | 1.6 | 6.50 | 45.1 |
| Other new (writes) | 825,000 | 4.1 | 4.13 | 28.6 |
| Cache reads | 18,900,000 | 94.3 | 3.78 | 26.2 |

The chart shows two stacked bars of 100%: one for token share and one for cost share. Hovering over a segment shows the type, its tokens or cost, and its share. A note states that cost uses the book's assumed prices ($20, $5, and $0.20 per million tokens).

Question feedback:

| # | Question | Correct answer | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Which token type is the largest share of tokens? | Cache reads | Cache reads are 18.9 million of 20.05 million tokens, or 94.3%, because the growing history is re-read on almost every turn. |
| 2 | Which token type is the largest share of cost? | Output | Output is only 1.6% of tokens but 45.1% of cost, because each output token costs $20 per million, 100 times a cache read. |

**Provenance:** Token counts and prices are from docs/course-description.md. Shares and costs are computed from the Rules and match the chapter table.

**Rules:** Share of tokens = type tokens / 20,050,000. Cost = tokens x price / 1,000,000, with prices $20, $5, and $0.20 per million. Share of cost = type cost / 14.405. Shares are shown to one decimal, so they may sum to 99.9% or 100.0%.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner chooses an answer to question 1 and then to question 2, before any chart is shown.
2. The learner presses Reveal. The two stacked bars appear, with correct and incorrect answers marked.
3. The learner hovers over each segment to read its tokens, cost, and share.
4. The learner should notice that the cache read segment is largest in the token bar and smallest in the cost bar.

**Feedback:** Two questions, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [type]." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text for that question. The correct answers are revealed together with the chart. A score "Questions correct: n of 2" is shown.

**Starting State:** The two questions are shown with three answer choices each and no chart. The prompt on screen is "Which kind of token is the biggest? Which kind costs the most?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states cache reads are 94.3% of tokens and 26.2% of cost, output is 1.6% of tokens and 45.1% of cost, and the whole session costs about $14.41.

The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 10: Tokens, Prompt Caching, and Token Pricing.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** token-split-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/token-efficiency/tree/main/docs/sims/interactive-tokenizer-explorer<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** compare<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will compare their predicted token count with the illustrative split for each of five short texts, and identify the one text that the four-characters-per-token rule underestimates by more than 50%.

**Prerequisites:** token, tokenizer, four-characters-per-token rule of thumb (all defined in the section "The Token" above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For each of the five texts, the learner commits a predicted token count before the split is revealed. After all five reveals, the learner answers "Which text did the four-character rule underestimate by more than 50%?" The answer is correct when it names the text in row 5 of the Content table. Reading the reveal and hovering over pieces are exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) One word is always one token. (2) The four-character rule works equally well for every kind of text. (3) Every tokenizer splits text the same way.

**Instructional Rationale:** Predicting before the reveal makes the learner commit to a mental model of tokens, and the reveal creates the mismatch that corrects it. Comparing prediction to split for five contrasting kinds of text lets the learner see where the rule holds and where it fails.

**Content:**

All token splits below are illustrative and the sim must label them "illustrative: real tokenizers differ".

| # | Text shown | Characters | Illustrative pieces | Tokens | Four-character estimate | Reason shown after reveal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grab only what you need! | 24 | Grab, " only", " what", " you", " need", ! | 6 | 6.0 | Common words are one token each, so the rule fits ordinary English. |
| 2 | ScreenGrab | 10 | Screen, Grab | 2 | 2.5 | A joined name splits at its natural word boundary. |
| 3 | Supercalifragilisticexpialidocious | 34 | Super, cal, if, rag, il, istic, exp, ial, id, ocious | 10 | 8.5 | A rare long word breaks into many short pieces. |
| 4 | swift build -c release | 22 | swift, " build", " -", c, " release" | 5 | 5.5 | Command-line text splits at spaces and symbols. |
| 5 | 1,150,000 | 9 | 1, ",", 150, ",", 000 | 5 | 2.25 | Digits and separators each become their own piece, so the rule underestimates numbers. |

**Provenance:** The five texts are chosen by the chapter author. The pieces and counts are illustrative, not the output of a named tokenizer. The characters and four-character estimates are computed from the Rules.

**Rules:** Four-character estimate = characters / 4, shown to two decimals. A prediction is an integer from 1 to 40 (min 1, max 40, step 1, default 5). A prediction is "close" when |prediction - tokens| <= 2. The rule underestimates a text when tokens > 1.5 x estimate. Only row 5 meets this (5 > 1.5 x 2.25 = 3.375); row 3 does not (10 < 12.75).

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads text 1 and sets a predicted token count.
2. The learner presses Reveal. The text is shown split into its pieces, with the true token count, the four-character estimate, and whether the prediction was close.
3. The learner repeats for texts 2 to 5 in order. A revealed split stays visible and cannot be re-predicted.
4. After the fifth reveal, a table of all five rows appears and the learner picks the text that the rule underestimates by more than 50%.
5. The learner should notice that the rule is good for ordinary English and poor for numbers.

**Feedback:** Five predictions, fixed order, one attempt each. After each reveal the sim states "Close" or "Off by N tokens" and shows the Reason text for that row. The final question allows two attempts. Correct: "Row 5: digit groups and commas each count as a token." Incorrect: "Compare tokens with the estimate in each row; the rule underestimates when tokens exceed 1.5 times the estimate." After the second wrong attempt the correct row is revealed. A score shows "Predictions close: n of 5".

**Starting State:** Text 1 is shown with the prediction at 5. The question on screen is "How many tokens will this take?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states one token is about four characters or three-quarters of a word. The chapter's table lists the same five texts with the same counts: 6, 2, 10, 5, 5.

The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** usage-feature-driver-sorter<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** distinguish<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will distinguish four reasons a vendor adds a feature by assigning each of 8 described situations to the correct reason, scoring at least 7 of 8.

**Prerequisites:** usage telemetry, product roadmap, competitive feature matching, feature checklist marketing (defined in the chapter sections "Measuring Feature Usage" and "Why Features Keep Arriving").

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns each situation to one of four reasons. An assignment is correct when it equals the Correct reason column in Content. Mastery is 7 of 8 correct on the first attempt through. Reading the reason definitions is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Every feature exists because customers asked for it. (2) A longer feature list always means a better product.

**Instructional Rationale:** Sorting similar-looking situations forces the learner to attend to the trigger behind each addition, which is the distinction at the Analyze level.

**Content:**

The four reasons, with the definition shown to the learner:

| Reason | Definition shown |
|---|---|
| Customer need shown by usage | The vendor adds the feature because telemetry or customer requests show many users need it. |
| Product roadmap | The vendor adds the feature because it is on a plan made to show progress and growth. |
| Competitive feature matching | The vendor adds the feature because a rival has it. |
| Feature checklist marketing | The vendor adds or counts the feature so the product wins a feature-by-feature comparison. |

The 8 situations, in this fixed order:

| # | Situation shown | Correct reason | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A rival announces AI summaries, and the vendor ships its own within a quarter. | Competitive feature matching | The trigger is the rival's move, not any request from users. |
| 2 | Telemetry shows 40% of users resize every grab by hand, so the vendor adds a resize handle. | Customer need shown by usage | Usage data shows a widespread need. |
| 3 | A three-year plan names cloud collaboration as the headline of next year's release. | Product roadmap | The feature comes from a plan, not from a stated need. |
| 4 | A package says "120+ features" and counts every menu item and setting. | Feature checklist marketing | The count is chosen to look large in a comparison. |
| 5 | Many support tickets ask for a delay timer, so the vendor adds one. | Customer need shown by usage | Repeated requests from users are a direct signal of need. |
| 6 | A comparison page ticks every row against the rivals, including a rarely used plug-in interface. | Feature checklist marketing | The row exists to earn a check mark, not to serve a job. |
| 7 | A planned platform release schedules a plug-in interface for the second half of the year. | Product roadmap | The date and scope come from the vendor's plan. |
| 8 | After a competitor adds screen recording, the vendor adds recording although no customer asked. | Competitive feature matching | The competitor's feature, not demand, is the cause. |

**Provenance:** All 8 situations are illustrative scenarios invented for this chapter; the sim labels them illustrative.

**Rules:** Each situation is assigned once to exactly one reason. The score is the number of correct assignments out of 8. Mastery is a score >= 7 on the first pass.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads the four reasons and their definitions.
2. The learner sees situation 1 and chooses one reason.
3. The sim shows whether the choice was correct, with the Why text, and the learner moves to the next situation.
4. After situation 8, the learner sees the score and which reasons they confused most often.

**Feedback:** Eight items in fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct" with the Why text. Incorrect: the correct reason and the Why text. The final screen shows "n of 8" and the message "Mastery reached" when n >= 7.

**Starting State:** The four reasons are listed with situation 1 shown. The question on screen is "Why was this feature added?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the sorter has 8 situations and 4 reasons, and that one reason, customer need shown by usage, is the healthy one.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 2: Feature Usage and the 95/5 Rule.

Type: chart
**sim-id:** usage-long-tail-explorer<br/>
**Library:** Chart.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Analyze<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** examine<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will examine an illustrative 20-feature usage distribution and state how many features are used by at least a chosen share of users, correctly for 3 of 3 thresholds.

**Prerequisites:** feature usage, power users, casual users, long tail of features (defined in the chapter sections above).

**Evidence of Mastery:** For 3 challenge thresholds, the learner enters how many of the 20 features are used by at least that share of users, before the sim highlights them. An entry is correct when it equals the Count column in Content. Mastery is 3 of 3 on the first attempt. Dragging the threshold freely and hovering bars is exploration and is not scored.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Most features are used by most users. (2) A feature used by few users is unimportant to the vendor's revenue.

**Instructional Rationale:** Counting features above a threshold makes the learner read the distribution rather than glance at it, and the threshold control lets them see how steeply the count drops.

**Content:**

All values are illustrative and the sim labels them illustrative. The chart shows the 20 features in this order, from most to least used, with the share of users in percent.

| Rank | Feature | Share of users (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Grab a region | 92 |
| 2 | Grab a window | 55 |
| 3 | Save to a file | 48 |
| 4 | Grab after a delay | 30 |
| 5 | Draw an arrow | 22 |
| 6 | Add text | 16 |
| 7 | Custom hotkeys | 12 |
| 8 | Blur a region | 11 |
| 9 | Scrolling capture | 9 |
| 10 | Record the screen | 8 |
| 11 | Extract text from an image | 6 |
| 12 | Upload to a cloud gallery | 5 |
| 13 | GIF export | 4 |
| 14 | Team library | 3 |
| 15 | Capture timeline | 3 |
| 16 | Comments | 2 |
| 17 | Image compare | 2 |
| 18 | Stamp library | 2 |
| 19 | Batch rename | 1 |
| 20 | Plugin interface | 1 |

The adjustable quantity is the threshold.

| Quantity | Min | Max | Step | Default | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Usage threshold | 1 | 100 | 1 | 50 | percent of users |

Challenges, in this order:

| # | Threshold (%) | Count | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 50 | 2 | Only grab a region (92) and grab a window (55) reach 50. |
| 2 | 20 | 5 | Adding save to a file (48), grab after a delay (30) and draw an arrow (22) gives 5. |
| 3 | 10 | 8 | Add text (16), custom hotkeys (12) and blur a region (11) bring the count to 8. |

**Provenance:** Illustrative numbers invented for this chapter, shared with the chapter's table; no real product is measured.

**Rules:** A feature is counted when its share is >= the threshold. The count is shown as "n of 20" and as the percentage n / 20, rounded to the nearest whole percent. At threshold 100 the count is 0. At threshold 1 the count is 20.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees the sorted bars and moves the threshold; bars at or above the threshold are marked as counted and the count updates.
2. The learner starts the challenges. For each, the sim shows the threshold and the learner enters a count.
3. The learner presses Check; the counted bars are marked and the Why text appears.
4. After challenge 3, the learner returns to free exploration and should notice that the count falls from 20 to 8 between thresholds 1 and 10, then from 8 to 2 between thresholds 10 and 50.

**Feedback:** Three challenges, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct: n features." Incorrect on the first attempt: "Not quite. Count the bars that reach the threshold." After the second wrong attempt the correct count and the Why text are shown and the challenge counts as missed. "Correct: n of 3" is displayed.

**Starting State:** The 20 bars are shown with the threshold at 50 and a count of 2 of 20. The question on screen is "How many features do most users really use?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states that the data has 20 features, that only 2 are used by more than half of the users, that 8 are used by at least 10%, and that the bottom 12 are each used by fewer than 1 user in 10.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 13: Bugs, Evidence, and Verification Plans.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** verification-status-classifier<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/unicorns/tree/main/docs/sims/claim-verification-tree<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** judge<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge the verification status of each of ten ScreenGrab claims from the evidence offered for it, with at least 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** automated test, manual testing, evidence-based reporting, verification status, the four status labels (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns one of the four status labels to each claim. An assignment is correct when it matches the Correct status in Content. Mastery is 8 of 10 correct on the first attempt per item. Reading the reasons after answering is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Passing automated tests verify the whole product. (2) A later success explains an earlier failure. (3) A claim with no evidence is false rather than unverified.

**Instructional Rationale:** Judging requires applying criteria to evidence, which is the Evaluate-level skill. Ten mixed cases make the learner apply the same four criteria repeatedly, and each reason models the correct justification.

**Content:**

The four labels: Verified automatically, Verified by hand, Not yet run, Claim exceeds evidence.

| # | Claim | Evidence offered | Correct status | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 94 automated tests pass | A test run reports 94 of 94 passing | Verified automatically | A program ran the tests and the output is on record. |
| 2 | ScreenGrab works | The 94 automated tests pass | Claim exceeds evidence | The tests cover logic, not the real key press, capture permission, or paste. |
| 3 | Control-Shift-4 starts a grab | A real key press at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, confirmed in the log | Verified by hand | A person pressed the keys and the log recorded the result. |
| 4 | Control-Shift-5 starts a delayed grab | None yet | Not yet run | No check has been done. |
| 5 | The earlier Control-Shift-4 failure is fixed | The key later worked, and nothing was changed | Claim exceeds evidence | The cause is unknown, so a later success does not show it is fixed. |
| 6 | The Intel (x86_64) half of the universal app works | The build contains the x86_64 slice, but it was never run | Not yet run | Containing the code is not the same as running it. |
| 7 | The app idles at about 0.0% CPU and 25 MB | A smoke check using `ps` on macOS 26.6.2 | Verified automatically | A script measured it and the output is on record. |
| 8 | The installer rolls back after a failed swap | A test with a stubbed move command | Verified automatically | A test confirmed the flow, with the stub noted. |
| 9 | A real grab pastes with correct orientation and colors | A 980 by 570 grab was pasted into another app and checked | Verified by hand | A person made the grab and looked at the pasted result. |
| 10 | The countdown cancel paths work | None yet | Not yet run | These need a person and have not been run. |

**Provenance:** Claims and evidence are from section 10.4 "Verification status" of the ScreenGrab design document. Items 2 and 5 are claims the chapter author wrote to illustrate the fourth label; the sim must label them "constructed example".

**Rules:** Four answer choices per item. An item is correct when the chosen label equals the Correct status. The score counts first answers only. The order is fixed as listed.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads claim 1 and the evidence offered.
2. The learner chooses one of the four labels.
3. The sim shows correct or incorrect and the Why text. An answered item cannot be changed.
4. After claim 10, the sim shows the score and a table of the ten claims grouped by status.
5. The learner should notice that "Not yet run" is a different label from "Claim exceeds evidence".

**Feedback:** Ten items, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [status]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 10" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" when n >= 8.

**Starting State:** Claim 1 is shown with its evidence and four unselected labels. The question on screen is "How well is this claim verified?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter's status table lists these labels and states that the Intel half has not been run, Control-Shift-5 has not been run, Control-Shift-4 worked at 14:48:56 on 2026-11-01, and the earlier failure is unexplained.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 15: The Final Decision and the Capstone Project.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** weighted-decision-matrix-explorer<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Template:** https://github.com/dmccreary/3d-printing-course/tree/main/docs/sims/concept-selection-matrix<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Evaluate<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** judge<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will judge how robust the winner of a weighted decision matrix is by finding which single-criterion weight changes flip the winner, answering both evaluation questions correctly.

**Prerequisites:** decision criteria, decision matrix, weight, score (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** After exploring, the learner answers two questions: "By how many points does the leading option win at the default weights?" and "For how many of the five criteria does changing that weight alone (to any whole number from 1 to 5) flip the winner?" Answers are correct when they match the Content (7 points; 2 criteria). Dragging weights is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) The option with the higher total is obviously right. (2) Every criterion can change the outcome equally. (3) Weights are facts rather than judgments.

**Instructional Rationale:** Evaluating a choice means testing it against alternative judgments. Letting the learner change weights one at a time exposes which criteria carry the result, and the two questions ask the learner to state a judgment about robustness.

**Content:**

Criteria, fixed scores (1 to 5, higher is better), and default weights:

| Criterion | Default weight | Subscribe score | Generate score |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cost over five years | 5 | 2 | 5 |
| Fit to what I use | 4 | 2 | 5 |
| Verification effort | 3 | 5 | 2 |
| Maintenance load | 3 | 5 | 2 |
| Risk if it fails | 2 | 4 | 3 |

Each weight can be changed: min 1, max 5, step 1, unit points. Defaults sit on the grid. At the defaults, Subscribe totals 56, Generate totals 63, and the maximum possible total is 85.

Weight changes of a single criterion (all others at default). Totals are weight x score summed over the five criteria:

| Criterion changed | New weight | Subscribe total | Generate total | Winner |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cost over five years | 1 | 48 | 43 | Subscribe |
| Cost over five years | 2 | 50 | 48 | Subscribe |
| Cost over five years | 3 | 52 | 53 | Generate |
| Fit to what I use | 1 | 50 | 48 | Subscribe |
| Fit to what I use | 2 | 52 | 53 | Generate |
| Verification effort | 5 | 66 | 67 | Generate |
| Maintenance load | 5 | 66 | 67 | Generate |
| Risk if it fails | 5 | 68 | 72 | Generate |

The table lists the boundary cases. Every other single-weight change from 1 to 5 also leaves Generate ahead.

Question feedback:

| # | Question | Correct answer | Feedback when wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | By how many points does the leading option win at default weights? | 7 | Generate 63 minus Subscribe 56 = 7. |
| 2 | For how many criteria does changing that weight alone flip the winner? | 2 | Only Cost (weight 1 or 2) and Fit (weight 1) flip the winner; changing Verification, Maintenance, or Risk alone does not. |

**Provenance:** Criteria and scores are the chapter's worked example and are illustrative; the sim must label them "illustrative judgments". Totals are computed from the Rules.

**Rules:** Total for an option = sum over criteria of weight x score. The leader is the option with the strictly higher total; equal totals show "tie". The single-criterion flip count is found by trying every whole weight from 1 to 5 for one criterion at a time with the others at default. Cost flips at weights 1 and 2, Fit flips at weight 1, and Verification, Maintenance, and Risk never flip. The sim computes every total from the formula.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner sees the matrix at default weights with both totals.
2. The learner changes any weight. Both totals, the margin, and the leader update at once.
3. The learner resets the weights with a Reset action, which returns all five to default.
4. When ready, the learner answers question 1 and question 2.
5. The learner should notice that most weights can change a lot without changing the winner, and a few cannot.

**Feedback:** Two questions, fixed order, two attempts each. Correct: "Correct." Incorrect: the "Feedback when wrong" text. After the second wrong attempt the answer is revealed. A count "Questions correct: n of 2" is shown.

**Starting State:** The matrix is shown at default weights. The question on screen is "Is Generate's lead solid, or does it depend on one weight?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states totals of 56 for Subscribe and 63 for Generate, a margin of 7 points, and a maximum of 85.

docs.text:
The full specification below is extracted from Chapter 12: Software Testing: Automated and Manual.

Type: microsim
**sim-id:** which-test-can-confirm-this<br/>
**Library:** p5.js<br/>
**Status:** Specified<br/>
**Bloom Level:** Understand<br/>
**Bloom Verb:** classify<br/>
**Learning Objective:** The learner will classify each of twelve ScreenGrab behaviors as confirmable by a unit test, an integration test, a smoke test, or a manual acceptance test, with at least 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt.

**Prerequisites:** automated test, unit test, integration test, smoke test, manual testing, acceptance test (all defined in the chapter above this block).

**Evidence of Mastery:** The learner assigns each behavior to one of four test kinds. An assignment is correct when it matches the answer column in Content. Mastery is 10 of 12 correct on the first attempt per item. Reading the reasons after answering is exploration, not evidence.

**Misconceptions:** (1) Automated tests can confirm everything about the software. (2) Passing unit tests mean the real screen behaves correctly. (3) A smoke test proves the software is correct.

**Instructional Rationale:** Classification requires the learner to reason about what a check can observe, which is the Understand-level skill of sorting examples under a concept. Immediate reasons after each answer let the learner repair the wrong rule at once.

**Content:**

The four kinds of test: Unit test, Integration test, Smoke test, Manual acceptance test.

| # | Behavior to confirm | Correct kind | Why (shown as feedback) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | A drag from bottom-right to top-left gives the same rectangle as top-left to bottom-right | Unit test | It is pure logic in one function, so it can be checked in isolation. |
| 2 | A synthetic image with known pixel colors is cropped through the real geometry and cropping functions, and the output pixels match exactly at 2 times scale | Integration test | Several real parts must agree about points and pixels. |
| 3 | Two grabs in the same second are saved with the second named with " (2)" | Unit test | File naming is pure logic with an injected "exists" check. |
| 4 | A hotkey that another app has already registered is reported as a conflict | Integration test | It calls the real operating system registration and checks the combined result. |
| 5 | Pressing the real Control-Shift-4 keys starts a grab while another app is in front | Manual acceptance test | A program cannot send a real key press without Accessibility permission. |
| 6 | The pasted image in a Keynote or Pages document is exactly the selected region at the expected size | Manual acceptance test | It needs a real other application and a person to judge the result. |
| 7 | The installed app runs with no Dock icon | Smoke test | A quick check of the installed app, with no permission prompt. |
| 8 | The selection overlay, rendered off-screen, dims outside the selection and leaves the selection undimmed | Integration test | The view and its drawing code are tested together, through pixels. |
| 9 | After Screen Recording permission is revoked, a grab shows an alert with a button to open System Settings and copies no image | Manual acceptance test | It needs the real operating-system permission, which a program cannot grant or revoke. |
| 10 | A delay of 99 seconds is clamped to the allowed maximum | Unit test | Delay clamping is a pure function of its input. |
| 11 | The app idles at about 0% CPU | Smoke test | A quick `ps` check of the installed app, with no permission prompt. |
| 12 | With two displays of different pixel density, the captured pixels match the highlighted area on both | Manual acceptance test | It needs two real displays and a person to compare. |

**Provenance:** Items come from the ScreenGrab design document section 10 and specification section 10 (acceptance tests AC-3, AC-4, AC-9, and AC-21), and from the chapter's examples. Item 10's maximum is illustrative; the sim must label item 10 "illustrative value".

**Rules:** Four answer choices per item. An item is correct when the chosen kind equals the Correct kind. The score counts correct first answers only. The order is fixed as listed.

**Learner Activity:**

1. The learner reads behavior 1 and chooses one of the four kinds.
2. The sim immediately shows correct or incorrect and the Why text.
3. The learner moves to the next behavior. An answered item cannot be changed.
4. After item 12, the sim shows the score and a table grouping the 12 behaviors by correct kind.
5. The learner should notice that the manual group is the one that touches real keys, real permissions, and real displays.

**Feedback:** Twelve items, fixed order, one attempt each. Correct: "Correct: [kind]." plus the Why text. Incorrect: "Not quite: [Why text]." The score "Correct on first attempt: n of 12" is shown at the end, with "Mastery" shown when n >= 10.

**Starting State:** Behavior 1 is shown with four unselected choices. The question on screen is "Which kind of test could confirm this?"

**Chapter Anchors:** The chapter states ScreenGrab has 94 automated tests and 34 acceptance tests (AC-1 to AC-34), and that the smoke checks report about 0.0% CPU and about 25 MB at idle.
